P-E30BF49C36.title: UPLiFT: Efficient Pixel-Dense Feature Upsampling with Local Attenders

descriptions.M1: v2 introduces UPLiFTFAST inference execution through BatchNorm folding, channels-last layout, a fused Triton Local Attender kernel, and graph compilation (Section 3.4, Appendix A.5). The architecture and training objective remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 documents the existing Local Attender rather than introducing another operator.
descriptions.E1: The training datasets and evaluated tasks and datasets are retained. New ResNet-50 and ConvNeXt-S evaluations use the existing COCO/VOC segmentation coverage; their pretraining-corpus descriptions identify backbone configurations rather than newly conducted dataset experiments.
descriptions.E2: v2 adds AnyUp-v2 to the main predictive and efficiency comparisons, its chunked variant to the scaling study, and NATTEN-based windowed cross-attention alternatives in Table 9. These introduce efficient local-attention comparators important to the central efficiency argument. The original AnyUp remains as AnyUp-v1.
descriptions.E3: New evaluations vary encoder/decoder widths, remove the encoder, test windowed attention with 1/4/8/12 heads and 5×5 windows, and add convolutional backbones and fast-mode execution. The efficiency study replaces the 48-GB A6000 with an 80-GB H100 alongside the retained A5000, and tests AnyUp-v2 chunk size 10. Existing main-benchmark training and metrics are retained.
descriptions.E4: Beyond the retained training-depth, neighborhood, and VAE ablations, v2 adds encoder/decoder capacity and encoder-removal tests (Table 8), Local Attender versus windowed-attention tests (Table 9), and multi-baseline PCA case studies (Figure 9). The efficiency analysis also expands to examine fast-mode and chunking tradeoffs.
descriptions.E5: Both versions report point-estimate task scores and averaged latencies. Appendix B.2 retains three warm-up batches followed by averaging ten measurement batches. No new seed counts, repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported.
descriptions.E6: Table 1 adds AnyUp-v2 and UPLiFTFAST results. Under the retained 448×448/A5000 setting, FAST reports 41.6 ms versus regular UPLiFT's 79.4 ms, with VOC mIoU 85.08 versus 85.21. Tables 8–10 add architectural and convolutional-backbone results; scaling curves and qualitative findings also expand. Original generative and DINOv3 scores are retained. H100 results replace A6000 results, preventing a same-hardware comparison there.
descriptions.T1: The Local Attender definitions, O(nT) scaling argument, and training equations (1)–(5) are unchanged. Algorithm 1 restates the existing operations as pseudocode; no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation is introduced.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: efficient iterative pixel-dense upsampling, semantic consistency through Local Attender, strong predictive performance, and competitive generative upsampling. Additional experiments support these retained claims.
descriptions.C2: v2 qualifies the efficiency interpretation by acknowledging AnyUp-v2's linear scaling and memory advantages over regular UPLiFT. It adds a stronger-inductive-bias hypothesis for Local Attender, capacity and chunking tradeoffs, and explanations of smoothness, feature bleed, and background artifacts. Appendix D.3 also cautions that visually cleaner features do not necessarily improve downstream performance.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds detailed tensor-shape and broadcasting pseudocode, specifies the encoder's ten and decoder's six convolutional layers, explains the fast-mode implementation, and reports approximately nine hours of UPLiFT training on one A5000. It also adds code/configuration access guidance. These expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the original training procedure.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds references to Neighborhood Attention Transformer and Segment Anything. Section 2.1 distinguishes Local Attender from AnyUp-v2/NATTEN, while the appendix discusses SAM supervision in LoftUp. The broader related-work structure and existing citations are retained.
descriptions.P1: Editorial changes are localized: Section 3.2 is shortened, wording and typographical errors are corrected, Section 3.4 is added, and Appendix A gains numbered subsections. The main narrative and section order remain largely intact; most expansion documents new experiments or technical details.
descriptions.P2: Figures 3–5 are redrawn with clearer feature visualizations, labels, and scale relationships. v2 adds Algorithm 1, Tables 8–10, and the PCA comparison in Figure 9. Efficiency plots receive additional curves, wider axes, and revised hardware panels; Table 1 gains rows. Retained appendix exhibits are also relocated and renumbered.

descriptions.M1: The model family, centered-logit construction, L1/L2 distillation objectives and linear identifiability dissimilarity are unchanged. The added student-dimension sweep evaluates existing methods under different model configurations.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate Synth, CIFAR100 and SUB for classification, representational alignment and concept recovery. The added analyses use retained datasets; Appendix H adds a mathematical counterexample, and language-model experiments remain future work.
descriptions.E2: The evaluated comparison methods remain KL-, L1- and L2-students with teacher references. Newly discussed similarity measures and distillation literature do not introduce evaluated competitors.
descriptions.E3: V3 adds a SUB protocol varying student dimension from 2 to 10 against a dimension-10 teacher, evaluating mCCA over the most aligned student-sized teacher subspace. It also evaluates the CIFAR bound at epochs 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. The original experiments retain their stated splits, architectures and training budgets.
descriptions.E4: V3 adds two substantive analyses absent from v1: the SUB dimension ablation tests how student capacity affects label accuracy, concept recovery and alignment (Appendix L.1, Figure 8), while the CIFAR checkpoint analysis tests the empirical behavior of Theorem F.1's bound (Appendix F.5, Figure 3). These expand the targeted evaluation beyond fixed-configuration comparisons.
descriptions.E5: The original five-teacher, five-student-seed reporting and inverse-variance aggregation are retained. V3 separately specifies one teacher and five student seeds for the dimension ablation, reporting means and standard deviations, and displays five individual seed trajectories for the bound check. These are additional replication designs, not an increase in the original experiments' run counts.
descriptions.E6: Under unchanged reported settings, Table 4 revises SUB mCCA from 0.787 to 0.417 for KL, 0.996 to 0.993 for L1, and 0.997 to 0.994 for L2, retaining ±0.001. Table 2 likewise changes KL from 0.79 to 0.42. Figures 3 and 8 add bound-check and capacity-sweep findings; Appendix G adds KL values of 0.002 and 0.0017. The KL-alignment finding changes materially, although the reason for the score revisions is unspecified.
descriptions.T1: The central bounds and their proofs, including unequal-dimension Theorem F.1, are retained. V3 requires diversity of only one model in Theorem 2.2 and supplies its proof in Appendix C.1. Remark E.3 revises an example's constant and extends the tightness argument to Jensen–Shannon divergence. New Appendix H constructs models with maximal embedding and unembedding mCCA but different distributions.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: logit distance controls linear representational similarity and concept preservation, KL provides weak practical guarantees, and logit-based distillation better preserves teacher representations. Additional evidence and qualifications do not redefine these contributions.
descriptions.C2: V3 expands the applicability discussion. It explains that matching unlikely labels can transfer teacher noise, explicitly discusses unequal representation dimensions and large-model optimization, and clarifies the last-layer focus and exclusion of cross-modal comparisons. It also explains why maximal mCCA need not imply matching distributions and why linear-invariant similarity measures suit this identifiability perspective without being universally preferable.
descriptions.D1: The implementation sections match across v1 Appendix K and v3 Appendix L: architectures, preprocessing, learning rates, training epochs, batch sizes, software and drep subsampling are retained. Both versions provide the same code-access link.
descriptions.R1: Appendix A expands positioning against orthogonal Procrustes, RSA and CKA invariances, and discusses further model families and multi-view research. New citations also support discussion of rank ordering, calibration and steering in Section 4. The central relationship to prior identifiability work remains unchanged; publication updates of existing references are not new works.
descriptions.P1: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. V3 adds explanatory passages, expands related work and limitations, introduces an Impact Statement and adds appendix subsections. Author presentation and citation formatting also change, without a wholesale narrative rewrite.
descriptions.P2: The main text and references change from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, with new headers, reflowed equations and relocated tables. V3 adds Figure 3's bound plot, Figures 6–7's counterexample and Figure 8's ablation panels. V1 Figures 3–4 are retained as v3 Figures 4–5.

P-DEC3D673CB.title: Exploiting Low-Dimensional Manifold of Features for Few-Shot Whole Slide Image Classification

descriptions.M1: The frozen random branch plus nonlinear low-rank residual mapping is retained under the MR name; GELU was already used in v1. The default ABMIL integration changes from replacing V alone to replacing both U and V (v1 Appendix D.3; v2 Appendix G.4), promoting a previously tested variant. Zero initialization of W1 is newly documented, not established as a changed procedure.
descriptions.E1: V2 retains the three original datasets and adds two evaluated treatment-response cohorts: Boehmk ovarian cancer and Trastuzumab HER2-positive breast cancer (Table 9; Appendix G.1). These extend coverage beyond tumor detection and subtyping to clinical outcome prediction.
descriptions.E2: The main comparison adds FOCUS, DGRMIL, and RRTMIL, including MR-enhanced versions of the latter two, while removing CLAM/SR-CLAM. ABMIL, TransMIL, CATE, and ViLaMIL remain. The feature-extractor comparison also replaces TransMIL with CATE (v1 Tables 5/9; v2 Tables 6/12). FOCUS was cited in v1 but was not evaluated there.
descriptions.E3: The reported TCGA split changes from 60/15/25 to 60/20/20. V2 removes 1-shot evaluation, retains 2-shot results in Appendix Table 7, and adds 32/64-shot experiments. It adds AUPRC, specifies macro F1, and introduces geometric diagnostics, capacity-matched controls, and computation measurements under varying bag sizes. These are substantive evaluation changes, not just relocated settings.
descriptions.E4: V2 adds spectral, clustering, and tangent-space analyses; trainable-anchor and identity-skip ablations; a capacity-matched comparison; and analysis beyond extreme few-shot learning. It removes v1's activation-function comparison and revises initialization and rank-sensitivity studies using different backbones. The heatmap analysis is also revised and described as a 2-shot MR-CATE example, rather than the earlier SR-CLAM example.
descriptions.E5: V1 reports means and standard deviations from three training runs and states that methods share random seeds. V2 reports means and standard deviations across five sampled few-shot subsets/runs and mentions cross-validation folds without specifying their number. The shared-seed statement disappears; confidence intervals and significance tests are not introduced.
descriptions.E6: Many existing results are replaced. For example, Table 1 reports 8-shot Camelyon16 AUCs of 53.9%/88.5% for TransMIL/SR-TransMIL in v1, versus 57.5%/65.3% for TransMIL/MR-TransMIL in v2. Revised sampling protocols prevent treating this as a controlled performance decline. V2 also adds geometric measurements, AUPRC, treatment-response, capacity-matched, larger-shot, and runtime results.
descriptions.T1: V2 introduces mathematical definitions for spectral entropy/effective rank and tangent-space drift in Sections 3.1.2–3.1.3. The approximation theorem and random-projection, full-rank, and low-rank-product arguments largely retain v1's substance after relocation to Appendices D–F. V1's explicit SR-specific forward/backward complexity bounds are no longer stated.
descriptions.C1: The central contribution shifts from a parameter-efficient block suppressing overfitting and spurious features to diagnosing low-dimensional feature-manifold degradation by linear layers and preserving geometry through a random anchor. This changes the abstract, introduction, and conclusion's scientific emphasis. The earlier arbitrary-approximation/no-worse-performance claim remains in Section 3.2.3 and Appendix E.
descriptions.C2: V2 develops a expanded geometric mechanism, including spectral sharpening and interpretations of differences between CONCH, UNI, and ResNet50 representations. It qualifies geometric statistics as diagnostics rather than predictors of performance gains. Appendix I adds limitations concerning the data-independent anchor and untested slide-level foundation models such as TITAN, alongside the retained rank and placement limitations.
descriptions.D1: V2 supplies project-code access information and a reproducibility statement, whereas v1 mainly promises later code-related details. It newly documents residual initialization, geometric-analysis procedures, treatment-response label construction, and insertion locations for additional backbones. Core optimizer and hardware information remains; v1's explicit batch-size statement is omitted. The PDFs establish the access disclosure, not the repository's contents or functionality.
descriptions.R1: V2 adds a dedicated geometric deep learning and representation-analysis subsection, supported by manifold, effective-rank, and tangent-space literature. It newly positions MR relative to LoRA and prototype-based classifiers and discusses TITAN's applicability limits. Earlier boosting and extreme-learning-machine connections are removed, changing the research positioning.
descriptions.P1: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around geometry. SR/SP terminology becomes MR/LRP, related-work sections are reorganized, geometric preliminaries are inserted, and the main approximation proof moves to the appendix. Reproducibility, acknowledgements, an appendix contents page, and an LLM-usage statement are added.
descriptions.P2: V2 adds geometric Figures 1, 4, and 5, redraws the architecture schematic and rank-sensitivity plots, and restructures and expands the tables. The heatmap moves from main Figure 3 to appendix Figure 6 with revised heatmaps and layout. Its original biopsy images are reused, although the caption changes the model and slide attribution from SR-CLAM/tumor049 to MR-CATE/tumor058 without explanation.

P-B29440CFF1.title: Bounding-Box Trajectories Matter for Video Anomaly Detection

descriptions.M1: Equation 3 changes the documented coupling operation from v*exp(s(u))+t(u) to (v+t(u))*a(u), where a(u)=sigmoid(s(u)+2)+epsilon. This revises a method component while retaining the trajectory features, flow framework, pose conditioning and scoring objectives. The PDFs do not establish whether the implementation or original runs changed.
descriptions.E1: The three datasets and their human-related subsets remain unchanged. v2 adds a ShanghaiTech test scenario with randomly missing detections, extending coverage to explicitly corrupted detection inputs.
descriptions.E2: Tables 2 and 3 broaden the supplied comparisons beyond pose and trajectory methods, adding 13 ShanghaiTech baseline rows and five UBnormal rows covering RGB, flow and multimodal approaches. Examples include MULDE, FPDM, BA-AED and SSMTL++. Table 7 also compares STG-NF and TSGAD under missed detections. v1 referenced broader comparisons in an unavailable supplement, so these are newly explicit comparisons in the supplied material, not established new baseline runs.
descriptions.E3: Section 4.3 changes the stated window length from T=16 throughout to T=12, 16 and 24 for UBnormal, ShanghaiTech and MSAD respectively. v2 also adds K=2 to the depth sweep and specifies random removal of 10% of detections per track. These are reported setting changes and additions; rerunning the original experiments is not established.
descriptions.E4: New Table 7 tests sensitivity to missed detections, supplementing the existing detector-quality discussion with a controlled corruption experiment. Figure 4 extends the depth analysis from K=6-22 to K=2-22. The feature-group ablation and qualitative cases are retained, although their presentation order changes.
descriptions.E5: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new randomized detection-removal experiment also reports only point results.
descriptions.E6: Previously tabulated benchmark, timing and feature-ablation values are retained. Added results comprise the broader baseline rows, K=2 measurements and Table 7: TrajVAD-T drops from 84.9 to 82.4 AUROC, STG-NF from 85.9 to 80.7, and TSGAD from 80.6 to 76.1 under detection removal. These extend the evidence without demonstrating a same-setting improvement over v1.
descriptions.T1: Equation 3 revises the mathematical coupling map, introducing a sigmoid-based scale and applying translation before scaling. This is not equivalent notation. The remaining likelihood, gating and normalization equations are retained, and no theorem or proof is added.
descriptions.C1: The central contributions remain multi-class bounding-box trajectories as a primary anomaly modality, eliminating mandatory pose estimation, and optionally adding reliability-gated pose information. Abstract and conclusion wording changes, but the principal performance and efficiency claims retain their meaning and scope.
descriptions.C2: v2 interprets Table 7 as evidence of stability under short detection gaps, particularly with smoothing, interpolation and track splitting. Section 5 explicitly adds missed detections and unstable track IDs as failure conditions. The earlier ShanghaiTech discussion connecting AP advantages to low-false-alarm deployment is removed; the main explanations of dataset-specific behavior remain.
descriptions.D1: Section 4.3 newly specifies Kalman smoothing, linear interpolation across gaps of at most 10 frames, and splitting at longer gaps. v1 only stated that coordinates were smoothed and deferred preprocessing details. These disclosures do not establish changed preprocessing. Conversely, v2 omits v1's explicit pose-weight value, lambda=1.0.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds seven cited works, including LSA, BA-AED, sRNN, CAE-SVM and VEC, and removes the CVPR 2021 self-supervised multi-task reference. Section 2.1 more carefully acknowledges spatial evidence from appearance methods while emphasizing persistent object-level cues. The central positioning around underused multi-class trajectories remains.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, appearance-based related work and conclusion are edited or rewritten, terminology and headings are standardized, and acknowledgements are added. Ablation and qualitative analysis exchange subsection order. The overall narrative structure and much of the prose remain intact.
descriptions.P2: Tables 2 and 3 gain modality groups and additional rows; Table 7 is added and Table 6 is reformatted. Figure 2 revises the operation ordering and pose-branch drawing, while Figure 4 adds K=2 and changes axis ranges. Existing displays are relocated, with the overall visual format preserved.

P-9E1564D6C1.title: Beyond Literal Mapping: Benchmarking and Improving Non-Literal Translation Evaluation

descriptions.M1: Section 4 and Appendix B retain the same reflective Core Agent, three specialized agents, context memory, anchor calibration, and stopping procedure. The detailed agent prompts are unchanged apart from figure numbering.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate the same four MENT domains in Chinese–English directions and the same WMT23 English–German task. The added measurements and comparators reuse this existing coverage.
descriptions.E2: WMT23 Table 5 adds MetricX-23, COMETKiwi, and MetricX23-QE to the retained comparators. These methods already appeared in MENT evaluations, but their participation in the WMT23 comparison is new. The MENT comparator set is unchanged.
descriptions.E3: V2 adds system-level Soft Pairwise Accuracy as a supplementary MENT evaluation metric in Appendix E and Table 7. The existing composite meta-score protocol, annotation rules, and model settings remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: Appendix A.3 adds a segment-level annotation-consistency check in Figure 7, complementing the previously displayed system-level agreement. The sub-agent ablations, invocation analysis, backbone comparison, and illustrative evaluation trajectories are retained.
descriptions.E5: V2 first reports average segment-level Pearson agreement for annotator pairs in Figure 7, supplementing agreement calculated from aggregated system scores in Figure 3 and Equation 1. This extends agreement estimation and reporting; no additional runs, seeds, or confidence intervals are specified.
descriptions.E6: New results include RATE's SPA scores of 100.0 and 94.7 for ZH-EN and EN-ZH, the segment-level agreement matrix, and three additional WMT23 comparator rows. Existing main, ablation, backbone, and per-domain results are unchanged, including RATE's 80.4 meta score in Table 3.
descriptions.T1: Equation 1 and its definitions remain unchanged. The added SPA evaluation cites an existing metric without introducing a new formal definition, derivation, theorem, or proof.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims about MENT, RATE, the 3.2-point advantage, and general-domain robustness. Replacing 'meta score' with explanatory wording about combined system- and segment-level correlation does not substantively redefine the contribution.
descriptions.C2: Section 3.3 newly explains choosing SQM over MQM because holistic misunderstandings of non-literal content make error-span annotation subjective. Section 6.3 narrows its WMT23 performance interpretation to system-level evaluation, better reflecting the reported results. The dedicated limitations discussion is unchanged.
descriptions.D1: The detailed prompts, backbone assignments, loop limit, anchor initialization, generation settings, annotation instructions, and code/data access statements are retained. Moving implementation material and renumbering its references do not add reproducibility information.
descriptions.R1: V2 adds agentic-evaluation context citing You et al., Peng et al., and Zhuge et al., plus references supporting evaluation and annotation choices. Much of Section 2.1's metrics background already existed in v1 Appendix E.2; the central novelty positioning remains stable.
descriptions.P1: Related Work is organized into three subsections, with metrics background moved from the appendix. V2 adds localized explanations and explicit references to numerical results, edits wording, and adds an acknowledgment. Most method and experimental prose is retained.
descriptions.P2: V2 adds the segment-level agreement heatmap and SPA table, and expands the WMT23 table with three rows and a QE category. Existing figures and appendix examples are preserved, with relocation and renumbering within the retained two-column layout.

P-1B5E858B31.title: Multimodal Protein Language Models for Enzyme Kinetic Parameters: From Substrate Recognition to Conformational Adaptation

descriptions.M1: The MRCA and G-MoE stages, ESDA alignment, and heteroscedastic regression objective in Sections 3.2–3.5 are unchanged. No algorithmic component or procedure is revised.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same BRENDA/SABIO-RK-derived datasets for kcat, Km, and Ki, and the same mutant-inclusive EITLEM OOD tests for kcat and Km. Citation corrections introduce no additional coverage.
descriptions.E2: The kinetic baselines, PLM comparisons, and appendix ablation comparators are unchanged. Concat & Self-Attention, standard MoE, and L2 loss already appear in v1's Tables 7–9; v2 supplies their missing citations.
descriptions.E3: The log10 evaluation metrics, preprocessing, backbone configurations, and training settings are unchanged. Section 7.2 retains the same one-tenth test allocation for the OOD datasets.
descriptions.E4: Both versions contain the same module and fusion-order ablations, EC-class analyses, error distributions, and MRCA/G-MoE visualizations. Appendix Tables 7–9 are relocated without changing their analyses.
descriptions.E5: Section 4.1 retains the same unspecified repeated-run averaging statement, and Figure 5 retains its error bars. v2 adds no run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
descriptions.E6: All numerical entries in Tables 1–9 and the plotted findings are unchanged. For example, Table 1 retains ERBA R2 values of 0.54/0.61/0.61 for kcat/Km/Ki, and Table 3 retains OOD R2 values of 0.50/0.55.
descriptions.T1: Equations (1)–(15), including the staged formulation, routing regularizer, MMD estimator, and training objective, are unchanged. No mathematical assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added or revised.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about staged conditioning, preservation of PLM priors through ESDA, improved prediction, and OOD generalization.
descriptions.C2: Interpretations of fusion order, geometry, ESDA, backbone scaling, and expert behavior are unchanged. Discussions of endpoint errors and challenges involving particular enzyme classes or limited data also remain unchanged.
descriptions.D1: Implementation hyperparameters and data-processing descriptions in Sections 4.1 and 7 are unchanged. The repaired citations identify already mentioned resources without adding implementation instructions or code/data access information.
descriptions.R1: v2 supplies seven missing references for resources and methods already mentioned in Sections 7 and 11: AlphaFold, KEGG, RDKit, PubChem, sparse MoE, attention, and the cited L2-loss source. The related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain unchanged.
descriptions.P1: Citation markers, bibliography entries, contents-page references, and the version/date stamp are updated. The bibliography also acquires eleven duplicate entries. Scientific prose, terminology, and section order remain unchanged.
descriptions.P2: All figures and tables retain their designs and content, but text and appendix floats reflow. Tables 7–9 move from v1's final page to v2 page 16, while their detailed discussion appears on page 18.

P-B6939F516F.title: Contrastive Conditional–Unconditional Alignment for Long-tailed Diffusion Model

descriptions.M1: The contrastive and timestep-weighted alignment losses and training algorithm remain substantively unchanged under new names. The procedural addition is optional batch resampling, introduced in Section 3.1 and enabled for ImageNet-LT and TinyImageNet-LT. The SiT implementation applies the existing losses to transformer representations.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate the same five long-tailed datasets: CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet, ImageNet, and Places, retaining conditional and unconditional generation. CIFAR experiments move to the appendix. ImageNet's changed resolution and backbone alter experimental settings rather than the represented dataset or conditioning task.
descriptions.E2: The ImageNet comparison changes from DDPM, CBDM, and OCLT in v1 to SiT and SiT with Dispersive Loss in v2. The CIFAR DDPM-1000-step comparison also adds the evaluated omega-scheduler baseline in Table 7. CBDM, OCLT, and ADA remain in corresponding retained DDPM comparisons.
descriptions.E3: ImageNet changes from 64×64 DDPM trained for 300k iterations to 256×256 SiT evaluated at 40–160 epochs. Sampling changes from DDIM-100 with tuned guidance to ODE-50 with guidance 7.5, and evaluation samples increase from 20k to 50k. v2 adds spatial FID, precision, recall, and batch-resampling settings, including factor 0.1 for ImageNet and TinyImageNet.
descriptions.E4: v2 Table 5 adds a controlled comparison of SiT and CCUA with and without resampling, testing whether contrastive regularization offsets resampling's diversity loss. New ImageNet and TinyImageNet qualitative comparisons appear. Conversely, v1 Appendix A.4's latent-covariance spectrum analysis disappears. The original loss-component ablation is retained as v2 Table 4.
descriptions.E5: The CIFAR100-LT comparison using seeds 0, 42, and 2025, its FID values, and the approximately 0.04 versus 0.01 deviation discussion remain unchanged, moving from v1 Table 7 to v2 Table 10. No additional uncertainty estimates or significance tests accompany the new experiments.
descriptions.E6: v2 replaces the low-resolution ImageNet results with a new SiT result series; at 160 epochs, Table 1 reports FID 19.95 for SiT and 16.41 for CCUA. TinyImageNet's reported FID/FIDtail change from 17.16/37.88 to 15.24/30.39, while head FID changes from 20.39 to 21.32. These replacements involve changed settings, including resampling. Most CIFAR and Places values are retained, with new scheduler and resampling results added.
descriptions.T1: Section 3.1 adds mathematical assertions that collapsed embeddings produce loss log N, that this is the maximum loss, and that optimal embeddings are uniform on a hypersphere. These claims have no accompanying proof. The existing contrastive-loss definition and KL-to-MSE derivation remain unchanged apart from notation.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion broaden applicability from DDPM-focused validation to U-Net and diffusion-transformer architectures, including SiT and 256×256 ImageNet generation. Batch resampling becomes part of the central framework description, and superiority over Dispersive Loss is newly claimed. The explicit claim of being first to adapt conditional-unconditional alignment to diffusion is removed.
descriptions.C2: v2 explains why resampling supplies more within-tail-class negative pairs and interprets its interaction with CCUA through precision and recall. The dimensional-collapse interpretation from v1 Appendix A.4 is removed, while the central knowledge-sharing explanation remains. The training-cost limitation is extended with a 1.48× SiT overhead alongside the retained 1.6× DDPM overhead.
descriptions.D1: Appendix A.1 adds explicit U-Net/transformer feature-extraction mappings, four-A6000 SiT hardware, batch size 48, training budgets, and resampling configuration. However, it removes v1's explicit DDPM noise schedule, Adam optimizer, learning rate, and warmup settings, plus CIFAR evaluation sample-count and tail-class details. Reproducibility information is revised in both directions.
descriptions.R1: v2 revises the closest-work positioning around Dispersive Loss and REPA: it distinguishes unconditional regularization coupled through alignment from conditional regularization, and direct feature regularization from using an external encoder. SiT and Dhariwal–Nichol are newly cited. The BYOL analogy and explicit first-adaptation assertion disappear; the guidance-scheduler work was already cited in v1.
descriptions.P1: The title, abstract, introduction, conclusion, and experimental narrative are revised to foreground transformer experiments. CLDM/InfoNCE/MSE terminology becomes CCUA/UCL/AL. CIFAR and unconditional results and limitations move to the appendix, qualitative sections are reorganized, and Appendix B adds a writing-assistance disclosure.
descriptions.P2: v2 replaces the opening illustration with SiT examples, adds an architecture diagram and ImageNet/TinyImageNet image grids, and introduces SiT and resampling tables. The original combined benchmark table is split across main text and appendix. CIFAR figures are relocated, nearest-neighbor panels are consolidated, and the latent-spectrum figure and several supplementary panels are removed.

P-4F7439D0DF.title: Why Do Vision Language Models Struggle To Recognize Human Emotions?

descriptions.M1: Balanced fine-tuning and the two-stage MSCE procedure remain unchanged, including four intermediate frames per gap and interleaved keyframe/text classification. Revised notation and the redrawn diagram do not establish an algorithm change.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use MAFW and DFEW for dynamic emotion recognition and English/Chinese Google Books Ngram frequencies for the bias analysis. The added comparisons and analyses use retained coverage.
descriptions.E2: Section 4.2 adds an evaluated TCoT comparator under a reported matched Qwen2.5-VL setup; v1 only discussed and cited TCoT. Other comparator sets remain unchanged. The newly cited specialist facial-expression methods are not evaluated.
descriptions.E3: Section S5 introduces a directional-asymmetry metric and selected class-pair controls. Existing settings remain unchanged, including the 495/700-video balanced test sets, FPS sweep, approximately 1,500 fine-tuning videos, and MSCE intermediate-frame count.
descriptions.E4: New Sections S5–S6 quantify directional confusion and examine per-class benefits and failures of balanced fine-tuning. These extend analyses already presented through confusion matrices in v1. Existing shuffling, FPS, and visual-prompting analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: The Pearson correlations, two-tailed significance testing, and p-values in Table 1 are unchanged. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or comparable uncertainty estimates for classification performance.
descriptions.E6: Existing Tables 1–3 and S1–S3 retain their values. v2 newly reports TCoT F1 of 0.241 on MAFW and 0.450 on DFEW, asymmetry scores, and fine-tuning summaries including macro-F1 of 0.245 zero-shot versus 0.315 after balanced fine-tuning. These are added results, not improvements between versions; Table S4 redisplays the existing Figure 3 confusion counts.
descriptions.T1: Section S5 adds the formal definition Δ(r,c) = f(r→c) − f(c→r), its antisymmetry property, and its interpretation for directional confusion. v1 discussed asymmetry qualitatively without this definition. Existing mathematics is otherwise retained.
descriptions.C1: The central long-tail-bias and temporal-bottleneck claims remain. v2 explicitly positions MSCE as a secondary diagnostic contribution and strengthens the conclusion from fundamental changes that 'may' be required to shifts that 'will' be required.
descriptions.C2: v2 softens proxy validation to suggestive support and adds explanations concerning English/Chinese lexical frequencies. Section S6 newly qualifies rebalancing as redistributing rather than eliminating bias, with Helplessness over-predicted and Disappointment still difficult. Gemini results are also clarified as bias measurement rather than mitigation.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds a project-page link and explicitly identifies MAFW in Figure 4's caption. The 7–8B model-size range repeated in the main text was already disclosed in v1 Section S2, alongside the unchanged A100 hardware information.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds a focused discussion of DK-CLIP, PE-CLIP, Fine-CLIPER, AU-DFER, ExpLLM, and FaVChat, positioning specialist successes as complementary to its diagnosis. It also sharpens distinctions from previously cited long-tail and SpookyBench research. Publication metadata updates concern retained works.
descriptions.P1: There are localized paragraph rewrites, terminology and punctuation edits, clearer contribution framing, and two new supplementary subsections. The main section sequence and most explanatory prose remain intact.
descriptions.P2: Figure 5 is redrawn using video frames, timestamps, stage labels, and an explicit prediction example. v2 adds Tables S4–S6, clarifies Figure 4's caption, and relocates retained displays through page reflow. Other figures and existing table structures remain substantially unchanged.

P-182450FDF1.title: Subject-level Inference for Realistic Text Anonymization Evaluation

descriptions.M1: SPIA's subject identification, subject-wise PII inference, matching, and scoring procedures remain unchanged. The new Figure 12 illustrates the pipeline already documented in Section 4.2 and Appendix C.3.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same English legal documents from TAB and online texts from PANORAMA, covering the same 15 PII categories and subject-level privacy tasks. No dataset, domain, or test scenario is added.
descriptions.E2: The evaluated methods remain TAB Longformer, DeID-GPT, DP-Prompt, and Adversarial Anonymization, with the same six backbones for generative methods. The inference-validation and multi-adversary comparisons also retain their comparator sets.
descriptions.E3: The TAB/PANORAMA test sets remain 144/151 documents. Certainty filtering, top-1 inference, evaluator models, matching rules, scoring thresholds, anonymization settings, and privacy/utility metrics are unchanged.
descriptions.E4: Appendix E retains the same adversary-robustness, PII-type, hardness, privacy–utility, and backbone-behavior analyses. Figure 12 supplies illustrative protocol examples without adding empirical analysis.
descriptions.E5: Statistical reporting is unchanged, including Table 11's rank correlations, n=38, and p<10^-26 reporting. Neither version adds or revises repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or uncertainty-estimation information relative to the other.
descriptions.E6: Reported results match throughout the tables and retained plots. For example, Table 4 retains CPR 0.330 for Longformer on TAB and 0.870 for Adversarial Anonymization with GPT-4.1 on PANORAMA.
descriptions.T1: The CPR/IPR definitions in Equations 1–2 and the worked calculation in Appendix C.3.3 are unchanged. Figure 12 repeats the existing CPR formula and scoring scheme without introducing mathematical reasoning or definitions.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same benchmark contributions and claims about masking overestimating protection, non-target subjects' exposure, and domain-dependent anonymization effectiveness.
descriptions.C2: The domain and backbone explanations, privacy–utility interpretations, and limitations concerning collective references, equal PII weighting, subject attribution, language, and dataset scope are retained unchanged.
descriptions.D1: Implementation settings, model versions, hardware, annotation instructions, prompt templates, and code/data access statements remain unchanged. The added diagram restates documented evaluation steps.
descriptions.R1: The related-work discussion, bibliography, benchmark positioning, and novelty claims are unchanged. Figure 12 repeats the existing attribution of the scoring scheme to Staab et al. (2024).
descriptions.P1: Appendix C.3 adds a short passage introducing the protocol overview. Figure references and the arXiv version/date stamp are updated; the section organization and remaining prose are preserved.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds Figure 12 on page 20, illustrating subject matching, PII scoring, and CPR calculation. Existing Figures 12–29 become Figures 13–30, with appendix page reflow. Existing tables and result graphics are retained.

P-1E6D7D6200.title: Responsible Evaluation of AI for Mental Health

descriptions.M1: The three support types and four evaluation dimensions remain unchanged in v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 3. Added examples and practical recommendations elaborate the framework without changing an algorithm, model, or implemented procedure.
descriptions.E1: Both versions retain the same 135-paper corpus and five illustrative case studies. The new 60-paper analysis samples the existing corpus, while v2 Table 1 provides illustrative tasks without adding evaluated datasets or domains.
descriptions.E2: The comparisons described in the five case studies are unchanged. Newly cited reviews and benchmarks support positioning or recommendations without adding evaluated comparators.
descriptions.E3: Section 5 adds an analysis using 60 randomly sampled papers classified under the existing maturity stages. This introduces a sampling and analysis setting; the original corpus-selection procedure and retained case-study settings are unchanged.
descriptions.E4: V2 adds a supplementary analysis of how sampled publications distribute across evaluation-maturity stages, extending v1's conceptual discussion with empirical classification. The five existing case studies remain unchanged.
descriptions.E5: Section 2 newly states that 50% of the review corpus was double-annotated and reports Cohen's kappa of 0.67. V1 provides no agreement statistic for these annotations; the disclosure does not establish that annotation effort increased.
descriptions.E6: Section 5 newly reports 68% early maturity and 32% intermediate maturity among 60 sampled papers, alongside an observation of increasing clinical-expert involvement in recent publications. The original summary-table percentages and all 135 appendix annotation records are unchanged.
descriptions.T1: The conceptual taxonomy and maturity-stage definitions are retained. Neither version introduces formal mathematical results or proofs, and the newly reported agreement statistic adds empirical evidence rather than mathematical theory.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and four stated contributions retain their scope. The conclusion narrows v1's assertion that responsible evaluation can ensure clinically meaningful, ethically grounded AI to the more limited claim that the taxonomy helps evaluation reflect intended use and risks.
descriptions.C2: Section 5 replaces a general discussion of shared infrastructure and research priorities with concrete guidance for researchers lacking clinical access, including simulations, bias audits, and rubric-based assessments. It explicitly qualifies these proxies as insufficient substitutes for real-world validation; the dedicated Limitations section is unchanged.
descriptions.D1: Section 2 newly documents the annotators' qualifications, senior adjudication of disagreements, and joint discussion of ambiguous cases. Corpus retrieval details and project access information remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: Five references are added. Section 1 connects the framework to social-science measurement and explicitly distinguishes it from reviews by Wang et al. and Zhang et al. and clinical benchmarking by Flathers et al.; the underlying interdisciplinary positioning is retained.
descriptions.P1: V2 locally revises the introduction and positionality discussion, replaces the closing Section 5 paragraph, rewrites the conclusion, and streamlines acknowledgments. The main section organization and most taxonomy and case-study prose remain intact.
descriptions.P2: V2 adds a sample-task table, orders appendix survey entries chronologically, and abbreviates some displayed paper titles. Existing tables retain their basic structure, with renumbering and a task-inventory header change from Application Type to Support Type.

P-F151D659B3.title: DPsurv: Dual-Prototype Evidential Fusion for Uncertainty-Aware and Interpretable Whole Slide Image Survival Prediction

descriptions.M1: Equation 15 removes the precision and distance-decay regularization terms, ξR1 and ρR2, leaving the weighted survival likelihood objective. The patch-prototype GMM, component-prototype evidence fusion, mixture aggregation, and prediction procedures remain substantively unchanged.
descriptions.E1: v1 Appendix B.1 and v2 Appendix G.1 report the same BRCA, BLCA, LUAD, UCEC, and KIRC cohorts with identical patient and WSI counts. The added analyses reuse this coverage; CONCH changes the feature extractor, while additional pathologist-rated examples extend the existing interpretability evaluation.
descriptions.E2: v2 adds evaluated MC Dropout and Deep Ensemble comparators in Appendix K, Table 9 and Figure 7. The nine principal baselines are retained. DSMIL is not newly evaluated: it already appears in v1's result tables and Appendix B.2 despite its omission from the main baseline-list paragraph.
descriptions.E3: v2 replaces cohort-specific learning rates with 1e-4, changes DPsurv's training budget from 50 to 30 epochs and λ from 0.1 to 0.5, and selects K from {1,2,3,4} through validation/early stopping instead of the earlier cohort/fold-size choices. It newly specifies a 15% validation holdout and explicitly reports retraining baselines under the shared selection protocol. New protocols include fixed-configuration ablations, CONCH evaluation on UCEC, and a two-pathologist, 10-point coherence assessment.
descriptions.E4: v1 has qualitative interpretation examples but no component-ablation or hyperparameter-sensitivity experiments. v2 adds component ablations in Table 2, K/C/λ/α sensitivity tests in Tables 6–7, feature-extractor robustness in Table 3, additional interpretation examples and expert ratings in Appendix I, and a targeted analysis of the lowest-rated case in Appendix L.
descriptions.E5: Five-fold cross-validation and mean-with-±-dispersion reporting are retained. The new sensitivity tables explicitly label their dispersion as standard deviation, extending the existing reporting pattern to additional results. Neither version reports random seeds, additional repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
descriptions.E6: The principal result entries and several rankings change substantially. DPsurv's reported mean C-index, IBS, and IBLL change from 0.685, 0.288, and 0.862 in v1 Tables 1, 2, and 4 to 0.704, 0.310, and 0.824 in v2 Table 1. These are revised results under changed training/selection settings, not controlled performance gains. v2 also adds ablation, sensitivity, CONCH, runtime, expert-rating, and alternative-uncertainty results.
descriptions.T1: v2 Appendix D.1 adds a short proof of the previously stated survival-function bound. The GRFN derivations, mixture proof, EM updates, and GMM limiting argument are retained across relocation and notation changes. Newly numbered definitions/propositions and the numerical toy example mostly explain existing mathematics.
descriptions.C1: Both versions claim dual-prototype evidential WSI survival prediction, explicit aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty, feature-to-decision interpretability, and state-of-the-art discrimination/calibration across five cancer cohorts. v2 rephrases the abstract and contributions, but retains their substantive scope; the added evaluations primarily support existing claims.
descriptions.C2: v1's limitations emphasize careful prototype-count selection. v2 instead interprets sensitivity results as supporting robustness and adds concrete boundaries concerning sparse tumor content, stronger domain shifts, and the pilot nature of clinical validation. It also explains the poor ablation performance of component prototypes without prevalence-weighted evidence mixing and develops λ's interpretation as controlling prediction conservativeness.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds a code-access link, explicitly states that GMM parameters remain fixed during evidential-network training, and provides validation/model-selection details and training-time information. Its configuration table is revised accordingly. Both versions already document initialization, baseline adaptations, optimizer settings, patch sampling, and A100 hardware.
descriptions.R1: Most related-work content is retained in v2 Appendix B. A new focused discussion distinguishes DPsurv's within-WSI component reasoning from Huang et al. (2024c)'s multimodal survival fusion. References are also updated through additions such as Lu et al. (2023) and several 2026 works, while some introductory citations are removed.
descriptions.P1: v2 rewrites and reorganizes the narrative: it condenses the introduction and main related work, adds a method overview, expands mechanism explanations, and restructures the appendices into dedicated terminology, theory, experimental, interpretation, and limitation sections. These changes extend well beyond inserting new experimental content.
descriptions.P2: The main paper changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. v1's separate C-index, IBS, and appendix IBLL tables are consolidated into v2 Table 1, and the configuration table is restructured. Numerous new tables and Figures 4–7 are added. Figures 1–3 retain the same graphics but are resized and repositioned.

P-7B5D472CFB.title: On-Policy RL Meets Off-Policy Experts: Harmonizing Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning via Dynamic Weighting

descriptions.M1: The hybrid GRPO/SFT objective and token weighting φ=p(1−p) remain unchanged. Appendix A.3 adds the evaluated CHORD-tune-both variant, combining φ with a warmup-then-decay µ schedule instead of fixed µ. This is a limited procedural variant within the existing framework.
descriptions.E1: v2 retains OpenR1 mathematical training and AMC, AIME, and MMLU-Pro evaluation, while adding single-turn ToolAce training and BFCL function-calling evaluation. This introduces substantially different task requirements beyond the earlier reasoning experiments.
descriptions.E2: SASR becomes an evaluated comparator in Table 1 and the detailed appendix tables; its paper was already cited in v1. Existing math comparators remain. LUFFY is explicitly unevaluated on the newly added tool-use task, rather than removed from an earlier corresponding comparison.
descriptions.E3: The new tool-use protocol introduces LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct, 500 SFT and 5,000 RL examples, batch size 96, 100 RL steps, binary correctness rewards, and instance-weighted BFCL accuracy. Appendix A also changes the stated maximum SFT budget from five to three epochs and qualifies the overlength penalty as applying without a final answer. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: Appendix A.3 and Figure 10 add a sensitivity comparison of fixed versus warmup-then-decay µ when φ is active. Response-length and learning-dynamics analyses also extend to tool use. The earlier fixed-versus-dynamic µ, entropy, base-versus-instruct, and case-study analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: Both versions report avg@32 for AIME and avg@8 for AMC, with unchanged uncertainty-reporting practices in retained plots. v2 adds no seed counts, repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Its added variance rationale explains the existing averaging practice.
descriptions.E6: Existing math/general-reasoning scores, math response lengths, and case-study outputs are unchanged. v2 adds SASR scores, detailed BFCL results, tool-use response lengths, and joint-scheduling results. Newly reported BFCL overall accuracy is 78.5 for CHORD-φ, 78.1 for CHORD-µ, and 77.1 for GRPO; these are new-task results, not gains over v1 under an existing setting.
descriptions.T1: Equations (1)–(6), the GRPO formulation, expert-probability approximation, and mathematical token-weight definition remain equivalent. Defining the existing stop-gradient notation and adding intuitive scheduling arguments introduce no new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The introduction now explicitly claims demonstrated effectiveness on practical tool-use tasks alongside mathematical reasoning, and specifies that the progression analysis concerns a separate SFT process. The central claims about SFT/RL unification, policy disruption, and dual control remain.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds interpretations that optimal SFT-to-RL timing and desirable response length depend on the task. Section 4.3 and Appendix A.3 argue that φ reduces sensitivity to µ scheduling. Appendix C additionally argues that starting from base models can be impractical for instruction-dependent tool use.
descriptions.D1: v2 newly documents Adam parameters, a 16k response limit, integer-answer filtering, H20 hardware, tool-use settings and prompt source, and 800-step case-study checkpoints. It removes v1's exact selected SFT learning rates. The new validation-based checkpoint statement also leaves ambiguity because Section 4.1 still defines SFT-best through test performance. The CHORD implementation link is retained.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds citations including RL-plus, iw-SFT, MiniCPM, ToolAce, and Gorilla/BFCL, while pruning several general application references. Appendix B incorporates limited additional related-method discussion. The central positioning around instruction-tuned models versus the base-model emphasis attributed to SRFT, LUFFY, and Reift remains unchanged.
descriptions.P1: Introduction and method prose are tightened, terminology shifts toward response patterns, and the experimental narrative accommodates both task families. The separate µ and φ analysis subsections are merged, and Appendix A is reorganized. The overall narrative and most appendix prose remain intact.
descriptions.P2: The central result displays are expanded: Tables 1–2 gain cross-task structure, Figure 6 gains a tool-use panel, and a BFCL table plus two appendix plots are added. The standalone µ-schedule plot is removed, three retained diagnostic plots are regrouped, and the MMLU table headers are reformatted. These changes extend beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

P-15FD3C9FD9.title: Landscape of Thoughts: Visualizing the Reasoning Process of Large Language Models

descriptions.M1: The visualization pipeline and original random-forest outcome verifier remain unchanged. Appendix D.4 adds a process-verifier variant that predicts whether individual states favor the correct answer, using current and preceding thoughts, then aggregates these predictions. This is a limited procedural extension.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use AQuA, MMLU, StrategyQA, and CommonsenseQA with the same task coverage. The additional StrategyQA analyses and newer-model case studies use these retained tasks; Figures 25–27 explicitly use AQuA.
descriptions.E2: Table 3 adds the process-verifier alternative alongside the original outcome-verifier and no-verifier conditions. CoT, LtM (also called L2M), ToT, MCTS, and unweighted voting remain. The new discussion of external reward models does not establish that those cited methods were experimentally evaluated.
descriptions.E3: The stated budgets remain 50 test questions, 20 verifier-training questions per dataset, and 10 sampled paths. Targeted additions introduce sentence-splitting controls and convergence/landscape-similarity metrics. Appendix E also evaluates QwQ-32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B/Qwen-1.5B configurations. No revision of the original benchmark protocol is established.
descriptions.E4: v2 expands validation: D.1 quantitatively examines visual observations; D.2 tests over-splitting and under-splitting thoughts; D.4 compares verifier variants; and D.5 investigates the StrategyQA anomaly across models and algorithms. Appendix E adds annotated self-evaluation and backtracking case studies for newer reasoning models.
descriptions.E5: Appendix D.1 newly reports log-linear convergence estimation and p-values of 0.008 for correct/incorrect convergence differences and 9.421e-11 for the speed–accuracy association. v1 has no corresponding significance reporting. The significance-test designs are insufficiently specified, and no additional repeated-run or seed counts are disclosed.
descriptions.E6: The original benchmark plots and scores are retained. v2 adds convergence and similarity measurements in Table 1, absolute transfer accuracies in Table 2, process-verifier entries in Table 3, and robustness/diagnostic findings. Table 3 is labeled AQuA, although its no-verifier and outcome-verifier columns reproduce Figure 5’s four-dataset averages; these entries therefore cannot establish a same-setting AQuA performance change.
descriptions.T1: Appendix D.1 newly defines a convergence coefficient through log-linear regression and a bounded path-speed measure using endpoint displacement divided by cumulative path length. The original mathematical formulation, Equations 2.1–2.8 and 4.1, is retained; no new theorem or proof is added.
descriptions.C1: The central visualization, reasoning-observation, and verifier-adaptation claims and the three contribution bullets retain their meaning. The added abstract sentence highlights accuracy and test-time scaling benefits already claimed and demonstrated in v1 Section 4.2.
descriptions.C2: New discussions materially expand the interpretation and qualifications. B.2 explains aggregation advantages over manual text analysis. B.3 distinguishes inexpensive verifier training from landscape construction requiring n × c forward passes. D.5 attributes StrategyQA anomalies to model instability and unreliable feature estimation. The existing multiple-choice limitation remains.
descriptions.D1: C.1 specifies that the correct-answer distance occupies the first feature coordinate, elaborating v1’s fixed-coordinate alignment. D.2 discloses period-based splitting and the comma/merging controls; D.4 explains automatic state-label construction. These add implementation information. The code-access statement and original sampling budgets remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds references to DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B, Luo et al. (2024), and Xu et al. (2025), supporting newer-model examples and discussion of process-reward-model costs. Section 5 and the existing research positioning otherwise remain substantially unchanged.
descriptions.P1: The main narrative and section sequence are retained with local rewrites, expanded explanations, and updated cross-references. The appendices are reorganized: the Impact Statement moves to A, existing discussion becomes B.1, and settings and visualizations become C and E, alongside new analysis subsections.
descriptions.P2: v2 expands the visual presentation with three tables, a tokenization comparison, four StrategyQA landscape figures, and three annotated reasoning-model figures. Existing Figures 1–7 retain their displays with caption/layout refinements; v1 Figures 8–19 are retained as v2 Figures 13–24.

P-9A89B04063.title: The Sample Complexity of Online Reinforcement Learning: A Multi-model Perspective

descriptions.M1: Algorithms 1–4 retain posterior-weighted model selection, periodic switching, Gaussian excitation and greedy covering. The MPC example instantiates the existing freedom to choose feedback policies. Corrected normalization indices align the pseudocode with v2's existing loss definition.
descriptions.E1: v2 evaluates only a 20-state, five-input linear system. v3 retains this coverage and adds nonlinear pendulum-on-cart swing-up with state and input constraints and 500 candidate models excluding the true dynamics, expanding both task and environmental coverage.
descriptions.E2: The retained linear experiments use the same optimal true-model controller reference. The pendulum experiment extends this oracle-reference comparison to control using the true pendulum dynamics. The expanded related-work citations do not introduce additional evaluated learning baselines.
descriptions.E3: The pendulum study introduces a distinct protocol with 0.02-second simulation steps, constrained MPC over 50 steps at 0.04-second discretization, and input perturbations. Separately, the retained parametric linear experiment changes its stated epsilon from p/T to sqrt(p/N); the PDFs do not establish that this experiment was rerun.
descriptions.E4: Appendix B.2 adds a targeted misspecification case study examining control, parameter errors and posterior behavior when the true model is absent. This provides illustrative robustness evidence beyond the retained linear model-count sensitivity analysis, without a systematic comparison across misspecification levels.
descriptions.E5: Both versions report averaging Figure 3's regret over 40 independent realizations. v3 adds no repeated-run counts for the pendulum, empirical confidence intervals or significance tests. Its model-posterior plots concern model selection rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.
descriptions.E6: Figures 4–5 add pendulum control, estimation and posterior trajectories, alongside approximately 60 ms per iteration. Figure 4's caption reports swing-up after about 80 steps versus 60 with true dynamics, while Appendix B.2.1 says 40 additional steps, leaving the exact delay inconsistent. The stated linear convergence and scalability findings remain.
descriptions.T1: New Appendix G introduces assumptions and loss-gap derivations for non-realizable model classes, changing the benchmark to policies associated with a suitable closest model. The theorem statements and excitation assumptions also revise dimensional and separation-factor accounting, and Section 2 adds an online-regression lower-bound argument.
descriptions.C1: Headline guarantees now expose input dimension and finite-model separation, including O(sqrt(d_u N p)) instead of O(sqrt(N p)). The introduction removes the model-based versus model-free complexity contribution and foregrounds frequentist posterior-sampling guarantees. Section 2 additionally claims optimality up to logarithmic factors.
descriptions.C2: v2 leaves non-realizability to future work; v3 explains conditional applicability when a suitable model is uniformly closest across the state-action space. It also qualifies logarithmic regret when candidate models are nearly indistinguishable and interprets the pendulum results as successful control despite multiple approximate models.
descriptions.D1: Appendix B.2 newly documents pendulum equations, physical parameters, candidate-generation ranges, costs, discretizations and MPC implementation using IPOPT through CasADi. It also reports runtime. The earlier MATLAB, linear-controller, recursive-estimation and laptop details are retained; no code-access change is reported.
descriptions.R1: The introduction and Appendix A reposition the work within posterior-sampling reinforcement learning and Hedge, expanding discussion of Osband, Ouyang, Xu and related research. New comparisons address Bayesian versus frequentist guarantees, mixing versus excitation assumptions, and Decision-Estimation Coefficient and Bellman-based complexity frameworks.
descriptions.P1: The introduction and related-work appendix undergo rewriting and thematic reorganization. Appendix B gains a linear/nonlinear hierarchy, and detailed S2 algorithm explanation moves from Section 3.2 to Appendix D. These narrative changes extend well beyond local copyediting.
descriptions.P2: v3 adds pendulum plots in Figures 4–5 and a geometric illustration of misspecification assumptions in Figure 6. Figures 1–3 are retained and relocated. These additional displays expand the visual presentation, alongside conference formatting and page reflow.

P-BF9FE44027.title: DynamicTree: Interactive Real Tree Animation via Sparse Voxel Spectrum

descriptions.M1: The sparse voxel spectrum, frequency-conditioned diffusion model, diffusion and LSS losses, two-stage training, mesh-bound Gaussians, and modal interaction procedure remain unchanged, including the appendix architecture parameters.
descriptions.E1: New Section 6.3 adds evaluation on clean 3D tree models for the traditional-animation comparison, introducing an input scenario distinct from reconstructed real trees. The 8,786-instance training dataset and 13-real-tree evaluation set remain unchanged.
descriptions.E2: v2 broadens the comparison methods: SV4D 2.0 joins 4DGen in Figure 3 and Table 1, and Weber and Penn's traditional animation method becomes an evaluated baseline in new Table 2. PhysGaussian and PhysFlow remain the interaction comparators.
descriptions.E3: The animation preference comparison expands from two methods to three. The new traditional-animation experiment uses clean tree models and the existing perceptual criteria. Training budgets, CLIP metrics, and the four-view interaction evaluation remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: The training-strategy ablation, resolution sensitivity experiment, and appendix demonstrations of different force directions and magnitudes are retained. The new traditional-method comparison does not include a controlled scanning-noise or robustness test.
descriptions.E5: Both versions report point estimates and preference percentages without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added comparisons introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: Additional comparative results are added: SV4D 2.0 scores 0.0081 CLIP-I and 0.0057 CLIP-T, while new Table 2 reports overall preferences of 57.86% for DynamicTree versus 42.14% for Weber. Table 1 replaces animation preference results, including DynamicTree's 95.7% becoming 94.6% under the expanded comparator set; these are not directly comparable performance measurements. Existing CLIP scores, interaction results, and resolution-ablation values are unchanged.
descriptions.T1: The spectrum definitions, loss formulas, Gaussian-binding equations, and modal-analysis derivation are unchanged. v2 numbers the previously unnumbered LSS equation and shifts subsequent equation numbers without revising the mathematics.
descriptions.C1: The central contributions remain long-term real-tree animation, sparse voxel spectra for generation and interaction, and the 4DTree dataset. Greater emphasis on structural consistency and physical plausibility restates properties already claimed in v1.
descriptions.C2: Section 6.3 adds a fairness rationale for using clean models and interprets the resulting preferences as evidence of effectiveness and robustness. The voxel-smoothing explanation and limitations concerning global linear motion, deformation artifacts, and limited large-deformation data remain unchanged.
descriptions.D1: v2 removes v1's explicit statement that quantitative animation evaluation uses only the input view, without specifying a replacement restriction. This reduces protocol documentation rather than establishing an actual view-selection change. Hardware, hyperparameters, architecture specifications, and appendix data-curation instructions are retained.
descriptions.R1: The related-work discussion adds SV4D and SV4D 2.0 and removes Animate124. It retains the same principal research families and positioning around learned 3D motion, physical simulation, and spectral representations.
descriptions.P1: Several abstract, introduction, and related-work passages are rewritten, and affiliations and citation formatting are updated. Limitations and conclusion become separate subsections in reversed order, and appendix A.1–A.3 becomes A–C. Most methodological and experimental exposition retains its wording and organization.
descriptions.P2: The paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, moves Figure 1 to the first page, and extensively resizes and relocates figures and tables. Figure 3 and Table 1 gain SV4D 2.0 entries, and a new traditional-animation table is added. Appendix visualizations are retained but redistributed.

P-0E35CA24A5.title: Distributional Machine Unlearning via Selective Data Removal

descriptions.M1: The distance-to-retained-mean scoring, top-f deletion, and Gaussian MLE steps remain unchanged, as do the cosine, Mahalanobis, and likelihood-ratio heuristics. Section 4.3 evaluates the existing selectors with established downstream unlearning methods without introducing a new proposed selection component.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same Gaussian configurations, Jigsaw profanity-defined subpopulation, SMS spam-versus-ham task, and CIFAR-10 cat-versus-other-classes task. Table 5 reuses Gaussian and CIFAR-10 coverage. Describing CIFAR-10 and Jigsaw as well-separated and intertwined scenarios reframes existing experiments; SMS moves to the appendix.
descriptions.E2: Table 5 adds centroid-based Coreset comparisons, and Section 4.3 reports evaluating k-center greedy with near-identical performance. The new comparison matrix evaluates Random, Coreset, and Selective selection with retraining, finetuning, NegGrad+, and SalUn on CIFAR-10, and retraining versus influence-function updates on Gaussians. These comparisons were absent from v1.
descriptions.E3: Table 5 introduces evaluation across downstream unlearning procedures, including a 20% CIFAR-10 forget-class accuracy target and method-specific training budgets documented in Appendix B.2.2. Table 2 also changes the savings metric from reduction relative to random deletion to reduction relative to full removal. Existing dataset splits remain unchanged. Jigsaw preservation is relabeled from macro-F1 to F1 without specifying whether averaging changed.
descriptions.E4: Section 4.3 adds a analysis of whether selection benefits persist across approximate unlearning procedures, extending validation beyond retraining. It also tests forget-set representativeness through coreset selection. The existing Gaussian separation sweep and Figure 6 comparison of scoring heuristics are retained.
descriptions.E5: The documented counts remain 20 Gaussian, five Jigsaw, ten SMS, and thirty CIFAR-10 seeds. Existing mean and standard-error reporting is retained. Table 5 adds deletion-budget point estimates but introduces no new uncertainty-estimation practice or explicitly increased run count.
descriptions.E6: Table 5 adds results without counterparts in v1: for example, CIFAR-10 Selective versus Random deletion budgets are 70% versus 88% with NegGrad+ and 55% versus 68% with SalUn; Gaussian influence-function budgets are 18% versus 91%. Original Table 2 deletion budgets and matched performance curves are retained. Savings changes such as 72% to 82% reflect the changed denominator, not improved same-setting performance.
descriptions.T1: The central definitions, frontier formulas, log-loss bounds, and Appendix A proofs are retained; v1's exponential-family Proposition 3 becomes v3's Theorem 2. Limited refinements include explicitly specifying positive shared covariance and removing v1 Section 3.2's reversed assignment of square-root and fourth-root deletion bounds, while retaining Table 1's original formulas.
descriptions.C1: v3 recasts the main efficiency contribution around reducing the forget set for computationally expensive sample-level unlearning and adds an explicit claim of compatibility with several such methods. The headline empirical claim changes from 15–72% savings versus random deletion to 15–82% versus full removal. This redefines the principal efficiency comparison while retaining the underlying KL framework.
descriptions.C2: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning Gaussian finite-sample guarantees, dependence on upstream domain identification, and the absence of privacy-oriented evaluation. Sections 4.2–4.3 develop interpretations based on concentrated statistical influence and explain coreset performance through ignoring retained data. Remarks 9–10 discuss the relationship between deletion budgets, downstream computation, and selection overhead, replacing much of v1's speculative concluding discussion.
descriptions.D1: Appendix B.2.2 newly documents optimizers, learning rates, epochs, batch sizes, SalUn's saliency fraction, NegGrad+ weighting, and influence-function damping. Appendix B.2.1 adds coreset implementation descriptions. v3 also replaces ResNet feature references with CNN terminology consistent with v1's detailed CIFAR-10 procedure. Existing dataset-processing and hardware disclosures are retained.
descriptions.R1: Research positioning shifts toward complementing computational unlearning methods and contrasting two-distribution selection with conventional coresets. New citations include Mirzasoleiman et al. and Gentile et al. for coresets, Fan et al. for SalUn, and Eldan and Russinovich for domain unlearning. The earlier distributionally robust optimization and spurious-feature-pruning discussion is removed, while the coreset relationship receives substantive new argument and empirical support.
descriptions.P1: The title, abstract, introduction, methodological explanations, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around CIFAR-10 and Jigsaw case studies followed by the new synergy section; SMS moves to Appendix B.1. Appendix B gains a nested structure separating additional results from implementation details.
descriptions.P2: The document adopts substantially different typography, heading styles, margins, and page rules, with resized and repositioned displays. The CIFAR-10 plot moves from v1's appendix Figure 5 to main-text Figure 3, alongside Jigsaw Figure 4. Other figures are relocated, and a new two-part Table 5 is added. Existing plotted curves are preserved.

P-077499579B.title: NaviAgent: Graph‑Driven Bilevel Planning for Scalable Tool Orchestration

descriptions.M1: Section 3.2.4 adds periodic probing and reactivation of recovered APIs alongside pruning. The four-action agent, HGT architecture, losses, and search procedures remain substantially unchanged. The three named recovery strategies mainly elaborate v2's existing path-recombination description.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use ToolBench, API-Bank, and 50 real APIs covering the same seven domains. V3 adds a distinct changing-availability scenario in Appendix F.2, with API outages followed by recovery. The larger real-API query count changes sampling rather than domain or task coverage.
descriptions.E2: V3 adds evaluated ToolNet and ToolPlanner comparisons to both the ToolBench comparison in Table 1 and the real-API comparison in Table 2. These broaden comparison with graph-based and structured planners beyond the retained ReAct, ToolLLM, and alpha-UMI baselines; both added methods were already cited in v2.
descriptions.E3: The real-API evaluation expands from 60 queries, equally divided by difficulty, to 303 queries comprising 101 easy, 102 medium, and 100 hard tasks. V3 also introduces component-removal controls and a 50-query, two-phase outage/recovery protocol with explicit pruning and reactivation settings. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, and fine-tuning settings are retained.
descriptions.E4: V3 adds tests separating the effects of bilevel planning, graph access, and search strategy (Table 3); removing clarification and merging retrieval with execution (Appendix H, Table 11); and enabling pruning/reactivation under changing API availability (Appendix F.2, Table 8). These extend the retained TWNM-variant and decision-pattern analyses substantially.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V3's additional results and average timings do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: V3 adds comparator, ablation, recovery, and maintenance-cost results, including 44.0% versus 48.0% TSR without versus with pruning/reactivation. Real-API NaviAgent TSRs change from 36.7/53.3/63.3% to 37.4/54.4/64.6% across the three backbones under the expanded query set, not identical settings. Retained ToolBench comparison rows, benchmark-variant tables, and runtime values match v2.
descriptions.T1: New Section 3.4 and Appendix I introduce context-dependent feasible action sets, a KL-minimal projection theorem with a support assumption and proof, an idempotence proposition, a hard-rule corollary, and a possible soft extension. This formal analysis is absent from v2; the existing HGT and loss equations remain mathematically equivalent.
descriptions.C1: The central bilevel-planning, TWNM, and closed-loop adaptation claims remain. V3 removes the claim to be the first bilevel framework, adds empirical validation as an explicit contribution, and foregrounds live-API generalization. The abstract replaces the 'up to 17 points' headline with an average 13.1-point complex-task gain.
descriptions.C2: V3 adds a local KL-projection interpretation and explicitly excludes characterization of the full evolving TWNM process. It also interprets the new ablations as complementary component benefits and distinguishes pruning's avoidance of failing APIs from reactivation's recovery of useful tools. Earlier interface, dynamic-environment, and heuristic-runtime limitations remain.
descriptions.D1: Appendix E.5 newly documents asynchronous local updates, tool insertion, and offline graph retraining with hot-swapping on a single NVIDIA P40. Appendix C clarifies the retrieval request and illustrates dependency-tree serialization; Table 4 clarifies that the static graph excludes historical invocation data. Existing fine-tuning details and prompts are retained.
descriptions.R1: V3 removes Qu et al.'s 'From Exploration to Mastery' reference and moderates the first-framework novelty claim. The introduction more explicitly distinguishes action-mode selection from standard planner–executor formulations. Most related-work discussion and cited works remain unchanged.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, baseline description, and results narrative undergo rewriting. Real-API evaluation moves from Appendix F.1 into a dedicated main-text section, and ablations are reorganized. The title and author information change, with acknowledgements and an impact statement added.
descriptions.P2: The main text changes from single-column preprint layout to two-column conference formatting. Earlier Figures 1–2 are replaced by a conceptual comparison, an architecture/recovery overview, and a redrawn evolution diagram. Comparison tables and plots expand, new ablation tables appear, and the real-API table moves into the main text.

P-59940FCC1C.title: MTSQL-R1: Towards Long-Horizon Multi-Turn Text-to-SQL via Agentic Training

descriptions.M1: Section 3.3.2 changes the stated reward aggregation from four separately weighted terms to two groups: EX plus EM, and all process rewards. The action loop, self-taught SFT algorithm, and GRPO procedure remain intact. This establishes a limited objective revision, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E1: v3 adds evaluation on Spider and BIRD using a CoSQL-trained model, plus a CoSQL scenario conditioned on model-generated prior SQL (Tables 6 and 12). These expand benchmark coverage and input conditions beyond v2. First-turn evaluation within CoSQL/SParC already existed; industrial scenarios discussed in v3 are not evaluated.
descriptions.E2: v3 Table 2 adds short-horizon Direct RL at 1.7B/4B and a LangGraph planning/tool agent, while dropping the Qwen3-8B rows and untrained long-horizon 14B row from that comparison. Table 12 introduces single-turn comparators including DAIL-SQL+GPT-4, CHASE-SQL+Gemini 1.5, and RESDSQL-3B+NatSQ. These expand the evaluated comparison methods.
descriptions.E3: v3 introduces a LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct setting, gold-versus-predicted-history testing, reward-component controls, and 2,000/4,000/6,000/8,000-token inference caps. Appendix D.6 specifies extracting intermediate SQL when truncation prevents completion.
