The efficiency comparison changes from v2 Table 8's averaged EX to CoSQL-specific evaluation in v3 Table 13; the original Qwen training configuration largely remains unchanged.
descriptions.E4: v3 adds reward-component ablations separating verification from proposal/correction rewards, token-budget sensitivity, and predicted-history robustness tests. Its error chart also adds the SFT-only stage between base and SFT+RL (Figure 6). The earlier tool ablations, turn/difficulty analyses, training dynamics, and case studies are retained, sometimes relocated.
descriptions.E5: v3 Table 10 introduces ± reporting for reward-ablation results, including 79.1±0.15 EX for the previously reported outcome-only result of 79.1. Neither the meaning of these quantities nor run counts or seeds is specified, so additional runs and statistical significance cannot be inferred.
descriptions.E6: Additional new results include predicted-history CoSQL EX of 76.5 versus Direct RL's 71.2, Spider/BIRD EX of 84.2/56.9, and architectural-transfer, reward-ablation, and token-budget outcomes. Most original Table 2 cells remain, but the full 4B model's out-of-domain CoSQL EM changes from 62.9 to 63.0, alongside edited averages. The replacement efficiency results use different settings and do not establish same-setting improvements.
descriptions.T1: The total-reward definition in Section 3.3.2 now imposes shared coefficients within outcome and process groups, replacing four coefficients with two. This changes the formal weighting specification. The MDP definitions, transition structure, and SFT/GRPO expressions otherwise remain substantively unchanged; Algorithm 1 is relocated rather than newly introduced.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: an MDP-based long-horizon SQL agent, execution/memory verification, self-taught SFT followed by RL, and superior CoSQL/SParC performance. Reworded contribution bullets and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these headline claims.
descriptions.C2: v3 expands interpretation of deployment robustness, efficiency trade-offs, truncation failures, and real-time applicability. Section 5 and Appendix C.3 discuss industrial schema retrieval, alternative memory backends, and compatibility with large-model distillation pipelines as untested extensions. v2 already acknowledged higher token costs, but lacked these detailed applicability arguments and qualifications.
descriptions.D1: v3 newly identifies basic vLLM as the latency-measurement implementation and describes absent inference optimizations. A configuration comment clarifies that KL loss was already disabled. The release promise changes from after internal review to upon acceptance, with the explicit artifact list removed. Hardware, learning rates, tool templates, and most configuration details are retained.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds references supporting DAIL-SQL, RESDSQL, CHASE-SQL, LLaMA, and production-agent latency discussion. Section 4.4 also changes attribution of the error taxonomy from prior work to the authors' design. The main related-work positioning remains stable; merged duplicate SQL-R1 references and publication updates do not represent different cited works.
descriptions.P1: RQ1 is reordered into grouped effectiveness, generalization/robustness, and efficiency arguments. Training dynamics moves from Section 4.5 to Appendix D.8, Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A, and a Discussion section is introduced. The appendix organization is extensively revised, alongside terminology standardization and prose tightening.
descriptions.P2: Table 2 is reorganized by backbone and reasoning horizon, removes its combined Average column, and adds comparison rows. v3 introduces several evaluation tables and two Pareto plots, and redraws the error chart with an SFT-only series. Original figures are extensively redistributed between main text and appendices, with difficulty accuracy also displayed separately.

P-7E44C659F0.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders

descriptions.M1: The pruning rule, retained frozen SAE, concept bottleneck, concept selection and three training objectives remain unchanged. The additional SAE variants and removal of the SAE component are evaluation settings and ablations, not revisions to the proposed procedure.
descriptions.E1: Both versions retain ImageNet-1K, the same concept-set coverage studies, and LLaVA text-generation and UnCLIP image-generation tasks. The new analyses use existing coverage; the 1329 shared concepts form a matched analysis subset.
descriptions.E2: Beyond v1's Matryoshka SAE comparisons, v2 Tables 3-4 evaluate Top-k SAE, Batch Top-k SAE and a standalone CB-AE without the SAE component. This broadens the evaluated alternatives to include other SAE architectures and a concept-only comparator.
descriptions.E3: Existing training and steering protocols remain unchanged. Added diagnostic protocols include a native-CLIP steering threshold of 0.173 alongside the original SAE-mean threshold of 0.232, individual neuron-zeroing controls, dead-neuron counting and a matched comparison across 1329 concepts.
descriptions.E4: Appendix C adds investigations of threshold sensitivity, reconstruction contributions of the four neuron groups, robustness across SAE architectures, the contribution of retaining an SAE, and cross-task steerability correlation. These expand the validation beyond v1's retained pruning, loss, sparsity and evaluator-sensitivity analyses.
descriptions.E5: Appendix C.3 newly reports a p-value of 0.035 for the Pearson correlation between LLaVA and UnCLIP steerability. This adds significance reporting; no additional repeated-run counts, seed variation or confidence intervals are documented.
descriptions.E6: Original scores are retained, including v1 Tables 3-4 as v2 Tables 5-6. Additional new findings include architecture-specific scores and dead-neuron counts; CB-AE versus CB-SAE interpretability of 0.308 versus 0.244 and unit-vector steerability of 0.238 versus 0.261; reconstruction-loss changes; and cross-task correlation of 0.06. The alternative threshold yields 29.14% high-interpretability/high-steerability neurons versus 18.84% under the original threshold, not a same-setting performance improvement.
descriptions.T1: The mathematical definitions, pruning-set construction, SAE/CB-SAE equations and cosine-cubed loss formula are retained. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is introduced.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contribution: combining SAE discovery with user-specified concept control through pruning and a concept bottleneck. The headline interpretability and steerability improvements of 32.1% and 14.5% are unchanged.
descriptions.C2: New interpretations connect low interpretability with larger reconstruction contributions, explain the CB-AE/CB-SAE tradeoff and characterize steerability as downstream-task/model dependent. Appendix A suggests feature splitting as a possible explanation for incomplete concept coverage. The existing CLIP-Dissect reliability limitation is relocated, not newly introduced.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds an explicit code repository link on page 1, whereas v1 only promises release. The documented training budget, hyperparameters and hardware remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish the repository's contents or availability of model weights.
descriptions.R1: v2 expands citations and explicitly distinguishes its approach from DN-CBM and SpLiCE, while adding feature-splitting and SAE-utility context. The LLaVA-Phi citation is removed. The overall positioning remains unchanged, and the AlignSAE comparison was already present in v1.
descriptions.P1: The introduction and conclusion are tightened, acknowledgements are expanded, and existing limitations move into a dedicated Appendix A. Original appendix sections A-B become B-C. Most technical prose and the main narrative structure are preserved.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds Tables 3-4 and renumbers the existing appendix tables as 5-6. Figures 2-4 receive clearer steering annotations, quadrant percentages and an explicit final inference diagram; Figure 8 labels are refined. These are localized display revisions within the retained document layout.

P-E9934CCCB0.title: Relational In-Context Learning via Synthetic Pre-training with Structural Prior

descriptions.M1: Section 5.1.3 changes the specified feature decoder from Gaussian/Softmax sampling to clipping/normalization and discretization/binning. Appendix D.2 adds optional gradient adaptation and chunked-support probability averaging. The three-stage prior and main Transformer architecture remain; revised parameter counts alone do not establish an architecture replacement.
descriptions.E1: Tables 1–3 retain the same 19 binary relational tasks from 13 databases and 23 single-table datasets. The additional experiments reuse this coverage, changing adaptation procedures, metrics, support sizes or component configurations without introducing new datasets or task requirements.
descriptions.E2: Figure 6a and Tables 6–10 add XGBoost-Tuned and AutoGluon-Best alongside the retained comparators; AutoGluon-Medium corresponds to v1's AutoGluon. Table 17 additionally evaluates fine-tuned TabPFNv2.5 against the adapted RDB-PFN variants. Griffin remains a reported reference, while RT remains discussion-only.
descriptions.E3: Appendix D introduces PR-AUC evaluation, target-task and cross-dataset fine-tuning, effective support sizes up to 8192, component ablations trained with 20k RDBs, and DFS sensitivity protocols. RDB-PFN fine-tuning uses 1000 steps with 1024 samples per step. Appendix C.2.2 also removes Sum from the specified DFS aggregation set. These extend the retained main few-shot protocol substantially.
descriptions.E4: Beyond v1's single-table-only comparison and qualitative visualizations, v2 directly ablates schema generation, link generation, temporal signals, locality, model capacity and attention ordering. It also tests DFS depth and aggregation choices, alternative metrics, adaptation and larger support sets (Appendix D, Figures 8–10 and Table 4).
descriptions.E5: Both versions specify ten random seeds for relational evaluation, mean and standard-deviation reporting, and ten repeated single-table trials in Appendix A.3. Shaded uncertainty bands already appear in v1. v2 introduces no new stated uncertainty-estimation procedure, significance test or increased run count.
descriptions.E6: All matched entries in the original ROC-AUC and single-table result tables remain unchanged. v2 adds extensive results for stronger baselines, PR-AUC, adaptation, support scaling and ablations; Table 17 reports average ROC-AUC of 0.7342 for target-task fine-tuning and 0.7261 for cross-task fine-tuning under those new conditions. Efficiency reporting also changes, including RDB-PFN's parameter count from 2.64M to 0.7M while retaining its 34-second timing.
descriptions.T1: The completeness and universality definitions, assumptions, theorems and proofs are unchanged after matching v1 Appendix D to v2 Appendix E. Assumption 4.2 replaces generic value/rest notation with explicit attribute and conditioning notation without changing the locality condition.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and introduction retain the same central claims: synthetic relational pretraining, universality within an assumption-defined family, gradient-free in-context learning and strong relational few-shot performance with efficient inference. The revised conclusion and additional experiments do not redefine the main contributions.
descriptions.C2: Section 6.2 now attributes much of the speed advantage to avoiding default ensembling. Section 6.3 treats single-table performance as a transfer and scope check instead of using the specialization gap to confirm the source of relational superiority. Appendix D adds interpretations of component importance, DFS sensitivity and adaptation/runtime trade-offs, while Section 7 explicitly discusses the binary, global-support and DFS applicability boundaries.
descriptions.D1: V2 newly specifies Kaiming-uniform initialization for learnable attention projections, running DFS before uniform row sampling, variable training/test ratios, the exact TabPFNv2.5 checkpoint, and budgets for additional experiments. The principal architecture hyperparameters, optimizer, hardware, pretraining corpus composition and code-access information remain.
descriptions.R1: The bibliography is unchanged. Sections 6.1 and B.3 refine positioning relative to Griffin and RT by explicitly treating them as contextual relational references and distinguishing RT's local graph-conditioned label access from RDB-PFN's fixed global support. The broader positioning against real-data pretraining and privacy-oriented generators remains.
descriptions.P1: Targeted paragraph rewrites clarify assumptions, attention terminology, efficiency and transfer interpretations, and remove duplicated implementation prose. Section 7 becomes Conclusion and Limitations, and a new experimental Appendix D precedes the retained, renumbered proof and raw-results appendices. The main narrative structure remains recognizable.
descriptions.P2: Figure 2 is redrawn with revised resource values and axis labels; Figure 6 becomes a two-panel baseline comparison. New Figures 8–10 display PR-AUC, adaptation, context scaling and ablations. Table 4 and Tables 12–30 add new displays, while existing relational result tables gain comparator rows. These exceed simple relocation or renumbering.

P-E4E3F9EF9F.title: VFScale: Intrinsic Reasoning through Verifier-Free Test-time Scalable Diffusion Model

descriptions.M1: The default linear loss, KL regularizer, backbone and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. V4 adds optional adaptive BoN-to-MCTS switching based on branch-energy variance (D.3) and quadratic, rank-based and fixed-transformation loss variants (D.2). These extend components without replacing the core method.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same Maze size-generalization and SAT-Net-to-RRN Sudoku settings. The added experiments use the existing 15×15 Maze task; they introduce no new dataset, task or input-environment scenario.
descriptions.E2: V4 expands comparisons with a learned external verifier for VFScale BoN, sparse and dense ground-truth verifiers for full VFScale hMCTS (Tables 10–11), and QRNCL, RBNCL and FTNCL loss variants (Table 12). V3's Original, DDPM and existing oracle comparisons remain.
descriptions.E3: Existing splits, training configurations, success metrics and matched-NFE comparisons are retained. Additional protocols compare verifiers on identical BoN candidates, measure Kendall tau across denoising steps 0–9, and profile peak memory and per-sample inference time (Tables 10, 19, 22–23). These supplement the original evaluation.
descriptions.E4: V4 adds analyses of verifier quality and reward density, alternative monotonic constraints, adaptive switching, permutation versus Gaussian negatives, and ranking alignment across denoising steps (Appendix D). V3's noise-scale, inner-loop and fixed-switch sensitivity studies remain, expanding the questions tested.
descriptions.E5: V3 reports no run counts or uncertainty estimates. V4 introduces means and standard deviations over ten random seeds for key Maze comparisons (D.5/Table 18), plus mean and standard-deviation rank correlations (Table 19). This establishes new statistical reporting, not an increase from a documented earlier run count.
descriptions.E6: Earlier tabulated results are retained, while v4 adds comparison, ablation, ranking and resource results. For example, Table 10 reports N=81 Maze success of 0.6562 with intrinsic versus 0.3203 with learned external verification; Table 18 newly reports N=81 hMCTS success of 0.8422±0.0147. These supplement rather than replace v3's headline scores.
descriptions.T1: The displayed core objectives, denoising equations, Appendix A consistency definition and linear-regression derivation are preserved apart from notation. V4's local-to-global discussion offers hypotheses and empirical evidence, without new formal assumptions, guarantees or proofs. Kendall tau is an added evaluation metric.
descriptions.C1: The training contribution broadens from specifically linear-regression NCL to monotonic-regression NCL, explicitly treating linear regression as its default instance. The main intrinsic-verifier and hMCTS contributions, task scope, and headline claims of approximately 88% Maze and 43% Sudoku success remain unchanged.
descriptions.C2: V4 adds interpretations of reduced single-sample performance as a scalability tradeoff, dense verification, structured negatives, and local constraints producing global ranking alignment (5.2 and Appendix D). Appendix F discusses quantified computational tradeoffs, and the contrastive-loss description changes from global to local minima. V3's standalone limitations paragraph is retained in Appendix I.
descriptions.D1: Appendix B.6 newly explains one-hot encoding, continuous denoising and argmax decoding; Appendix F adds memory and inference-time information. Appendix L explicitly states availability of datasets and pretrained checkpoints alongside code, whereas v3 already linked the same repository. These are additional disclosures, not established changes to the existing implementation.
descriptions.R1: The same 28 cited works and principal positioning relative to energy-based reasoning and externally verified diffusion scaling are retained. Updated titles, venues and author-year citation formatting do not introduce new related work.
descriptions.P1: V4 makes localized introduction and method rewrites, revises loss terminology, moves the experimental overview to Appendix B.1, and organizes appendix analyses into named subsections with a contents page. It adds acknowledgment and disclosure statements while retaining the main section sequence and much existing prose.
descriptions.P2: V4 expands tables displaying verifier comparisons, variants, uncertainty, rankings and computational costs, and redraws Figure 2's intermediate states as continuous predictions. Existing plots and case studies remain with relocations, label updates and conference-format reflow. Table 21 redisplays training times already reported in v3's prose.

P-9E391D26B3.title: Autoregressive Language Models are Secretly Energy-Based Models: Insights into the Lookahead Capabilities of Next-Token Prediction

descriptions.M1: The ARM and EBM definitions, bijective mappings, training objectives and Transformer implementations are unchanged. C.6 evaluates the existing model classes without introducing a method component.
descriptions.E1: The reported coverage remains synthetic sequence modeling with Zipfian and softargmax-normal distributions and the vocabulary/length configurations in C.2. C.6 adds optimization diagnostics without identifying a new dataset, domain or task.
descriptions.E2: All retained comparisons are unchanged, and Figures 6–8 continue comparing EBMs with ARMs. No additional comparison method is evaluated.
descriptions.E3: C.1 retains the original three-rate search and selected-rate reporting. New C.6 evaluates nine learning rates from 0.00001 to 0.1 and introduces gradient noise scale, gradient coherence and coordinate-wise SNR measurements. These are added protocols; the retained experiments' settings are unchanged.
descriptions.E4: C.6 adds a substantive investigation of optimization robustness: learning-rate sensitivity in Figures 6–7 and mini-batch gradient-noise behavior in Figure 8. These address questions absent from v3's model-size, sequence-configuration and distribution/logit-convergence analyses.
descriptions.E5: No repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests are added. Figure 8 reports gradient variability as a diagnostic outcome, without adding uncertainty estimates for the experimental comparisons or explaining their statistical estimation procedure.
descriptions.E6: Figures 2–5 remain identical. New Figure 6 places both models' best final losses at learning rate 0.01; C.6 reports slightly greater learning-rate robustness for ARMs and broadly similar gradient-noise sensitivity. These are additional findings, not revised performance under the retained settings.
descriptions.T1: The formal model definitions, bijection, equivalence-of-minima result, KL bounds and proofs in Appendices A–B are unchanged. Figure 8 supplies standard formulas explaining empirical gradient diagnostics without adding a theoretical construction, derivation or guarantee.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions concerning ARM–EBM equivalence, the soft Bellman connection, teacher forcing and distillation bounds. C.6 adds supporting evidence without redefining these claims.
descriptions.C2: C.6 frames its diagnostics as further confirmation of the already stated interpretation that ARMs can behave similarly to EBMs. It adds no distinct mechanism explanation or limitation; the conclusion's qualifications about optimization and approximation error remain identical.
descriptions.D1: Figure 7 documents the additional learning-rate values, and Figure 8 specifies the gradient-diagnostic formulas. Existing implementation details remain unchanged. C.6 does not identify its particular model/data configuration or mini-batch sampling details.
descriptions.R1: The related-work discussion and bibliography are identical. C.6 introduces no citations or revised positioning relative to prior research.
descriptions.P1: v4 appends the short Optimization dynamics subsection with explanatory paragraphs and captions, and updates the publication footer and arXiv stamp. The existing narrative and section organization remain unchanged.
descriptions.P2: v4 adds a learning-rate summary plot, a nine-panel training-curve figure and a four-panel gradient-diagnostic figure. Existing Figures 1–5 and pages 2–30 retain their layout; the first page undergoes limited reflow.

P-6EE5F30CD7.title: Beyond Chunking: Discourse-Aware Hierarchical Retrieval for Long Document Question Answering

descriptions.M1: v4 introduces language adaptation through translated Chinese RST-DT data and multilingual parser training, replacing the XLNet-base-cased backbone with gte-multilingual-base (Sections 3.1.1 and 4.1; Appendix B.2). This extends parser construction. The downstream tree integration, node enhancement and evidence-selection algorithms remain.
descriptions.E1: Coverage expands from English training and evaluation to Chinese-augmented parser training and MultiFieldQA-zh evaluation. The added benchmark includes Chinese legal texts, government reports, encyclopedias and academic papers (Appendix B.1). The three English QA benchmarks are retained.
descriptions.E2: The QA comparator set remains flatten-chunk, flatten-sentence, RAPTOR and Bisection, including on the added Chinese benchmark. However, v4 Table 8 adds RAPTOR as an actually measured runtime comparator; v2 Appendix C.1 reported only DISRetrieval timing measurements.
descriptions.E3: The reported parser configuration changes to multilingual training. Added evaluation protocols include 200 Chinese test examples with two generators and 200/300/400 context settings, plus five hardware- and model-matched runtime comparisons spanning 10K–90K words. The retained English QA splits, metrics and context budgets remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: Appendix C.1 extends the existing scalability analysis to test preprocessing efficiency directly against RAPTOR. The hierarchy-selection, enhancement-model, parser-training-scale, Top-K and threshold ablations remain, with revised numerical evidence rather than substantially different analytical questions.
descriptions.E5: Both versions state that Figure 6 timing results average 10 documents per length range and report standard deviations. Neither introduces new QA seed counts, repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added timing table does not establish a new uncertainty-reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: v4 revises DISRetrieval results across the English benchmarks, enhancement-model ablation, node statistics and Figures 4, 8 and 9. For example, Table 1 QASPER F1 with UnifiedQA-3B, OpenAI embeddings and 400-word contexts changes from 41.14 to 40.74; the parser configuration also changes, limiting direct performance interpretation. New results include Chinese QA F1 of 35.25 with GPT-4.1-mini at context 400 and preprocessing times of 103.0 versus RAPTOR's 338.5 seconds at 50K words.
descriptions.T1: The transition-system definitions, node representations, action probabilities, training loss and tree-integration mathematics are retained. Two explicit parsing equations disappear from the main text but their relationships remain in prose and Appendix A. No substantive assumptions, derivations or proofs are added or revised.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction and conclusion elevate language-universal discourse parsing and cross-lingual QA to central contributions. Claims expand from improvements across three English datasets to applicability across languages, explicitly including English-to-Chinese generalization. The original discourse-guided hierarchical retrieval contribution remains.
descriptions.C2: v4 adds interpretations of cross-language discourse transfer and attributes runtime advantages to fewer LLM calls and selective summarization. Its limitations explicitly restrict demonstrated language coverage to English and Chinese, discuss additional translation requirements and dataset scarcity, and acknowledge possible translation-model bias.
descriptions.D1: v4 adds a translation prompt, training-corpus composition and the multilingual backbone identifier. It replaces the future code/model-release promise with reported public code/dataset availability and a repository address. Documentation remains inconsistent about the translation model: Sections 3.1.1 and 4.1 name GPT-4o, whereas Appendix B.2 names GPT-4o-mini.
descriptions.R1: Section 2 adds focused discussion of earlier discourse-based QA work, including Santhosh and Ali, Xu, Nair and Du, and distinguishes evidence retrieval from prior discourse applications to answer generation. References also add Tang's hierarchical work and multilingual representations while removing Chen et al. (2024). These refine the existing research positioning.
descriptions.P1: Beyond the scientific additions, v4 compresses and rewrites Related Work and the tree-construction exposition, revises the abstract and conclusion, and reorganizes the contribution list and experimental setup. Section 3.1.1 becomes RST Adaptation with separate granularity and language discussions, and Appendix B gains a translation subsection.
descriptions.P2: v4 adds Chinese QA and runtime tables, extends the dataset table, relocates existing figures, and revises captions and plot axes or labels. Table 1 now explains the Bisection control explicitly. The principal diagrams, table formats and overall two-column layout remain recognizable.

P-0FF1A03652.title: SignBind-LLM: Multi-Stage Modality Fusion for Sign Language Translation

descriptions.M1: The expert-routing, CTC, gated-fusion, and LLM pipeline remains. v3 changes manual inputs from hand crops to full frames and changes the main-text gate from manual-only conditioning to concatenated manual/lip features (v1 Equation 10; v3 Equation 12). It also describes independent decoder training on generated gloss/text pairs instead of v1's final training on fusion outputs.
descriptions.E1: v3 adds training and evaluation on BOBSL, extending coverage from American Sign Language to British Sign Language and interpreted broadcast footage. YouTube-ASL, How2Sign, and ChicagoFSWildPlus remain in use.
descriptions.E2: Geo-Sign is newly included in the How2Sign comparison, having only been cited in v1. The new BOBSL comparison includes GFSLT, Sign2GPT, Albanie, Sincan, and Lost in Translation. Appendix B additionally compares concatenation/MLP and cross-attention fusion alternatives and multiple YouTube-ASL baseline configurations. The fingerspelling comparator set is retained.
descriptions.E3: v3 adds zero-shot transfer and How2Sign-only training controls, standalone phoneme evaluation, and POS accuracy analysis. It drops BLEU-2/3 from the main benchmark comparison and no longer reports sequence-classification accuracy. Optimization is reported as AdamW rather than v1's Adam; most other newly supplied hyperparameters are disclosures, not established changes to existing experiments.
descriptions.E4: v3 adds fingerspelling, fusion, and sequencer removal ablations; standalone expert tests; alternative fusion comparisons; pre-training/transfer analysis; POS analysis; and label-length analysis. Qualitative cases are replaced and extended to BOBSL. Conversely, v1's quantitative comparison of random, frequency-based, keyword, and LLM glossing methods is removed rather than relocated.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional v3 results continue to use point estimates.
descriptions.E6: Reported How2Sign BLEU-1/BLEU-4 changes from 46.0/23.5 to 49.4/22.1, while ROUGE remains 41.2 and fingerspelling accuracy remains 73.2%. The no-lipreading BLEU-4 changes from 16.6 to 13.6. v3 adds BOBSL BLEU-4 of 6.8, zero-shot 8.3, How2Sign-only 13.7, and numerous analytical results. These are revised or newly reported results, not established same-setting performance gains.
descriptions.T1: Appendix B.1 adds a mathematical complexity comparison between O(T) gating and O(T²) cross-attention operations. Expanded CTC formulas mostly unpack losses already present in v1. Neither version presents a theorem or proof framework.
descriptions.C1: The central claim that specialized signing, fingerspelling, and lipreading experts improve translation through fusion remains. v3 extends the headline state-of-the-art claim to BOBSL and adds provision of generated pseudo-gloss and phoneme annotations for BOBSL and How2Sign as a contribution.
descriptions.C2: v3 adds substantive interpretations concerning gating's suppression of irrelevant mouth signals, benefits of diverse pre-training, and the tradeoff between content-word accuracy and function-word reconstruction. Appendix C discusses instructional-domain bias, while Appendix E explains proper-name hallucinations and semantic drift through weak conditioning and LLM priors. v1's discussion was narrower.
descriptions.D1: v3 adds exact glossing prompts, phonemization tools and fallback handling, parameter counts, fusion architecture dimensions, training schedules, LoRA configuration, hardware, computational costs, and decoding settings. These expand v1's sparse implementation documentation. However, v3 contains conflicting descriptions of epochs, full fine-tuning versus LoRA, and training-time totals.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds related-work coverage including SAGE, SLTUNET, hierarchical feature alignment, and Lost in Translation, alongside component references such as DINOv2, Gumbel-Softmax, and LoRA. The underlying positioning remains the absence of explicit fingerspelling/lipreading integration in prior SLT systems; publication and bibliographic updates do not constitute additional scientific changes.
descriptions.P1: Beyond the title and model rename, v3 extensively rewrites the introduction and method, reorganizes the pipeline into numbered stages, and develops a structured appendix with a contents list and dedicated analysis and implementation sections. This is narrative restructuring, not merely added experimental content.
descriptions.P2: v3 adds an opening modality illustration, redraws the architecture diagram, replaces the earlier routing visualizations with different translation displays, and introduces a POS heatmap and label-length plots. Comparison tables are restructured, and new appendix tables document analyses, configurations, and intermediate fused outputs.

P-1D1B0D7CCE.title: SceneDiff: A Benchmark and Method for Multiview Object Change Detection

descriptions.M1: The core geometry, segmentation, scoring, and association pipeline remains. Sections 4.2–4.3 change the region exclusion threshold from 60% to 50%, reduce the region-matching weight from 0.2 to 0.1, and replace accepting any sufficiently similar counterpart with one-to-one greedy matching for change classification.
descriptions.E1: V2 adds actual evaluation on PASLCD, previously only discussed as prior work. This extends testing to densely captured indoor and outdoor scenes under similar and different lighting conditions. SceneDiff, RC-3D, ChangeSim, and the existing dynamic-content and robotic scenarios remain.
descriptions.E2: SceneDiff comparisons add MV3DCD and both pretrained and fine-tuned CYWS-2D. The retained Qwen2.5-VL baseline replaces Grounding SAM localization with SAM3. RC-3D adds CYWS-2D and removes the reported VLM comparison. PASLCD comparisons additionally include SplatPose, CSCDNet, CYWS-2D, and MV3DCD, with baseline scores explicitly sourced from prior work.
descriptions.E3: V1 evaluates prediction centroids inside ground-truth boxes, tolerates two detections per object, and uses the highest-confidence point for scene matching. V2 introduces pixel IoU and mask-based object AP, one-to-one matching at IoU 0.5, and scene matching through aggregated IoU with mean confidence. It also adds CYWS-2D fine-tuning on 3,125 validation frame pairs and direct-box versus SAM-mask evaluation controls.
descriptions.E4: V2 expands sensitivity testing from change and merging thresholds to three scoring weights and four thresholds. Sections 8.6–8.7 add checks of whether SAM conversion disadvantages CYWS baselines, while Section 8.4 adds trajectory evidence explaining rendering failures. Existing dynamic-person, repetitive-object, lighting, and geometry stress analyses remain; change-type-aware evaluation is revised and relocated rather than newly introduced.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. V2's discussion of mask confidence concerns detection ranking, not statistical uncertainty reporting.
descriptions.E6: Main benchmark and ablation results are extensively revised. For SD-V, v1 reports point-based per-view/per-scene AP of 49.6/46.3, whereas v2 reports mask-based obj/im and obj/sc AP of 43.8/22.8; these are not directly comparable scores. Reported RC-3D Both AP50 changes from 68.7 to 65.3 and ChangeSim F1 from 57.6 to 57.0. New PASLCD results report 47.3 mIoU versus MV3DCD's 46.1.
descriptions.T1: Equations 1–6 retain their mathematical forms apart from equivalent notation and parameter retuning. Neither version adds theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations. The revised AP matching criteria are experimental protocol changes rather than new theoretical results.
descriptions.C1: The benchmark, training-free method, and superior-performance contributions remain. V2 explicitly elevates cross-domain generalization without retraining and improvement with advancing foundation models into abstract and conclusion claims. The reported headline relative AP margins change from 84%/37.4% to 53.0%/30.6% alongside revised comparisons.
descriptions.C2: V2 distinguishes geometry cues' usefulness for pixel segmentation from their weaker object-level performance, elaborates interpolation versus extrapolation as an explanation for rendering-based baseline failures, and acknowledges possible disadvantage from adapting MV3DCD. It broadens the claimed hyperparameter robustness, although Figure 19 still shows substantial change-threshold sensitivity. The principal ambiguity and reconstruction limitations remain.
descriptions.D1: V2 expands baseline reproduction instructions, including CYWS-2D training-pair construction, MV3DCD's 60% region assignment rule, and confidence sources. It newly documents scene-consistent splits, collection effort, and using validation-selected parameters across benchmarks. V1 promises future code release; v2 states a self-contained codebase accompanies the supplement, although that attachment cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.
descriptions.R1: Related work expands coverage of sensor-depth, point-cloud, and TSDF approaches, including POCD and Khronos, and adds SAM3 and SplatPose references. GPT-4 and Grounded SAM references disappear with their associated comparison changes. The central positioning around training-free object-level detection remains, with a more qualified account of rendering-based methods' strengths.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, related work, experimental discussion, and conclusion undergo rewriting. The benchmark section is reorganized to introduce metrics before dataset and annotation details, and the appendix structure is revised. Method explanations and terminology are also refined beyond simple renumbering.
descriptions.P2: V2 replaces the two-column main layout with a single-column design and restructures displays. Table 2 groups methods by output type, and ablations use colored differences from the full method. New displays cover scene diversity, PASLCD, expanded sensitivity tests, trajectories, and training examples; the old point-based evaluation illustration is removed and qualitative comparison panels are revised.

P-0AEA9EF3C2.title: Empowering Multi-Turn Tool-Integrated Agentic Reasoning with Group Turn Policy Optimization

descriptions.M1: Equation 7 changes the specified advantage normalization from normalization across trajectories at a fixed turn to pooling all turns across sampled trajectories, also reflected in Algorithm 1. This revises one calculation within the retained three-component GTPO design; it does not establish that experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E1: Section 6.2 adds GPQA Diamond, BBEH-mini, and EvalPlus HumanEval/MBPP evaluations, extending coverage beyond mathematical reasoning to non-math reasoning and program synthesis. The five original math benchmarks and training datasets remain. Removing OlympiadBench from Table 2's caption corrects an unsupported listing rather than removing reported results.
descriptions.E2: v2 Table 5 adds evaluated DAPO and SimpleTIR comparators on MATH 500 and AIME 2024 under the ablation training budget. This broadens the trained-method comparison beyond GRPO. The original prompting and GRPO baselines remain; v1's conceptual DAPO comparison was not an empirical evaluation.
descriptions.E3: Added experiments introduce Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, EvalPlus testing, a three-embedding correlation protocol, and runtime-success rate as a tool-quality metric. These broaden the evaluation design. Existing numerical training and evaluation settings in Section 5.1 and v1 Appendix A.2, retained as v2 A.4, remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: Sections 6.3–6.4 add analyses testing whether code-similarity scores agree across embedding models and whether increased tool use accompanies executable code. These address robustness and tool errors beyond the original analyses. Existing component, discount, reward-shaping, and turn-count ablations remain, including the reward-shaping analysis relocated to Appendix A.5.
descriptions.E5: Section 6.3 newly introduces Pearson and Spearman correlation estimation for embedding-based similarity scores, reported in Table 8. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the statistical addition does not quantify uncertainty in performance gains.
descriptions.E6: Original math scores and ablation values are retained, including v1 Tables 5–6 as v2 Tables 10–11. New Tables 5–9 add results: Llama averages are 21.18 for GRPO versus 23.01 for GTPO, and non-math averages are 46.1 versus 47.9. Tool-execution success improves on average, but GTPO scores lower on AMC23: 69.49 versus GRPO's 72.17.
descriptions.T1: Equation 7 substantively revises the mathematical normalization set to include all trajectory-turn pairs. Section 4.3 also specifies the previously undefined no-positive-sample case. The turn-level MDP and discounted-return formulation remain, with no new theorem or proof.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the contribution from demonstrated mathematical-reasoning gains to non-math generalization, explicitly claiming 3.9% relative improvement on reasoning and program-synthesis tasks. They also foreground negligible overhead. The original three methodological contributions and 3.0% relative math-improvement claim remain.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds interpretations connecting embedding-score correlations to reward-shaping robustness and execution success to reliable tool use. It explicitly acknowledges runtime success as a proxy that cannot establish logical correctness, and adds a qualitative overhead rationale. Table 4 also corrects gamma=1's interpretation from disabling turn-level rewards to disabling discounting.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds procedural pseudocode in Algorithm 1, documents global normalization and zero-positive handling, and identifies additional embedding models with access links. Appendix A.3 describes one embedding per trajectory and a rough seconds-level cost. Original hyperparameters and evaluation-setting disclosures are retained.
descriptions.R1: The redesigned Table 1 and new Appendix A.1 expand positioning against GRPO/DAPO/GSPO and ReTool/ToRL/Search-R1, including an explicit first-formulation claim for the combined design. New benchmark and temporal-credit-assignment citations are added, while the SFT-related discussion and several associated references are removed.
descriptions.P1: Most existing prose and the core narrative remain. v2 updates the title and affiliations, shortens parts of Related Work and Background, clarifies notation, adds a Discussion section and appendix explanations, and moves the reward-shaping discussion into the appendix. Rewriting of retained material is localized.
descriptions.P2: v2 redesigns the conceptual comparison table and expands experimental displays through Tables 5–9 and a full-width Algorithm 1. Several existing figures and tables are relocated, including the reward-shaping table becoming Appendix Table 10. All eight original figures retain their graphical content.

P-EB39325FAB.title: Self-Soupervision: Cooking Model Soups without Labels

descriptions.M1: The supervised mixing option changes from v1's Instant Seasoning, which samples mixture weights and selects by labeled kNN accuracy, to cross-entropy-trained labeled seasoning in v2 Section 4.6. The central Self-Soup construction and entropy-based Self-Seasoning procedure remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same ImageNet evaluation variants, LAION-C, and 21 VTAB tasks with their corruption variants. Ratatouille uses four already represented VTAB datasets; the additional sample counts and augmentation configurations change protocols within retained coverage.
descriptions.E2: v2 adds logit ensembles to the ImageNet comparisons, continued-SSL soups trained on the corresponding corruptions to Table 2, and an evaluated Ratatouille baseline in Table 5. The few-shot comparison adds full fine-tuning, replaces random-search seasoning with gradient-based labeled seasoning, and removes the best-ingredient comparator; stock and uniform-soup results remain in Appendix Table 9.
descriptions.E3: ImageNet experiments expand from three SSL algorithms to four with LeJEPA, and Section 4.1 evaluates 64 mixtures instead of 52. The revised few-shot study varies training size from 25 to 1,000, matches six-configuration tuning budgets, tunes Self-Seasoning's k and temperature, and reports held-out selection. Appendix A adds RandAugment and a doubled ingredient pool combining augmentation schemes.
descriptions.E4: New Appendix Tables 6–7 examine sensitivity to augmentation choice and increased ingredient diversity. Figure 4 and Table 9 add training-sample sensitivity analyses comparing seasoning with full fine-tuning across VTAB domains. The existing corruption evaluations and Franca connectivity analysis are retained.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports seed-based repetitions, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The six runs per method in v2 are different hyperparameter configurations, rather than repeated runs for uncertainty estimation.
descriptions.E6: Figure 2 and Table 1 report revised results with four SSL ingredient types: uniform Self-Soup accuracy changes from 32.23/22.40 to 32.34/22.92 on IN-C/LAION-C under the changed configuration. v2 adds shifted-data comparator scores, Ratatouille results, augmentation results, and extensive few-shot results with revised mixture coefficients. Table 4 and the Franca curves retain their earlier results.
descriptions.T1: The linear mode connectivity definition and Self-Soup equation are unchanged. New Equation 3 expresses the neighbor-entropy objective already described and implemented in v1 Appendix D; it adds mathematical exposition without a new derivation, assumption, or proof.
descriptions.C1: The central claims remain that SSL ingredients can be mixed productively, unlabeled shifted data improves robustness, and Self-Seasoning learns mixtures without training labels. The abstract retains the +3.5%/+7% robustness claims; adding LeJEPA extends the supporting demonstration without redefining these contributions.
descriptions.C2: v2 interprets comparable Ratatouille accuracy as a practical advantage because Self-Soups avoid auxiliary labels. It also identifies a specific use case where seasoning outperforms fine-tuning: natural VTAB tasks with fewer than 500 training samples. The limitations paragraph remains unchanged.
descriptions.D1: v2 documents LeJEPA's lambda=0.02 and the revised few-shot search grids, batch-size rule, and held-out selection. It omits v1's explicit zero initialization and softmax parameterization of mixture weights. The entropy code and code/data access links are retained; repeating the code link in the abstract does not establish new availability.
descriptions.R1: V2 adds the LeJEPA citation and incorporates it as an SSL ingredient. The new Ratatouille experiment adds a comparison against supervised inter-training, while the related-work discussion otherwise remains substantially unchanged.
descriptions.P1: Local revisions consolidate the seasoning explanation, rewrite the few-shot section, give the retained Franca analysis its own subsection, and reorganize the appendices. Most introductory and discussion prose is retained. Several stale references are introduced, including Table 7 references associated with Table 1 results and a Table 4 reference for the few-shot finding.
descriptions.P2: Figure 2 changes from triangular three-ingredient plots to square four-ingredient heatmaps. v2 adds few-shot curves, a Ratatouille table, augmentation tables, and comparator rows in existing tables. The seasoning presentation is reorganized into Figure 4 and Appendix Tables 8–9; the Franca figure is retained and renumbered.

P-EDC8469DCC.title: A Training-Free Style-Personalization via SVD-Based Feature Decomposition

descriptions.M1: v1's three-path system uses feature initialization, Key Stage Attention Sharing at steps 2–3, and similarity-weighted Adaptive Query Sharing at steps 4–7. v2 replaces this with two generation streams conditioned on the same prompt, SVD-based Principal Feature Blending at the third feature, and Structural Attention Correction replacing content queries and keys at steps 3–12. These change the inference procedure, rather than merely renaming components.
descriptions.E1: The 190-prompt Parti benchmark, ten quantitative reference styles, and image-guided and text-only generation tasks remain. Qualitative artistic-style coverage changes: v2 includes geometric flat illustration, metallic 3D, neon comic art, and retro sci-fi examples, while earlier Mesopotamian-relief examples disappear. Additional backbones change model settings rather than task coverage.
descriptions.E2: Table 1 and Figure 5 add CSGO and StyleAR to the six retained external baselines. B-LoRA joins the user-study comparison. For text-only style-aligned generation, v2 Figure 14 adds comparisons against StyleAligned and AlignedGen, whereas v1 Figure 8 displays only the proposed method.
descriptions.E3: v2 adds the harmonic mean of prompt and style fidelity as an evaluation metric. The user study changes from 40 participants choosing among four methods to 30 choosing among five. New experiments introduce mixed object/color prompt-pair controls and evaluation on Infinity-8B and Switti. The primary Infinity-2B benchmark, output resolution, and stated GPU remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: The step-wise prompt-injection analysis is retained, but the query/key/value replacement analysis is replaced by baseline, full-feature replacement, and SVD-guided controls. Component ablations are redesigned around replacement, PFB, and SAC. Appendix A adds top-k singular-component and exponential-decay sensitivity studies, and Appendix D tests qualitative generalization across backbones.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Additional averaged CLIP results and the revised user-study sample size do not introduce uncertainty reporting.
descriptions.E6: On the retained benchmark, Table 1 changes the proposed method's prompt fidelity from 0.330 to 0.334, style fidelity from 0.603 to 0.630, and reported runtime from 6.44 to 3.58 seconds; the six shared baselines' corresponding values remain unchanged. v2 adds baseline, harmonic-score, spectral-analysis, sensitivity, and backbone results. User preferences change from 57.5%/30.5% to 35.3%/32.0% for prompt/style fidelity, but the changed participants and candidate set preclude interpreting these as comparable gains or losses.
descriptions.T1: The mathematical construction changes from attention concatenation and cosine-weighted query mixing to principal/residual feature decomposition, an exponentially weighted SVD operator, and residual-preserving reconstruction in v2 Section 5.2. Appendix A additionally defines top-k decompositions and interventions. These substantively revise the formal definitions; neither version provides theorems or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion replace the central claim about content-specific query representations and attention sharing with a claim that dominant singular components of the third feature encode style, motivating PFB and SAC. Training-free personalization from a single reference and efficient autoregressive generation remain the overarching goals.
descriptions.C2: v2 explains style/content separation through leading versus higher-rank singular components and interprets weaker spectral decay as increasing content leakage. It also adds an explicit limitation: heterogeneous reference styles can become blended because the method cannot selectively isolate sub-styles. v1 instead emphasizes query-based content control and ends with general future directions.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds Algorithm 1, the spectral-decay setting, and extensive baseline implementation information, including repository provenance, default configurations, the unofficial StyleDrop implementation, and a shared A6000/PyTorch environment. Table 1 and Appendix C explicitly explain that tuning-based runtimes include style-specific training plus one generated image. These expand documentation without establishing that retained baseline experiments were rerun.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds targeted references including CSD-VAR, FLUX, multimodal diffusion editing, CSGO, StyleAR, and AlignedGen, and connects the revised mechanism to prior feature decomposition and attention editing. Most of the three-part related-work discussion remains. Publication updates and duplicate entries for existing works do not constitute additional research coverage.
descriptions.P1: The title, abstract, introduction passages, mechanism analysis, method description, ablation discussion, and conclusion are rewritten around the SVD formulation. The appendix is reorganized into analysis, algorithm, implementation, backbone experiments, limitations, and qualitative-results sections. This changes the narrative beyond adding scientific content.
descriptions.P2: v2 redraws the pipeline schematic and replaces the attention-feature illustration with a spectral-analysis display. It expands the comparison table, changes the ablation-table structure and placement, adds sensitivity plots and a user-preference table, and revises qualitative grids. Typography, author presentation, references, and overall page layout also change substantially.

P-1425C016CE.title: CoMeT: Collaborative Memory Transformer for Efficient Long Context Modeling

descriptions.M1: The chunk-processing procedure, residual low-rank adapters, gated global memory, FIFO temporary memory, and layer-level pipeline parallelism remain unchanged. The added scheduling illustration and hyperparameter experiments document and evaluate the existing method.
descriptions.E1: v2 extends length-extrapolation evaluation from synthetic passkey retrieval to realistic GovReport and NarrativeQA inputs exceeding the 32k training length, reaching 484k tokens (Appendix D). Table 9 also adds NQ and NarrativeQA evaluations explicitly distinguished from SCROLLS. Original task coverage is retained.
descriptions.E2: Appendix G adds RWKV-7-Goose-World-2.9B-HF as an efficiency comparator; v1's efficiency comparisons used Full Attention. Comparator membership in the original Tables 2–4 is unchanged.
descriptions.E3: New evaluation configurations include Qwen3-14B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, a 4,854-example SCROLLS subset above 32k tokens, and sweeps over adapter rank, chunk size, compression interval, and temporary-memory budget. The existing training settings remain unchanged; the agent experiment already used Qwen3-8B in v1.
descriptions.E4: v2 adds analyses of backbone generalization, realistic length extrapolation, adapter-rank sensitivity, and chunk/compression/memory choices (Tables 5–7 and 9). Appendix J adds four Qasper failure cases examining detail loss, causal reasoning, and information aggregation. Existing memory ablations and gating analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The added tables continue reporting point estimates.
descriptions.E6: Original Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results. Additional new results include CoMeT SCROLLS averages of 43.14 on Qwen3-14B and 40.55 on Llama-3.1-8B, and long-subset NarrativeQA F1 of 13.2 versus SWA's 5.8. Tables 6 and 8–10 add sensitivity scores, runtime measurements, and qualitative failure outcomes under additional settings.
descriptions.T1: The mathematical definitions, RLA and gated-update equations, and complexity reasoning remain unchanged. The new pipeline diagram and empirical analyses introduce no new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The introduction narrows the claim that overall performance surpasses existing efficient methods to achieving the highest average score among the methods evaluated. The abstract and conclusion retain the same principal architecture, complexity, extrapolation, and application claims.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds substantive interpretations of model-dependent performance, the remaining Full Attention advantage on long documents, and RWKV7's prefill/memory tradeoff. Appendix J offers compression-related explanations for Qasper failures and qualifies their uniqueness. A new societal-impact section discusses privacy risks tied to processing user histories; the original limitations paragraph remains.
descriptions.D1: v2 changes the advertised code location from an anonymous host to a named GitHub repository. It additionally documents the 3.95M-parameter overhead, xRAG's vector encoding, 5–7-digit passkeys, and RWKV implementation details and kernel limitations. These disclosures do not establish changes to the retained experiments.
descriptions.R1: The bibliography and Related Work section are unchanged. The introduction qualifies its previously categorical criticism of context compression to typical settings, while Appendix G adds direct positioning against RWKV7's efficiency tradeoffs.
descriptions.P1: Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained. Changes include localized wording clarifications, expanded abbreviations and affiliation information, additional analysis subsections, ethics and acknowledgments sections, and reorganized appendix labels.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds six tables covering generalization, extrapolation, sensitivity, efficiency, and failure cases, plus a pipeline execution diagram. Existing illustrations and tables are repositioned, and captions gain clarification. The original graphics are retained, including the all-layer gating visualization renumbered from Figure 11 to Figure 12.

P-1F1438CC01.title: OmniFall: From Staged Through Synthetic to Wild, A Unified Multi-Domain Dataset for Robust Fall Detection

descriptions.M1: v2 introduces controlled Wan 2.2 synthetic-video generation and reports end-to-end VideoMAE-K400 classification, replacing v1's frozen-backbone approach. Supervised segmentation changes from MS-TCN++ to ASQuery. However, v2's end-to-end description is not clearly reconciled with Appendix A.5's classifier operating on extracted features.
descriptions.E1: The eight staged datasets and OOPS-derived wild corpus are retained under revised names. v2 adds 12,000 synthetic videos with demographic and environmental variation, expands the taxonomy from 10 to 16 classes, reports full-taxonomy wild evaluation beyond v1's binary wild labels, and evaluates cross-age and cross-BMI scenarios.
descriptions.E2: v1's classification comparison among I3D, VideoMAE-Pre and VideoMAE-K400 is replaced by VideoMAE-K400 training-source comparisons. SigLIP2 enters the feature comparisons, ASQuery replaces MS-TCN++ for supervised segmentation, and Appendix Table 8 adds evaluated TW-FINCH and KMeans baselines.
descriptions.E3: The staged CS/CV partitions are retained in Appendix A.2. Reported classification settings change from 150 epochs, batch size 256 and learning rate 5e-4 to 50 epochs, batch size 32 and 1e-5. v2 adds single-source, synthetic and combined-source controls and demographic protocols; embedding smoothing changes from 18-feature averages to five-frame means.
descriptions.E4: v2 adds training-source ablations, cross-age/BMI robustness tests in Figure 7, and temporal trajectory and recovery-completeness analyses in Appendix A.5.1 and Figure 8. Existing domain-shift analyses incorporate synthetic data and SigLIP2. Conversely, v1's qualitative segmentation prediction example becomes an annotation-only illustration in v2 Figure 3.
descriptions.E5: Appendix A.3.5 newly documents deterministic, hash-based seeding for synthetic attribute selection. This is limited seed information, not evidence of repeated experimental runs. Neither supplied PDF reports confidence intervals, significance tests or run-to-run variability for the benchmark scores.
descriptions.E6: v1 reports wild Fall F1 of 0.76/0.82 for I3D and 0.34/0.26 for VideoMAE-K400 under CS/CV training. v2 replaces these comparisons with scores of 52.3% for CMDFall training, 61.2%/60.5% for OF-Staged, 64.2% for synthetic and 65.6% for combined training. These are different experimental conditions, not same-setting improvements. New segmentation, demographic and temporal-analysis results further expand the evidence.
descriptions.T1: v1 Section 4.2 explicitly defines capped dataset weights as w_i = min(max_j |D_j| / |D_i|, 20); v2 omits this mathematical specification. Neither version develops theorems or proofs, so the change is limited to removal of a formal training rule.
descriptions.C1: v1 principally claims a unified staged-to-wild benchmark and identifies differences between frozen representations. v2 makes controlled synthetic data a central contribution and claims synthetic training can match or surpass staged training on wild transfer. The abstract and conclusion also expand the benchmark claim to three domains, 16 classes and privacy-amenable data generation.
descriptions.C2: v1 explains transfer through I3D's simpler motion representations and transformer overfitting. v2 emphasizes demographic/environmental diversity, synthetic appearance versus staged motion, and differences in recovery coverage. Its limitations newly discuss generator-induced biases and incomplete synthetic realism, extending the retained concerns about wild coverage and deployment privacy.
descriptions.D1: v2 documents generation prompts and attributes, annotation tooling and review, source permissions, feature extraction, four H100 GPUs and extraction time. Some precise v1 classifier and loss details disappear. Access wording changes from direct dataset/code links to a project page and an Appendix A.5 release-on-acceptance statement; actual availability cannot be established from the PDFs.
descriptions.R1: The review of existing fall datasets remains largely intact. v2 adds references supporting Wan, SigLIP2, ASQuery, VIA and demographic attribute design, while removing the class-balanced-loss and MS-TCN references. These are targeted additions supporting the expanded benchmark rather than a comprehensive restructuring of the prior-work landscape.
descriptions.P1: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around three domains. Experiments are reorganized around training sources, and dataset splits, search details and limitations move into a appendix. This changes the narrative and document organization beyond simply inserting new results.
descriptions.P2: v2 changes the single-column layout to two columns, introduces a three-domain overview, redraws distribution and embedding plots, and reorganizes result tables with colored rankings. It adds demographic and trajectory figures and appendix tables. Figures 9–20 enlarge the existing embedding analysis rather than constituting separate experiments.

P-2B8BB4A4AF.title: iLRM: An Iterative Large 3D Reconstruction Model

descriptions.M1: The viewpoint tokenization, per-view cross-attention, global self-attention, token uplifting, mini-batch attention, Gaussian decoder, and training loss remain unchanged. The added optimization interpretation and implementation disclosures do not establish a revised algorithm.
descriptions.E1: v3 adds Tanks&Temples and Mip-NeRF360 evaluations for novel-view synthesis and depth, plus NRGBD and ETH3D pointmap evaluations. It also introduces corrupted-camera-input scenarios. This extends the original RE10K, ACID, and DL3DV coverage beyond image synthesis into geometric accuracy and imperfect inputs.
descriptions.E2: Mip-Splatting is removed from the 16-view and 32-view wide-coverage comparisons in Table 5. The other principal reconstruction comparators remain. MoGe-2 supplies pseudo-depth reference targets rather than serving as a newly evaluated reconstruction baseline.
descriptions.E3: v3 introduces a 51-scene DL3DV evaluation split, tests 32-view-trained models with unseen view counts, and adds depth, pointmap, and translation-noise protocols. Geometry evaluation specifies an F1 threshold of 0.1 and downsampling ground-truth pointmaps for iLRM. Long-LRM is explicitly re-evaluated using released checkpoints except for 16-view metrics. Reported AdamW beta2 changes from 0.095 to 0.95, without establishing that training was rerun.
descriptions.E4: v3 adds layerwise attention-correspondence analysis, camera-translation perturbation tests, generalization beyond the training view count, and latency scaling through 256 views. It extends post-prediction optimization analysis to additional datasets. These investigate mechanisms and robustness beyond the retained architectural, overlap, and representation-density ablations.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new Gaussian-noise standard deviations specify input perturbations, not uncertainty in estimated results.
descriptions.E6: Numerous new results accompany the added evaluations. Retained eight-view MC results also change: Table 1 RE10K PSNR increases numerically from 30.96 to 31.24, and Table 2 ACID/DL3DV PSNR changes from 30.47/29.03 to 30.72/29.33. Table 5 revises baseline results: 32-view 3D-GS PSNR changes from 23.60 to 24.43, while iLRM remains 24.30. Its timings and Long-LRM results are revised, and the 50-epoch iLRM row is removed; these should not be interpreted as demonstrated same-setting performance gains.
descriptions.T1: The model equations, training objective, and FLOPs calculation are retained. v3's added approximate-gradient expressions illustrate the existing optimization analogy; they introduce no defined energy function, formal guarantee, proof, or substantive derivation.
descriptions.C1: The three central architectural contributions remain unchanged. The introduction narrows the wide-coverage claim from outperforming optimization-based 3D-GS in reconstruction quality to achieving comparable performance in approximately 0.5 seconds versus approximately eight minutes.
descriptions.C2: v3 clarifies refinement under fixed image evidence and interprets attention visualizations as progressive correspondence formation. It adds static-scene and geometry-supervision limitations, explicitly qualifies pseudo-depth agreement as indirect evidence, and attributes faster post-prediction optimization partly to geometric quality. The original scalability and camera-pose limitations remain.
descriptions.D1: v3 newly specifies 50,000 high-resolution fine-tuning iterations, post-prediction optimization learning rates, and Long-LRM checkpoint provenance, while correcting the reported AdamW beta2. It removes v2's explicit training disclosure of FlashAttention-2, BFloat16, and gradient-checkpointing use. The project-page destination is unchanged.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds references including Perceiver, sparse transformers, state-space alternatives, MoGe-2, DUSt3R, Rayzer, FLARE, and newly evaluated benchmarks. Mip-Splatting and several implementation references disappear. The principal related-work discussion is substantially retained from v2 Appendix A, now in main Section 2.
descriptions.P1: Related work moves into the main text, experimental-setup subsections become condensed run-in paragraphs, and several method explanations are shortened. Affiliation and acknowledgement text also changes. The existing introduction, method narrative, ablation explanations, and conclusion largely retain their structure and wording.
descriptions.P2: v3 replaces the single-column presentation with a two-column layout and reorganizes tables and illustrations. It adds attention, depth, geometry, and optimization visualizations plus new evaluation tables. Existing displays are also resized, reordered, or relocated; for example, v2 Figure 7's high-resolution comparison becomes v3 Figure 15.

P-B0E1B7929A.title: Deterministic Bounds and Random Estimates of Metric Tensors on Neuromanifolds

descriptions.M1: Equation (8) changes the rank-k estimator from a shared probe ξx to independent probes ξxi for each input and eigendirection. This corrects the procedure as written for k greater than one and reconciles it with v2's existing statement that k|Dx| probes are needed. An implementation change or experimental rerun is not established; the other estimator constructions are retained.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate SST-2, DBpedia, MNLI, CIFAR-100, and SpeechCommands using the same six model-task combinations. Appendix C's reference to AG News concerns an earlier draft in both PDFs, not a coverage change between these versions.
descriptions.E2: Table 2 retains the same comparison among empirical Fisher, unbiased Hutchinson, diagonal-core, rank-one, and rank-two estimators. Monte Carlo remains excluded from the empirical comparison. No new comparator or reevaluation of a revised comparator is reported.
descriptions.E3: Section 4.5 retains the model initialization and fine-tuning states, 128 batches of 64 samples, exact diagonal-FIM reference, single-backward-pass comparison, and RelMAE with epsilon 10^-12. Section 4.4 makes T=30 illustrative rather than definite, but does not report a different tested budget; this weakens disclosure rather than establishing a changed experiment.
descriptions.E4: The component-level FIM distribution analyses in Figures 1 and 2 and Appendix B's qualitative comparison with the square-root estimator are retained. No ablation, robustness test, sensitivity study, or case study is added or removed.
descriptions.E5: Both versions report point estimates in Table 2 without repeated-run counts, numerical seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The analytical variance and coefficient-of-variation guarantees remain; reorganizing their proofs does not introduce empirical uncertainty reporting.
descriptions.E6: All Table 2 error values and speed ratios, and the histogram results in Figures 1 and 2, are unchanged. For example, unbiased Hutchinson retains RelMAE 0.18 on SST-2 and 0.16 on MNLI. No result entries or substantive empirical findings are added or removed.
descriptions.T1: The existing bounds and variance results are retained, including Proposition 11 renamed Theorem 11. Limited mathematical corrections include Equation (8)'s probe indexing and replacing an erroneous pjpj term with pipj in Lemma 12's proof. Conversely, Section 1 drops the Monte Carlo estimator's 'up to scaling' qualification: under its stated uniform sampling, the displayed average estimates F(theta)/|Dx|, whereas Equation (1) defines F(theta) as a sum.
descriptions.C1: The introduction describes the empirical contribution as covering modern classifiers rather than just DistilBERT, matching experiments already present in v2. The conclusion narrows evaluating the Hessian to approximating it. Section 5 also strengthens novelty by asserting that no previous method simultaneously offers unbiasedness, explicit variance bounds, and scalability.
descriptions.C2: The conclusion explicitly limits the demonstrated work to static FIM computation at fixed parameters, refining v2's broader lack-of-downstream-application caveat. Section 4.5 qualifies the recommendation for low-rank estimators as offering potentially improved accuracy. The existing explanations of histogram patterns and low-rank performance remain.
descriptions.D1: A new footnote in Section 4.5 provides a code-access reference described as a PyTorch library for Hutchinson FIM estimation. Section 4.4 states total power-iteration cost explicitly, but changes the definite T=30 implementation budget to an example, reducing hyperparameter specificity. The hardware disclosure remains NVIDIA H100 SXM5.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds Kupeli's Singular Semi-Riemannian Geometry to clarify the metric terminology and revises the Hutchinson-related positioning into an explicit three-property exclusivity claim. The surrounding literature coverage is largely retained; removed reference URLs do not represent removed cited works.
descriptions.P1: v3 revises the abstract and selected discussion passages, copyedits terminology, and renames Proposition 11 as Theorem 11. Lemma 12's proof moves beside its statement in Appendix A, while Propositions 13 and 14 are consolidated with their proofs in Appendix O. The six main sections and overall narrative remain.
descriptions.P2: The same figures and tables are retained with limited caption edits and relocation. Figure 1 and Table 2 move into the experimental discussion on pages 10 and 11, respectively; Figure 2 moves from page 18 to page 19. Plot designs, axes, and table structures remain unchanged.

descriptions.M1: v3 adds text/CLAP conditioning, latent classifier-free guidance, and backbone latent distillation (Sections 4.6–4.7), and adopts Lagrangian Self-Distillation for TTS sampling. Pocket TTS distills a 24-layer teacher backbone into six layers while retaining its sampling head. These extend the procedure. The original continuation architecture remains; explicitly adding WavLM distillation to Equation 2 documents a component already described in v1.
descriptions.E1: v1 evaluates speech and music continuation. v3 additionally evaluates text-to-speech on LibriSpeech test-clean and conditioned music generation using CLAP, including text-to-music evaluation on MusicCaps. These introduce different conditioning requirements and benchmark coverage. The original French/English speech continuation and LAION-Disco music coverage are retained.
descriptions.E2: New TTS comparisons include F5-TTS, DSM, DiTAR, and SALAD; Pocket TTS additionally includes Chatterbox Turbo and Kokoro. MusicCaps comparisons add MusicLM, AudioLDM2, Noise2Music, Jen-1, MusicFlow, and the original text-conditioned MusicGen. DiTAR/SALAD and several MusicCaps baseline scores are explicitly borrowed from publications. Comparator membership in the original continuation experiments remains unchanged.
descriptions.E3: v3 introduces TTS training/evaluation settings, WER/CER and speaker-similarity measurements, MUSHRA evaluations, and PANN-based KLD/CLAP music metrics. Speech compression gains PESQ, STOI, and human evaluation. Pocket TTS uses enhanced 24 kHz inputs for all its baselines, separating that comparison from Table 3. The runtime table also reverses the RTF convention while retaining the measured generation times.
descriptions.E4: Appendix E.5 adds substantive TTS ablations comparing LSD with consistency and varying absent, text-only, and text-plus-audio guidance. Table 3 adds a reference-through-VAE diagnostic investigating low speaker-similarity scores. The original component, context-window, scaling, sampling-step, temperature, and head-batch analyses are retained; their relocation does not constitute new evidence.
descriptions.E5: v3 removes the PPX and VERT confidence intervals from Table 2 while retaining their point estimates. It also removes v1's general statement that all reported intervals use 95% confidence. The Bayesian Elo estimation procedure and its 95% posterior intervals remain unchanged. Neither version establishes additional repeated runs or seeds.
descriptions.E6: v3 adds results for compression, conditioned generation, TTS ablations, and Pocket TTS: examples include CALM's 1.81 WER in Table 3, 2.14 MusicCaps FAD in Table 11, and Pocket TTS's 1.84 WER, tied with DSM, in Table 12. These are newly reported experiments, not gains over v1 under identical settings. Original continuation point estimates and plots remain; changed RTF values reflect the inverted convention.
descriptions.T1: Appendix A adds the two-time LSD flow-map definition and combined flow-matching/self-distillation objectives. Section 4.6 formalizes latent guidance. Section 4.5 replaces v1's Jacobian-based temperature argument and stated variance 1/sqrt(tau) with standard-deviation scaling by sqrt(tau), correcting the mathematical description without establishing that experiments were rerun. Existing consistency and Bayesian Elo formulations are retained.
descriptions.C1: The introduction expands the contribution list to include latent guidance and distillation and explicitly claims application to four tasks. The abstract and introduction add the open-source, approximately 100M-parameter Pocket TTS contribution and faster-than-real-time laptop CPU operation. The earlier claim of being the first application across both speech and music is removed; the general efficiency/fidelity thesis remains.
descriptions.C2: v3 adds a localized explanation attributing poor automatic TTS speaker similarity partly to the VAE and uses human evaluation to qualify that metric. It also discusses guidance-related quality/similarity tradeoffs and LSD's suitability at the tested smaller scale. The original explanations concerning error accumulation, noisy long-term context, clean local detail, and incomplete scaling evaluation remain substantially intact.
descriptions.D1: v3 documents the 88k-hour TTS dataset mixture, SentencePiece vocabulary, LSD loss-batch allocation, guidance settings, and TTS architecture/training hyperparameters in Table 14. It provides Pocket TTS distillation details and tested CPU models, reports a model release with repository and enhanced evaluation-data links, and promises CALM training code. Existing continuation and VAE hyperparameters are largely unchanged.
descriptions.R1: v3 broadens positioning through continuous word-sized and spectral speech representations, IMPACT, MingUni-Audio, and other newer work. It connects temperature sampling to GAN truncation, credits latent guidance to SoundReactor, and incorporates Boffi et al.'s LSD framework. It also drops v1's first-across-both-domains assertion and its near-exclusivity statement about accelerating continuous autoregressive sampling.
descriptions.P1: The narrative is reorganized around four task evaluations. Music VAE details, the temperature study, and several efficiency analyses move from the main text into dedicated appendices. Noise-injection exposition moves within the method section, temperature sampling is rewritten, and the appendix structure is expanded and reorganized. Much original prose and the conclusion remain unchanged.
descriptions.P2: v3 adds TTS, conditioned-music, MusicCaps, Pocket TTS, and TTS-ablation tables, expands speech-compression metric columns, and adds a TTS hyperparameter column. Several existing tables are relocated or reformatted. All three original figures are retained; the two analysis plots move to the appendix and exchange numbering. Title, headings, running headers, and page layout also change.

P-BDDF8741C4.title: SCORE: A Unified Framework for Overshoot Refund in Online FDR Control

descriptions.M1: The SCORE and SCORE+ procedures in Sections 3–5 retain their update rules. V2 Appendix C adds discounted-memory versions of their FDP accounting, introducing decayed discovery totals and modified denominators. This is a limited methodological extension, presented as an outline rather than an implemented, evaluated procedure.
descriptions.E1: The Gaussian, exponential, AR(1), yeast, and clinical settings are retained. Appendix B.2 adds a distinct adversarial stream in which a null rejection suppresses subsequent alternative signals, deliberately violating CPQD. The target-level sweep reuses existing data-generating settings.
descriptions.E2: Comparator membership is unchanged in matched experiments. This includes the e-value families and the six classical p-value comparators: LOND, LORD, SAFFRON, ADDIS, Alpha-investing, and SupLORD. The new checks use existing SCORE/SCORE+ procedures.
descriptions.E3: V2 adds pointwise power ratios relative to each family's baseline and a sensitivity sweep over alpha = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20. The new stress-test protocol specifies alternating null/non-null hypotheses and a rejection-triggered signal trap. Previously reported main-experiment settings are retained.
descriptions.E4: Appendix B adds two substantive investigations absent from v1: a CPQD-violation stress test examining SCORE+ failure versus basic SCORE control, and target-FDR sensitivity analyses across both main simulation settings.
