descriptions.E1: V2 adds a ground-truth outdoor benchmark using Laval Outdoor HDR crops (Section 4.2, Table 2, Figure 11), extending quantitative single-image coverage beyond v1's indoor benchmarks. Outdoor training and qualitative outdoor examples already existed; the other datasets remain.
descriptions.E2: DiffusionLight and 4D Lighting remain the single-image comparators, and 4D Lighting remains the dynamic-scene comparator. The outdoor benchmark uses the same comparator set. V2's new capability matrix is research positioning, not additional empirical baseline evaluation.
descriptions.E3: Added protocols include 26 randomly rotated outdoor crop sequences with three frames selected for metrics, and controlled FOV offsets from -50% to +50% on Infinigen. Existing training budgets, metrics, and original benchmark settings remain unchanged as reported.
descriptions.E4: V2 adds FOV-error sensitivity testing (Section 8, Figure 8) and extends component ablations to Laval Indoor SV (Section 9, Table 6). These broaden analysis of geometric-input robustness and real-data component behavior, including an intensity/color tradeoff absent from v1's synthetic ablations.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's sensitivity curves contain point estimates without uncertainty reporting.
descriptions.E6: V2 adds outdoor scores, FOV-sensitivity results, and real-data ablation outcomes. For example, outdoor diffuse RMSE is 0.12 for LIMO(image), versus 0.23 for DiffusionLight and 0.25 for 4D Lighting. Retained Laval Indoor SV printed values also change: LIMO(image) glossy RMSE 0.22 to 0.21, and diffuse/glossy angular errors 2.7 to 2.6. Original video and Infinigen ablation scores remain identical.
descriptions.T1: Equations 1–15, including geometric-map definitions, depth sampling, reconstruction losses, and rendering expressions, are retained. Calling the HDRI sequence a spatiotemporal volume clarifies existing mathematics; no new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs are introduced.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and central contributions retain the same claims about spatiotemporal HDR estimation, geometric grounding, and combined mirror/diffuse predictions. The introduction's five capabilities and conclusion's state-of-the-art claim retain their scope; new evidence supports existing claims.
descriptions.C2: V2 interprets the FOV experiment as evidence of robustness. Its real-data ablation discussion qualifies diffuse-sphere benefits: color improves while intensity accuracy worsens for some materials, hypothesized to reflect bias from predicting spheres larger than ground truth. The earlier finite-sphere and facial-cue limitations are largely retained.
descriptions.D1: Section 9 newly discloses that Laval Indoor SV predictions use spheres larger than the ground-truth probes to increase prediction resolution. This documents an implementation choice without establishing that it changed between versions. Existing hardware, training-time, data-generation, and HDRI-optimization details remain.
descriptions.R1: V2's Table 1 explicitly categorizes six prior methods against five capabilities, refining the existing positioning narrative. The additional bibliography entry duplicates the already cited Deep Sky Modeling paper rather than introducing a distinct work.
descriptions.P1: V2 tightens wording in the introduction, related work, method, and conclusion, adds acknowledgements, and inserts two supplementary analysis sections. The main section order and narrative remain substantially intact; the changes are localized editing and expansion.
descriptions.P2: V2 adds a capability matrix, Light Stage demonstration, FOV plot, real-data ablation table, and outdoor qualitative figure, and expands the image-results table. It also moves v1's training-example Figure 3 to supplementary Figure 7. This expands and redistributes the visual material; other matched displays are largely retained.

P-C94596D537.title: PETAR: Localized Findings Generation with Mask-Aware Vision-Language Modeling for PET Automated Reporting

descriptions.M1: The core encoding, focal cropping, feature fusion and autoregressive objective remain unchanged. Section 4.4 changes the stated alignment order from mask-then-projector to projector-then-mask and describes repeating the three-stage sequence on both training datasets. However, v2's stage headings contradict their descriptions, leaving the implemented order uncertain.
descriptions.E1: V2 adds evaluation on 32 external autoPET instances, extending coverage beyond the internal PET/CT dataset. The supplement identifies an additional imaging difference: primarily contrast-enhanced CT externally versus primarily non-contrast CT internally. Renaming PETAR-11K to PETARSeg-11K does not itself change coverage.
descriptions.E2: Compared with v1 Table 3, v2 Table 2 adds QoQ-Med and fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B and MedGemma-4B comparisons. Expanded names for retained baselines are not counted as new methods.
descriptions.E3: The reported internal test size changes from 1,170 to 1,175, and the stated anatomical pretraining size changes from approximately 5,000 to 100,000 segmentations. V2 reports ten epochs for all stages instead of five for initial pretraining, although supplementary Table 9 still lists five. It also specifies three-view inputs for the new fine-tuned 2D comparisons and changes retained ablation rows' TS flags from enabled to disabled. These are reported setting revisions, not evidence that all experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: V2 adds an explicit full-model comparison with and without TotalSegmentator pretraining, which v1's populated ablation rows did not isolate. It also adds external distribution-shift evaluation, replaces the original qualitative cases with broader baseline error comparisons in Figure 4, and supplies autoPET examples in supplementary Figure 5.
descriptions.E5: V1 reports point estimates, whereas v2 Table 5 adds plus/minus quantities to physician ratings. Their statistical meaning is not specified. Neither version reports training-run uncertainty, seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.
descriptions.E6: PETAR's reported BLEU, CIDEr and GREEN change from 0.531, 0.415 and 0.246 to 0.535, 0.457 and 0.257; changed settings prevent interpreting these as controlled performance gains. GREEN's human correlation changes from 0.608 to 0.592, and other metric correlations and rankings change. V2 additionally reports new comparator results, internal physician scores and preference counts (15 preferred, 54 tied, 47 not preferred), external ratings and cohort statistics.
descriptions.T1: The cropping, encoding, fusion and likelihood equations retain their mathematical substance. V2 makes mask embeddings and notation more explicit and numbers more equations, but introduces no substantive theoretical result, proof or changed formal assumption.
descriptions.C1: The central dataset, mask-aware model and improved findings-generation claims remain. V2 adds an explicit novelty claim in the abstract that its five-physician evaluation is the first human study of automated PET reporting.
descriptions.C2: V2 explicitly acknowledges hallucinated numerical measurements and qualifies the reader evaluation by explaining their exclusion. It also discusses PET domain shift, possible overrating by automated metrics and external generalization. Dependence on supplied masks and a future fully automated reporting pipeline were already discussed in v1.
descriptions.D1: V2's supplement supplies acquisition and deidentification details, the formatting prompt, software libraries, LoRA placement, precision, batch size, learning rate and other hyperparameters. It also documents reader blinding, numerical masking, viewing software and scoring rubrics. These are new disclosures, although conflicting epoch counts and training descriptions limit reproducibility.
descriptions.R1: V2 expands citations supporting baseline models, PET datasets, evaluation metrics, implementation tools and segmentation workflows. It sharpens the distinction from Reg2RG's organ-level, single-modality setting and develops the relationship to Describe Anything's focal prompting; Describe Anything was already cited in v1.
descriptions.P1: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, results and explanatory passages. It reorganizes experimental setup and human evaluation, replaces the standalone PETAR-Bench and Discussion sections with revised setup and limitations sections, renames the dataset, and adds a structured supplement.
descriptions.P2: Figures 1–3 are redrawn, and Figure 4 becomes a larger comparison matrix with anatomical error annotations. V2 removes the model-capability table, redesigns the dataset comparison table, reorganizes experimental tables and adds physician-results and supplementary displays. These changes extend well beyond numerical updates and renumbering.

P-F114353673.title: Omni-View: Unlocking How Generation Facilitates Understanding in Unified 3D Model based on Multiview images

descriptions.M1: Appendix A.5 introduces a generation variant that packs four consecutive views into one grid and generates grids autoregressively; B.4 identifies its use in stage 2. This locally modifies generation while retaining the three-module architecture, losses, and principal training recipe.
descriptions.E1: V2 adds targeted cross-scale, reference-conditioned depth-prediction examples from SPAR-7M, illustrated using Structured3D and ScanNet++ scenes (A.3), and explicit outdoor generation and depth-estimation scenarios (A.4). The training mixture and main benchmark coverage remain unchanged.
descriptions.E2: The comparator sets in Tables 1–3 remain identical. Figure 3 adds a direct comparison of grid generation against the original frame-by-frame procedure, whose corresponding output was only a standalone failure example in v1. The activation comparison reuses BAGEL-FT.
descriptions.E3: New qualitative generation demonstrations extend through View-48, beyond v1's displayed View-24 examples, and Figure 3 compares grid and framewise configurations. Main quantitative evaluation settings remain unchanged. Appendix B's filtering rules and training budgets are newly disclosed details, not evidence that existing experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: Beyond retaining all original ablations, v2 adds analyses of scale consistency, grid generation versus framewise generation, indoor/outdoor depth quality and failures, training convergence, and BAGEL-FT versus Omni-View activations (A.3–A.5, B.4–B.5). These broaden the diagnostic evidence.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added raw and exponentially smoothed training-loss curves do not provide uncertainty estimates across runs.
descriptions.E6: All numerical entries in Tables 1–7 remain unchanged, including the 55.4 VSI-Bench average. V2 adds supplementary outcomes: depth predictions such as 2.0 meters against 2.2 meters ground truth, grid-consistency examples, outdoor failures, loss and activation patterns, and inference timings. These extend the results without changing benchmark rankings.
descriptions.T1: Equations 1–6 retain the same mathematical content; changes to module-name typography are cosmetic. Neither version presents theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new appendices add no substantive theoretical derivation.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims that generation facilitates 3D understanding, that the texture/geometry decomposition enables a unified model, and that Omni-View achieves 55.4 on VSI-Bench. The added appendix evidence does not redefine these central claims.
descriptions.C2: V2 adds specific qualifications about outdoor scenes with substantial camera movement, hypotheses connecting camera-loss spikes to learnable-query optimization, and broader attention as a possible explanation for improved understanding. It also suggests reducing the geometry-loss weight for stability. The original limitations paragraph remains unchanged.
descriptions.D1: New Appendix B documents filtering rules, tokenizer and backbone details, parameter sizes, packed sequence lengths, 10,000/20,000 training iterations, and 32-H100 training costs. It also reports inference timings. The abstract now provides a repository and states that code and models are released, although the reproducibility statement still promises future release.
descriptions.R1: Section 2 adds three Hu et al. image-restoration references alongside a short extension from inpainting to restoration. The broader positioning relative to unified models and 3D understanding/generation work is retained; MV-AR's changed citation suffix identifies the same work.
descriptions.P1: The main narrative and section order remain largely verbatim, with limited wording, affiliation, header, and cross-reference edits. The appendix is expanded and organized into additional qualitative and technical subsections, and the existing LLM-use disclosure becomes Appendix C.
descriptions.P2: V2 expands visual presentation with Figures 2–6, additional qualitative panels, architecture diagrams, and seven training-loss plots. The original NVS failure sequence is reused within Figure 3, while the original successful example is replaced. Tables are repositioned, and Table 3 gains explicit best/second-best highlighting.

P-7A1215A9A8.title: Chorus: Multi-Teacher Pretraining for Holistic 3D Gaussian Scene Encoding

descriptions.M1: The core encoder, teachers, losses, augmentations, and rendering-based adaptation remain unchanged. However, v3 Appendix C.2 describes reducing the VLM task-guided sparsifier to one attention block, whereas both versions' Section 4.1 says components other than the backbone remain unchanged. This inconsistency prevents distinguishing an architectural revision from a newly disclosed implementation detail.
descriptions.E1: The datasets and principal tasks are retained. v3 extends evaluation to ScanNet++ iPhone RGB-D captures rather than only laser-derived point clouds, and adds tests on differently optimized Gaussian representations. These broaden input conditions within the existing indoor-scene coverage.
descriptions.E2: The comparator membership in corresponding main experiments is unchanged. SceneSplat's retraining changes its settings and scores, not its method identity. The added analyses use existing comparators such as Sonata and SceneSplat; teacher combinations are method ablations.
descriptions.E3: v3 reports retraining the joint-data SceneSplat baseline using updated Matterport3D reconstructions, revising a comparison control. Added tests vary Gaussian optimization, density, and capture source, while Appendix D introduces DINO-first probing and a specified UMAP sampling protocol. The main benchmark metrics remain unchanged. Most appendix training budgets, splits, and processing settings are newly disclosed rather than established changes to existing experiments.
descriptions.E4: Beyond the retained ablations, v3 adds optimization/density and iPhone robustness tests in Tables 10–11. The supplement adds DINO-first teacher ablations, visibility-crop analysis, UMAP comparisons, additional scene-feature examples, and before/after adaptation diagnostics. These expand evidence about teacher contributions, input robustness, feature organization, and adaptation failures.
descriptions.E5: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or experimental error bars. The added pose-sampling averages describe data characteristics, not uncertainty in performance estimates.
descriptions.E6: Table 1 replaces SceneSplat's joint-training scores: ScanNet200 f-mIoU/f-mAcc changes from 21.4/38.7 to 22.5/41.7, while Chorus remains 24.6/47.7. These accompany revised baseline training, not a same-setting Chorus improvement. v3 also adds results in Tables 10–11 and C, including iPhone scores of 45.7/57.6 for Chorus versus 39.5/52.0 for Sonata, plus new qualitative findings. Most retained main results are unchanged.
descriptions.T1: v1 motivates the augmentations qualitatively and refers to unavailable supplementary equations. v3 Appendix A.3 supplies a Taylor-expansion and covariance argument for rendering-equivalent perturbations, and a projection/Fourier derivation relating scale inflation to Gaussian blur. These add substantive mathematical justification beyond notation changes or standard metric formulas.
descriptions.C1: The central contributions remain multi-teacher 3DGS pretraining, transferable and data-efficient scene embeddings, and rendering-based adaptation. Adding Q&A to the abstract restates a capability already claimed and evaluated in v1. The introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain their scientific scope.
descriptions.C2: v3 adds a localized explanation of teacher compatibility through shared representations, separate projectors, and PHI-S balancing. It interprets the new robustness tests and explicitly discusses lamp/ceiling confusion and blurred boundaries after low-resolution adaptation in Appendix D.4. The existing point-cloud transfer hypotheses and offline pseudo-label-cost limitation remain.
descriptions.D1: The new supplement documents augmentation parameters, camera selection and cropping, teacher feature resolutions, Matterport3D reconstruction, InteriorGS label assignment and splits, prediction transfer, and downstream training settings. It specifies VLM optimization and two-H200 training hardware, among other details absent from v1. The abstract also replaces a future code/model-release promise with a linked code-release statement; repository availability is not independently established by the PDFs.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds citations including Occam's LGS, SAM 2, UMAP, OPT, evaluation metrics, Rosetta Neurons, and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. The latter two support a new discussion of shared representations across teachers. The principal positioning relative to SceneSplat, point-cloud pretraining, and multi-teacher distillation is retained.
descriptions.P1: v3 expands brief descriptions and references to supplementary material into organized, step-by-step explanations of adaptation, augmentation, dataset construction, and evaluation, with a contents list and Sections A–E. This changes the explanatory structure. The main narrative order remains stable, alongside grammar, terminology, notation, affiliation, and acknowledgement edits.
descriptions.P2: v3 adds robustness Tables 10–11, supplementary Tables A–C, Algorithm 1, and Figures A–I covering pipelines, data processing, and feature analyses. The expanded PCA gallery includes a reused main-paper example alongside additional scenes. Existing main figures are largely retained; Figure 6 moves, Table 4 gains an explanatory caption, and the runtime table becomes Table 12.

P-C0823925BC.title: Memory-R1: Enhancing Large Language Model Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via Reinforcement Learning

descriptions.M1: The two-agent architecture, operation set, memory distillation and PPO/GRPO objectives remain. The published construction pseudocode locally changes UPDATE/DELETE from editing an individual m_j in v1 Algorithm 1 to merging/removing the retrieved set M_ret in v4 Algorithm 3. Removing Appendix B's operation-label language clarifies the RL approach already described in v1; it does not establish a new training regime.
descriptions.E1: Evaluation expands from LoCoMo alone to modified MSC and the oracle version of LongMemEval. These add distinct conversational data and evaluation requirements involving preferences, knowledge updates and multi-session information integration. Training remains confined to LoCoMo.
descriptions.E2: Table 1 removes LangMem and adds Memory-SFT for both backbones. Memory-SFT uses the same architecture and training data with behavior cloning from GPT-5 trajectories, introducing an important supervised-versus-RL control. LoCoMo, Zep, A-Mem and Mem0 remain; renaming LoCoMo to LoCoMo (RAG) does not introduce another comparator.
descriptions.E3: v4 introduces transfer evaluation without additional training on modified MSC and LongMemEval-oracle, and adds Qwen 3B/14B configurations. The LoCoMo split, metrics and principal decoding settings remain. Appendix B changes the stated memory-history window from 50 to 24 turns, but v4 Algorithm 1 still specifies 50; this is a reported setting revision with unresolved implementation.
descriptions.E4: New analyses test cross-dataset transfer, model-size sensitivity and Judge-based versus exact-match rewards. Figure 5 also adds PPO without memory distillation, whereas v1 Table 4 reports that comparison only for GRPO. The original component ablations, stronger-manager comparison, training curves and Appendix A case studies are retained, often reformatted.
descriptions.E5: v1 Section 4.1 states that every configuration is evaluated three times and mean scores are reported. v4 omits this statement while retaining surrounding settings in Appendix D, and supplies no replacement repeat-count or uncertainty-reporting practice. This establishes reduced reporting, not that fewer evaluations were performed.
descriptions.E6: All shared Table 1 rows retain identical numbers; LangMem results are removed and Memory-SFT results added. v4 additionally reports model-scale, MSC, LongMemEval and reward-comparison outcomes. These include mixed findings: LongMemEval Qwen Judge scores are 53.2 for BASE, 47.4 for PPO and 57.8 for GRPO. Appendix Table 3 also gives Qwen-7B results differing from retained Table 1 without clearly distinguishing conditions, preventing a same-setting version-performance interpretation.
descriptions.T1: The policy, PPO/GRPO objective, group-relative advantage and exact-match reward definitions remain mathematically equivalent. Moving the advantage formula into prose and renumbering equations do not change theory. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and conclusion expand the generalization claim to three named benchmarks, 3B–14B model scales and transfer without retraining. The central contributions—two-agent RL memory management, data efficiency with 152 training examples and strong LoCoMo performance—remain.
descriptions.C2: v4 adds a substantive explanation that Judge-based rewards encourage verbose answers and conflict with string-overlap metrics. New limitations identify dialogue-focused evaluation, untested multimodal applicability and the complexity of separately training the agents. Existing interpretations of memory consolidation, filtering and stronger upstream memory are largely retained.
descriptions.D1: v4 newly names VERL, specifies eight H100 GPUs for the 14B model, adds training pseudocode and expands explanations of staged training and frozen components. It also documents dataset licensing and segmentation. Most existing hyperparameters and prompt contents are retained or relocated rather than newly introduced.
descriptions.R1: The introduction adds Tensor Brain and traces memory operations through database CRUD, MemLLM and AIOS, explicitly attributing the adopted operator set to Mem0. New benchmark and implementation references appear, while LangMem and several general agent references disappear. v1's characterization of A-Mem as RL-based is removed, but the main RL-memory novelty positioning remains.
descriptions.P1: Much of the main text is rewritten and condensed. The pipeline overview is integrated into Section 3, implementation details move into Appendix D, and dataset documentation is reorganized into testing and training subsections. The evaluation narrative gains a generalization section, with separate limitations and extended-results sections.
descriptions.P2: v1's three ablation tables are reorganized into v4's four-panel Figure 5. New scaling and transfer plots, a reward-comparison table and extended-results tables change the evidence presentation. Existing plots and algorithms are relocated, prompt displays gain shaded boxes, and the document is extensively reflowed.

P-240E4DEFBC.title: ChatHLS: Towards Systematic Design Automation and Optimization for High-Level Synthesis

descriptions.M1: v3 extends generation inputs from C algorithms to include natural-language descriptions and changes SFT from LoRA adaptation to full-parameter tuning. The VODA workflow, hierarchical diagnosis/fixing/judging, DPO and three-directive optimization loop remain. The expanded reasoning-to-instruction and QoR-aware reasoning descriptions largely elaborate existing mechanisms.
descriptions.E1: v3 adds 108 natural-language-to-HLS generation tasks, comprising 85 HLS-Eval designs and 23 custom designs. Optimization expands beyond v2's five linear-algebra kernels to broader kernel workloads and MobileNet and Transformer accelerators. Kernel/Vitis/Manual debugging coverage is retained; changed case counts alone do not establish new coverage.
descriptions.E2: Debugging comparators change from GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama3.1-8B and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B to Gemini-3-pro, Claude-opus-4.5, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and DeepSeek-V3.2. v3 also adds matched RAG variants and C2HLSC/HLSRewriter comparisons; Appendix D.3 identifies the latter baselines as published scores. RALAD and the DSL/learning-based optimization comparators remain.
descriptions.E3: Training changes from Llama3-8B with 11 SFT/3 DPO epochs to Qwen2.5-Coder-14B with 3/2 epochs; training sample counts and the debugging test size also change. v3 introduces staged pass@k evaluation, matched retrieval controls, an explicit 80% resource ceiling and post-route checks. Optimization is reported as 15 trials, although five-iteration descriptions remain, leaving the exact budget relationship unresolved.
descriptions.E4: Beyond the retained HLSFixer component ablation, v3 adds train–test similarity analysis, controlled retrieval studies, model-family/size sensitivity, token-cost analyses and optimization trajectories in Appendices D–G. Table 4 adds physical-feasibility validation after place-and-route. The per-error analysis expands from 24 displayed error types to 33.
descriptions.E5: v2 reports aggregate pass rates without repeated-sampling counts or uncertainty bars. v3 specifies five candidates per debugging case and 20 generation repetitions, uses sampled pass@k estimation, and adds error bars to Figure 6 and token-cost Figures 15 and 17. These are newly reported practices; seeds and the statistical meaning of the bars remain unspecified.
descriptions.E6: Reported debugging performance changes from 82.7% on 612 cases to 93.4% pass@1 on 591 cases. Figure 9's optimization headline changes from 5.4× over baseline on five kernels to 18.1× over broader workloads. These use changed models and evaluation conditions, so they are not same-setting gains. v3 adds generation, accelerator, retrieval and physical-implementation results and removes the energy-efficiency proxy results.
descriptions.T1: V2's bespoke nonlinear Energy Efficiency definition and its latency/resource penalty construction in Equation 2 are removed. V3 instead formalizes resource-constrained speedup in Appendix D.4. Neither version contains theorems or proofs; v3 also adds standard metric formulas.
descriptions.C1: The headline claims expand from debugging and constrained-kernel optimization to demonstrated natural-language generation gains and neural-accelerator optimization. v3 claims a 41.8% relative generation improvement over Gemini-3-pro and replaces v2's 82.7% repair and 3.6× DSL/learning comparison headlines with 32.6% relative debugging improvement and 3.3× over RALAD. The overall ChatHLS purpose remains.
descriptions.C2: v3 adds interpretations of retrieval's differing effects on generation and debugging, model-scaling behavior, optimization trajectories and physical feasibility. Appendix G acknowledges greater hardware costs and lower resource efficiency than methods such as Allo. New limitations explicitly identify unsupported DATAFLOW/AXI directives and validation on only one FPGA platform, qualifying v2's generalization discussion.
descriptions.D1: Appendices A–D newly disclose retrieval chunking, embedding/vector-store choices, top-k retrieval, log parsing, full prompts, teacher inputs, sampling temperatures, detailed SFT/DPO settings, software environment and training durations. These greatly extend v2's brief training description. Appendix H adds asset licensing and intended-use information without establishing a new public artifact release.
descriptions.R1: Section 2.2 expands positioning beyond retrieval-based assistance to recent LLM-based Bayesian directive optimization and GNN-supervised LIFT, emphasizing design–directive–QoR relationships. References add HLS-Eval, C2HLSC, HLSDebugger and other recent work while removing several earlier general code/HDL and retrieval references. This revises the competitive context beyond bibliographic updates.
descriptions.P1: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around three challenges, and contributions are reordered. Method exposition changes from workflow–VODA–HLSFixer–HLSTuner to workflow–HLSTuner–HLSFixer–VODA. Numbered sections, expanded explanations, structured appendices and dedicated limitations/ethics sections reorganize the narrative; author and affiliation text also changes.
descriptions.P2: v3 redraws introductory visuals, expands the optimization chart, and adds generation/accelerator/RAG tables plus prompt, similarity, scaling, cost and trajectory figures. v2's Table 2 is retained as v3's Table 6, and its per-error Figure 6 is expanded and relocated as Figure 14. The energy-efficiency chart is removed, alongside extensive plot and page-layout changes.

P-C98E742F29.title: WorldWander: Bridging Egocentric and Exocentric Worlds in Video Generation

descriptions.M1: The Wan2.2-5B backbone, LoRA adaptation, clean conditional latents, collaborative attention, shared temporal position encoding, and flow-matching objective remain unchanged. Reference-conditioned ego-to-exo generation is already present in v1; expanded explanations and corrected task-variable labels do not establish a changed procedure.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the synthetic GTA-5 and real-world EgoExo-8K subsets for bidirectional perspective translation. Dynamic navigation and human-object interaction already appear in v1's dataset coverage; v2's cooking and manipulation examples in Figure 8 provide additional cases within that scope.
descriptions.E2: v2 Table 1 adds an untuned ReCamMaster comparator for synthetic scenarios alongside the retained fine-tuned version. AnyV2V, I2VEdit, TrajectoryCrafter, and the existing fine-tuned ReCamMaster comparisons remain; newly discussed ego/exo methods are not actually evaluated.
descriptions.E3: The added experiments introduce a uniform-timestep variant, LoRA ranks 64 and 128 alongside the retained rank 80, and a ReCamMaster comparison without fine-tuning. Existing metrics, clip settings, held-out triplet counts, and user-study sample size remain unchanged. Removing the stated 6,000-step budget does not establish that training changed.
descriptions.E4: v2 extends the existing analyses with timestep and LoRA-rank tests in Table 2, a fine-tuning control in Table 1, and human-object interaction cases in Figure 8. These are focused additions; the earlier component ablations, convergence comparison, failure cases, and out-of-domain gallery are retained.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The added result rows retain the existing point-estimate reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: Previously reported scores in Tables 1 and 2 remain unchanged. Added results include untuned ReCamMaster synthetic FVD values of 738.7 for exo-to-ego and 915.7 for ego-to-exo, uniform-timestep and rank-64/128 results, and Figure 8 interaction examples. These are additional results under additional conditions, not improved same-setting WorldWander scores.
descriptions.T1: The substantive mathematical formulation remains unchanged, with no new theorem, proof, or derivation. v2 adds the standard inference ODE in Section 3 to explain the existing flow model; the remaining equations correspond to v1 after renumbering.
descriptions.C1: v2 revises the novelty claims: v1 broadly introduces ego/exo translation and claims no existing paired dataset, whereas v2 acknowledges prior datasets and emphasizes bidirectional dynamic navigation, reference-guided synthesis, and the first dynamic open-world wandering benchmark. The core framework and performance claims remain, although several novelty passages incorrectly reverse ego/exo direction labels.
descriptions.C2: Section 4.1 replaces the rationale that typically fixed perspectives make camera parameters less important with an argument about geometry-free generalization across moving cameras. v2 also interprets the new fine-tuning control as evidence of dataset usefulness and the rank sweep as supporting rank 80. The appendix limitations concerning physical consistency and limited human diversity are retained.
descriptions.D1: v2 documents the GTA-5 two-player/spectator collection protocol, names the real-world cameras, and reconciles the camera-mounting description with the earlier appendix. It adds approximately two-day training and three-minute inference times but removes the exact 6,000-step training budget. The code-access link and most implementation settings remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: The general video-diffusion survey is replaced by a dedicated exo-to-ego related-work section, with added discussion and citations concerning 4Diff, EgoWorld, EgoExo4D, H2O, and TACO. v2 positions the contribution against prior static, unidirectional, or auxiliary-input settings and explains exclusions from direct comparison, revising the research positioning.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, related work, task formulation, and dataset narrative are extensively rewritten. Supplementary Sections 7–11 become Appendices A–E before the bibliography, and acknowledgements are added. These are narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.
descriptions.P2: The paper changes from a two-column to a single-column layout, redistributing and resizing figures and tables throughout. v2 adds the positional-encoding illustration and interaction examples, reorganizes the dataset mosaics, and expands both results tables with rows and fine-tuning markers. Most existing comparison and appendix images are retained.

P-40E366546B.title: Self-Improving Skill Learning for Robust Skill-based Meta-Reinforcement Learning

descriptions.M1: The decoupled policies, skill-learning objectives, maximum return relabeling, buffer mixing, and periodic refinement remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 now explicitly show initial skill training and the frozen final task encoder, both already described in v3’s Appendix B.
descriptions.E1: The four original environments and their noise, dataset-size, and data-quality settings remain. Appendix G.6 adds explicit-goal evaluation scenarios for HER in Maze2D and AntMaze. The new Kitchen visualizations and interval sweep use existing task coverage.
descriptions.E2: Table G.2 adds SAC+HER as an evaluated comparator in Maze2D and AntMaze. Appendix E extends the timing comparison to four existing SISL ablation variants. The main Table 1 comparator set remains unchanged.
descriptions.E3: Appendix G.5 adds a Kitchen noise-0.3 sweep over refinement intervals {100, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000}. G.6 introduces HER training directly on test tasks with explicit goals and no offline data. Appendix E reports total training hours instead of per-iteration seconds. Existing benchmark splits, budgets, and default settings remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: v4 supplements the existing extensive ablations with refinement-frequency sensitivity in Figure G.4, comparative microwave and bottom-burner failure cases in Figures F.5–F.6, and component-level runtime analysis in Table E.2. These are focused extensions to retained analyses.
descriptions.E5: Both versions specify averaging over five random seeds, with standard deviations shown through shading and table uncertainties. v4 introduces no changed run-count disclosure, confidence intervals, significance tests, or distinct uncertainty-estimation practice.
descriptions.E6: Table 1 and existing appendix scores remain unchanged. v4 adds SAC+HER results of 0.37±0.09 in Maze2D and 0.00±0.00 in AntMaze, total training times of 42.16 hours for SiMPL and 48.96 for SISL, ablation timings, and interval and trajectory findings. Table G.2 repeats existing SISL scores; its differing comparator conditions do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.
descriptions.T1: The mathematical setup and objectives in Equations (1)–(7) and (B.1)–(B.6) are retained. Correcting the covariance-symbol explanation from I to Σ and introducing θ_final clarify notation without changing assumptions or mathematical reasoning. No new theorem or proof appears.
descriptions.C1: v3 qualifies its 'first framework' claim with 'through both exploration-guided refinement and principled relabeling.' v4 drops that qualification, broadening claimed priority to explicitly addressing suboptimal demonstrations in skill-based meta-RL generally. The two main contributions and robustness claims otherwise remain.
descriptions.C2: Section 5.4 adds explanations connecting relabeling stability to shared subtask reward semantics and softmax sampling. Appendices E and G.5 add interpretations of runtime overhead and the adaptation-versus-refinement-frequency tradeoff. G.6 discusses differences from goal-conditioned RL. Section 6’s existing limitations are retained.
descriptions.D1: Alongside the existing anonymized supplementary-code statement, v4 adds a direct SISL repository link. It newly specifies a 50/50 allocation of sampled training tasks between the two policies, expands runtime information, and clarifies parameter freezing in pseudocode. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun; Appendix C’s hardware and hyperparameter tables remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: v4 adds citations on exploration, meta-RL, robustness, and goal-conditioned learning, including Pathak et al. (2017), Kim et al. (2025), Hwang et al. (2025), and HER. Appendix G.6 expands positioning against goal-conditioned RL, alongside the slightly broader introductory priority claim. The main related-work organization remains.
descriptions.P1: Targeted edits expand the introduction, methodological explanations, runtime discussion, and ablation summaries. v4 adds appendix subsections, acknowledgments, the full institutional name, and publication-status headers. Most prose and the overall section sequence are retained.
descriptions.P2: v4 adds Tables E.1–E.2 and G.2, plus Figures F.5–F.6 and G.4. It expands captions for Figures 2–4 and reformats the algorithms. Existing graphics are retained, with local resizing, spacing changes, and relocation through page reflow.

P-FA8F4ACB13.title: Hierarchical Successor Representation for Robust Transfer

descriptions.M1: v2 introduces online option construction in Appendix B.2 and Algorithm S2: agents begin without options, learn a primitive-action SR, construct eigenoptions after warm-up, and periodically refresh them while learning HSR. v1 assumed pre-acquired options and left iterative discovery to future work. This extends the procedure while retaining the underlying HSR/NMF framework.
descriptions.E1: Transfer evaluation expands beyond the canonical four-room environment to an asymmetric four-room layout with barriers, a Loop maze, a Corridor maze, and a Multi-pairwise-bottleneck maze (v2 Figure S3). These test materially different environmental geometries and connectivity structures. The original transfer and procedural-maze exploration scenarios remain.
descriptions.E2: Section 4.3 and Figure 5 add an actual SR-GPI comparison, evaluating policy composition with one-hot, HSR-row, and HSR-NMF representations against linear Q-learning. v1 discussed successor-feature research but did not evaluate this comparator family. The original representation and exploration baselines are retained.
descriptions.E3: New evaluation designs include withholding the target reward vector until first goal discovery before switching to GPI, testing agents without preconstructed options, and varying option budgets across 4, 8, 16, and 32. Figure S6 adds a 10,000-action coverage analysis; the retained main exploration figure still reports 100,000-action coverage. These are added protocols, not demonstrated reruns of the original experiments.
descriptions.E4: v2 expands robustness analysis: Figure S3 tests dependence on environmental topology; Figure S4 compares eigenoptions, covering options, random target options, and option counts; Figure 2i-l and Figure S6 test transfer and exploration with online-discovered options. These address dependencies that v1's representation and offline-versus-online analyses did not test.
descriptions.E5: Mean ± standard error reporting and the 20-seed default remain, while several added experiments explicitly use 10 seeds. Figure S6 introduces two-way ANOVA interaction tests. Figure 5 describes a paired t-test but reports df = 18 for 10 seeds, leaving the exact test unclear. There is no evidence that retained experiments used fewer runs.
descriptions.E6: Additional new results include online-option transfer benefits (Figure 2l, p = 0.026), no significant difference between one-hot SR-GPI and HSR-NMF Q-learning (Figure 5c, p = 0.199), and benefits from combining GPI with HSR-row/NMF (p = 0.003/0.007). New appendix results report robustness across geometries and stabilisation beyond eight options. These supplement largely unchanged original results.
descriptions.T1: v2 removes the leading discount factor from the main-text termination-kernel formula, matching v1's appendix expression. Appendix A changes the intra-option occupancy sum from ending at τ to τ−1, restores discounted continuation terms, explicitly conditions on termination states, and revises the contraction argument. These are mathematical revisions within the existing framework; Theorem 3.1's conclusion is retained.
descriptions.C1: The abstract's central transfer, representation, and exploration claims remain. However, the introduction now explicitly claims robustness to environmental geometry, option definition, and absence of preconstructed options. The discussion replaces v1's pre-exposure restriction with demonstrated operation using online option construction, materially broadening claimed applicability.
descriptions.C2: v2 interprets HSR representations and GPI policy composition as complementary, explains weak covering-option performance through restricted initiation sets and sparse rewards, and discusses stability beyond a modest option budget. It also qualifies online option construction as heuristic with unresolved theoretical foundations. These extend interpretation and applicability boundaries while retaining the original topological explanation.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds a code-repository access statement, online-option initialisation and update pseudocode, and the reward-discovery implementation used for GPI comparisons. Existing transfer and exploration hyperparameters remain. Numerical warm-up and option-refresh intervals are not supplied, so the additional reproducibility documentation remains incomplete.
descriptions.R1: The relationship to successor-feature/GPI research is substantively revised: v1 emphasised its allegedly shared diffusion limitations, whereas v2 positions GPI as complementary algorithmic machinery and studies combinations with HSR. Carvalho et al. (2023) is added to this discussion, alongside new predictive-map connections citing Yu et al. (2020) and Piray and Daw (2021).
descriptions.P1: Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain. v2 adds a GPI results subsection, organises Appendix B into subsections, inserts GPI implementation details, and locally rewrites related work and discussion. Typographical corrections, acknowledgements, and conference-header changes accompany these additions, without a wholesale language or structural rewrite.
descriptions.P2: Figure 2 expands from eight to twelve panels, and v2 adds a GPI schematic/comparison figure, topology and option-sensitivity figures, an online-exploration figure, and another algorithm display. These expand the visual presentation. The original exploration Figure 5 becomes Figure 6, and the original spectral Figure S3 becomes Figure S5; neither is removed.

descriptions.M1: Algorithm 1 is identical. The implemented GMPO procedure retains geometric averaging, token-level clipping in log space, and the default exp(-0.4)/exp(0.4) thresholds. The main objective is rewritten without changing this default procedure.
descriptions.E1: Appendix B adds CountDown arithmetic puzzles for training and validation. The five mathematical benchmarks, Geometry3K, MATH training data, and DeepScaleR were already used in v1; the additional model configurations do not themselves constitute new task coverage.
descriptions.E2: The untuned Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct-7B comparator, scoring 38.1% in v1 Table 2, is omitted from v2's corresponding Geometry3K comparison. Mathematical comparators are retained across v2 Tables 1 and 3. The added MoE experiments compare GMPO with the existing GRPO baseline.
descriptions.E3: V2 adds reported 32B and adapted 200M MoE configurations, DeepScaleR-to-MATH500 evaluation, and CountDown holdout validation, with distinct batch settings in Table 6. Validation-score monitoring replaces the earlier training-reward plots. The documented unnormalized ablation loss also changes, although identical scores do not establish that it was rerun.
descriptions.E4: Figures 4–5 add gradient-norm and validation diagnostics, including the CountDown instability case and MoE stability comparisons. Appendix C adds sequence-level importance ratios versus response length to investigate normalization. Existing objective and clipping ablation scores remain, while v1's training-reward curves are no longer presented.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The importance-ratio ranges and training trajectories are diagnostics, without a newly specified uncertainty-estimation procedure.
descriptions.E6: The original mathematical benchmark and ablation numbers are retained. V2 Table 2 newly reports 96.7% for GMPO versus 94.6% for GRPO on MATH500 in the 32B setting. New diagnostics report GRPO's CountDown collapse around 250 steps, steadier GMPO gradients, and increasing unnormalized sequence ratios with response length.
descriptions.T1: Appendix A adds three explicit gradient derivations where v1 supplied final expressions. The ablation formulas also revise sign and advantage handling: the unnormalized objective now places the advantage inside the product, changing its power relative to v1 Table 3. The original AM–GM objective-range argument remains.
descriptions.C1: V2 extends the introduction's performance claims to a reported 32B MoE setting, claiming a 2.1-point MATH500 advantage. The central geometric-mean stability contribution and the original 4.1-point mathematics and 1.4-point multimodal gains remain unchanged.
descriptions.C2: V2 explicitly connects premature entropy collapse to validation plateaus and explains normalization through response-length-dependent growth of sequence importance ratios. These extend the existing stability and exploration interpretation. V1's discussion that MATH is too easy for the 7B model is removed.
descriptions.D1: Table 6 adds model identities, total and activated expert counts, and batch/mini-batch sizes. Appendix B describes DeepScaleR's approximate size and composition and the CountDown holdout. The hardware statement is narrowed to models described as under 7B; Algorithm 1 and the code-access URL remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: Section 2.1 expands related work across uncertainty-aware updates, efficiency, rollout selection, replay, and exploration, including Seed-GRPO, GRPO-lead, CPPO, RePO, and INTUITOR. New policy-gradient and entropy references are added to the conceptual discussion. The OlympiadBench citation also replaces v1's citation to OlympicArena.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, and diagnostic interpretations undergo widespread rewriting. Importance-ratio notation and clipped versus unclipped objectives are standardized. The main section sequence remains, while Appendices A–C organize derivations, MoE experiments, and normalization analysis.
descriptions.P2: V2 adds a conceptual Figure 2 and appendix Figures 5–6, redraws the importance-ratio plots, and replaces the six-panel diagnostic figure with eight panels. The original mathematical comparison is distributed across Tables 1 and 3; Table 2 gains a MoE panel, and Table 6 adds settings. Typography and page styling also change.

P-219A550654.title: For-Value: Efficient Forward-Only Data Valuation for finetuning LLMs and VLMs

descriptions.M1: The scoring rule, Algorithm 1, batching, vocabulary restriction and averaging over valuation examples already appear in v1. v3 makes the restriction explicit in Equation (2) and clarifies the last-layer gradient interpretation without changing the scoring procedure.
descriptions.E1: v3 retains the original sentence/math, image subject/style and cat–dog tasks. It adds fine-tuning data selection on GSM8K, Noise-Huatuo-Complex-CoT and PMC-Reasoning, with five medical QA and six VLM evaluation datasets.
descriptions.E2: Tables 1–2 retain Hessian-free, DataInf, HyperINF and Emb. New fine-tuning comparisons add base-model and full-data training references, including a PMC full-data row attributed to Huang et al. (2025). These new comparisons use the three existing gradient baselines and exclude Emb.
descriptions.E3: New protocols select 1%/5% of GSM8K, 5%/10% of Huatuo and 10%/20% of PMC data, with warm-up training, full-parameter fine-tuning and greedy-decoding accuracy evaluation. GSM8K uses test examples for valuation; medical experiments use separate valuation pools and held-out tests. Original detection settings are retained.
descriptions.E4: v3 extends robustness evaluation to fine-tuning selection under corrupted medical reasoning data. It adds clean-data recovery among the top 10% of selected samples (Table 8) and mislabel-ratio sensitivity at 40% and 60% alongside the original 50% (Table 7). Existing prediction-error ablation, model-size analyses and qualitative examples remain.
descriptions.E5: v1 already contains plus/minus values and error bars. v3 explicitly identifies mean and standard deviation in Table 1 and Figure 3 and explains nonzero deviations after rounding. No seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests are added.
descriptions.E6: All numerical entries in the original Tables 1–2 are retained. New results include 48.3% GSM8K accuracy with 5% selected data and 62.35% mean medical QA accuracy with 10% Huatuo data. On PMC, For-Value leads at 10% selection but trails HyperINF at 20%: 52.67% versus 53.04%. These are newly reported experiments.
descriptions.T1: Theorem 2, Equation (3), explicitly adds an unembedding-dependent term. Related mathematics existed conditionally in v1's proof, but v3's standalone statement omits the matching-input/prefix restriction retained in its derivation. This is a limited formal revision with an unresolved condition; the principal assumptions and most proof equations remain unchanged.
descriptions.C1: The central claim of efficient forward-only data valuation remains. v3 emphasizes last-layer gradient approximation and batch scalability and extends its advertised empirical contribution to selecting useful subsets for actual fine-tuning, beyond the identification and detection claims demonstrated in v1.
descriptions.C2: New limitations identify pretraining as outside direct applicability and acknowledge that data value changes during training (Section 7). v3 also interprets the Hessian-free comparison as support for last-layer valuation and attributes noisy-data baseline failures to convergence or uniqueness assumptions (Appendix A.4).
descriptions.D1: Appendix A.3 adds warm-up procedures, LoRA ranks, learning rates, epochs, batch sizes, gradient accumulation and GPU counts for the fine-tuning experiments. v3 also documents new data-pool sizes and corruption construction and supplies a GitHub code-access link. Earlier detection settings and licensing information are retained.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds references including Bae et al. (2024), LAVA by Just et al. (2023), Razin et al. (2024), and literature supporting the new benchmarks. The basic positioning against gradient, Hessian and Shapley approaches remains. Wang's Data Shapley in One Training Run is retained with updated publication metadata.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, contributions and method explanations are rewritten around last-layer gradients and batch scalability. Preliminaries move into Appendix B, and the appendices are reorganized into experimental details/results and proofs. Contents, limitations, acknowledgments and an LLM-use disclosure are added; the title and author block also change.
descriptions.P2: v3 adds the performance–efficiency overview in Figure 1, fine-tuning Tables 3–5, diagnostic Tables 7–8 and corruption examples in Figure 7. The original complexity table and qualitative figure move into the appendix as Table 6 and Figure 5. Table styling, figure sizing and appendix layout are also revised.

P-41114F7DE5.title: Visual Prompt Discovery via Semantic Exploration

descriptions.M1: The abstract-idea search tree, novelty-guided UCT, implementation loop, semantic backpropagation, expansion rules, and Appendix A prompts are unchanged. The restricted-tool variant is an experimental control; the proposed default procedure remains intact.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate the same four BlindTest tasks and five BLINK tasks described in Section 4.1 and Appendix B. The added backbone, toolbox, and split experiments reuse this coverage without introducing different data populations or task requirements.
descriptions.E2: Table A1 adds Basic-tool SEVEX as an internal comparison variant against full-tool SEVEX and Naive. The existing Naive, SketchPad, SketchPad+APE, and search-component comparisons remain; Table 5 reuses the Naive and SketchPad comparator set.
descriptions.E3: v2 expands evaluation beyond v1's single-task cross-backbone transfer experiment with full-discovery comparisons across four BlindTest tasks using GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.0. It also introduces a restricted-tool control and two additional 30-image CircledLetter development splits, excluding their union from testing. These extend the evaluation design while retaining the original metrics and main search settings.
descriptions.E4: The original component ablations and qualitative analyses are retained. New Appendix C tests whether gains depend on external pretrained tools, examines sensitivity to development-set selection, and presents a per-trial search trace. These add substantive evidence about attribution, robustness, and search behavior.
descriptions.E5: v1 already reports Figure 5 averages over five independent runs. v2 additionally specifies five runs per new development split and reports means with within-split standard deviations in Table A2. This adds explicit variability reporting for one study without revising the original run counts.
descriptions.E6: Original Tables 2–4 retain their values. Table 5 adds backbone/task results, including SEVEX averages of 62.4% for GPT-4o and 75.2% for Claude, while reusing Gemini and some LineIntersections entries. Table A1 adds a 73.3% basic-tool average versus 72.4% with full tools. Table A2 reports test accuracies of 88.00 ± 4.30% and 85.98 ± 3.86% under the new split protocol. These are additional results, not revised same-setting performance gains.
descriptions.T1: The search-tree definitions and priority equations (1)–(2) are unchanged. The added explanation of search behavior introduces no new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims about automated task-wise discovery, semantic exploration, performance and efficiency, and model-specific prompting. The added experiments provide further support without redefining these main contributions.
descriptions.C2: v2 interprets the toolbox ablation as evidence that external models are not the main source of BlindTest gains, while acknowledging task-specific benefits. It also acknowledges the Claude CircledLetter exception, explicitly limits split-stability conclusions to CircledLetter, and explains how initially weaker search nodes can support useful refinements.
descriptions.D1: Appendix C specifies the permitted and excluded tool functions and explains construction of the additional development splits and held-out test set. The original hyperparameters, tool descriptions, Appendix A prompts, and Appendix B development indices remain unchanged. No new code or data access instructions are supplied.
descriptions.R1: Section 2.1 softens the research-gap description from lacking research to being underexplored and replaces the claim of the first agent-driven system with an agent-driven system. The same 25 cited works remain; bibliography corrections do not add related research.
descriptions.P1: v2 condenses Section 2.1, corrects grammar and terminology, and consistently identifies the CircledLetter ablation. It inserts a backbone subsection and an additional-analyses appendix, moves the existing Discussions appendix from C to D, and adds contact information and acknowledgements. The overall narrative structure remains recognizable.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds Table 5, Tables A1–A2, and Figure A1 using the established presentation style. Existing displays are retained, with localized resizing and relocation, corrected captions and the Figure 5 task label, and changes to reference-link coloring. The original figures and tables are not substantially redesigned.

P-505B500047.title: Transition Matching Distillation for Fast Video Generation

descriptions.M1: The decoupled backbone, conditional flow head, TM-MF pretraining, DMD2-v objectives, and flow-head rollout remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 move to Appendix A without changing their procedures.
descriptions.E1: Both versions retain the teacher-generated video dataset with VidProM/Qwen prompts, 480p text-to-video generation, and VBench evaluation of Wan2.1 1.3B and 14B models. The added timing and pretraining-budget analyses introduce no new dataset, domain, or task.
descriptions.E2: Comparator membership remains unchanged in the matched benchmark and ablation comparisons. New Table 13 reuses the existing two-step rCM and DMD2-v baselines and scores; Table 12 uses the existing teacher architecture as its timing reference.
descriptions.E3: Table 12 introduces component timing with M=1 and batch size 1 on a single H100. Table 13 evaluates 0.5k, 1k, and 3k TM-MF pretraining budgets with distillation reported as under 6k iterations. These supplement the retained evaluation protocols; the original Table 7 defaults are unchanged.
descriptions.E4: Sections B.7–B.8 add analyses of component latency and sensitivity to pretraining duration. Conversely, v1 Figure 13's gated-versus-concatenated fusion convergence plot is removed, although Table 9's final-score comparison and the stability discussion remain.
descriptions.E5: Both versions retain the same five generation seeds per prompt for the 60-prompt user study. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates; its new tables report point estimates.
descriptions.E6: Table 2 changes the Wan2.1 14B TMD-N4H5 result at NFE 2.75 from 84.62/85.09/82.72 to 84.92/85.54/82.42 for overall/quality/semantic scores under the same reported configuration. Tables 12–13 add timings and reduced-pretraining results, including overall scores 84.52 and 84.59 at 0.5k and 1k pretraining iterations. The fusion convergence traces in v1 Figure 13 are removed.
descriptions.T1: The transition-matching definitions, MeanFlow derivation, distillation equations, effective-NFE formula, finite-difference approximation, and appendix curvature definition are retained. No substantive mathematical correction, assumption, or proof is introduced.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same architectural and two-stage training contributions and speed–quality claims. The highlighted near-one-step 14B VBench result remains 84.24 at NFE 1.38.
descriptions.C2: Section B.7 newly interprets measured latency ratios as validating effective NFE as an efficiency proxy. Section B.8 adds the argument that TMD is training-efficient relative to rCM and remains competitive with substantially reduced pretraining. Existing mechanism explanations and qualifications are largely retained.
descriptions.D1: The new analyses disclose timing hardware, batch size, component runtimes, and additional training-budget information. Existing implementation details and Table 7 remain. The project-page link supplied with v1's abstract is absent from v2, removing an access pointer without establishing any change in the underlying resource's availability.
descriptions.R1: The same 70 cited works and the related-work discussion are retained. Section B.8 adds limited training-efficiency positioning against rCM, contrasting TMD's 3k pretraining plus 1k distillation iterations for 14B with rCM's cited 10k iterations.
descriptions.P1: v2 lightly edits the abstract, introduction, and conclusion, moves Algorithms 1–2 from the main text to Appendix A, and adds two appendix subsections. The principal section order and explanatory narrative remain substantially intact.
descriptions.P2: v2 replaces the NVIDIA report styling with a conference-style layout, changes typography and abstract columns, removes running headers and footers, and resizes or relocates figures and tables throughout. Figure 2 changes from full-width to single-column presentation. Tables 12–13 are added and v1 Figure 13 is removed; retained qualitative images are unchanged.

P-1316010E21.title: ModTrack: Sensor-Agnostic Multi-View Tracking via Identity-Informed PHD Filtering with Covariance Propagation

descriptions.M1: Appendix K adds a tested MLP radar-perception variant alongside the previously reported Doppler and oracle front ends, although its architecture is unspecified. The analytical tracking core, covariance propagation, fusion equations, and identity-assignment and lifecycle procedures remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate pedestrian tracking on WildTrack and MultiviewX and automotive radar tracking on RadarScenes. The additional experiments retain these datasets and modalities. Evaluating all 400 existing WildTrack frames changes the sequence length and evaluation protocol, without introducing a new dataset or population.
descriptions.E2: v3 adds vanilla GM-PHD comparisons on both camera datasets in Table 10 and adds MOT and CA-Net to the RadarScenes comparison in Table 4. Appendix C also adds a reported runtime comparison with MCBLT, previously an accuracy comparator only. These additions expand comparisons relevant to the filtering core and radar performance; Table 1's comparator membership is retained.
descriptions.E3: The original splits, training settings, and evaluation thresholds are retained. Appendix I adds inference across all 400 WildTrack frames using perception trained on the original 90/10 split, explicitly including training frames. New diagnostics specify single-component substitutions and a MultiviewX gate sweep; v3 also reports identity-switch counts and radar GOSPA. These extend the evaluation protocol without replacing the original experiments.
descriptions.E4: Appendix H adds isolated tests of covariance-aware clustering, propagated covariance, and precision-weighted fusion. Section 4.4 adds a MultiviewX gate sweep measuring missed clusters versus merge errors. Appendices I-K add longer-sequence behavior, comparison with vanilla GM-PHD to assess the practical consequences of departing from formal PHD filtering, and an MLP radar-perception diagnostic. These extend the existing matching-mode, dropout, sensitivity, and calibration analyses.
descriptions.E5: Camera-subset means and standard deviations, runtime uncertainty, and the NEES confidence-interval and coverage procedures are retained. No new repeated-run counts, random-seed reporting, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation practices are introduced. The deterministic RANSAC description concerns algorithm execution rather than repeated-run statistical estimation.
descriptions.E6: The original camera scores, dropout results, runtime measurements, and calibration statistics remain unchanged. New Table 9 reports IDF1/MOTA of 92.8/90.8 for RANSAC clustering, 95.0/90.7 for fixed covariance, and 93.0/89.5 for mean fusion, against 95.5/91.4. Table 10 adds vanilla-filter results and identity-switch counts; additional radar scores and the 400-frame results further expand the evidence. Table 10 reports ModTrack's MultiviewX IDF1 as 85.2, whereas retained Tables 1-2 report 86.2, with no explanation establishing a comparable-setting performance change.
descriptions.T1: The projection derivations, covariance flooring, fusion equations, filtering equations, and calibration mathematics are retained. Renaming Rdepth to Rindep is not a mathematical change. Appendix J explains departures from formal RFS/PHD guarantees and evaluates them empirically, without introducing a new theorem, proof, or revised recursion.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, three principal contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about modular tracking, traceable uncertainty, sensor flexibility, and competitive accuracy. The introduction adds an explicit assertion that the modifications to GM-PHD improve identity consistency while preserving state-estimation accuracy, extending the claimed validation of the heuristic backend.
descriptions.C2: v3 develops several substantive interpretations and qualifications. Section 4.4 diagnoses the MultiviewX gap as a structural missed-cluster/merge tradeoff rather than merely crowding-related ambiguity. Section 3.3 explains the overlapping-camera rationale for singleton rejection and the radar exception. Appendix J explicitly states that component weights lose their expected-target-mass interpretation. Appendix I additionally claims no compounding tracking error from the longer-sequence experiment, despite its acknowledged training-data overlap.
descriptions.D1: Appendix L newly supplies a code-availability statement and repository address. Appendix H documents the deterministic consensus-clustering implementation, fixed covariance, and averaging substitutions, while Section 3.3 discloses radar singleton handling. The existing training recipes, hardware, and hyperparameter tables are retained. The added MLP experiment lacks architecture and training details.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds references to Mahler's foundational PHD work, Marcuzzi et al.'s CA-Net work, and Weng et al.'s tracking baseline. The introduction refines its criticism of earlier multi-view RFS trackers toward missing covariance propagation across the pipeline. The broader related-work organization and positioning between learned tracking and RFS filtering remain intact.
descriptions.P1: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes comprise localized clarifications, revised subsection labeling, an explicit supplementary-material heading, new Appendices H-L, and expanded author, affiliation, keyword, and acknowledgement text. The revision does not extensively rewrite the existing narrative.
descriptions.P2: v3 comprehensively reformats the document with narrower text blocks, running headers, and resized and redistributed figures and tables. Table 4 gains comparator rows and a GOSPA column, and Tables 9-10 are added. Table 7 moves to the final page. The underlying images for Figures 1-14 are unchanged, so their relocation and scaling are presentation changes.

P-326D643383.title: Branch-and-Browse: Efficient and Controllable Web Exploration with Tree-Structured Reasoning and Action Memory

descriptions.M1: Section 4.2 introduces a SteP-augmented variant that replaces the ReAct-style policy at node expansion with SteP sub-policies. Search, replay, background reasoning, pruning and memory retain their default logic. The expanded scoring description documents details without establishing a change to the original implementation.
descriptions.E1: Evaluation expands from WebArena to VisualWebArena, covering Classifieds, Reddit and Shopping with multimodal observations and visual grounding requirements. This materially broadens the tested task and observation conditions while retaining the original WebArena coverage.
descriptions.E2: Table 2 adds Branch-and-Browse + SteP as an evaluated comparison variant alongside the original framework. All earlier WebArena baselines remain; standalone SteP was already included in v1.
descriptions.E3: The stated success-rate metric, successful-task timing rule, 812-task WebArena evaluation, default depth and branching factors of 5, and 10-step budget are retained. The added VisualWebArena evaluation explicitly uses the same model and budget conventions.
descriptions.E4: Section 4.2 adds a component-combination analysis testing whether SteP policies complement the existing search framework. The replay/background-reasoning ablations and depth/branching sensitivity experiments remain unchanged; the latter moves from Table 3 to Table 4.
descriptions.E5: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.
descriptions.E6: Existing WebArena and ablation values are unchanged, but new results are reported. Table 2 adds the SteP hybrid at 39.8% overall success alongside the original method's 35.8%. New Table 3 reports VisualWebArena overall success of 18.9% for the GPT-4o reactive baseline, 26.4% for Tree Search and 32.7% for Branch-and-Browse, plus site-specific results.
descriptions.T1: Section 3.1 adds a bounded specification of the previously abstract utility score, v in [0,1], and describes retaining best-so-far values per subtask. This is a limited elaboration of the scoring definition. No proofs or theorems are added; renaming the transition operator from T to Trans is only notational.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims about subtask-aware tree exploration, replay/background reasoning and page action memory. Their headline WebArena claims remain 35.8% success and a 40.4% execution-time reduction.
descriptions.C2: New discussion explains how subtask-conditioned scoring distinguishes progress from redundant retries, attributes the hybrid's benefits to SteP interaction routines, and interprets VisualWebArena results as evidence of multimodal applicability. The existing limitations paragraph is retained.
descriptions.D1: The abstract adds a code repository link. Section 3.1 newly documents the LLM evaluator's conditioning inputs, score normalization and per-subtask bookkeeping, while Section 4.2 explains the SteP integration interface. These disclosures do not establish that the original implementation changed.
descriptions.R1: The new hybrid discussion explicitly connects the approach to prior policy-layer composition and develops its relationship to SteP beyond v1's suggested complementarity. The cited-work set is retained; updates to the VisualWebArena publication entry and LASER year are bibliographic corrections.
descriptions.P1: Localized revisions expand the scoring explanation and organize Section 4.2 with WebArena, SteP-combination and VisualWebArena subheadings. v2 also adds acknowledgements and corrects terminology, grammar, author-block punctuation and bibliographic details. The main section structure and most prose remain intact.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds the VisualWebArena table and a hybrid row with an updated caption in Table 2. The sensitivity table is retained as Table 4 and relocated within the layout. Figures 1–4 retain their content; other layout differences mainly reflect text reflow.

P-62AB495AD4.title: Theory of Minimal Weight Perturbations in Deep Networks and its Applications for Low-Rank Activated Backdoor Attacks

descriptions.M1: New Section 7.4 introduces a procedural adaptation for noninvertible downstream maps: estimating minimum-norm perturbations through local linearization and the Jacobian pseudoinverse, using autograd. The original exact construction, backdoor losses, SVD compression, and finite-difference power-iteration algorithm remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use synthetic four-class classification, CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, and SQuAD 1.1 question answering. Phi-2 and compression across additional layers expand model configurations and evaluation procedures without introducing a documented new dataset or task.
descriptions.E2: The standard-backdoor control defined by Equation 11 remains the comparator for compression-activated attacks, including the new Phi-2 experiments. Existing comparisons are retained in the appendices. Newly discussed prior work, including Tsai and Weng, is not added as an evaluated baseline.
descriptions.E3: v2 adds substantially different evaluation configurations: 32-block Phi-2, pruning at 20–40%, single-layer compression at ranks 1800/1700/1500, and compression of all fc2 layers at ranks 2000/1900/1800. Section 7.4 also introduces a layer-wise Jacobian-based evaluation. Existing RoBERTa and vision protocols remain documented.
descriptions.E4: Section 7.4 and Figure 4 newly examine whether local perturbation estimates remain informative across Phi-2 layers despite failure of exact invertibility assumptions. Table 11 additionally tests backdoor activation under simultaneous compression of all fc2 layers and exposes its clean-accuracy cost. The earlier synthetic-network and spectral-energy analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: Both versions state five repetitions and retain the existing appendix means and standard deviations. However, the new Phi-2 Tables 8, 10, and 11 display means without deviations; Tables 10–11 still claim standard deviations in their captions. This changes reporting consistency without establishing any change in run counts.
descriptions.E6: The matched original detailed results are unchanged, but v2 adds Phi-2 evidence. Table 10 reports ASR increasing from 45.5% at full rank to 86.0% at rank 1500; Table 11 reports 99.5% ASR with 55.0% clean accuracy at rank 2000 across all fc2 layers. Figure 4 adds sensitivity findings. These are new settings, not same-setting improvements over v1. Phi-2 pruning ASR at 20% is inconsistently reported as 99.3% in Table 2 and 99.5% in Table 8.
descriptions.T1: Theorems 3.1, 4.1, A.1, and A.2, Corollary 5.1, and their mathematical assumptions and proofs are retained. Appendix renumbering, incorporating the row-space remark into the theorem presentation, and a notation correction do not alter the mathematics. Section 7.4 describes an approximation procedure without adding a formal derivation or proved guarantee.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and central contributions remain stable. The conclusion narrows the practical defense claim: v1 says estimated Lipschitz constants can certify safe compression regimes, whereas v2 emphasizes robustness diagnostics based on sensitivity estimates. This qualifies practical applicability without replacing the central theoretical or backdoor claims.
descriptions.C2: v2 explicitly discusses the restrictive single-layer setting and labels the new local approximation a sensitivity tool rather than a formal certificate. Section 7.3 also replaces the broad practical safety wording with a statement tied to the particular sample, estimated Lipschitz constant, and 10% pruning. Existing appendix limitations are retained.
descriptions.D1: Appendix C.1 newly supplies a code-repository address and a reference to running instructions. Table 4 adds Phi-2 architecture and compression-location details, and Section 7.4 identifies autograd for the approximation. Existing hardware and software disclosures remain unchanged; Table 5 does not add Phi-2-specific loss constants.
descriptions.R1: New Appendix A.1 develops the relationship to prior weight-perturbation research, contrasting Theorem 3.1 with Tsai et al. and Theorem 4.1 with Weng et al. Expanded Section 4 and Appendix B also position the work against input-space and parameter-space Lipschitz research, including newly cited Herrera, Bartlett, Fazlyab, Pauli, and Tsuzuku.
descriptions.P1: Most existing prose and section ordering are retained. Localized edits expand the applicability discussion, rewrite and rename the Summary as Conclusion, add an Impact Statement and related-work subsection, and update cross-references. These do not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.
descriptions.P2: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column conference formatting, resizing and relocating displays and changing headers and typography. v2 adds Figure 4 and three Phi-2 result tables and expands the architecture table. The five original figures remain visually unchanged apart from placement and size.

P-35310D7F3D.title: View Space: Learning Representation across Arbitrary Graphs

descriptions.M1: The GVT encoder, recurrent architecture and training objective remain unchanged. Appendix L adds RGVT+TabPFN as an optional predictor variant, replacing per-dataset classifier fitting with in-context prediction. This is a limited extension of the inference procedure.
descriptions.E1: Both versions cover the same 28 main benchmark graphs, six non-attributed graph settings and seven graphs with LLM-embedded features. V2's new 17- and 23-dataset comparisons use subsets of existing coverage; they introduce no additional graph domains or prediction tasks.
descriptions.E2: V2 adds comparisons with NodeFormer, LSGNN, DirGNN and SGFormer in Table 14, and TS-Net variants, TAG and NodePFN in Tables 16–17. Those tables also introduce the Products-pretrained GraphAny variant. The original comparisons remain, expanding the evaluated comparator set.
descriptions.E3: The original experimental settings are retained, but v2 adds separate RGVT evaluations under TAG and NodePFN pipelines, a TabPFN comparison restricted to 17 compatible datasets, and transfer-depth sweeps. Figure 9 also introduces Elo and improvability metrics. These expand the evaluation design without establishing changes to the retained experiments.
descriptions.E4: New appendices analyze predictor substitution, transfer-depth sensitivity across 28 graphs, and t-SNE representations on Amazon Photo and Coauthor CS. The transfer-depth analysis differs from the retained pretraining-depth ablation. The aggregation heatmaps also replace the first-versus-eighth-layer comparison with a comparison between random-walk and symmetric-normalized views.
