descriptions.E5: Both versions report five independent runs with means and standard deviations and retain the identical Wilcoxon signed-rank analysis in Appendix A. Additional result tables and plots do not establish a changed repetition count, uncertainty-estimation procedure or significance-testing practice.
descriptions.E6: The original table means and standard deviations are unchanged, but results are added. Table 13 reports 70.70% for RGVT+TabPFN versus 70.03% for RGVT+MLP on 17 datasets; Table 14 reports 71.00% for SGFormer versus 71.13% for RGVT+MLP. Tables 16–17 add pipeline-specific comparisons with newer GFMs, rather than same-setting improvements over v1. V2 also introduces a 5 ms inference statement that conflicts with the retained 0.052 seconds in Table 10.
descriptions.T1: The formal view-space definitions, permutation-equivariance statements, linear-aggregation analysis, local-linearization result and proofs in Appendices B–E are substantively retained. Notation, equation numbering and explanatory wording change without adding or revising formal results.
descriptions.C1: Despite the new title and revised framing, the abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: FI-NRL, view space, GVT and RGVT. The headline claims of +8.93% over GraphAny and at least +3.30% over 12 individually tuned GNNs also remain unchanged.
descriptions.C2: Section 9 expands the discussion of absent explicit cross-feature mixing, its scalability tradeoff, predictor-training requirements, TabPFN limitations and recurrent-depth selection overhead. New analyses support interpretations about preserving feature structure and using fixed depths. Appendix O acknowledges narrower accuracy margins against newer GNNs and emphasizes adaptation efficiency.
descriptions.D1: V2 newly supplies a code-and-checkpoint link in the abstract and reports approximately three days on four H200 GPUs for the additional GNN comparisons. Existing hyperparameters, optimizer, stopping rules and A6000 runtime setup remain unchanged. The added pipelines receive limited implementation detail.
descriptions.R1: V2 adds substantive positioning relative to tabular foundation models and recent fully inductive graph models, particularly TAG and NodePFN. Previously cited TS-Net becomes an evaluated comparator. New discussion and citations for recent GNNs broaden the assessment of competitiveness and adaptation cost beyond the original GraphAny-centered comparison.
descriptions.P1: The title, abstract and introduction are rewritten, contributions become an explicit numbered list, and several section headings and explanations are revised. The ablation and visualization subsections exchange order, a dedicated Discussion section is introduced, and new appendices shift the dataset-details and full-results sections.
descriptions.P2: The main text changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column proceedings layout. The original overview figure is split into two figures, aggregation heatmaps are redesigned, and new depth, representation and comparison plots and tables are added. Table 1 loses its relative-improvement rows, while the original full GNN table is enlarged and split across Tables 20–21.

P-8260FD36A0.title: Render-of-Thought: Rendering Textual Chain-of-Thought as Images for Visual Latent Reasoning

descriptions.M1: The rendering procedure, visual projection head, two-stage training, losses, and dynamic/fixed-budget decoding procedures remain unchanged. Applying existing baselines to another backbone does not establish a change to RoT.
descriptions.E1: v3 retains GSM8k-Aug, GSM-Hard, SVAMP, MultiArith, and MATH, and adds actual evaluations on GPQA and ProsQA in Appendix F. These extend the evaluated coverage from mathematical problems to scientific question answering and logical reasoning.
descriptions.E2: The original comparator sets remain intact. New Tables 8-9 reuse Coconut, CODI, and CoLaR-2, already evaluated in v1. The documented differences concern backbone settings and task coverage; no comparator-algorithm revision is specified.
descriptions.E3: Appendix E adds a controlled comparison placing RoT and three baselines on Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, addressing the differing backbones in retained Table 2. Appendix D introduces training-time measurements with matched three-epoch budgets, batch size 16, and one H20 GPU. Existing experimental protocols are retained.
descriptions.E4: Appendices D-E add analyses of training overhead and whether backbone differences explain RoT's advantage, extending the efficiency and attribution evidence. Existing stage, projection-head, rendering, decoding, and case analyses remain unchanged. Appendix G adds discussion, not another termination experiment.
descriptions.E5: The five-seed/95% confidence-interval statement and existing uncertainty entries remain unchanged. New appendix tables report point values, as earlier appendix ablation tables already did; no changed run counts or statistical estimation procedures are specified.
descriptions.E6: Tables 7-9 add training times of 56.1 hours for RoT versus 36.9 for SFT-CoT, VLM-based comparator results including CoLaR-2's 45.3 average versus RoT's retained 55.4, and RoT Pass@1 scores of 60.5 on GPQA and 100.0 on ProsQA. Original Tables 1-6 and plotted findings are unchanged. The new backbone results are additional evaluations, not corrections or same-setting performance changes.
descriptions.T1: The loss equations, termination definition, and special-token normalization remain unchanged. Appendix G's continuous-space explanation introduces no formal assumption, theorem, derivation, or proof.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and introduction replace claims of maintaining competitive performance with an efficiency-accuracy Pareto framing, qualifying the performance claim around a tradeoff. The novelty, analyzability, plug-and-play, and compression contributions remain unchanged; logical-reasoning coverage was already claimed in v1.
descriptions.C2: New discussion interprets the shared-backbone results as evidence against a pretraining-only explanation and argues that inference savings offset training overhead. Appendix G strengthens the termination explanation into an asserted intrinsic continuous-space difficulty, without a new causal test. Existing limitations and case interpretations are retained.
descriptions.D1: v3 adds homepage and model-collection access links and documents hardware, epoch allocation, and measured costs for the training-time comparison. Original implementation hyperparameters remain unchanged. The new GPQA/ProsQA evaluation receives only a general statement that implementation details are consistent with the existing setup.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds the GPQA reference by Rein et al. and expands discussion connecting termination difficulties to the already cited LVR work. The related-work section and central novelty positioning otherwise remain unchanged.
descriptions.P1: Changes include limited abstract/introduction wording, author-order and affiliation edits, and four new appendix sections with an expanded contents list. The case study becomes Appendix H, with updated cross-references. The existing narrative is largely retained.
descriptions.P2: v3 adds three compact appendix tables and a title-page resource strip. Figure 2 moves earlier, some tables become more compact, and appendix material shifts. Original figure content and existing table structures remain intact.

descriptions.M1: The hard, soft, and update-driven interruption procedures and the prompt-guidance intervention already appear in v1 and remain in v4. The paraphrase ablation, additional comparators, and proprietary-model proxy do not establish a revision to the proposed core method.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24/25, and LiveCodeBench-v6, including their augmented update-driven problems. The added controls, model evaluations, and annotation checks use this existing coverage; no additional application domain or benchmark task is evaluated.
descriptions.E2: v4 evaluates Chain of Draft against ordinary Qwen3-8B reasoning under all three interruption modes (Section 6.4); v1 only cites it. Appendix F.2 also adds evaluated DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama and Nemotron-3-Nano comparisons beyond the original model families, expanding the comparative evidence.
descriptions.E3: v4 adds paragraph-boundary interruption experiments, an augmented-problem/no-update control, larger model configurations, and a GPT-5.4-Mini proxy with internal reasoning disabled. Human validation introduces two 50-sample checks and multiple panic thresholds. Appendix F.4 re-bins existing runs by absolute character length; it does not establish new fixed-token-budget experiments.
descriptions.E4: New analyses test guidance paraphrasing, possible benchmark memorization, interruption boundaries, and dependence on relative indexing. Appendix E adds panic-threshold sensitivity and human checks of panic and self-doubt labels. The original scaling, turn-role, and speedup analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.
descriptions.E5: Appendix E newly reports coefficients of variation across panic thresholds and human agreement estimates for the automated labels. Both versions retain 16 AIME trials, single runs elsewhere, and bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals; v4 does not establish increased repeated-run counts or specify a new significance-testing procedure.
descriptions.E6: v4 adds extensive model, comparator, and robustness results, including 90% panic-label agreement and 88% self-doubt-label agreement in Appendix E. Section 6.4 newly reports AIME panic rates of 13.1% with Chain of Draft versus 3.8% with regular reasoning at position 0.3. Existing LiveCodeBench update-driven curves also change substantially in Figures 4, 6, and 8, without an explanation establishing whether these are corrections or reruns.
descriptions.T1: The inference formalization, interruption-conditioned accuracy and length definitions, and necessary-update condition in Section 3 are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the new operational labeling criteria and empirical analyses do not revise the mathematical framework.
descriptions.C1: v4 narrows the contribution framing from a new analytical framework for persistent interruptible agents to an evaluation setting, benchmark, and error taxonomy, explicitly emphasizing single-round experiments. The central claims about dynamic fragility, the three failure modes, and drops of up to 60% remain.
descriptions.C2: v4 adds substantive interpretations concerning memorization controls, prompt sensitivity, problem difficulty, and why compact reasoning does not eliminate interruption failures. It narrows the coding-fragility discussion particularly to Qwen3 and explains that the proprietary-API proxy cannot establish native-reasoning behavior. The limitations also clarify the diagnostic scope and requirements for future interruption-aware training.
descriptions.D1: v4 discloses the 1% remaining-context panic criterion, GPT-5 self-doubt classification, annotation sample counts, a paraphrased guidance prompt, and the dataset acceptance rate. It specifies an MIT license and replaces the dataset-collection link with a direct benchmark-dataset link. The original prompts and general hardware/hyperparameter descriptions largely remain.
descriptions.R1: v4 adds model and software references, including Nemotron-3-Nano, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3, SillyTavern, and text-generation-webui. It explicitly connects the study to Chain of Draft through evaluation, while retaining the overall positioning against efficient reasoning under static contexts.
descriptions.P1: The overall narrative sequence and much existing prose remain. v4 revises the abstract, contribution bullets, experimental rationale, and conclusion; separates limitations from the conclusion; and adds an impact statement and human-validation appendix. These are localized editorial and structural changes rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.
descriptions.P2: v4 converts the main paper to a two-column conference layout, resizing and relocating existing multi-panel figures. It adds baseline and robustness figures, extensive appendix plots, and two validation tables. The original appendix plots are matched to Figures F.23–F.27, with some revised displays and results.

P-E3633DE5CC.title: ECHO: Ego-centric Modeling of Human-Object Interactions

descriptions.M1: Sections 3.1–3.3 replace window-based canonicalization with per-frame head-centric representations and conveyor inference with smooth overlapping-window inpainting. Human root transformation is inferred through head alignment rather than diffused. Binary contacts become continuous, conditioning changes, and training uses clean/noisy modality combinations with synchronized noise. Appendix losses replace object vertex reconstruction with object-motion smoothness.
descriptions.E1: BEHAVE, OMOMO and AMASS remain the principal training and evaluation datasets. v2 adds intermittent hand-tracking scenarios and qualitative evaluation on one Aria Digital Twin sequence with novel motion and objects (Figure 6), providing a limited extension of the existing HOI task coverage.
descriptions.E2: Tables 1–2 revise the comparator set. Standalone BoDiffusion disappears from both comparisons, and the original AMASS EgoAllo comparison is replaced by EgoAllo+H+O, which also enters the HOI comparison. BoDiffusion+Obj is retained as BoDiffusion+O; that renaming alone is not an addition.
descriptions.E3: Reported model size, training steps and learning rate change from 47.3M, 400k and 1e-4 to 57.7M, 300k and 5e-4. Contact accuracy replaces quaternion difference in Table 1. Sparse-observation percentages change from 1/5/10/25/100 to 10/25/50/100, and new hand-dropout protocols are introduced. Dataset splits, 30-fps processing and 60-frame training windows remain.
descriptions.E4: v2 adds hand-dropout robustness tests on both HOI datasets, a smooth-inpainting ablation, and NoAMASS evaluation on AMASS. It removes the NoAuxLoss and NoCan ablations from both dataset-specific ablation tables. Appendix Table S2 also extends the additional-modality analysis to OMOMO.
descriptions.E5: Section 4.1 changes the reported aggregation for Tables 1–2 from four runs to three. Table 1 newly supplies uncertainty values for foot-contact scores. Both versions otherwise retain the same general mean-and-variance reporting approach.
descriptions.E6: Results are extensively replaced under revised models and settings. ECHO's BEHAVE MPJPE changes from 61.4 mm to 6.8 cm, object vertex error from 29.5 to 33.5 cm, and AMASS MPJPE from 93.9 mm to 7.4 cm. v2 adds contact-accuracy, dropout and additional conditioning results. Changed configurations and comparator membership prevent interpreting these as controlled same-setting gains or losses.
descriptions.T1: v2 revises mathematical definitions of human state, contacts and egocentric conditioning, changes the loss formulation, and adds explicit guidance and smooth-inpainting equations in Appendix Section 9. These change the formal specification. The new skating equation, Eq. 18, sums consecutive joint positions, which appears inconsistent with its stated skating-penalty purpose.
descriptions.C1: The first unified sparse-tracking HOI framework claim remains. However, the abstract, introduction and conclusion replace the conveyor-inference contribution with smooth inpainting, remove the standalone novelty claim for the head-centric representation, and explicitly add robustness claims concerning intermittent hand tracking and sensor noise.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds explanations of overlap blending and training stability, interprets substantial hand-tracking degradation as emerging around 75% missing input, and refines limitations concerning dynamic environments, finger detail and missing RGB-based datasets. The central interpretations about contacts connecting modalities and AMASS supplying human-motion priors remain.
descriptions.D1: v2 expands implementation documentation: rotary embeddings, AMASS conditioning tokens, guidance weights and update scale, a 30-frame overlap, and blending factor 0.4 are specified. Loss weights, training hardware and timing reports are revised; inference timing now includes guidance. Both versions still promise future code and model release.
descriptions.R1: v2 explicitly positions its representation as extending EgoAllo and its inference as extending HMD2, replacing the earlier conveyor lineage through Diffusion Forcing and The Matrix. Related work adds distinctions from EgoGrasp and WHOLE and expands coverage of recent egocentric methods. These change methodological attribution and positioning beyond bibliographic updates.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work gains numbered subsections, and the appendix gains a roadmap and separate implementation-details and metrics sections. This is narrative restructuring beyond edits required by the new experiments.
descriptions.P2: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figures 2–4 are redrawn; qualitative comparisons are reorganized between Figure 5 and Figure S1 with an added comparator. Figure 6 and dropout tables are added, while existing tables receive revised columns, rows and captions.

P-DBA7C8B88B.title: Reliable Evaluation Protocol for Low-Precision Retrieval

descriptions.M1: The HPS operation and TRM computations remain unchanged. However, Section 2.3 relaxes the protocol's prescribed outputs: v3 recommends expectation plus range, whereas v4 permits an expectation or conventional tie-oblivious score alone after HPS or internal TRM stability verification.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use MIRACLReranking's English subset, AskUbuntuDupQuestions, and the same ten English MTEB-R datasets. The new Appendix C diagnostics reuse existing coverage; moving dataset descriptions into Section 3.1 does not add tasks or populations.
descriptions.E2: The corresponding benchmark comparisons retain the same five models and precision regimes. 'multilingual-e5-large-large' is corrected to 'multilingual-e5-large.' Random tie-breaking, raw logits, and temperature scaling remain conceptual alternatives rather than newly evaluated baselines.
descriptions.E3: New Appendix C evaluates unique-score counts and average tie-group sizes at cutoffs from 1 to 1000, plus Spearman correlation against FP32 rankings. Existing splits, input lengths, batch size, and retrieval metrics are retained. The BM25/top-1000 statement supplies previously undocumented settings for the existing MTEB-R experiment.
descriptions.E4: Appendix C adds supporting analyses asking how frequently scores collide, how large tie groups become, and whether HPS preserves FP32 ordering. These extend the existing score examples and metric-stability analyses without introducing broader robustness scenarios or component ablations.
descriptions.E5: Section 2.3 changes the uncertainty-reporting recommendation from expectation plus range to permitting a single score after HPS or internal stability verification. The experimental tables retain their range/bias reporting; neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
descriptions.E6: All 25 existing benchmark result rows and the result plots are unchanged. New Tables 3–5 report additional diagnostics, including 81.34 versus 84.09 unique scores at k=100 for BF16 versus BF16+HPS, and corresponding FP32 rank correlations of 0.998960 versus 0.998961. These are newly reported measurements, not improvements over v3's results.
descriptions.T1: Appendix C.2 newly defines the tie-size diagnostic as k divided by the number of unique scores. Otherwise, the closed-form expectations, complexity arguments, and raw-logit/sigmoid derivation are unchanged. The upcast definition is relocated, and equation renumbering does not alter the mathematics.
descriptions.C1: The conclusion newly claims to be the first to identify and formally analyze the low-precision evaluation problem. It also replaces the direct claim of enabling more stable retrieval in RAG with a more qualified claim of providing a foundation for downstream applications. The central HPS/TRM contributions remain.
descriptions.C2: v4 explicitly acknowledges the absence of downstream RAG evaluation, removes the limitation about untested TRM interpretability, and adds a non-interval-scale caveat for nDCG/MRR. Appendix G.2 weakens the unconditional metadata-independence fairness guarantee, while Appendix C interprets rank agreement as recovery of meaningful distinctions.
descriptions.D1: v4 replaces the promised post-review code release with a repository location and specifies BM25 retrieval of 1000 candidates for MTEB-R. Existing implementation settings and the HPS code example are mostly relocated into the main text. The PDFs establish the access statement, not the repository's contents or functionality.
descriptions.R1: v4 adds citations to Ash and Doléans-Dade, Goldberg, Guo et al., and Micikevicius et al. in existing methodological discussions, and removes Salton's reference. It also adds the explicit priority claim in the conclusion. The relationship to McSherry and Najork's tie-aware expectations remains unchanged.
descriptions.P1: v4 moves the upcast explanation and experimental details into Sections 2.2 and 3.1, consolidates appendices, and transfers detailed-results guidance into captions. Reporting, conclusion, and limitations paragraphs are revised, but most prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.
descriptions.P2: v4 adds three diagnostic tables, moves the HPS implementation figure into the main text, and expands figure/table captions. The retained MTEB-R table gains performance underlining. Existing scientific graphics are unchanged, and the two-column layout is retained.

P-5DD71D7FFC.title: DataMIL: Selecting Data for Robot Imitation Learning with Datamodels

descriptions.M1: Both versions use clustered regression or metagradient datamodels, the behavior-cloning proxy, target-data splitting for OXE, ranked selection and downstream policy training. v2 provides operational details and pseudocode for the existing estimators; it does not establish a replacement algorithm, architecture or objective.
descriptions.E1: MetaWorld, LIBERO and the OXE subsets, robot embodiments and target tasks are retained. LIBERO-5 comprises five already evaluated LIBERO-10 tasks, and the extended proxy tests use tasks already covered by MetaWorld. These additions change analyses and experimental subsets rather than task or domain coverage.
descriptions.E2: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain the same retrieval methods and Target-Only, All-Data or Random controls. New ablations reuse existing comparators. CUPID and COLLAGE enter the related-work discussion but are not evaluated as baselines; longer All-Data training changes its budget rather than its identity.
descriptions.E3: Appendix C introduces controlled evaluations varying selection percentages from 5% to 30%, clustering at 15 steps, 30 steps or whole trajectories, co-training ratios of 0.3/0.5/0.7, and All-Data training budgets of 1×/2×/4×. Main benchmark protocols are retained. Regression sampling is also reported as p=0.1 in v2 Appendix H, versus Bernoulli(1/2) in v1 Appendix B.2; this documentation change does not establish reruns.
descriptions.E4: v2 expands tests of the method's design choices: proxy-versus-rollout selection extends from one to four MetaWorld tasks, Figure 13 tests selection budget, clustering and co-training sensitivity, and Appendix C.6 checks whether longer training helps All-Data. Appendix A.2 adds LIBERO selection case studies. The no-goal MetaWorld analysis already existed in v1.
descriptions.E5: Both versions report three MetaWorld seeds, five LIBERO seeds and one real-world seed. Figure 13 continues five-seed averaging. There is no new significance-testing or confidence-interval procedure; correction of an individual uncertainty value changes a result, not the reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: The LIBERO/OXE benchmark means in v1 Table 3 are retained in v2 Table 1, but v2 adds sensitivity, proxy-comparison and qualitative results. Appendix C.6 reports All-Data success of 43.36, 44.13 and 38.40 at 1×, 2× and 4× training. The malformed STRAP Soup-Sauce uncertainty entry is also corrected to 15.7.
descriptions.T1: v2 Appendix B.3 adds explicit definitions of training-count perturbations and stochastic metagradient updates in Equations 11–12. Appendix B.2 generalizes inclusion probability from 1/2 to p. The underlying datamodel objective and first-order influence approximation were already present; moving the Taylor expansion into the main text is not new theory, and no theorem or proof is added.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adapting datamodels to offline robotic data selection through a differentiable surrogate, scaling to larger policies and heterogeneous datasets, and improving task success. The additional evidence supports these existing claims without redefining their scientific scope.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds interpretations connecting reduced selection advantages at larger budgets to inclusion of more useful data, finer clusters to more precise selection, and excessive All-Data training to overfitting. It also interprets LIBERO retrieval through scene and object similarity. The computational, hyperparameter and target-scale limitations already existed in v1 and are consolidated into the conclusion.
descriptions.D1: Algorithms 1–2 and Appendices G–H expand reproducibility information: estimator pseudocode, gradient averaging, 10,000 regression fits, sampling probability, MLP dimensions, metagradient iteration counts, training steps, the final 100-step differentiation window, optimizers and schedules. Hardware and runtime estimates are newly documented across the experimental settings.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds COLLAGE, CUPID, DataRater and work on scale transfer and robot dataset factors, while pruning several broad background references. It replaces v1's statement that robotic data attribution was unknown with a comparison to concurrent CUPID, emphasizing offline selection from heterogeneous datasets. The broader datamodel-versus-heuristic positioning remains intact.
descriptions.P1: Targeted rewrites expand the metagradient explanation, tighten introductory and experimental prose, and revise appendix cross-references. The separate limitations section is merged into the conclusion, and existing appendix results are regrouped before implementation details. The overall narrative and most existing exposition remain recognizable.
descriptions.P2: v2 expands the visual presentation with LIBERO selection plots, the extended proxy comparison, a three-panel ablation figure, two algorithm displays and a hyperparameter table. The real-world sample montage moves from v1 Figure 7 in the main text to v2 Figure 10 in the appendix. Existing benchmark tables and plots are largely retained.

P-5545494030.title: Toward Culturally Aligned LLMs through Ontology-Guided Multi-Agent Reasoning

descriptions.M1: The main pipeline and agent prompts remain substantially unchanged. However, v1 Section 3.2.1 filters retrieval through top-p subclasses Fq, whereas v3 describes retrieval across subclasses of selected top-level classes. v3 Section 3.3 still specifies top-3 fine-grained category selection. This inconsistency prevents determining whether retrieval actually changed or its description was corrected.
descriptions.E1: v3 Appendix C.3 adds ISSP 2023 as a cross-national survey evaluation described as a post-cutoff control, covering five continents including Oceania. The WVS retrieval corpus and six original regional evaluations remain, so coverage expands within the existing survey-response task.
descriptions.E2: v3 Appendix D.1 adds CultureLLM as a post-training comparator on the six regional datasets. The five original Table 1 baselines remain unchanged. CultureLLM uses Qwen 3.5-9B, whereas the displayed OG-MAR results use the original four backbones, limiting direct method-level comparison.
descriptions.E3: v3 adds EMD, Proportion Correlation, and TVD evaluation, including a separately evaluated persona-vote distribution variant. New protocols include 500 ISSP respondents sampled across five continents, CultureLLM fine-tuning, and component-removal controls. Section 4.3 also clarifies response-type scoring and ordinal-scale MAE; this clarification does not establish that the original evaluations were rerun.
descriptions.E4: v3 adds topic-classifier error propagation analysis, ontology and demographic-removal ablations, a controlled single-agent demographic comparison, and analysis of information retained in persona vote proportions. It also adds an ISSP contamination control and comparative mechanism case studies. The original retrieval-size, value-inference, and single-judge analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: Appendix H.1.3 newly reports inter-group ontology-selection reliability using Cohen's kappa, with κ = 0.68. Both versions already specify paired t-tests with Holm–Bonferroni correction. Newly added significance markers on Table 1 averages are additional outcomes, not evidence of a changed testing procedure or increased run count.
descriptions.E6: v3 adds distributional, ISSP, CultureLLM, classifier-error, component-ablation, and qualitative results. ISSP accuracies for OG-MAR are 0.6879, 0.5760, 0.6693, and 0.5318 across the four backbones, leading the reported comparisons. Original main accuracies are largely retained, but Table 1 changes EXAONE ValuesRAG's average from 0.5631 to 0.5613 and adds average-score significance markers. Some displayed evidence in retained case traces also changes.
descriptions.T1: The written mathematical specification changes: v3 removes the explicit Fq selection definition and its retrieval restriction, and corrects the persona-output set from respondent–triple indexing to respondent-only indexing. These are limited formal-definition revisions without new theorems or proofs. The explicit 12-plus-64 hierarchy otherwise restates the taxonomy already documented in v1 Table 16.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: ontology-guided, demographically grounded multi-persona reasoning improves cultural alignment and interpretability. The additional evaluations support this existing contribution rather than redefine its central scientific claim.
descriptions.C2: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning taxonomy mismatch, minority-profile retrieval, propagation of inaccurate ontology relations, and inference cost. Its Impact Statement addresses demographic profiling, stereotypes, privacy, and oversight. New analyses also introduce interpretations of classifier-error resilience, distributional information loss, and backbone-dependent component contributions, while the cost discussion narrows the framework's intended use.
descriptions.D1: v3 newly documents ontology candidate counts and filtering criteria, senior-expert review, and blinded topic-label annotation. It supplies CultureLLM hyperparameters and regional language mappings, ISSP source and sampling details, and repository and classifier access links. These supplement the extensive prompts, core training settings, hardware information, and dataset links already present in v1; they do not establish that the existing implementation was rebuilt.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds CultureLLM and explicitly positions OG-MAR against culture-specific post-training, alongside new citations for Cohen's kappa and ISSP. The original related-work discussion and ontology-based positioning remain substantially unchanged. Consolidating and updating the WVS reference is bibliographic maintenance.
descriptions.P1: v3 standardizes top-class/sub-class terminology, revises selected method, metric, and discussion passages, and adds limitations, impact, availability, and acknowledgement sections. Appendix headings and cross-references are updated. Most existing prose and the overall narrative order remain, making the editorial changes targeted rather than a wholesale rewrite.
descriptions.P2: v3 adds tables for classifier errors, distributional evaluations, ISSP, CultureLLM, component ablations, and comparative cases, plus a new ontology-construction schematic in Figure 14. Figure 1 receives graphical refinements, and existing displays are reflowed or relocated. The original ontology visualizations and sensitivity plots are retained rather than newly introduced.

P-3C10B80CE9.title: Remaining-data-free Machine Unlearning by Suppressing Sample Contribution

descriptions.M1: The basic sensitivity-gap objective remains, but Algorithm 1 replaces v1's loss-change stopping criterion with a criterion tracking recovery of irrelevant-class sensitivity relative to its initial value and minimum. Appendix C-D also introduces dynamic loss reweighting, using kappa=80 for Tiny ImageNet and early sequential subclass requests. These alter termination and optimization, rather than merely documenting the existing method.
descriptions.E1: v2 adds Tiny ImageNet, SVHN, and the Lamp subclass evaluation while retaining the earlier datasets and task families. It also introduces sequential deletion of five distinct classes or five related subclasses. These scenarios add the requirement that previous forgetting survive subsequent unlearning requests, which v1 does not evaluate.
descriptions.E2: v2 retains v1's five comparators, with Blindspot renamed Bad Teacher (BT), and adds Boundary Expand, EU-k, CF-k, SCRUB, DUCK, SalUn, NG, RL, JiT, and SCAR in reported comparisons. Boundary Shrink also enters subclass comparisons, where v1 excluded it. This broadens the evaluated comparator set.
descriptions.E3: Random-subset deletion changes from 100 CIFAR-10 samples to 10%. v2 adds VGG-16 and ImageNet-initialized ViT configurations, test accuracy, average-gap and output KL-divergence metrics, and sequential-request evaluation procedures. Reported MU-Mis learning rates also differ from v1's stated range. These are substantive evaluation changes, separate from newly disclosed implementation details.
descriptions.E4: v2 adds sequential-unlearning robustness analyses examining recovery of forgotten knowledge and accumulated utility damage, plus learning-rate and stopping-threshold studies in Figures 4–7 and 9. The attention-map and pairwise-gradient analyses are retained. The loss ablation is revised: v1's two-stage TC-then-OC experiment is removed, as is its Appendix A.2 trajectory comparing forgetting-data and remaining-data sensitivity gaps.
descriptions.E5: v1 presents point estimates without specifying repeated-run counts or uncertainty. v2 introduces means and standard deviations over five independent trials in Table I and carries this reporting format into other benchmark tables. This is a substantial change in statistical reporting; v1 supplies no prior run count from which an increase in repetitions could be established.
descriptions.E6: Benchmark results are extensively revised and expanded. For CIFAR-20 Sea, MU-Mis forgetting accuracy changes from 97.66 to 81.00 ± 2.95, while the retrained reference changes from 97.05 to 80.93 ± 2.20 (v1 Table 4; v2 Table II). New architecture, dataset, sequential-unlearning, and hyperparameter results add findings. Changed protocols and reference models prevent interpreting these revisions as same-setting performance gains.
descriptions.T1: The central contribution/residual decomposition is retained. v2 explicitly states approximations neglecting probability derivatives and changes in the training-dependent gradient mapping, distinguishes infinitesimal self-influence from leave-one-out memorization, and adds an MLP/ReLU derivation in Section III-B, Eqs. (6)–(7). These are limited mathematical extensions and refinements within the existing approximate theoretical framework.
descriptions.C1: v1 already claims effective, efficient unlearning without remaining data. v2 adds an explicit claim to be the first remaining-data-free method to outperform state-of-the-art methods using remaining data, alongside claims of sequential-unlearning resilience and easy hyperparameter tuning. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion thus expand the claimed novelty and practical capabilities.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds interpretations of sequential failures as knowledge recovery, knowledge residue, and utility breakdown, and connects input sensitivity to generative classifier interpretations and privacy. It acknowledges weaker random-subset competitiveness of remaining-data-free methods. Conversely, v1's concluding limitations about unexplained utility preservation and imperfect contribution estimation disappear, although v2 still describes the sensitivity surrogate as approximate.
descriptions.D1: Appendix C adds training schedules, optimizers, batch sizes, frozen batch-normalization instructions, baseline implementation sources, and extensive hyperparameter settings and search ranges. Hardware changes from RTX 2080Ti to RTX 4090. Much of this is newly disclosed information rather than demonstrated changes to earlier procedures. v1's promise to release MU-Mis code is absent; v2's implementation links identify baseline sources.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds a dedicated remaining-data-free related-work subsection positioning MU-Mis against JiT and SCAR. It expands connections to influence estimation, sequential-unlearning evaluation, input curvature, memorization, privacy, and generative interpretations of classifiers. These change the research positioning beyond citation formatting or publication-metadata updates.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around remaining-data-free unlearning. v1's unified Method section becomes separate analysis and proposed-method sections; experiments and appendices are reorganized, and the Broader Impacts section is removed. The title and author block also change. This is narrative restructuring.
descriptions.P2: v2 adopts a different document template and replaces compact benchmark tables with broader tables containing additional metrics, comparator groupings, and uncertainty displays. v1 Figures 3–4 are combined and expanded into v2 Figure 3; attention maps move from Figure 6 to Figure 8, and the gradient histograms become Appendix Figure A2. New sequential and hyperparameter plots change the visual presentation.

P-28ED89B51A.title: AFFMAE: Scalable Vision Pre-Training for High-Resolution Microscopy Segmentation on Desktop Hardware

descriptions.M1: V2 introduces cached, quantized-grid KNN retrieval in place of separate neighbor searches for decoder queries (Sections 3.3 and 7.1). This is a localized procedural change to the retained framework of adaptive merging, stable interpolation, Perlin masking, and deep supervision.
descriptions.E1: V2 adds evaluations on Lucchi++, Kasthuri++, and the 2012 ISBI EM Challenge, broadening microscopy coverage beyond FPW. The reported FPW segmentation task also narrows from four foreground classes to the basement-membrane interface and filtration slits, retaining background.
descriptions.E2: The FPW comparison expands from ViT-MAE in v1 Table 1 to include SimMIM, MixMAE, GreenMIM, HiViT, and nnU-Net V2 in v2 Table 2. These are evaluated comparators, whereas several appeared only as related work in v1.
descriptions.E3: Reported main models increase from approximately 22M to 65M parameters, with pretraining/fine-tuning schedules changing from 300/700 to 400/400 epochs. FPW test size changes from 164 to 235, and resolutions from 448/512/768 to 512/768/1024. V2 also introduces CLAHE preprocessing, UperNet baseline heads, Slits IoU and FPW-error metrics, revised memory-measurement batch sizes, and public-benchmark protocols.
descriptions.E4: V2 adds controls for initialization source, deepest-stage-only reconstruction, ViT with the point decoder, and cached versus standard decoder execution. It removes v1's training-data-fraction study (Figure 11) and the 65% masking-ratio ablation entry. Existing representation-collapse and spectral analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: V2 Table 2 first reports main FPW scores as mean ± standard deviation across four random seeds. Table 4 additionally reports timing variation over 30 trials. V1 provides point estimates without corresponding model-run or uncertainty information; an increase from a known v1 run count cannot be established.
descriptions.E6: Main and ablation results are extensively replaced: AFFMAE's 512-pixel mIoU is 0.6030 in v1 Table 1 versus 0.608 ± 0.002 in v2 Table 2 under revised settings, not a same-setting gain. V2 adds FPW errors, decoder timings, and public-benchmark results, including AFFMAE mIoUs of 0.8829, 0.8870, and 0.8661 in Table 6.
descriptions.T1: V2 adds limited complexity arguments: cached KNN retrieval is effectively O(1) per query after table construction, and the volumetric discussion derives O(n^6) versus O(n^4) dense-attention scaling. Core interpolation and normalized-effective-rank mathematics remain equivalent; no theorem or proof framework is introduced.
descriptions.C1: The central contribution remains efficient, mask-agnostic hierarchical pretraining with ViT-level microscopy segmentation. V2 refines the headline contributions toward reusable segmentation decoding, 2× pretraining and 5× fine-tuning speedups, and better slit segmentation than grid-based hierarchies, replacing v1's emphasis on up to 7× FLOP reduction.
descriptions.C2: V2 adds substantive discussion of token-location interpretability, volumetric applicability, and bandwidth/cache limitations that can erode efficiency at very high resolutions. It also replaces v1's interpretation of robustness at 75% masking with an account of noticeable degradation and explains the failure of deepest-stage-only reconstruction.
descriptions.D1: Supplementary Sections 7.1–7.7 add architecture configurations, cached-neighbor implementation details, preprocessing parameters, segmentation-head adaptation, benchmark-specific optimization settings, and measured pretraining hours. Hardware disclosure also expands to identify H100-trained baselines, although this conflicts with the main text's blanket RTX 5090 description.
descriptions.R1: Research positioning shifts toward kidney ultrastructure and comparisons with sparse hierarchical masked-modeling approaches. V2 adds GreenMIM, HiViT, clinical FPW, public-benchmark, and segmentation-decoder references while removing the separate adaptive-token survey covering DynamicViT, A-ViT, and AdaViT. The earlier broad criticism of competing hierarchical methods is rewritten.
descriptions.P1: The title, introduction, related work, method explanations, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Method subsections are reorganized, ablations precede main results, and dedicated discussion/limitations and supplementary sections replace the earlier compact structure.
descriptions.P2: V2 switches to a single-column layout, merges existing collapse and masking figures, redesigns efficiency displays, and expands comparison-table structure. New architecture/cache diagrams and qualitative panels are added, while v1's data-efficiency plot is removed. These are substantive display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

P-AC8F5D883F.title: Simulated Students in Tutoring Dialogues: Substance or Illusion?

descriptions.M1: The seven metrics, student and evaluator models, SFT procedure, and offline DPO pipeline are unchanged. Appendix B.2 newly explains the development of the dialogue-act taxonomy, but the final definitions in Table 6 and associated prompts remain identical.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate student-turn simulation using the same Question-Anchored Tutoring Dialogues 2k dataset of UK middle-school mathematics tutoring. No additional datasets, populations, domains, or task scenarios are evaluated.
descriptions.E2: Table 1 retains the same SFT/DPO models and Zero-Shot, OCEAN, ICL, Reasoning, and Oracle comparators. Membership also remains unchanged in the human evaluation and reward ablation. Newly cited methods are not added as evaluated baselines.
descriptions.E3: Both retain the 1,147/382/382 train/validation/test dialogue split, seven evaluation metrics, and training and decoding settings. Human evaluation still covers 190 turns across 38 dialogues with three evaluators. The ablation still uses a random 20% test subset.
descriptions.E4: Section 4.3 adds a brief case comparison of Reasoning, SFT, and real-student replies to illustrate differences in grammatical formality and punctuation. The reward ablations, label-distribution analyses, and performance-by-turn analyses remain unchanged.
descriptions.E5: The Cohen's kappa and Pearson correlation reporting remains unchanged, with no added repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing procedures. The new discussion of unpredictable student behavior concerns interpretation rather than statistical uncertainty estimation.
descriptions.E6: Quantitative results in the tables and figures are unchanged. Section 4.3 newly reports a qualitative example: Reasoning produces 'Yes, thanks — I'll enter D.', SFT produces 'yes thank you', and the real student says 'yes', supporting the added observation about prompting methods' formal language.
descriptions.T1: The mathematical definitions and equations for simulation, training, and evaluation are unchanged. The new suggestion that attainable metric scores may fall below one is an informal qualification, without a formal bound, derivation, or proof.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and main findings: reference-based evaluation of simulated student turns, benchmarking prompting and fine-tuning, and improved but still limited realism from fine-tuning and preference optimization.
descriptions.C2: Section 2.3 newly warns that training against LLM-evaluated metrics can exploit evaluator errors and recommends expert human checks. Section 4.2 qualifies the interpretation of poor scores by acknowledging an unknown attainable ceiling arising from randomness in student behavior.
descriptions.D1: Appendix B.2 newly documents internal labeling and comparison with LLM labels when refining dialogue acts, including dropping an Other category and merging correct/incorrect math-answer categories during development. These disclose the origins of the unchanged taxonomy; hyperparameters, hardware, prompts, and resource access remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: Appendix A expands discussion of prior work, including Cao et al. on student-response refinement, Song et al. on unlearning, Dou et al. on LLM-conducted realism tests, and Yuan et al. on the competence paradox. The central positioning around reference-grounded, turn-level simulation remains intact.
descriptions.P1: v2 makes localized explanatory additions, corrects wording such as the duplicated 'student student', and adds acknowledgments. The title, section organization, and overall narrative remain substantially unchanged.
descriptions.P2: Text reflow moves Tables 2 and 3 lower within PDF page 7 and changes surrounding page composition. The figures and tables retain their contents, captions, and designs; the later appendix pages match visually after accounting for pagination.

P-910A814CF9.title: SpatialScore: Towards Comprehensive Evaluation for Spatial Intelligence

descriptions.M1: V2 adds supervised fine-tuning on SpatialCorpus using cross-entropy, absent from v1. SpatialAgent retains Plan-Execute and ReAct but changes its toolbox: Rex-Omni replaces OWLv2 localization and supports counting, while DetAny3D and MapAnything add 3D detection and metric-distance capabilities (Sections 3.2–3.4).
descriptions.E1: Coverage expands from 11 integrated datasets to 23, adding tasks such as maze navigation, paper folding, mental rotation, velocity estimation, and size compatibility. V2 also introduces real-world and simulated training coverage through SpatialCorpus. Geometry tasks persist within the repurposed data; that component adds Omni3D and PointOdyssey and stops sourcing ScanNet.
descriptions.E2: V2 adds evaluated comparators including Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, SpaceThinker, and SpaceR, while Cambrian-8B and SpatialBot-Phi2 disappear from the quantitative comparisons. Proprietary comparisons shift from GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Haiku, and Gemini-2.0-Flash to newer systems. Human, random, and text-only baselines are also added.
descriptions.E3: V1's 28,093 samples and 1,400-sample Hard subset give way to 5,025 samples selected using text-only filtering and manual verification. SpatialScore numerical scoring changes from factor-two tolerance to MRA with parser/LLM score averaging; MRA already appeared in v1's separate VSI-Bench evaluation. Video sampling changes from eight frames by default to 32 for open models and 16/8 for proprietary models. The agent token limit increases from 2,048 to 4,096.
descriptions.E4: Beyond the retained Figure 4 cases, v2 adds annotation-error examples (Figure 5), analyses of fine-tuning versus agent generalization across OpenSource and Repurpose subsets (Appendix C.1), quantitative reasoning-failure analysis (Appendix B.3), and new qualitative cases (Figures 9–10). These provide new evidence about data quality, distribution dependence, and agent reliability.
descriptions.E5: Both versions specify a fixed random seed and deterministic decoding. Neither reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's human-participant count and agent failure percentages do not introduce uncertainty estimation.
descriptions.E6: The original benchmark and source-dataset result tables are replaced by results for the redesigned benchmark and new training/agent comparisons. For example, v2 Table 3 reports Qwen3-VL-8B scores of 45.48 zero-shot, 54.71 after fine-tuning, and 53.81 with ReAct; Table 2 adds human performance of 86.60. These are newly reported results under revised conditions, not direct gains over v1's scores.
descriptions.T1: The Plan-Execute and ReAct mathematical formulations remain equivalent apart from notation and explicit backbone bookkeeping. Neither version develops theorems or proofs. V2's standard fine-tuning description and MRA scoring instructions add method and evaluation documentation rather than substantive mathematical reasoning.
descriptions.C1: V1 foregrounds VGBench as the first dedicated visual-geometry benchmark, the 28K SpatialScore collection and Hard subset, and SpatialAgent. V2 redefines the central contributions around a curated 30-task benchmark, the 331K SpatialCorpus training resource, and complementary fine-tuning and expanded agent approaches. VGBench and SpatialScore-Hard cease to be separately claimed contributions.
descriptions.C2: V2 attributes larger fine-tuning gains on Repurpose to training-distribution alignment, discusses potential forgetting and uneven task improvements, and adds limitations concerning SpatialCorpus diversity. It also interprets measured failure rates as evidence of ReAct's greater stability. The RGB-input and rudimentary-toolbox limitations already existed in v1; their relocation to Section 7 is not a new limitation.
descriptions.D1: V2 documents the new fine-tuning recipe: one epoch, batch size 512, learning rate 1e-5, 3% warm-up, and a frozen visual encoder. It expands construction templates, distractor rules, scoring prompts, and tool specifications, and reports eight rather than four A100 GPUs. Explicit code and dataset links are added, although the PDFs do not establish actual resource availability.
descriptions.R1: V2 expands engagement with recent spatial benchmarks, training approaches, and perception tools, including SpatialEval, OmniSpatial, SPAR-Bench, MMSI-Bench, Rex-Omni, and MapAnything. The new benchmark-comparison Table 1 and revised related work position the contribution as a comprehensive evaluation and improvement framework, replacing the earlier emphasis on VGBench's visual-geometry novelty.
descriptions.P1: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and portions of the main text are rewritten. Baseline evaluation moves into the benchmark section, methodology is reorganized around two improvement approaches, limitations move into the main text, and six appendix sections are reorganized into three.
descriptions.P2: V2 redraws the overview, construction pipeline, toolbox diagram, and dataset-flow visualization. Result tables adopt new task columns, grouping, rankings, and highlighting; benchmark-comparison, annotation-error, and additional qualitative displays are added. Figure 4 is substantially retained and relocated, while the document typography, prompt boxes, and page layout are extensively reformatted.

P-57AAEFFDC4.title: TimeLens: Rethinking Video Temporal Grounding with Multimodal LLMs

descriptions.M1: The timestamp encoding, thinking-free RLVR objective, difficulty-aware sampling, early stopping, and data-curation procedures are retained. The Qwen3-specific preliminary SFT stage was already documented in v1 Appendix B.2.
descriptions.E1: v2 Appendix D adds evaluation on the external, human-annotated VUE-TR temporal-grounding benchmark. Existing training sources, TimeLens-Bench, original benchmark evaluations, and Video-MME coverage are retained.
descriptions.E2: Table 1 broadens the evaluated open-source comparison set by adding TRACE, TRACE-uni, TimeSuite, Grounded-VideoLLM, and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B. These introduce additional grounding approaches and a much larger general-purpose comparator; all previous comparators remain.
descriptions.E3: The added VUE-TR evaluation is explicitly labeled 0-200s and reports IoU in Table 10. Previously reported splits, training settings, resolution budgets, and evaluation metrics remain unchanged. The new explanation that Table 2 uses RLVR-trained models clarifies an existing experiment.
descriptions.E4: The timestamp, training-paradigm, training-data, and model-size ablations, training curves, and thinking-process observations are retained. VUE-TR supplies additional benchmark scores, while the new appendix discussion adds interpretations without new ablations or robustness tests.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports evaluation seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The training reward standard-deviation curve in Figure 6 is retained unchanged.
descriptions.E6: Existing numerical results and plotted findings are unchanged. v2 adds scores for the five Table 1 comparators and a VUE-TR comparison: TimeLens-7B reports 45.1 IoU, versus Gemini-2.5-Pro's 41.6, Qwen2.5-VL-7B's 36.0, and GPT-4o's 34.5. These are additional results, not improvements to previously reported scores.
descriptions.T1: The task formulation and Equations 1-9, covering the RL objective, rewards, difficulty definition, and density-corrected Gaussian sampling, are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or derivation is introduced.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and relocated conclusion retain the same contributions and claims about data quality, TimeLens-Bench/100K, training recipes, and competitive grounding performance. Additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining the main contribution.
descriptions.C2: New Appendix F explains VideoChat-R1 and Time-R1's differing benchmark behavior and the interaction between timestamp encoding and post-training. It also qualifies early stopping as a practical single-task recommendation that may require different treatment in multitask training. Appendix D interprets VUE-TR results as evidence of external generalization.
descriptions.D1: Appendix F explicitly documents that all timestamp-encoding methods in Table 2 are compared after RLVR training. Implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware, prompts, and release statements otherwise remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds LLaVA-ST and Grounded-VideoLLM citations to the related-work coverage and discusses differences from VideoChat-R1 and Time-R1 in Appendix F. The central positioning as a systematic investigation and baseline remains unchanged.
descriptions.P1: The conclusion moves from main-text Section 6 to Appendix A. v2 adds acknowledgements, an external-evaluation paragraph, and Appendix F, with corresponding section renumbering and limited wording edits. Most existing prose is retained.
descriptions.P2: Table 1 gains five comparator rows, and a new VUE-TR Table 10 is inserted. The previous Video-MME Table 10 becomes Table 11. Existing figures and table designs are retained, with local relocation and page reflow.

P-073730B4DC.title: NSF-SciFy: Mining the NSF Awards Database for Scientific Claims

descriptions.M1: Both versions use joint zero-shot extraction with Claude-3.5, LoRA fine-tuning of Mistral and Qwen, and GPT-4o-mini pairwise evaluation. Renaming verifiable_claims to claims preserves its definition. Applying the approach to NSF-SCIFY-20K and proposing future remedies do not establish a changed extraction or training method.
descriptions.E1: v1's downstream experiments use the materials-science subset. v3 additionally trains and evaluates on NSF-SCIFY-20K, spanning MPS, GEO, ENG, CSE, and BIO, and evaluates extraction quality across six areas by separating materials science from the rest of MPS. This broadens the empirically studied domains while retaining the three tasks.
descriptions.E2: The Mistral and Qwen comparisons in Tables 2–4 remain unchanged. Section 7 and Appendix I newly use Claude-extracted claims as a comparison in the error analysis of fine-tuned Mistral outputs; Claude previously served as the dataset generator without this reported error comparison.
descriptions.E3: v3 adds a validation protocol sampling 20 awards from each of six areas, using GPT-4o to identify missing or incorrect extractions and manually checking its outputs on 20 abstracts. It also reports pairwise-judge validation and a separate 120-award error-analysis sample. These extend evaluation design; the original materials-science split, preprocessing, training budget, and metrics remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: v3 adds claim and proposal taxonomies, extraction precision/recall analyses across scientific areas, human-assisted judge validation, a reported evaluation-prompt robustness check, and detailed error categories with examples in Appendix I. v1's abstract-style analysis and qualitative joint-versus-separate extraction observation are retained.
descriptions.E5: v1 already reports 95% confidence-interval ranges for Tables 2–4, which v3 retains. v3 additionally specifies standard-deviation error bars from 1,000 bootstrap resamples in Figures 5–6. Appendix F displays per-score uncertainties without clearly identifying their interpretation. No increase in training runs or seeds is documented.
descriptions.E6: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results. New NSF-SCIFY-20K results in Tables A5–A7 include base versus fine-tuned Mistral claim F-scores of 0.5247 versus 0.7268, alongside lower recall of 0.8141 versus 0.7354. v3 also adds domain-specific extraction-quality results, taxonomy distributions, and error rates. These are additional results under new coverage, rather than improvements over v1 under identical conditions.
descriptions.T1: The pairwise support functions and mathematical precision/recall definitions are retained. The new true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative description explains standard evaluation quantities; neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs that change.
descriptions.C1: v1 describes the full 2.8-million-claim corpus as an estimate awaiting comprehensive processing. v3 presents that size without the estimate qualification, adds NSF-SCIFY-20K as an explicit contribution, and foregrounds high-precision extraction with lower recall. This materially strengthens and broadens the dataset contribution while retaining the three-task and fine-tuning claims.
descriptions.C2: v3 introduces limitations concerning funded-US-proposal coverage, availability bias, older publication links, generalizability, limited baselines, and LLM evaluation validity. It interprets lower claim recall as a deliberate precision-first choice and discusses error mechanisms and possible remedies. These qualifications go substantially beyond v1's advantages and brief future-work discussion.
descriptions.D1: V3 adds explicit code and checkpoint locations, stated Apache-2.0 release terms in Appendix A, and approximately one hour of training per epoch. Much of the release description and the extraction/evaluation prompts already existed and is relocated. These are changes to access documentation; resource availability has not been independently verified.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds Gu et al.'s LLM-as-judge survey, Liu et al.'s G-Eval, and GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini references, and explicitly connects its claim definition to the already-cited Tang et al. The principal related-work comparison and grant-abstract novelty positioning remain largely unchanged; publication updates to existing references are bibliographic changes.
descriptions.P1: v3 rewrites the abstract, expands short task descriptions into explanatory paragraphs, recasts the conclusion, and reorganizes the narrative around dataset validation, error analysis, and structured limitations. The appendices are reorganized to include reproducibility and separate analyses, with existing prompts and release material moved.
descriptions.P2: v3 adds two taxonomy treemaps, two extraction-quality plots, three results tables, two taxonomy-example tables, and formatted error-example panels. The original t-SNE figure moves to Appendix E as Figure A7, and existing example tables become A8–A9. Table 1 gains a subset row, and numerous captions gain emphasized summaries.

P-EA0F671C36.title: MMControl: Unified Multi-Modal Control for Joint Audio-Video Generation

descriptions.M1: The MMCU inputs and masks, dual-stream bypass architecture, modality-specific guidance, and two-stage inference remain unchanged in Section 3. The new ablation variants test the existing method rather than revise the proposed model.
descriptions.E1: Both versions train on 30,000 Hallo3 samples and cover reference-image/audio, depth, and pose conditioning. Pose control already appears in v1 Figure 6. Its new quantitative evaluation and the added appendix experiments do not introduce a new dataset, domain, or task.
descriptions.E2: v3 adds AVControl as a comparator for depth and pose control in Table S5. Existing comparator sets are retained; Text2Video-Zero, ControlVideo, and VACE already participated in v1's qualitative pose comparison.
descriptions.E3: v3 extends evaluation with quantitative pose MAE and temporal consistency, component comparisons on 90 paired samples, an AVControl comparison on 60 samples, and guidance sweeps over 0.5, 1.0, and 1.3. The original training settings, 200-sample audio/depth benchmarks, human-study design, and 150-case audio evaluation remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: Beyond the retained qualitative guidance study in Figure 7, Appendix C adds quantitative validation. Table S3 tests masks, projector initialization, unified attention, removal of each bypass branch, and added cross-attention across audio/depth/pose tasks. Table S4 adds guidance-strength sensitivity analysis.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new 90- and 60-sample counts describe evaluation samples, not repeated runs or uncertainty estimation.
descriptions.E6: Tables 1, 2, S1, and S2 retain their values. Additional new results include pose MAE ×100 of 3.07 versus VACE's 3.29 in Table 3, component and guidance results in Tables S3–S4, and AVControl comparisons in Table S5: depth MAE 11.49 versus MMControl's 4.52 and pose MAE 7.57 versus 3.07. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under matched settings.
descriptions.T1: Equations 1–5 retain the same task mapping, conditional representations, masks, projection, and residual guidance formulation. No new theorem, proof, derivation, or substantive mathematical revision appears.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and introduction narrow broad references to scene layout and diverse control scenarios to depth-guided scene structure and reference/depth/pose conditioning. The central MMCU, dual-stream bypass, guidance-scaling, and state-of-the-art claims remain.
descriptions.C2: Appendix C adds interpretations connecting component removals to synchronization, speaker similarity, and structural errors. Appendix D explains the loudness-versus-timbre distinction limiting the AVControl comparison and acknowledges its pose-aesthetics advantage. Section 4.3 also qualifies VACE comparisons and separates visual structural evaluation from joint audio-video capability.
descriptions.D1: Appendix C specifies the six ablation modifications and exact guidance values, including fixing the other scale at 1. These add limited reproducibility information. The original backbone, optimizer, training budget, hardware, preprocessing, and audio-evaluation tools remain unchanged; no new code or data access information appears.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds references for AVControl and Text2Video-Zero. Appendix D positions AVControl as concurrent work using task-specific IC-LoRA adapters and distinguishes its acoustic control target. The main related-work discussion otherwise retains its existing positioning.
descriptions.P1: v3 tightens wording throughout the method, experiments, and conclusion while retaining the main section sequence and narrative. It adds a main-text summary of existing human/audio results, expands the appendix outline, and changes citation style and author/header presentation.
descriptions.P2: The document is comprehensively reformatted with different typography, text width, running headers, and figure/table placement. Four tables are added: Table 3 and Tables S3–S5. The seven existing figures retain their illustrated content but are resized or relocated, with several captions revised.

P-BA20B2B606.title: Learning to Bet for Horizon-Aware Anytime-Valid Testing

descriptions.M1: The main three-action DQN and its architecture remain unchanged. Sections 4.4 and F.1 add trained DQN-EB and DQN-U variants with early-rejection rewards, while F.4 tests an expanded nine-action policy. These are limited extensions of the existing learning procedure.
descriptions.E1: Beyond the retained Beta/Beta-mixture experiments, v2 evaluates transfer to logit-normal distributions and six real-data sources: three DNA methylation samples and three relative-humidity stations. It also adds Bernoulli-family training and evaluation, using a separately trained policy.
descriptions.E2: The external comparator set remains empirical Kelly, Linear-ε, Hedge, STaR-Bets, and STaR-Hoeffding. Figure 6 adds DQN-EB and DQN-U as internal comparators in the retained Beta-mixture setting, and Figure 15 compares the original DQN with its nine-action variant.
descriptions.E3: v2 adds empirical-distribution resampling protocols with N=100 and null controls, a matched-budget action-space comparison, evaluation at N=250, 300, and 350, and retraining/evaluation at α=0.01. These extend the evaluation design; the original experiments and main training settings remain intact.
descriptions.E4: Appendix F adds reward-function and action-space ablations, distribution-transfer tests, deadline and significance-level sensitivity experiments, and explicit Type-I error checks. These address design choices and robustness questions beyond v1's training curves and qualitative trajectories, which are retained.
descriptions.E5: The new real-data curves use the existing practice of estimating frequencies over 5,000 trials. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across independently trained DQN seeds. The fixed-seed checkpoint evaluation remains unchanged; null-calibration curves are new outcomes, not uncertainty estimates.
descriptions.E6: Existing results are retained, while Figures 6–18 add new findings. These include improved power on additional distribution families, the highest deadline rejection probability in five of six real-data cases, earlier rejection versus terminal-power tradeoffs from reward shaping, and no overall improvement from nine actions.
descriptions.T1: Equation 1 generalizes deadline power to expected utility E[u(τ)1{τ≤N}] for nonnegative, nonincreasing u, with an expected-wealth constraint at bounded stopping times. The subsequent analysis specializes to u=1. The Bellman recursion, principal theoretical results, and Appendix A–B proofs are retained.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and headline contributions remain the finite-horizon control formulation, three-regime betting theory, and a universal DQN that improves deadline power and confidence sequences while preserving validity. The expanded experiments primarily provide additional support for these retained claims.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds substantive interpretations of reward tradeoffs, optimization difficulty with larger action spaces, transfer beyond training distributions, and use of the Type-I error budget. It explicitly limits real-data evidence to resampled marginal distributions and adds an interpretability limitation. The conclusion replaces the Beta-only experimental limitation with broader remaining distributional questions.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds a code-repository link, GEO sample identifiers, humidity station/date information, humidity normalization and resampling instructions, and specifications for the new policy variants. The original implementation descriptions, architecture, hardware information, and Table 1 hyperparameters remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: Section 2 adds Koning and Van Meer (2026), discussing their Doob-martingale construction and distinguishing this paper's restriction to multiplicative betting processes. Other reference changes largely update metadata for existing works rather than introduce new research positioning.
descriptions.P1: v2 makes localized wording edits, expands Section 4.4, adds an Impact Statement, and organizes Appendix F into nine subsections. The original training and trajectory subsections move to F.8–F.9. Most existing prose and the overall section structure are retained.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds thirteen multipanel figures, Figures 6–18, displaying new comparisons, data histograms, calibration curves, and ablations. Original Figures 1–5 remain, while v1 Figures 6–9 become Figures 19–22. Table 1 is retained.

P-55230F72B6.title: One Persona, Many Cues, Different Results: How Sociodemographic Cues Impact LLM Personalization

descriptions.M1: The six persona-cue procedures, demographic controls, and response-generation approach remain unchanged. Presenting the setup as a flexible benchmark and renaming the name-based non-binary condition to unisex do not establish procedural changes.
descriptions.E1: Both use SBB and its five domains, MMMD, AITA, and IssueBench, with the same demographic coverage and PRISM, ImplicitPersona, and voter-registration sources. The unisex relabeling retains the existing name-selection population.
descriptions.E2: The same six cue conditions and no-persona baseline are evaluated across the same seven models. Newly cited studies do not participate as experimental comparators.
descriptions.E3: Both retain 1,666 evaluation questions, five indicators per persona-cue combination, temperature 1.0, the same preprocessing and controls, and the same outcome metrics. Llama-3.3-70B remains the IssueBench judge; the detailed model descriptions move to Appendix C.
descriptions.E4: The persona-, model-, and task-specific correlation analyses and ANOVA/Tukey-Kramer comparisons are retained. Tables 5–7 provide detailed outputs of those existing comparisons; no distinct ablation, robustness test, or case study is added.
descriptions.E5: Three sampled responses, 1,000 bootstrap resamples, confidence intervals, and statistical tests remain unchanged. However, new Tables 5–6 label significance as 0.01%, conflicting with alpha = 0.01 in the methods, Appendix H, and Table 7. This introduces a reporting inconsistency without establishing a changed testing procedure.
descriptions.E6: Section 4 corrects the invalid-response percentage from 0.57% to 0.98%, matching Appendix D in both versions. Tables 5–7 newly report exact pairwise differences, including a 0.071 AITA accuracy difference between male and non-binary personas under explicit-user cues. Main trends remain stable, although the new 'up to 5,000$' salary summary understates the 7,848.817 difference reported in Table 6.
descriptions.T1: No formal theory, proofs, or new mathematical definitions are introduced. Adding 'for the same persona' to the correlation null hypothesis clarifies the existing comparison.
descriptions.C1: The introduction and conclusion newly identify a flexible, reusable benchmark as an explicit contribution, and the recommendation now also addresses engineers testing models before deployment. The central claims about correlated cues producing different bias findings remain.
descriptions.C2: Section 5.2 adds explanations involving prompt position and internal demographic representations, without direct mechanism tests. The limitations newly discuss legitimate demographic differences in medical advice, while Appendix A.1 expands the qualification of unisex names as a proxy. Appendix H adds a warning against comparing effect sizes across datasets.
descriptions.D1: Prompt templates, demographic controls, preprocessing, model identifiers, hardware, runtimes, judge instructions, and repository access remain substantively unchanged. V2 relocates model details and adds reasons for existing choices, including the budget-based selection of GPT-4o-mini.
descriptions.R1: V2 adds discussion of Neumann et al. (2025), concurrent Tonneau et al. (2026), and several supporting studies. It explicitly acknowledges conflicting findings about system versus user prompts. Publication updates and deduplicated Gautam and Wang references retain the same underlying works.
descriptions.P1: V2 adds a contribution paragraph and discussion, reorganizes limitations under topical headings, moves detailed model descriptions into Appendix C, and edits terminology, affiliations, and prose. The overall section sequence and narrative remain recognizable.
descriptions.P2: The visual presentation is systematically revised: heatmaps are recolored and reordered, outcome plots receive aligned scales and revised markers, legends, and baseline displays, and the setup diagram is updated. V1 Figure 13 becomes main-text Figure 5; v1 Figures 5–7 become appendix Figure 11. Three new numerical tables are added.

P-9AEC8D36FC.title: PnP-CM: Consistency Models as Plug-and-Play Priors for Inverse Problems

descriptions.M1: v2 implements nonlinear data-fidelity optimization, including a differentiable JPEG surrogate, whereas v1 left nonlinear implementation to future work. Supplement B.1 also adds phase-retrieval output disambiguation and specifies median-filter initialization for inpainting, contrasting with v1's explicit zero-initialization/no-heuristics description. The ADMM-CM core remains; the explicit CM noise-scale parameter mainly formalizes separately tuned noise levels already mentioned in v1.
descriptions.E1: v2 adds CelebA-HQ training and evaluation and evaluates JPEG restoration, nonlinear deblurring, and coded-mask phase retrieval on both natural-image datasets. LSUN Bedroom's original linear restoration tasks and fastMRI PD/PD-FS reconstruction remain.
descriptions.E2: Linear natural-image comparisons add DiffPIR, DPnP, and PnP-DM. The new nonlinear comparisons evaluate DPS, ΠGDM, and DPnP. MRI comparisons now include quantitative and visual CM4IR results alongside DPS and DDS; v1 only described CM4IR's failure without corresponding comparative entries.
descriptions.E3: The reported MRI CM distillation budget changes from 7M iterations in v1 Appendix D.1 to 700k in v2 Supplement C; this establishes a revised stated setting, without establishing retraining. New protocols include CelebA-HQ training/evaluation splits, JPEG quality factor 5, eight-NFE phase retrieval, MRI momentum controls at 4/10/20 NFEs, and randomized hyperparameter perturbations up to 25%.
descriptions.E4: v2 adds an MRI study testing whether momentum benefits diminish with increasing NFEs and a CelebA-HQ deblurring hyperparameter-sensitivity study (Supplement D.1–D.2). The four-way component ablation and noise/NFE sweep move from LSUN Bedroom experiments to CelebA-HQ experiments, replacing their evidence rather than merely relocating it.
descriptions.E5: Both versions use averaged reconstruction metrics and retain plus/minus reporting for MRI. Neither introduces seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new randomized sensitivity study changes experimental design without adding uncertainty estimation.
descriptions.E6: v2 adds extensive CelebA-HQ, nonlinear-task, baseline, and sensitivity results while revising retained entries. For example, four-NFE LSUN deblurring changes from 28.10/0.237 to 27.49/0.285 PSNR/LPIPS, and MRI PD R=4 PnP-CM mean PSNR changes from 32.69 to 35.57. These are revised reported results, not established controlled performance gains. Original two-NFE comparator entries and LSUN ablation/sweep results are removed or replaced.
descriptions.T1: Section 2.1 removes v1's specialized empirical ODE, dx/dt = -t sϕ, and instead describes sampling through the general drift/diffusion probability-flow equation. This is a limited mathematical-formulation revision. Theorem 1, its Lipschitz and summable-noise assumptions, and Appendix A's convergence argument remain substantively unchanged.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion broaden the work from demonstrated linear restoration/MRI reconstruction to a unified framework with demonstrated linear and nonlinear applications. Nonlinear implementation was explicitly future work in v1. The proximal-prior interpretation, few-NFE efficiency, and first MRI-trained CM claims remain.
descriptions.C2: v2 removes the LSUN-only limitation and nonlinear-future-work discussion as coverage expands. It adds interpretations of comparable visual quality to diffusion-PnP methods, robustness to hyperparameter perturbations, and phase-retrieval ambiguity. Its new MRI analysis qualifies momentum as especially useful at low NFEs and not the primary performance driver, replacing v1's emphasis on momentum dominance in its LSUN ablation.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds a code-repository link, explicit noise/penalty/momentum schedules, coefficient values for CelebA-HQ and MRI in Table 3, nonlinear implementation instructions, additional baseline tuning details, and training losses and budgets. v1 largely described empirical tuning and referenced external implementations. Conversely, v1's explicit [0,1] input-normalization statement is no longer stated.
