descriptions.R1: Section 2.3 replaces the Schrödinger-bridge discussion of I2SB/CDDB with substantive positioning against diffusion-based PnP approaches, including newly cited work by Graikos, Park, Wu, and Xu/Chi. v2 also expands nonlinear-imaging references and more explicitly positions noise and momentum as established acceleration techniques, including momentum-ADMM prior work.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, contributions, related-work discussion, acceleration narrative, and results discussion are rewritten. v2 introduces separate Final Algorithm and Ablation Studies subsections, removes the standalone Discussion section, and reorganizes the appendices into experimental details, training details, and further results. These changes extend beyond renaming and renumbering.
descriptions.P2: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the introductory overview, and merges the original natural-image and MRI tables into an expanded multipart Table 1. It adds nonlinear comparisons, a sensitivity plot, and CelebA-HQ image grids. Retained LSUN and MRI grids are expanded with comparator columns and rearranged; new hyperparameter and momentum tables further change the presentation.

P-5834D0DEB7.title: STAGE: Storyboard-Anchored Generation for Cinematic Multi-shot Narrative

descriptions.M1: Section 4 retains the same STEP2 model, multi-shot memory pack, dual-encoding strategy, supervised and preference-alignment training, and director/refiner video-generation workflow.
descriptions.E1: Both use the same ConStoryBoard and ConStoryBoard-HP data derived from Condensed Movies for storyboard-conditioned multi-shot generation. No dataset, task, domain or test scenario is added or removed.
descriptions.E2: Tables 1–2 retain the same five comparators: CineTrans, IC-LoRA + WanX, StoryDiffusion + WanX, VideoGen-of-Thought and MovieAgent. Their participation in the quantitative, qualitative and human comparisons is unchanged.
descriptions.E3: The 100K training/1K testing pairs, 100K supervised plus 20K preference-training iterations, evaluation metrics and procedures are unchanged. Both human studies specify 20 samples and 25 volunteers per experiment.
descriptions.E4: Section 5.4, Table 1 and Figure 5 retain the same removals of the memory pack, dual encoding and two-stage training. Section 5.5 and Figure 6 retain the same nine-shot generation example.
descriptions.E5: Both report the same point-score and preference-percentage reporting practices. Neither supplies repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests.
descriptions.E6: All numerical entries in Tables 1–2 match, as do the qualitative examples and findings in Figures 4–6. For example, STAGE's TVS remains 0.2732 and its shot-consistency preference remains 72.8%.
descriptions.T1: Equations (1)–(10), including memory compression, flow matching, preference optimization and workflow definitions, are unchanged. No mathematical assumption, derivation or proof is added or revised.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims about controllable generation, cross-shot coherence, cinematic transitions and ConStoryBoard. The added code-access sentence does not change a scientific claim.
descriptions.C2: The interpretations of comparisons and ablations are identical. Both retain the limitation that off-the-shelf video infilling can introduce temporal inconsistencies and the proposed future integration into an end-to-end backbone.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds 'Our code will be available at this url' at the abstract's end on page 2, linked to a specific GitHub repository; v1 has no code pointer. This adds prospective access information without establishing that code is released. Implementation details and the dataset-release promise are unchanged.
descriptions.R1: Both contain the same 60 cited works and identical related-work positioning. Differences in reference back-reference page numbers reflect pagination, not changed citations.
descriptions.P1: The substantive prose and section sequence are unchanged. v2 adds the short code-availability sentence and updates the arXiv version/date text, without broader rewriting or narrative restructuring.
descriptions.P2: Text and equations reflow across columns and pages, and Table 2 moves from page 7 to page 8. All six figures, both table structures and their captions remain unchanged.

P-B208830EDC.title: ProactiveBench: Benchmarking Proactiveness in Multimodal Large Language Models

descriptions.M1: Benchmark construction, environment actions, and GRPO training with the same reward choices remain unchanged. The added multi-turn open-ended experiment extends the evaluation protocol rather than modifying the trained models.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same seven datasets and scenarios, with QuickDraw and COCO supplying training data. The additional multi-turn open-ended evaluation reuses this coverage.
descriptions.E2: Model membership is unchanged in the retained MCQA, single-turn open-ended, reference, and hinted comparisons. The new multi-turn experiment evaluates 12 models already represented in the existing suite; it introduces no new baseline method.
descriptions.E3: Section 4.2 adds a supplementary multi-turn open-ended protocol that maps inapplicable suggestions to random valid actions and measures trajectory accuracy and intervention rate. This replaces the earlier cross-format comparison using aggregate accuracy. The original evaluation settings remain.
descriptions.E4: v2 examines whether weak open-ended performance persists with multiple interaction turns. Appendix A.8 also adds a modeled recall comparison for filtering thresholds. Existing invalid-action, hint, history, few-shot, and reward analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: Appendix A.8 adds binomial-based recall estimates: 92.8% for the chosen filtering rule versus 37.6% for a binomial-test alternative at a 0.05 threshold, assuming 40% first-turn success. Neither version reports experimental confidence intervals or repeated-run uncertainty.
descriptions.E6: The MCQA aggregate results in v1 Table 10 are removed and replaced by multi-turn open-ended results for 12 models. Qwen2.5-VL-7B leads the new comparison with 3.9% accuracy and 0.1 intervention rate. These are different-protocol results, not performance changes. Retained numerical tables and single-turn component scores are unchanged.
descriptions.T1: Appendix A.8 introduces binomial-model reasoning under an assumed 40% success probability to justify the six-of-22 filtering cutoff. v1 supplied empirical filtering curves without this mathematical rationale. The MDP formulation and training reward rules remain unchanged.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: current models lack proactiveness, prompting provides limited benefits, and reinforcement learning can improve proactiveness with transfer to unseen scenarios.
descriptions.C2: v2 more explicitly distinguishes frequent suggestions from successful proactive behavior and explains why single-turn OEG and MCQA metrics are not directly comparable. Results sections narrow the scaling statement to no simple monotonic relationship within tested families. Appendix A.8 adds arguments about filtering-pool dependence and future evaluation.
descriptions.D1: Filtering documentation explicitly identifies first-turn MCQA predictions, the six-of-22 cutoff, and the pool spanning ten model families. These clarify the existing procedure. Training hyperparameters, hardware, runtime information, prompts, and code/data access links remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: Both versions cite the same 72 works and retain the same positioning relative to MLLM benchmarks and active vision. Reference formatting and bibliographic metadata changes do not alter research positioning.
descriptions.P1: Targeted rewrites clarify metrics, interpretations, and filtering. Terminology distinguishes MCQA intervention rate from OEG suggestion percentages; affiliations and keywords are also updated. The main section and appendix organization remains intact.
descriptions.P2: The document is comprehensively retypeset with a narrower text block, different typography and headers, and widespread resizing and relocation of displays. Table 2 now separates category and suggestion scores, Figure 6c displays suggestion percentages instead of aggregate accuracy, and Table 10 presents a different experiment.

descriptions.M1: The proposed after-posterior-update stopping rule and PBGI/LogEIPC acquisition definitions remain unchanged in Equations (4)–(10). The theoretical corrections and expanded experimental documentation do not establish a revised algorithm.
descriptions.E1: LCBench evaluation expands from Fashion-MNIST, adult, and higgs to all 35 datasets, broadening the represented classification problems and dataset sizes. The synthetic scenarios and three NATS-Bench datasets are retained.
descriptions.E2: The comparator roster is otherwise retained, but v2 Figure 19 labels the unknown-cost acquisition LogEIPC-exp, whereas v4 Figure 18 labels it LogEIPC-inv and changes some plotted entries. v4's caption and Appendix D.3 still specify LogEIPC-exp and expected-cost substitution, leaving actual comparator replacement unresolved.
descriptions.E3: v4 adds min–max normalization across acquisition–stopping pairs for aggregate LCBench evaluation and dataset-specific regression slopes for the full benchmark's runtime proxies. The original three-dataset 0.001-times-parameter-count setup remains in the appendix; initialization and iteration budgets are retained.
descriptions.E4: Appendix D.3 adds failure and sensitivity analysis distinguishing seven datasets with persistent underperformance across all three cost scales from three that recover at the smallest scale. Existing posterior-update, smoothing, runtime, and cost-mismatch analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: Both versions specify 50 random seeds and means with error bars of twice the standard error. Added plots and changed error-bar values do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice or statistical testing procedure.
descriptions.E6: v4 adds aggregate and per-dataset results for the full LCBench benchmark at three cost scales, reporting competitive matched-pair performance on roughly 75% of datasets and identifying persistent failures. Some unknown-cost LogEIPC entries also change, with variant ambiguity preventing direct performance attribution. Table 1 and the retained synthetic appendix curves are unchanged.
descriptions.T1: Lemma 1 generalizes the constant prior mean to a mean function and corrects the expected-improvement time indexing. Appendix B replaces the optional-stopping invocation with an explicit indicator/tower-property calculation and completes the regret-plus-cost bound. New Corollary 3 proves high-probability finite termination under a positive cost floor; the previous budget-scaling corollary is retained as Corollary 4.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and contributions broaden the empirical recommendation from pairing the rule with PBGI to pairing it with PBGI or LogEIPC. The introduction also explicitly frames applicability to classical and cost-aware Bayesian optimization. The central stopping-rule contribution remains the same.
descriptions.C2: v4 adds the hypothesis that small datasets contribute to model misspecification and poor performance, while acknowledging two larger-dataset exceptions. It also explicitly states that the matched stopping rationale does not automatically extend to KG or MES. v2's general model-mismatch discussion and NATS failure interpretation are retained.
descriptions.D1: v4 adds a code-repository link on the first page, documents regression-based runtime proxies for the full LCBench evaluation, and clarifies that 20-iteration averaging applies to all acquisition-value-based stopping rules. These are additions to access and implementation information, without establishing reruns of retained experiments.
descriptions.R1: v4 adds the OpenML reference by Vanschoren et al. and sharpens the connection to Nguyen et al.'s existing EI stopping rule and the distinction from other acquisition-design principles. The broader Pandora's Box and PBGI positioning remains intact.
descriptions.P1: The abstract and contribution paragraphs are rewritten, acquisition definitions receive clearer explanations, and the stopping-rule taxonomy changes from a numbered list to paragraph headings. Cross-references and terminology are refined, while the overall section and appendix organization remains stable.
descriptions.P2: v4 merges the separate 1D and 8D main-text plots into Figure 2, replaces the main LCBench panels with aggregate comparisons, and adds three full-page grids covering 35 datasets with failure highlighting. Retained appendix plots are relocated and regrouped; these are display changes beyond renumbering.

P-AD73F6FDFB.title: SAFA-SNN: Sparsity-Aware On-Device Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning with Fast-Adaptive Structure of Spiking Neural Network

descriptions.M1: Equation (7) changes the reported threshold update from subtracting A(r_new-r_base) to adding it, reversing its feedback direction. This is a localized procedural correction. The three components, ZOO estimator, loss and prototype-projection rule remain; Algorithm 1 also clarifies the previously described base-training and incremental-learning stages.
descriptions.E1: The five FSCIL datasets and classification tasks remain CIFAR-100, MiniImageNet, CIFAR10-DVS, DVS128 Gesture and N-Caltech101. Added studies vary methods, architectures and evaluation settings within retained coverage rather than introduce another benchmark or input scenario.
descriptions.E2: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with FSLL, SoftNet and WSN in Table 12; six surrogate gradients in Table 17; and Subspace-reg in Table 18. Table 19 newly evaluates ANN versions of ASP, CoACT and PriViLege, extending beyond v1's SNN-adapted comparisons. The principal existing comparator sets remain.
descriptions.E3: Section 6.1 changes the reported neuromorphic batch sizes from 128 throughout to 32 for CIFAR10-DVS and 8 for DVS128 Gesture and N-Caltech101. Added evaluations introduce SEW ResNet-18/34/50 configurations, pretrained ANN versus SNN comparisons, and peak-memory and projection-execution-time measurements. The PDFs do not establish that retained results were rerun under the revised batch sizes.
descriptions.E4: Beyond retaining the original component ablations, shot counts, hyperparameter sweeps and firing-rate analyses, v2 directly tests ZOO against six surrogate gradients and compares projection mechanisms. It also investigates depth degradation using SEW residual architectures and training-time scalability across additional architectures.
descriptions.E5: Both versions specify three repetitions with different seeds and use the same existing uncertainty-reporting format. Additional tables extend that practice without introducing a new run-count policy, confidence-interval procedure or significance test.
descriptions.E6: The principal retained scores remain unchanged, including Table 1's MiniImageNet final accuracies of 48.70% for SAFA-SNN and 44.69% for CLOSER. Additional new results appear in Tables 11, 12, 15 and 17–19. For example, Table 17 reports 50.13% final accuracy with ZOO versus 46.71% with the triangle surrogate. These are added comparisons, not demonstrated version-to-version performance gains.
descriptions.T1: v2 revises the MSE bound from O(delta^2)+O(b delta^2 d^2) to O(delta^2)+O(d/(b delta^2)), and replaces convergence to the original gradient with convergence to the smoothed-objective gradient. Appendix D substantively revises the transformed-density and surrogate-recovery derivations. New Appendix E introduces noise assumptions, error decomposition and covariance bounds. v1's extended continuous-time IF/LIF derivation is removed.
descriptions.C1: The first general on-device SNN FSCIL contribution, three-component approach and claimed 4.01-point MiniImageNet advantage remain. The abstract narrows the energy claim by explicitly locating the 20% reduction on CIFAR-100.
descriptions.C2: v2 replaces the suggestion that deeper networks need more epochs with an identity-mapping explanation and SEW residual remedy. It expands explanations of homeostatic preservation, prototype projection and ZOO overhead, discusses pretraining differences in ANN comparisons, and newly interprets the retained misclassification results as evidence that projection introduces no additional bias.
descriptions.D1: V2 adds an explicit code-availability link, dataset sizes and image resolutions, fuller baseline-adaptation descriptions, and clarification that the initialization mask remains fixed. The PDFs alone do not verify repository contents. Core hardware, optimizer and epoch information was already present.
descriptions.R1: The positioning expands substantially through comparisons with soft-subnetwork learning, surrogate-gradient training, trainable subspace regularization and ANN PEFT approaches. Added references and discussion connect neuronal dynamics to homeostatic plasticity and distinguish the method from FSLL, SoftNet, WSN and Subspace-reg. This exceeds bibliographic updating.
descriptions.P1: The introduction, methodological motivation, neuronal-dynamics explanation and several appendix discussions are extensively rewritten. The appendix changes from A.1–A.16 to separately organized A–T sections, with revised baseline descriptions and navigation. Section 6.4, acknowledgments and an LLM-use disclosure are added, alongside affiliation and terminology edits.
descriptions.P2: Six new tables present the added comparisons, while retained tables are relocated and reformatted. Figures 4 and 5 are redrawn with different styling, legends and axes, including a truncated energy axis in Figure 4. Other figures receive labeling refinements, and Algorithm 1 is restructured and relocated.

P-68D3697367.title: Understanding In-Context Learning on Structured Manifolds: Bridging Attention to Kernel Methods

descriptions.M1: The embedding, positional encoding, empirical-risk objective, and five-block construction implementing Gaussian Nadaraya–Watson regression are retained. The construction still uses ReLU attention followed by masked softmax attention. v1 Appendix C.1 and v2 Appendix E.1 contain the same construction; the new experimental configurations do not introduce a new proposed method.
descriptions.E1: v1 has no empirical dataset or task coverage. v2 adds regression tasks generated from combinations of ten spherical harmonics on S^2 and diagnostic analysis of pretrained GPT-2 on five authored English sentences. These introduce actual synthetic and language-data evaluation.
descriptions.E2: v2 newly evaluates Gaussian-kernel scores as a reference comparator for learned attention scores in Figures 1 and 5 and Table 1. v1 connects these quantities only theoretically. This is a diagnostic comparison, without a benchmark comparison against alternative trained regressors; GPT-2 serves as a case study.
descriptions.E3: v2 introduces experimental protocols absent from v1: spherical-harmonic task generation, 50,000 tasks in each training/testing set for the correlation study, Pearson-correlation and MSE evaluation, prompt-length/task-count sweeps, and sorted GPT-2 attention analysis. Appendix F specifies model configurations and 100-epoch Adam training. These are new protocols, not revisions of earlier experiments.
descriptions.E4: v2 adds mechanistic checks comparing learned attention with Gaussian kernels, distributions of per-sample correlations, additional examples in Appendix F, and a GPT-2 case study. Figure 4 also investigates sensitivity to prompt length and training-task count. v1 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.
descriptions.E5: v2 first reports correlation means, standard deviations, and associated p-value statistics over 5,000 independent testing samples in Table 1. The scaling study reports 30 repetitions and displays mean curves with standard-deviation bands in Figure 4. v1's probabilistic theoretical bounds do not constitute empirical uncertainty reporting.
descriptions.E6: All empirical results are new. Table 1 reports mean correlations of 0.86, 0.75, 0.69, and 0.67 for prompt lengths 4, 8, 16, and 32. Figure 4 reports decreasing testing MSE and fitted prompt-length slopes of -0.071, -0.080, and -0.103 for 400, 1,600, and 6,400 training tasks. GPT-2 attention curves and additional kernel-comparison examples are also added.
descriptions.T1: Lemma 1 replaces the manifold, uniform-sampling, and Hölder assumptions inherited from Assumptions 1–2 with a bounded domain, a supported sampling distribution, and a bounded target function. The kernel bandwidth is stated as h > 0 instead of 0 < h < 1. Theorem 1 makes logarithmic factors explicit, while the main assumptions, construction proof, and supporting derivations are retained.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and introduction newly claim that learned query–prompt scores are highly correlated with a Gaussian kernel and present numerical validation as a contribution. The principal claims about exact kernel implementation, intrinsic-dimension dependence, and near-minimax regression rates remain.
descriptions.C2: v2 interprets attention correlations and GPT-2 curve shapes as support for the existing kernel perspective. It also explains flattening with increasing task count and faster prompt-length decay through the balance between the two existing error terms. The limitations concerning fixed prompts, noisy data, broader function classes, and limited training tasks are essentially unchanged.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds data-generation instructions, experimental embedding dimensions, layer and head counts, batch size 100, Adam learning rate 0.0005, 100 training epochs, activation choices, and the five sentences with truncation instructions. Its new reproducibility statement reports supplementary training/evaluation code; actual code availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.
descriptions.R1: Section 6 adds discussions and citations to Cheng et al., Geshkovski et al., Han et al., Lu and Yu, and Tai et al. It acknowledges earlier kernel-based ICL interpretations and specifies the exact construction and manifold generalization bound as distinguishing contributions. The existing comparisons with Kim et al. and Li et al. remain.
descriptions.P1: The main narrative is reorganized: the kernel connection precedes the generalization theorem, related work becomes a separate section, and the entire proof roadmap moves from Section 5 to Appendix C. The abstract and introduction are revised, and reproducibility, language-model-use, and experimental-detail sections are added.
descriptions.P2: v2 introduces five numbered figures and Table 1 where v1 has none. These include attention/kernel comparisons, correlation histograms, language attention curves, and six-panel scaling plots with uncertainty bands; Appendix F adds twelve example panels. This changes the visual presentation beyond ordinary text reflow.

P-243869DBDE.title: SpecAgent: A Speculative Retrieval and Forecasting Agent for Code Completion

descriptions.M1: The retriever–forecaster combination, cached contexts, and main nine-retrieval/three-prediction composition remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and Appendix B document the existing procedure more explicitly; they do not establish an implemented method revision.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same REPOCOD-based function-completion coverage: 980 problems from 11 repositories, with the retained indexing-time and inference-time scenarios. Appendix G analyzes cases from this existing benchmark.
descriptions.E2: The SpecAgent comparisons retain no context, BM25, RepoMap, BM25 + RepoMap, UniXcoder, CodeSage v2 large, and the oracle. Appendix G separately analyzes BM25 and RepoMap against an earlier oracle without adding a competitor to the SpecAgent evaluations.
descriptions.E3: Appendix G adds a diagnostic protocol selecting cases where only one retrieval method yields a passing completion. Claude 3.7 Sonnet judges failure causes, context helpfulness, and context decisiveness using an explicitly earlier oracle. This supplements the retained benchmark evaluation.
descriptions.E4: The existing ablations and examples are retained. New Appendix G adds systematic BM25/oracle and RepoMap/oracle failure analyses, success-factor breakdowns, and detailed cases examining missing dependencies, type information, usage examples, and repository conventions.
descriptions.E5: V2 newly documents confidence outputs: a 0–1 self-assessment from the function-removal scorer and high/medium/low confidence from the diagnostic judge (B.6 and G.1). These are agent judgments; calibration, confidence intervals, and repeated-run uncertainty for benchmark scores remain unreported.
descriptions.E6: Appendix G adds judge-reported context-decisiveness rates: 98.8% versus 25.5% for oracle/BM25 and 97.8% versus 41.7% for oracle/RepoMap, plus helpfulness findings and case outcomes. For Qwen3-8B with the Qwen3-Coder agent, reported latency changes from 39.99 seconds to 3.80 seconds (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 8). Existing pass@1 values remain unchanged.
descriptions.T1: Algorithm 1 introduces notation for the already-described context composition and caching procedure. No substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are added or revised.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and summary retain the same contributions and claims about speculative indexing-time context, future-context leakage, and approximately 9–11 percentage-point accuracy gains.
descriptions.C2: Appendix G adds interpretations of baseline failures involving lexical mismatch, missing implementations and usage information, and multi-hop dependencies. Section 4.1 adds cache-refresh and cost-amortization considerations. The original limitations and risk discussions are retained.
descriptions.D1: New Appendix B supplies agent prompts, tool workflows, parsing, caching, deterministic composition, oracle filtering, and validation details. Appendix H newly specifies decoding parameters, retrieval chunk and candidate limits, exploration budgets, and serving settings. These expand reproducibility documentation.
descriptions.R1: The related-work text and bibliography are unchanged after accounting for reflow. The positioning relative to code models, repository retrieval, and indexing-time computation remains the same.
descriptions.P1: The original main narrative and retained appendix prose are largely unchanged. V2 adds an appendix contents page, dedicated sections, updated cross-references, and localized method and deployment explanations while preserving the existing narrative order.
descriptions.P2: V2 changes the appendix from full-width single-column pages to a continuous two-column layout, reflowing code listings and tables. It adds Algorithm 1 and Figures 4–5, redraws Figure 2 while retaining its example, and rearranges the Appendix A tables.

P-77997A6854.title: G2P: Gaussian-to-Point Attribute Alignment for Boundary-Aware 3D Segmentation

descriptions.M1: Both versions retain Mahalanobis-weighted attribute aggregation, combined scale/semantic boundary labels, the Sonata teacher, PT v3 with the BFANet B–S block, and the same losses. Algorithm 1 and the clarified teacher inputs expand implementation documentation without establishing an algorithmic revision. The instance experiment uses G2P within a common PointGroup framework.
descriptions.E1: v3 adds actual ScanNet200 instance-segmentation evaluation, extending coverage from semantic classification to grouping individual objects (Table 5). ScanNet v2, ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, and SceneSplat-7K remain represented. ScanNet200 hidden-test semantic evaluation was already present in v2.
descriptions.E2: For ScanNet v2, v3 Table 1 adds SPG and PT v3 + PPT and removes DeepViewAgg. For ScanNet200, v3 Table 2 adds PT v2, SPG, and PT v3 + PPT while removing OneFormer3D. Table 6 adds MinkUNet and OctFormer to the existing ScanNet++/Matterport3D comparisons. Table 5 adds instance-segmentation comparisons using MinkUNet, PT v2, and PT v3 backbones.
descriptions.E3: v3 introduces PointGroup-based instance evaluation with mAP25, mAP50, and mAP, plus new controlled protocols: boundary tests without distillation at fixed boundary-loss weight and attribute-distillation tests without the B–S block. Main semantic tables remove mAcc and several OA columns, although supplementary tables retain these metrics. Section 4.1 reports AdamW instead of v2's Adam; this reported setting revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: Beyond retained module and correspondence ablations, v3 tests semantic versus scale-based boundary supervision, appearance-encoder fine-tuning, individual Gaussian attributes and combinations, conventional-feature teachers, pruning ratios, loss weights, and class-group tradeoffs (Tables 8–9 and 14–17; Figure 11). Supplementary Sections B–D also add reconstruction-quality analysis, feature PCA visualizations, and boundary case studies.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added scene-wise PSNR/mIoU comparison is descriptive analysis and does not introduce uncertainty estimation.
descriptions.E6: G2P's core validation mIoUs remain 78.4, 36.6, 48.7, and 55.9 across the four semantic benchmarks. However, Table 4's hidden-test row changes from 35.5/55.3/28.6/18.7 to 35.7/54.3/28.7/20.2 for mIoU/Head/Common/Tail, making G2P highest on Tail. v3 adds instance results of 41.8 mAP25, 33.3 mAP50, and 23.2 mAP, plus extensive ablation and cost results. Several reproduced baseline scores are replaced by reference scores, and some secondary metric entries disappear; these replacements are not same-setting performance gains.
descriptions.T1: The covariance, aggregation, boundary-selection, and loss definitions remain mathematically equivalent in Equations 1–9. Pruning-ratio notation is clarified, and pseudocode is supplied, but neither version introduces formal theorems or proofs, nor does v3 add a substantive mathematical derivation.
descriptions.C1: The central alignment, distillation, and boundary contributions remain. v3 narrows the blanket absence-of-2D-supervision claim to no pretrained 2D features or language supervision in the segmentation pipeline, drops the 'first approach' claim, and replaces overall state-of-the-art assertions with competitive-performance claims. Opacity's contribution is specified more precisely as visibility cues.
descriptions.C2: v3 develops opacity as structural/visibility confidence, explains why SH and rotation are excluded, and acknowledges texture-induced small-scale boundary noise. It adds interpretations of reconstruction-quality dependence and geometry-versus-appearance tradeoffs. Sections A and E explicitly discuss offline preparation costs, Gaussian availability, and outdoor scale variability, extending v2's brief indoor-coverage qualification.
descriptions.D1: v3 supplies teacher batch size and learning rate, B–S channel dimensions and attention heads, boundary-head architecture, explicit training-only split usage, and the nearest-Gaussian fallback. It specifies the 0.06 m search radius and default k=20. Table 13 documents preparation costs, including 22 minutes per scene for GS optimization and 27.9 hours per dataset for teacher training. A project-page link replaces the future code-release statement, without establishing code availability from the PDFs alone.
descriptions.R1: The related-work organization and distinction from UniPre3D remain largely intact. v3 adds references including SPG, PT v2, PointGroup, Segment then Splat, DNGaussian, and Speedy-Splat, replaces the Bhattacharyya citation with Mahalanobis's distance paper, and removes the first-approach novelty wording. Publication and bibliographic updates to retained works are not additional research coverage.
descriptions.P1: The main five-section organization and much of the prose remain. v3 revises the abstract, contribution wording, opacity terminology, method explanations, and ordering of experimental discussions. It also updates the title, authors, and affiliations and organizes the additional supplementary material into Sections A–E.
descriptions.P2: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting. v2's combined overview becomes separate preparation and training diagrams in v3 Figures 2 and 4, while Figure 3 is expanded. The existing qualitative comparison is retained as Figure 5. Tables are extensively restructured, including reduced metric columns and a transposed correspondence ablation, and numerous supplementary plots, tables, and qualitative panels are added.

P-6519877D31.title: Double: Breaking the Acceleration Limit via Double Retrieval Speculative Parallelism

descriptions.M1: Section 4 and Algorithms 1-3 retain the same iterative draft retrieval, target-guided verification, parallel execution and hierarchical datastore procedures, including the greedy and stochastic verification rules.
descriptions.E1: HumanEval, GSM8K, CNN/DM, Alpaca, MT-Bench, the ShareGPT prior and the appendix deployment scenarios are unchanged. The newly discussed multimodal and agentic applications are future directions, not evaluated coverage.
descriptions.E2: Comparator membership is unchanged within corresponding experiments: SpS, Lookahead, PLD, Token Recycling, Ouroboros, PEARL, EAGLE-3 and the appendix NANO-PEARL/Vanilla comparisons are retained. Newly cited methods are not added as evaluated baselines.
descriptions.E3: Section 5.1 and Appendices C-D retain the same model configurations, hardware, metrics, batch sizes, temperature settings and testing procedures. Retrieval depth d=10, prior rounds K=10 and n-gram size n=3 are unchanged.
descriptions.E4: The component ablations, retrieval-depth and prior-size sweeps, rejected-cache ablation, losslessness checks, runtime profiling and batching/memory analyses already appear in v1 and remain unchanged.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Point-estimate reporting and the qualitative uncertainty explanation accompanying Table 6 are unchanged.
descriptions.E6: Result entries in Tables 1-10 and the empirical figures are unchanged. For example, Table 1 retains HumanEval speedups of 5.33× for LLaMA3.3-70B and 2.84× for Qwen3-32B under the same settings.
descriptions.T1: The mathematical definitions, speedup derivations, Theorems 1-3, Appendix B proofs and Appendix D.2 losslessness reasoning are unchanged. Equation movement reflects text reflow.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about training-free lossless decoding, overcoming the PSD speedup ceiling, resolving the retrieval trade-off and the headline speedups.
descriptions.C2: Appendix E adds prospective applicability discussion covering multimodal inference, agentic reasoning and further Transformer/hardware parallelism. Existing result interpretations and limitations remain unchanged, and these extensions are not demonstrated.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds a concrete repository link and code-availability statement in the abstract; v1 only promises a later release in Appendix C. That older promise remains in v2, creating inconsistent availability wording. Implementation details are otherwise unchanged.
descriptions.R1: Appendix E adds citations to LongSpec, Jakiro and TALON, plus literature supporting the new multimodal, agentic and systems directions; the EAGLE-2 citation and reference are removed. The established comparative taxonomy and central novelty argument remain intact.
descriptions.P1: v2 adds the abstract code statement, a funding Acknowledgements section and a future-work paragraph in Appendix E. The existing scientific narrative and section organization are largely preserved.
descriptions.P2: All eight figures and ten tables retain their content, captions and design. Added text causes limited column and page reflow around existing figures and equations; the expanded references shift the appendix pagination.

P-C1B4AEE9DB.title: Beyond Transcripts: A Renewed Perspective on Audio Chaptering

descriptions.M1: Section 3.4.1 adds MLLM inference formulations producing timestamps and titles, either directly or alongside transcription. These extend the output procedure. AudioSeg's architecture, feature fusion and existing training objectives remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: V2 extends v1's YTSeg-only coverage to AMI multi-party meeting segmentation, including training and evaluation in this distinct domain. It also tests explicit timestamp prediction with and without transcription. Title generation itself was already present in v1.
descriptions.E2: Table A11 adds BART as a title-quality comparison reference, with results attributed to Retkowski and Waibel (2024). Its oracle segmentation and reference-transcript setting are explicitly identified. The original segmentation comparator sets remain unchanged.
descriptions.E3: V2 adds AMI-only versus YTSeg-to-AMI training comparisons, short-meeting and all-meeting evaluations, T1 evaluation at 8/10/12 seconds, and T2 scoring at ±3/±6 seconds. It also introduces temporal-matching and global-concatenation title evaluation using BERTScore and ROUGE-L. Original six-second evaluations and documented training settings are retained.
descriptions.E4: New analyses test pretraining transfer to AMI, sensitivity to evaluation granularity, and timestamp-localization errors using predicted versus forced-alignment timestamps. Duration analysis gains segment-density and speaker-composition statistics. Existing acoustic-feature, DeepFilterNet and MLLM failure analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: Existing plot bands and dataset summary reporting are retained. Neither new run counts or seeds nor new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures are documented. Added performance tables report point scores.
descriptions.E6: V2 adds AMI, timestamp, title-quality, granularity and continuous-time results. For example, Table 7 reports 12.52 F1 using Qwen3-Omni's predicted timestamps versus 43.84 using forced alignment of the same outputs. Table A8 reveals AudioSeg/MiniSeg-with-features ranking reversals at 8/10 seconds. Original table scores are retained; Section 5.1 corrects 37.74 to 37.76, matching the unchanged Table 4.
descriptions.T1: New Appendix B formally defines temporal title matching through endpoint tolerances and global title comparison through chronological concatenation, including unequal chapter counts. Existing segmentation definitions and alignment mathematics remain unchanged; no proofs are added.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, three stated contributions and conclusion retain their scientific claims about AudioSeg, acoustic cues, ASR robustness and transcript-invariant evaluation. The added experiments support and investigate these claims without redefining the central contribution.
descriptions.C2: V2 identifies temporal localization as an MLLM bottleneck, interprets transfer to meetings, explains re-discretization artifacts, and connects duration with speaker complexity. It also adds an explanation for adapted encoders' weaker standalone performance. Limitations now acknowledge small-scale AMI validation while retaining generalization concerns.
descriptions.D1: V1 promises a future AudioSeg release; v2 reports its release and supplies a model-access link in the first-page footnote. Existing hyperparameters, hardware information, prompts and feature-extraction details are retained across appendix renumbering. Availability is reported by the PDF, not externally verified.
descriptions.R1: Section 6 adds positioning against VAD and ASR chunking, while Appendix B discusses prior segmentation and title-evaluation approaches. Additional citations cover AMI, downstream chapter applications and encoder adaptation. The central novelty framing remains stable.
descriptions.P1: V2 makes localized language and cross-reference corrections, adds a temporal-grounding research question and subsection, and inserts a title-quality appendix. Subsequent sections and appendices are renumbered, while most existing prose and the overall organization are retained.
descriptions.P2: The results presentation expands substantially: Table 7 gains a timestamp-variant block and explanatory notes, and new appendix tables display AMI comparisons, granularity sensitivity, continuous-time scores, title metrics and duration statistics. Existing figures and tables are retained, with several relocated.

P-B327C00E18.title: AVA-VLA: Improving Vision-Language-Action models with Active Visual Attention

descriptions.M1: Sections 3.1–3.4 and Appendix A retain the recurrent-state construction, state-based action initialization, AVA architecture, attention reweighting, training losses, and inference procedure. The additional experiments test existing components and alternative training conditions without revising the proposed method.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate the same four LIBERO suites, CALVIN ABC-to-D setting, seven LIBERO+ perturbation dimensions, and four Mobile ALOHA tasks. The new ablations and failure cases use this existing coverage rather than introducing another dataset, domain, or test scenario.
descriptions.E2: v3 adds VLA-Adapter to the CALVIN comparison in Table 2, reporting an average completed length of 4.42. The existing benchmark and real-robot comparator sets otherwise remain intact. Newly discussed methods such as MemoryVLA are not added as evaluated baselines.
descriptions.E3: New Table 7 introduces a controlled LIBERO comparison: both methods start from the same pretrained OpenVLA checkpoint and train for 100,000 steps with batch size 256. This supplements the retained main recipe, which initializes AVA-VLA from trained OpenVLA-OFT and fine-tunes for 40,000 steps with batch size 64. Existing task splits, metrics, and real-robot trial counts remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: v3 adds analyses of the extra-training confound (Table 7), the attention regularizer (Table 8 and Figure 12), component contributions on CALVIN (Table 9), and manipulation failures (Figure 13). These expand the questions investigated. The LIBERO+ robustness study and earlier attention visualizations are retained and relocated, not newly introduced.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both use point estimates, and the stated real-robot trial counts are unchanged. The added experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.
descriptions.E6: Table 1 revises AVA-VLA's per-suite-policy Goal score from 98.2% to 97.9% and its average from 98.3% to 98.2%. Table 2 revises OpenVLA-OFT's CALVIN average from 4.10 to 4.28; AVA-VLA remains at 4.65. New results include 98.3% versus 96.8% under matched training, 97.5% without the regularizer versus 98.0% with it, and CALVIN component-only averages of 4.63 and 4.61. These additions expand the findings; the matched-training result is not a same-setting improvement over the earlier main experiment.
descriptions.T1: The POMDP formulation, recurrent-state definition, attention equations, and loss definitions in Equations 1–14 remain substantively unchanged. Notational corrections and expanded explanations introduce no new assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same core contributions: POMDP-inspired recurrent conditioning, active visual attention, strong benchmark performance, and transfer to real-world manipulation. The new supporting experiments do not redefine these claims or their scope.
descriptions.C2: v3 adds substantive interpretations concerning architectural benefits versus additional training, complementary component roles across task horizons, and the regularizer's role in suppressing distracting attention. New Appendix E attributes precision-sensitive failures to accumulated perception errors and belief drift, connects this limitation to long-horizon pruning sensitivity, and discusses possible remedies. v1 lacks this explicit limitations analysis.
descriptions.D1: v3 supplies a project-page link, reports that the added modules contain fewer than 50 million parameters and under 1% of the full model, and documents the new matched-training settings. The existing architecture descriptions, hardware, principal hyperparameters, and real-robot implementation details are retained.
descriptions.R1: New Appendix C expands positioning beyond v1's general VLA and sequential-VLM discussion. It distinguishes AVA-VLA from MemoryVLA's explicit memory retrieval and discusses its relationship to VLN-BERT, SafeVLA, NaVid, and recurrent reinforcement-learning approaches. These are substantive comparisons concerning memory representation and visual processing, alongside additional citations such as VLA-Adapter.
descriptions.P1: The abstract and conclusion are rewritten, introductory and technical prose is polished, and explanations of component roles are expanded. The supplement gains dedicated discussion and limitations sections, while execution trajectories move into Appendix B. The main five-section narrative and most technical exposition remain recognizable.
descriptions.P2: The manuscript changes from a predominantly single-column preprint layout to a two-column layout, with extensive table and figure resizing and relocation. v1 Figure 4 becomes supplementary Figure 6, and the existing attention figures are redistributed. v3 also adds Tables 7–9, a robot-platform image, regularizer visualization, and failure-case panels, and expands several captions.

P-90DFCFF0D8.title: Fixed Aggregation Features Can Rival GNNs

descriptions.M1: The core aggregation equations and MLP pipeline remain unchanged. Appendix B.3 introduces an evaluated optional Drop-Span step that removes linearly dependent feature columns; v1 only suggested dimensionality reduction as a possible remedy.
descriptions.E1: Appendix F adds preliminary evaluations on GraphBench's quotes and replies tasks, measured by MAE. The fourteen main benchmarks and four GraphLand datasets are retained, making this a limited extension of coverage.
descriptions.E2: New Table 4 evaluates PCA as a feature-reduction comparator alongside Drop-Span and unreduced FAF4. Existing GNN, GESN and GraphLand comparator sets remain unchanged. The GATv2-to-GAT prose edit matches the GAT labels already present in v1's unchanged tables, rather than establishing a baseline replacement.
descriptions.E3: The added compression experiment compares alternative feature preprocessing and input dimensions. GraphBench introduces test MAE and uses GraphLand-derived hyperparameters without further tuning. Existing experimental splits, hyperparameter grids and training budgets are unchanged.
descriptions.E4: Appendix B.3 and Table 4 add an analysis of whether feature reduction preserves prediction performance across five retained datasets, comparing Drop-Span with PCA. Existing reducer, hop, classifier, rewiring, KA and SHAP analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: New Table 4 introduces performance reporting through point estimates without variability or a stated repeat count, unlike the retained performance comparisons. Existing run/split descriptions and uncertainty reporting remain unchanged; GraphBench uses the existing ± format without specifying its repeat count.
descriptions.E6: Existing results are unchanged. New Table 4 reports Cora performance of 0.818, 0.8226 and 0.6632 for FAF4, Drop-Span and PCA. Table 17 adds FAF MAEs of 0.661 and 0.579 versus GNN values of 0.768 and 0.694 on quotes and replies. Tables 18–19 reproduce prior-work results.
descriptions.T1: Theorems 4.1–4.2, the proof and the two-hop example are retained. v2 clarifies multiset notation and that orthogonality concerns distinct feature states, consistent with the existing proof; it adds no substantive mathematical result or revised derivation.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and principal contributions retain the claim that FAFs compete on twelve of fourteen main benchmarks, with Roman-Empire and Minesweeper as exceptions. The theoretical message and recommendations for stronger tabular baselines and harder benchmarks remain unchanged.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds explanations concerning information discarding versus injectivity and why PCA may obscure sparse predictive signals. Appendix F adds substantive qualifications about incomplete tuning and why preliminary GraphLand results cannot establish that learned aggregation is necessary.
descriptions.D1: v2 documents the feature-column removal procedure and original/reduced input dimensions, and explains that GraphBench uses transferred GraphLand hyperparameters without retuning. Existing code access, hardware and main training details are retained; the new experiments remain only partly specified.
descriptions.R1: Section 2 expands positioning against close alternatives: SIGN, GAMLP and HOGA, plus a dedicated discussion of graph tabularization for foundation models by Eremeev, Choi and Hayler. It distinguishes FAF's nonlinear reducers and analytical aims from these approaches. Appendix A also expands the comparison with GIN's injectivity argument.
descriptions.P1: The revision makes localized prose expansions, clarifies terminology, refines appendix headings and adds Appendix G. It also updates the publication footer and reorders acknowledgments and the impact statement. Most prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds feature-reduction Table 4, GraphBench Table 17 and reproduced Tables 18–19. Existing figures and tables are retained, with renumbering and relocation, including Figure 4. Figure 1's caption is expanded; the existing plots are unchanged.

P-F9A7C76E44.title: Graph-R1: Towards Agentic GraphRAG Framework via End-to-end Reinforcement Learning

descriptions.M1: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the multi-turn policy, dual entity/hyperedge retrieval, reciprocal-rank fusion, and GRPO with format/F1 rewards. Appendix J expands construction documentation without establishing a revised Graph-R1 procedure.
descriptions.E1: V2 retains the six original QA benchmarks and adds zero-shot evaluation on Medicine, Agriculture, CS, Legal, and Mix datasets in Appendix K.2. These broaden the evaluated domains.
descriptions.E2: The main comparator membership is unchanged. Added experiments reuse Search-R1 and the existing GPT-4o-mini comparator set; Table 6 explicitly imports the latter's scores from HyperGraphRAG. Newly cited graph methods are not added as evaluated baselines.
descriptions.E3: V1 Table 5 specifies three epochs for R1, Search-R1, R1-Searcher, and Graph-R1; v2 Table 3 specifies one. Appendix K adds combined-dataset training with controlled total data volume and specialized-domain zero-shot testing. These extend the protocols; the unchanged main scores do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: Existing ablations, sensitivity comparisons, case study, and transfer heatmaps remain. Appendix K adds a controlled comparison of dataset-specific, single-source transfer, and mixed-dataset training, plus specialized-domain transfer tests, extending the generalization analysis.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional tables continue to report point estimates.
descriptions.E6: Table 2 and the original transfer heatmaps retain their numerical results. V2 adds result sets: combined-training average F1 is 48.19 for Graph-R1 versus 35.25 for Search-R1, and specialized-domain average F1 is 39.26 versus 24.32. These concern newly reported conditions, not same-setting improvements between versions.
descriptions.T1: Appendix B retains the three propositions and their mathematical arguments, and Appendix C retains the complexity analysis. Equation consolidation, renumbering, and shortening the standard F1 explanation do not revise the mathematics.
descriptions.C1: The central contribution and claims about accuracy, retrieval efficiency, and generation quality remain. V2's abstract emphasizes being the first such framework, but v1 already makes that novelty claim in Section 2. Generalization claims remain in the relocated and expanded appendix discussion.
descriptions.C2: V2 removes v1 Appendix H's explicit limitations concerning construction cost, missing structural reasoning in retrieval, and text-only knowledge. Appendix K adds interpretations about transferable relational biases and the benefits of domain-aligned versus mixed supervision. Together these materially change the discussion of applicability and limitations.
descriptions.D1: Appendix J newly specifies 1200-token chunks with 50-token overlap and explains the construction and vector-storage pipeline. The abstract extends the availability statement from code to software and data, and Appendix G revises the epoch setting. Conversely, Section 4 omits v1's explicit answer-reward tokenization preprocessing note.
descriptions.R1: Section 2 adds works including G-Reasoner, Youtu-GraphRAG, and GraphSearch, while removing examples such as VLM-R1 and ZeroSearch. The overall research positioning remains similar; numerous other bibliography edits are publication updates to retained works.
descriptions.P1: V2 condenses wording and subsection titles, moves the case study and generalization section into Appendices H–I, and adds acknowledgments and an impact statement. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain recognizable.
descriptions.P2: The main text changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. V2 combines the cost table and generation radar chart into Figure 6, relocates existing displays, and adds Figure 12 and experimental Tables 5–6. Relocated Figure 11 also replaces informative method/metric subcaptions with misleading generic labels.

P-14803FA4E1.title: Efficient Prediction of SO(3)-Equivariant Hamiltonian Matrices via SO(2) Local Frames

descriptions.M1: The specified SO(2) tensor-product computation changes from componentwise products and index flips in v1 Eqs. 5–8 to complex-product and conjugate-product formulas with cross terms and signs in v2 Eqs. 7–9. This is a localized correction to a component; the surrounding architecture and nearest-neighbor frame selection remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish an implementation change or experimental rerun.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate the same four QH9 settings and MD17 trajectories for water, ethanol, malondialdehyde and uracil. PubChemQH remains unevaluated future work in both versions.
descriptions.E2: Table 1 retains QHNet across QH9, WANet on stable-id, and SPHNet on stable-id and stable-ood. Table 2 retains PhiSNet, QHNet and SPHNet for MD17, and Table 3 retains the same efficiency comparators. The new gate-comparison table is conceptual, not an evaluated baseline.
descriptions.E3: The splits, sample sizes, metrics, training budgets, schedules and model configurations match between v1 Appendix C and v2 Appendix F. The relocated efficiency study retains the single-A6000, maximum-available-batch-size protocol.
descriptions.E4: Table 4 retains the same three SO(2) TP/FFN configurations and ablation results; the accompanying study moves from Section 5.4 to Appendix A.2. The added frame-discontinuity discussion contains no new robustness test or sensitivity analysis.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The empirical tables retain the same point-estimate reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: In Table 1, QHNet's diagonal/off-diagonal MAEs on QH9-dynamic-300k-mol change from 108.70/261.63 to 261.63/108.70, in units of 10^-6 Hartree. This swaps the reported values and reverses the diagonal-error ranking against QHNetV2. The remaining benchmark, efficiency and ablation values are retained.
descriptions.T1: Beyond the retained frame-averaging argument, v2 adds Appendix D derivations relating SO(2) linear operations to SO(3) tensor products and comparing gate expressivity, plus Appendix E's irrep-mapping equivariance argument. Section 3.2 also revises the tensor-product algebra. These expand and revise the mathematical treatment.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: QHNetV2 uses SO(2) local-frame operations to preserve global SO(3) equivariance, avoid costly SO(3) tensor products, and perform strongly on QH9 and MD17. The symmetric-contraction analogy removed from the abstract remains in the introduction and method.
descriptions.C2: v2 newly acknowledges discontinuities from nearest-neighbor frame selection and discusses averaging neighboring frames as a possible remedy. It also explicitly states that SO(2) and SO(3) tensor products are non-equivalent and that lower complexity does not guarantee better performance. Appendix D adds an expressivity explanation for SO(2) gating.
descriptions.D1: v1's abstract promises code release through AIRS and supplies a repository URL; v2 removes both without replacement. Software versions, hardware and appendix hyperparameters remain unchanged. This changes access information, without establishing whether code availability actually changed.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds Pozdnyakov and Ceriotti's work on smooth rotational symmetrization and expands the discussion of continuity and relationships to eSCN. It drops v1 Section 3.1's explicit claim to be the first to connect eSCN with frame averaging. The Hamiltonian-prediction related-work survey is otherwise retained.
descriptions.P1: Section 3.1 is rewritten into explicit global-frame, local-frame and irrep-mapping explanations. Hamiltonian equivariance moves from v1 Appendix A.3 into Section 2.1, while efficiency and ablation studies move into v2 Appendix A. Most existing prose remains, alongside small abstract edits and removal of acknowledgments.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds Table 5 comparing SO(2) and SO(3) gates, relocates Tables 3–4 to the appendix, and adjusts benchmark-table sizing and emphasis. Figures 1–2 retain their drawings, with resizing or placement changes. The overall visual format remains similar.

P-3797F32E4C.title: Beyond Simple Graphs: Neural Multi-Objective Routing on Multigraphs

descriptions.M1: Section 4 and the matched architecture/training appendices retain the GREAT encoders, edge-based and dual-head decoders, preference conditioning, REINFORCE objectives and curriculum. The additional tasks and expanded implementation explanations do not establish a changed algorithm.
descriptions.E1: v5 adds MGMOCVRP on FLEX2/FIX2, combining capacity constraints with two conflicting total-distance objectives. It also adds tri-objective MOTSP and MGMOTSP across several distributions and instance sizes (Tables 11, 16–17). v3's multigraph experiments covered TSP-family problems, and all its evaluations were bi-objective.
descriptions.E2: v5 adds evaluated GREAT-based GRBM and GOAL-based GOBM comparators, including augmented variants, across retained routing tasks and MGMOCVRP (Table 6). It also introduces HGS for MGMOCVRP (Tables 1 and 11). The existing MBM, Euclidean CNH, evolutionary algorithms and relevant heuristics remain.
descriptions.E3: The existing bi-objective evaluation and training protocols are retained. Added tri-objective experiments use 105 heuristic subproblems and 105 or 1035 neural preferences, with three-dimensional hypervolume reference points (Tables 16–17; Appendix E). MGMOCVRP also receives task-specific reference points. These extend protocols for new experiments rather than revise the earlier evaluations.
descriptions.E4: The learned-versus-simple pruning and reward ablations, training analyses and zero-shot tests already appear in v3 and are retained. v5 extends the pre-pruning ablation to MGMOCVRP (Table 1) and compares 105 versus 1035 neural preferences on tri-objective tasks (Tables 16–17), adding evidence about pruning and inference-budget sensitivity.
descriptions.E5: Both versions average hypervolume over test instances and report runtimes. Neither reports repeated training-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests; the added results introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: Matched earlier benchmark results retain their values and runtimes, but v5 adds results for new tasks and comparators. For example, MGMOCVRP FLEX2-50 yields HV 0.89 for HGS and 0.86 for augmented GMS-EB (Table 1). Tri-objective XASY100 yields 0.64 for GMS-DH versus 0.68 for MBM with 105 preferences (Table 16). These are newly reported settings, not performance changes under v3's settings.
descriptions.T1: v5 explicitly requires the Chebyshev reference value to lie strictly below the minimum of each objective, whereas v3 only calls it an ideal value. New Appendix B.2 provides graph-size and decoding-complexity arguments for line-graph and virtual-node transformations. The Pareto definitions, scalarizations and Proposition 1 remain otherwise unchanged; its proof is still omitted.
descriptions.C1: The central contributions remain the first neural multigraph-routing solvers, their two construction strategies and competitive performance with different scalability tradeoffs. v5's introduction additionally claims that naive extensions of existing single-objective asymmetric solvers perform poorly, extending v3's comparison of existing methods' supported inputs and tasks.
descriptions.C2: v5 adds explanations involving parallel-edge permutation invariance and graph transformations, and explains the existing omission of MatNet from large-instance evaluations. Appendix H.4 newly attributes the retained FIX10-100 weakness to the selection decoder's growing action space; H.5 qualifies objective-count scalability with the new GMS-DH XASY100 failure. Earlier training-cost and pruning-context limitations remain.
descriptions.D1: v5 replaces the promised future code release with a stated public implementation link. It also specifies uniform training-preference sampling, evenly spaced evaluation preferences, and construction details for GRBM/GOBM and the added tasks. Existing hardware, hyperparameters, curriculum and parameter counts remain documented as before. Repository contents were not independently verified.
descriptions.R1: Appendix A.2 and new Appendix B expand research positioning, including POCCO, EFormer and hierarchical graph-partitioning work. v5 distinguishes encoding incompatibility from theoretically extendable edge-based methods and develops explicit novelty comparisons against prior AR/NAR combinations and dual-decoder systems. This goes beyond adding citations to the existing review.
descriptions.P1: The introduction is rewritten around encoder and decoder incompatibilities, and multigraph-related discussion is consolidated into Section 2.2. A dedicated Extended Motivation appendix reorganizes the architectural rationale, graph-transformation alternatives and technical novelty. Experimental subsections and appendices are reorganized, although most method exposition is retained.
descriptions.P2: The document changes from two-column to single-column conference formatting. Architecture diagrams are redrawn with example graphs and autoregressive loops, and a graph-transformation figure is added. Table 1 gains MGMOCVRP, new comparison/result tables appear, and v3's separate time-window tables are merged into v5 Table 12. Training plots are retained and relocated.

P-E33DCEF7FB.title: Beyond RAG vs. Long-Context: Learning Distraction-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Knowledge Grounding

descriptions.M1: The core architecture, band-selection procedure and policy-gradient update are retained. Appendices D.5 and D.9 add evaluated variants with token-cost regularization, standard learnable embeddings and a pooled MLP encoder. These extend the studied procedures without replacing the main LDAR method.
descriptions.E1: v2 adds Ada-LEval's BestAnswer task, requiring selection of the most helpful answer among StackOverflow candidates (D.7, Table 8). The existing LaRA tasks and HELMET HotpotQA/NQ coverage are retained.
descriptions.E2: v2 adds RankZephyr to the main LaRA comparisons and all nine per-model tables, and adds cache-augmented generation, CAG, to efficiency comparisons. These substantively broaden evaluated alternatives to include listwise reranking and document-cache reuse while retaining the previous comparator suite.
descriptions.E3: New protocols measure end-to-end latency and cumulative training/inference costs at 10K, 100K and 500K inference calls. Additional designs include embedding-model swaps, misaligned task transfers, clustering 100 similarity distributions and sliding windows of 20, 50 and 100 passages. The original split and correctness judging remain unchanged; newly disclosed chunking details do not establish changed preprocessing.
descriptions.E4: Beyond the retained band-versus-Bernoulli and hallucination-training analyses, v2 adds cost-objective and architecture ablations, cross-embedder generalization and task-alignment tests. New case studies, clustering and sliding-window experiments investigate when broader or non-top-ranked retrieval helps (D.2–D.10).
descriptions.E5: Figure 11 newly specifies standard-deviation bands across examples for similarity distributions. Existing standard-error reporting across LLMs is retained. Neither version provides explicit seed or repeated-run counts.
descriptions.E6: Original LDAR accuracy results are retained, while v2 adds baseline, efficiency, ablation and transfer results. New Table 3 reports open-source LDAR/LC latency of 3.9/15.4 seconds, and Table 8 adds BestAnswer results. A retained entry also changes: GPT-4o Top-5's 128K overall token ratio goes from 0.082 to 0.025 (v1 Table 10; v2 Table 16).
descriptions.T1: Section 4's equations and Algorithm 1 retain the same mathematical content. The added mechanism and transfer discussions are empirical; no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations are introduced.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction's contributions and conclusion retain the central claim that capacity-adaptive band retrieval balances coverage and distraction, improving accuracy with fewer tokens. Added experiments support this existing contribution without redefining it.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds substantive explanations involving similarity-scale/rank alignment, task-structure alignment, mid-ranked informative passages and cost-penalty-induced collapse. It also interprets deployment volume as determining training-cost amortization. These expand applicability conditions and mechanism explanations; the original limitations paragraph is merely relocated to Appendix B.
descriptions.D1: v2 newly documents 600-token chunks with 100-token overlap, RankZephyr's top-50-to-top-5 procedure, and per-document caching for CAG. The anonymous code-access link is replaced by the named GitHub repository. Core LDAR hyperparameters and hardware disclosures are retained.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds references and discussion for CAG, RankZephyr, Ada-LEval, C-pack and Deep Sets. These support added comparisons and analyses; the main related-work organization and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.
descriptions.P1: Most original prose and the main narrative are preserved. Local revisions clarify baseline descriptions and task alignment, move limitations into Appendix B, reorganize the appendices, and update author, affiliation and publication information. Added scientific sections do not constitute extensive rewriting of the existing text.
descriptions.P2: v2 expands visual presentation with efficiency plots, an annotated case study, rank-agreement and clustering figures, sliding-window plots and ablation tables. Existing comparison tables gain RankZephyr rows. v1 Figures 5–6 are retained as v2 Figures 6–7, while new Table 3 is redisplayed as Table 6.

P-A9551C0D7D.title: xRFM: Accurate, scalable, and interpretable feature learning models for tabular data

descriptions.M1: v2 routes each prediction to one leaf. v3 Appendix B adds optional temperature-tuned routing that averages predictions from up to eight leaves using products of node weights. Appendix D also introduces validation-based selection among xRFM and GBDTs. These add substantive prediction procedures, while the original leaf learner and Algorithms A.1–A.5 remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: The three benchmark suites and interpretability tasks remain. New Table E.2 includes Diabetes130US and KDDCup99 beyond v2's ten named meta-test classification datasets. However, v2 does not enumerate its 300 TALENT datasets, so whether these introduce new underlying data or reuse previously evaluated coverage cannot be established.
descriptions.E2: Tables E.1–E.2 add explicit comparisons of AGOP, AGOP+TT, PCA+TT and RF+TT splitting variants. Table E.3 adds an original-RFM comparison on large TALENT classification datasets, and E.17 compares validation-selected portfolios. The principal benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged; TabDPT was already present in v2.
descriptions.E3: The new split study uses a 40,000-sample split threshold and validation tuning over hard routing plus 15 temperatures. The portfolio evaluation introduces validation-based model selection on 200 datasets with available validation results. These are additional protocols; the existing benchmark search spaces, including the 60,000-sample threshold, are retained.
descriptions.E4: v3 adds quantitative split-method and temperature ablations, including runtime tradeoffs (E.1–E.2), a large-dataset RFM comparison (E.3), benchmark-overlap analyses (E.14–E.16), portfolio analyses (E.17), and performance versus dataset metafeatures (F.3). These expand investigation of the method's design and behavior beyond v2's benchmark and interpretability evidence.
descriptions.E5: Table E.13 newly reports asymmetric Elo uncertainty bounds, whereas v2's corresponding table contains point estimates only. Their confidence level and estimation procedure are unspecified. The existing Wilcoxon comparison and five-split averaging for the retained meta-test results remain unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is established.
descriptions.E6: v2's binary TabArena Table B.10 duplicates its regression Table B.8; v3 replaces it with distinct binary results in E.13, including xRFM (T) Elo 1251 instead of 1504. This is a reporting correction. Numerous supplementary results are also added, while matched TALENT, original meta-test, and TabArena regression/multiclass tables retain their values.
descriptions.T1: Appendix B introduces mathematical definitions for temperature-scaled sigmoid node weights and path-product leaf weights, relating hard routing to zero temperature. Existing kernel, AGOP and metric definitions remain unchanged. No theorem or proof is added.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal claims: strong tabular prediction, scalable tree-based local feature learning, and native AGOP interpretability. Additional supporting experiments do not redefine these core contributions.
descriptions.C2: Appendix B newly explains how globally simple targets or poor splits can make partitioning harmful and discusses the cost of leaf ensembling. Appendix C considers tuning, cross-validation, baselines and metrics as possible explanations for benchmark differences after examining dataset overlap. Existing AGOP interpretations and principal future-work discussions remain.
descriptions.D1: v3 supplies temperature-grid limits of 0.025–4.5, the eight-leaf ensemble cap, and supplementary split settings. A.3 also documents 50 sampled configurations and coordinate standardization for TabPFN-v2 embedding experiments, although corresponding outcomes are not reported. Existing implementation descriptions, main search spaces and code-access information are retained.
descriptions.R1: The cited works and principal positioning relative to RFMs, scalable kernels, GBDTs and tabular foundation models remain unchanged. Switching from numbered to author-year citations does not add related work.
descriptions.P1: Main section order and most prose remain intact. v3 expands selected results paragraphs, introduces focused appendix sections B–D and F, and updates author affiliations, acknowledgments, headers and citation style. These are localized editorial and organizational changes.
descriptions.P2: Figure 3 expands from six to nine panels, adding normalized-error versus training-time plots. Seven supplementary tables and Figures F.1 and F.3 are added; existing tables and figures are redistributed under the ICLR layout. The original runtime Figure B.1 is retained as F.2, rather than newly introduced.

P-8D6A5D7CA6.title: XR-1: Towards Versatile Vision-Language-Action Models via Learning Unified Vision-Motion Representations

descriptions.M1: Section 3.2 revises the stated motion-decoder inputs: v1 specifies language and observations alongside the motion code, whereas v2 permits optional conditions and explicitly uses proprioceptive states in its implementation. The dual-branch UVMC architecture and three-stage framework otherwise remain stable.
descriptions.E1: Appendix F adds CALVIN D-to-D evaluation, extending coverage to simulated, language-conditioned manipulation using CALVIN's 34-task repertoire. The original real-world embodiments and tasks remain. Identifying XR-D as a RoboMIND 2.0 subset does not establish a change to its represented training data.
descriptions.E2: The new CALVIN comparison in Table 17 introduces evaluated comparators OpenVLA, Qwen-π0, and Qwen-GR00T, alongside RDT-1B, π0, and π0.5. This adds a distinct comparison suite; comparator membership in the retained real-world and ACT/DP adaptation experiments is unchanged.
descriptions.E3: v2 introduces CALVIN testing on 1,000 five-instruction sequences and new retrieval and controlled-ablation protocols. It also changes Stage-2 from absent to downstream-task training for Exps. 2 and 4–9 in v1 Table 4/v2 Table 3. This is a substantive reported-setting revision, without establishing that experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: Appendix D adds codebook-size, embedding-dimension, modality-only, shared-versus-separate-codebook, and Ego4D ablations. Appendices G–I add nearest-neighbor retrieval, t-SNE analyses, and baseline/XR-1 failure cases. The earlier cross-embodiment transfer analysis is retained as Table 16, rather than newly introduced.
descriptions.E5: Appendix G.2 and Table 18 newly summarize normalized nearest-neighbor similarity distributions using modes and averages, extending descriptive statistical reporting beyond success-rate averages. Neither version reports repeated-training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
descriptions.E6: New results include motion-only, vision-only, and unified-code success rates of 35.0%, 50.0%, and 66.7% in Table 14; Ego4D ablation results of 32.5% versus 38.3% in Table 15; and CALVIN scores of 4.256 for XR-1 versus 3.885 for π0.5 in Table 17. Retrieval statistics and failure findings are also added. Matched original real-world scores remain unchanged.
descriptions.T1: Appendix G.2 introduces a formal construction of the cross-task retrieval statistic: a pairwise motion–vision similarity matrix, column-wise maxima, and a normalized nearest-neighbor vector. Existing training mathematics is mostly compacted or renotated; no new theorem or proof is introduced.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: unified vision–motion codes, heterogeneous-data exploitation, a model-agnostic three-stage framework, and strong performance across six robot embodiments and over 120 tasks. Additional evidence does not redefine these main claims.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds interpretations of codebook saturation, comparable shared/separate codebooks under alignment, human-video benefits, and action-semantic clustering across embodiments. It also explicitly identifies XR-1's precision failures on tiny screws, adding a concrete applicability limitation absent from v1's discussion.
descriptions.D1: v2 identifies XR-D's relationship to RoboMIND 2.0, specifies the motion-decoder conditioning used, and documents feature extraction and similarity aggregation for the new retrieval analyses. Existing architecture tables, hyperparameters, hardware, training costs, inference speeds, and project access information are retained.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds citations to CALVIN and RoboMIND 2.0 and connects XR-D to the latter. It removes the Weblab xArm reference by Matsushima et al., replacing the corresponding dataset citations with Oh et al. The broader positioning against action-only and video-only representation learning remains.
descriptions.P1: The introduction, related work, methodology, and experimental narrative undergo condensation and rewriting. Ablations precede generalization, appendices are reorganized into A–J, and an Additional Analyses section is added. The LLM-writing disclosure is removed and an Impact Statement appears.
descriptions.P2: The main paper changes from a single-column layout to two columns. Figure 2 is redrawn with explicit conditioning and token labels, the ablation table's stage columns are restructured, and existing displays are relocated. New CALVIN, retrieval, t-SNE, and failure-case figures accompany four additional tables.

P-D1172FA39A.title: What Matters in RL-Based Methods for Object-Goal Navigation? An Empirical Study and A Unified Framework

descriptions.M1: v2 introduces tested procedure variants using detector-plus-SAM2 segmentation, nearest/farthest frontier selection, and a height-map channel replacing the binary obstacle channel. These extend the framework; its principal architecture, reward functions and test-time algorithms remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: v2 extends the Gibson navigation evaluation to HM3D, using five test scenes for perception comparisons and the full 20-scene HM3D v1 validation split for component evaluation (A.4). This materially broadens environmental coverage. MP3D and AI2-THOR evaluations remain proposed future work.
descriptions.E2: Table 1 expands perception comparisons by adding RF-DETR-Seg, RF-DETR+SAM2 and YOLO11-XL under both corner and frontier policies. The new HM3D comparison also evaluates YOLO11-N. Table 4 retains the same ten named prior navigation baselines and the human baseline.
descriptions.E3: New experiments specify five-scene detector testing, 20-scene zero-shot testing without retraining, FPS reporting, and PPO clipping settings of 0.2 and 0.001. These extend the established evaluation procedures. The original 500-step limit, dynamic-step calculation, success criterion, navigation metrics and two-million-frame training budget remain unchanged; expanded human-study controls are newly disclosed details.
descriptions.E4: v2 adds analyses of frontier-goal selection, PPO update constraints and height information (Tables 7–9), plus cross-dataset component ablations on HM3D (Table 6). New Figures 7–9 illustrate untrapping, dynamic-goal and remapping behavior. The original failure analysis and perception visualizations are retained.
