descriptions.E5: Neither version reports independent-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates; the expanded human-study description introduces no new statistical estimation procedure.
descriptions.E6: Retained Gibson results are unchanged, including the continuous policy's 84.4% SR/48.2% SPL and humans' 98.0% SR/53.3% SPL. Additional new results appear in the expanded Table 1 and Tables 5–9: RF-DETR-Seg obtains 52.4% SR/24.2% SPL on five HM3D scenes, and the height-map ablation reports 75.1% SR versus 78.3% with the obstacle map. These are added comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.
descriptions.T1: The reward definitions, map and action formulations, and dynamic-step equation remain unchanged. The new PPO and height-map discussions provide empirical analysis and intuitive explanations, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.
descriptions.C1: v2 qualifies v1's claim that policy improvements yield only marginal gains: the abstract now says perception and test-time strategies often yield larger gains, while the introduction and conclusion emphasize reliable policy comparisons under unified configurations. The conclusion drops the 'first' empirical-study claim. The central decomposition, performance and human-gap contributions remain.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning cross-dataset transfer, frontier information-gain/travel-cost trade-offs, restrictive PPO updates, and why height information may require more training data. It also proposes that structured maps explain similar CNN/Transformer performance. Some interpretations overreach: A.4 asserts a shared detector ordering that is not consistent across the metrics in Tables 1 and 5.
descriptions.D1: v2 supplies project and repository links, explicitly identifies PPO, and expands human-study documentation with the interface, observation restrictions and prohibition on repeated episodes. These clarify existing work without establishing that the human experiment changed. Hardware and training-budget disclosures are retained; release wording remains inconsistent between the introduction and A.2.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds connections to MOPA for random/frontier goal selection, PPO and broader robotics learning, contemporary detectors, and 3D-LLM/ForesightNav for spatial representations. These broaden supporting context and attribution while retaining the central positioning as an empirical study of modular ObjectNav components.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, conclusion and most recommendation passages are rewritten, and policy-learning and human-study explanations are expanded. Numbered experimental subsubsections become paragraph headings, the appendix is reorganized, and references move after the appendix. These constitute extensive narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds Tables 5–9 and Figures 7–10, expands Table 1, and redraws Figure 2 with failure-mode annotations. Table 4 becomes a full-width summary containing one own-policy row instead of four; the other policies' results remain elsewhere. Typography, margins, headers and recommendation boxes change throughout, while original perception Figures 7–9 reappear as Figures 11–13.

P-15AA5D444A.title: QuantSparse: Comprehensively Compressing Video Diffusion Transformer with Model Quantization and Attention Sparsification

descriptions.M1: MSAD, its loss, and the SSAR/SVD correction procedure are retained. Equation 7 explicitly adds aggregation over attention heads before salient-token selection, whereas v1 omits head indexing. The PDFs do not establish whether this changes the implemented selection procedure or clarifies its earlier description. Algorithm 1 otherwise documents the existing pipeline.
descriptions.E1: v3 Appendix K adds text-to-image generation on DrawBench using Hunyuan-DiT. This extends evaluation beyond the video-generation tasks covered in v1. Existing OpenSORA-prompt and VBench video coverage remains; moving HunyuanVideo results into Table 2 does not add coverage.
descriptions.E2: v3 Table 13 adds full-attention distillation as a performance comparator to MSAD; v1 Figure 3 only compared its attention-memory cost. The established quantization and sparsification baseline sets remain. Evaluating QuaRot and Q-VDiT on DrawBench extends their coverage without introducing new baseline methods.
descriptions.E3: The original 50-step video evaluation and 20-sample, 15-epoch calibration settings remain. Added experiments introduce cache intervals 3–6, attention densities 10–25%, a 1000-sample attention-MSE diagnostic, a full-attention distillation control, and W4A8 evaluation of the 1.5B Hunyuan-DiT. These are targeted protocol extensions.
descriptions.E4: v3 expands validation of the framework's rationale and design choices: Table 8 isolates quantization, sparsification, and their interaction; Figures 8–9 add four paired attention-error examples; Table 5 tests cache-interval and density trade-offs; Table 13 compares MSAD against full-attention distillation. Existing saliency, SVD, and component ablations are retained.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing temporal singular-value mean/variance plots are retained. The new 1000-sample diagnostic specifies sample size, not repeated-run uncertainty.
descriptions.E6: Additional new findings accompany the added experiments. v3 reports attention MSE of 0.685 for combined compression versus 0.216 and 0.134 separately; full-attention distillation and MSAD achieve 15.25 and 15.22 PSNR respectively at substantially different resource costs; DrawBench results give QuantSparse 20.34 PSNR versus Q-VDiT's 19.32. New sensitivity results and baseline latency entries also appear. Matched original video benchmark scores remain unchanged.
descriptions.T1: Equation 7 revises the written saliency definition from summation over one token index to explicit summation over heads and tokens. The other substantive equations, Propositions 3.1–3.3, Theorem 3.4, and its Appendix A proof remain unchanged.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about amplified attention shift, MSAD, SSAR, and compression-quality benefits. The headline HunyuanVideo result remains 20.88 PSNR with 3.68× storage compression and 1.88× acceleration.
descriptions.C2: Section 4.2 newly attributes occasional improvements over full precision to emphasizing task-critical tokens, suppressing irrelevant attention, and stabilizing temporal behavior. New discussion explains cache-interval and density choices and interprets DrawBench results as evidence of applicability to image generation. No substantive new limitations discussion is added.
descriptions.D1: v3 adds calibration-to-inference pseudocode and specifies A800 80GB hardware, CUDA 12.4, and CUTLASS integer matrix multiplication through PyTorch. Table 13 also documents attention-map dimensions. Existing calibration hyperparameters remain, and both versions still describe the same code repository as forthcoming.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds citations including S2Q-VDiT, MPQ-DMv2, AffineQuant, Hunyuan-DiT, DrawBench's source work, and CUTLASS, while removing the Krishnamoorthi whitepaper reference. The central positioning around combining quantization and sparsification remains. Q-VDiT's publication update refers to the same work.
descriptions.P1: Changes are localized: a new overall-pipeline subsection, expanded experimental explanations, an image-generation appendix, acknowledgements, affiliation updates, and some terminology corrections. Appendix H reorders existing discussions. Most of the original narrative and section organization are preserved.
descriptions.P2: Table 2 is restructured to combine both large video models with quality and latency columns, incorporating existing appendix results. v3 also adds four experimental tables, paired attention-map figures, and an algorithm display, and reformats the SVD ablation table. Existing video examples and earlier analytical figures are retained.

P-FBA29E1EB3.title: GAP-MLLM: Geometry-Aligned Pre-training for Activating 3D Spatial Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models

descriptions.M1: Section 7.5 introduces sliding-window inference for dynamic videos, processing each window independently in its first-frame coordinate system. The encoders, gated fusion, joint pre-training, and two-stage grounding procedure remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: Coverage expands beyond the retained indoor datasets to degraded first-frame inputs and dynamic outdoor driving scenes from nuScenes. The outdoor evaluation is qualitative only, but introduces a substantially different domain and scene conditions.
descriptions.E2: Corresponding existing comparisons retain their comparator membership. The new small-object analysis uses VG-LLM, already evaluated for detection. Table 3 relabels the larger VG-LLM row from 7B to 8B with identical scores; this is a reported model-size revision rather than an established new comparison method.
descriptions.E3: New protocols corrupt only the first frame using blur at sigma 8/12 or occlusion covering 30%/50%, and report category-specific and averaged metrics for eight small-object classes. Table 3 also revises the stated VG-LLM size from 7B to 8B without establishing reruns. Existing training budgets, splits, and metrics remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: New Sections 7.3–7.5 expand supplementary analysis: sensitivity to first-frame corruption, small-object performance under patch merging, and qualitative dynamic-scene/domain-shift testing. Existing component, fusion, supervision, and grounding ablations are retained.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing reconstruction mean/median summaries are unchanged, and the new tables continue reporting point estimates without uncertainty.
descriptions.E6: Existing numerical entries are retained, but new results broaden the findings. Table 15 reports F1 declining from 50.6 on clean inputs to 47.5/46.0 under blur and 50.1/48.4 under occlusion. Table 16 reports small-object average F1 of 31.2 versus VG-LLM's 16.0, and Figure 12 adds qualitative outdoor detections. These are additional conditions, not improved scores on the original benchmarks.
descriptions.T1: The token definitions, fusion equations (1)–(3), and coordinate formulations are unchanged. No mathematical derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or revised.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about activating geometric priors through sparse joint pre-training and multi-level gated fusion. The appendix extensions do not redefine these central contributions.
descriptions.C2: The added analyses interpret corruption tolerance as effective multi-frame aggregation and small-object performance as preservation of information after patch merging. Section 7.5 newly states the static-scene assumption, attributes preliminary outdoor generalization to VGGT priors, and acknowledges missing motion modeling and temporal association. Section 9's existing limitations remain unchanged.
descriptions.D1: V2 adds a project-page address, specifies that the existing ten-scene reconstruction evaluation uses random ScanNet scenes, and documents corruption settings and window-based inference. The random-scene statement is additional disclosure, not evidence of changed sampling. The PDFs do not establish code availability through the new address.
descriptions.R1: V2 adds references to nuScenes and Li et al.'s work on causal tracing of object representations. All 61 earlier references are retained, and the positioning relative to geometric reconstruction and prior 3D MLLMs remains substantially unchanged.
descriptions.P1: V2 makes limited wording and terminology edits, updates affiliation and author-note text, adds acknowledgments, and inserts Sections 7.3–7.5 within the existing supplementary structure. The main narrative and section organization are largely preserved.
descriptions.P2: Tables 15–16 and Figures 10–12 expand the appendix's visual presentation of robustness, small objects, and dynamic scenes. Figure 11 redisplays detections already shown in Figure 7 with enlarged crops. Original appendix Figures 10–12 are retained as Figures 13–15 and relocated. Smaller teaser, architecture-label, and front-matter layout edits also occur.

P-F016033310.title: Leveraging Multispectral Sensors for Color Correction in Mobile Cameras

descriptions.M1: The LPIENet and cmKAN adaptations retain the same spectral encoders, fusion operations, model configurations and training objectives. Figure 2 is redrawn without changing the depicted procedure.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same hyperspectral scene sources, 102 illuminants and seven simulated RGB camera sensitivities. Aligned, spatially misaligned and exposure-scaled evaluations are retained.
descriptions.E2: The comparator sets remain identical within each experiment: the statistical, FC4, ConvMean, QU and spectral baselines in Table 1, the spectral baselines in Table 2, and SpectralConvMean in Table 4.
descriptions.E3: The scene-wise splits, input resolutions, optimization settings, evaluation metrics and camera aggregation remain unchanged. Both versions use the same spectral-encoder adaptation for misalignment and the same exposure factors.
descriptions.E4: Both retain the misalignment experiment in Table 2, multispectral-input ablation in Table 3, exposure robustness tests in Table 4 and qualitative cases in Figure 4. No analysis is added or removed.
descriptions.E5: Both report the same distribution summaries and averaging across cameras. Neither introduces repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.
descriptions.E6: All numerical entries in Tables 1–4 are unchanged; for example, Table 1 retains cmKAN-light mean ΔE00 values of 1.60 for mirrorless and 1.47 for mobile sensors. Visual inspection confirms that Figure 4 retains the same examples and displayed error values.
descriptions.T1: The image-formation equation (1) and associated mathematical reasoning remain unchanged. No formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added or removed.
descriptions.C1: Both claim a unified RGB–multispectral correction framework, a 116,688-pair dataset and adaptations of two architectures. The abstract retains the claim of up to 50% error reduction, and the conclusion retains the same generality and robustness claims.
descriptions.C2: The explanation still attributes reflectance–illumination ambiguity to limited RGB spectral information, although v2 drops the term metamerism. Experimental interpretations and the limitation concerning reduced interpretability without explicit intermediate estimates remain unchanged.
descriptions.D1: The abstract replaces a promise to release data, code and models upon acceptance with a statement of availability and a concrete project-page link. Actual resource availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.
descriptions.R1: v2 removes the Wyszecki and Stiles Color Science reference previously cited for metamerism. The remaining research positioning is unchanged; the subsequent Zhou et al. reference is retained and renumbered.
descriptions.P1: v2 makes limited edits to the abstract and shortens the introductory explanation of RGB ambiguity. Section order and the overall narrative remain unchanged, with some text reflow across pages.
descriptions.P2: Figure 2 gains explicit architecture names and an operation-symbol legend, with adjusted spacing and a revised caption. Figure 4 changes label and colorbar rendering while preserving its examples; table structures remain unchanged.

P-7B060AA48E.title: Towards In-Context Tone Style Transfer with A Large-Scale Triplet Dataset

descriptions.M1: The two-stage tone scorer, dataset-filtering procedure, FLUX.1 Fill in-context model, training losses and inference procedure remain unchanged. The architecture and LUT-based high-resolution processing were already documented in v1, including Appendices B–C.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same source datasets, TST100K training data, TST2K and PST50 benchmarks, and IFFI scorer evaluation. Reference-guided colorization and the illustrated scene categories already appear in v1; v2 adds no dataset or task coverage.
descriptions.E2: Table 1 and Figure 6 add CSGO and Nano Banana2. Table 4 adds CSD, which was previously cited but not evaluated there. Existing comparators are retained, while the seven-method user study and appendix comparison tables retain their original membership.
descriptions.E3: The reported preprocessing, metrics, training budgets, model configurations and sampling settings are unchanged. The user study still uses 20 image pairs and 20 participants. Added comparator results use the existing evaluations; no revised evaluation protocol is specified.
descriptions.E4: The tone-scorer effectiveness analysis in Section 4.3.2 is extended with CSD retrieval and preference results, adding evidence about general versus tone-specific style representations. The filtering and reward-learning ablations, cross-dataset testing and appendix analyses otherwise remain unchanged.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, uncertainty intervals or statistical significance tests. The user-study aggregation and point-estimate reporting practices remain unchanged.
descriptions.E6: New comparator results are added without changing existing scores. In Table 1, CSGO's PST50 Aes of 0.3607 exceeds ICTone's 0.2820 and GT's 0.3305. Table 4 adds CSD Recall@1 of 63.13 and PAcc of 70.89. Figure 6 adds CSGO and Nano Banana2 outputs; appendix results remain unchanged.
descriptions.T1: Equations 1–14 retain the same losses, mathematical definitions and optimization formulations. Added equation references and citations do not alter the mathematics; neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about TST100K/TST2K, the two-stage tone scorer, in-context transfer and state-of-the-art performance. Added comparisons support existing contributions without redefining their scope.
descriptions.C2: v2 attributes Nano Banana2's low content preservation to reference-foreground leakage and explains how CSGO's oversaturation can inflate aesthetic scores without improving fidelity. It interprets the CSD comparison as supporting tone-specific representations and adds an image-concatenation efficiency limitation. Aesthetic-filtering bias was already discussed in v1 Appendix E.
descriptions.D1: Appendices B–C retain the same architecture, hyperparameters, hardware, training and inference details. v2 adds ICEdit attribution for the already reported four denoising steps and guidance scale of 50. The project-page hyperlink retains the same destination; no new reproducibility settings or resource access are supplied.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds nine references, including CSGO, Nano Banana2, PerTouch and DiffRetouch, and expands discussion of CSD through direct comparison. The central research positioning remains unchanged. UniChange and ICEdit publication updates concern already cited works.
descriptions.P1: Several introductory paragraphs are rewritten, experimental explanations and grammar are refined, and comparison-method, limitations and acknowledgment paragraphs are added. Author affiliations and contribution markers change. The overall section structure and most main-text and appendix prose remain intact.
descriptions.P2: Tables 1 and 4 gain comparator rows, and Figure 6 expands to include the new methods. Figures 4–5 move into a side-by-side arrangement, Table 2 moves, and appendix Figures 7–8 exchange order and numbering. Figure 6 loses its scene-panel labels despite retained textual panel references; other illustrations retain their content.

P-7FDBF43C24.title: Bridging Language and Items for Retrieval and Recommendation: Benchmarking LLMs as Semantic Encoders

descriptions.M1: v1's proposed RoBERTa-based BLAIR models and review–metadata contrastive-plus-MLM pretraining are removed. v2 instead defines BLAIR as a benchmark using frozen external encoders with downstream UniSRec, AlphaRec, and representation adaptation.
descriptions.E1: The Amazon dataset, Beauty/Games/Baby categories, ESCI, and Amazon-C4 remain. v2 adds MovieLens-1M and Yelp to sequential recommendation, collaborative filtering across six datasets including Book-Crossing, and real-world Reddit-Movies complex-query retrieval.
descriptions.E2: RoBERTa-large and SimCSE-large remain, while v2 adds Sentence-T5, three Qwen3 sizes, E5, SFR-Embedding-Mistral, GritLM, Gemini, and text-embedding-3-large. v1's BM25, GRU4Rec/SASRec, smaller encoders, and BLAIR/MLM comparison entries disappear from the corresponding evaluations.
descriptions.E3: Amazon item inputs change from concatenated titles, features, and descriptions to titles alone. v2 introduces protocols for the added tasks, including collaborative-filtering splits of 4:3:3 and filtered leave-last-out datasets, and adds NDCG@20 and Borda aggregation while dropping v1's additional sequential Recall and NDCG@50 reporting.
descriptions.E4: v1's MLM-only, multi-domain-training, and initialization-curriculum analyses are removed. v2 adds metadata and PCA-versus-MRL comparisons, encoder-scaling and cross-benchmark correlation analyses, and a concrete GritLM retrieval failure case in Appendix F.
descriptions.E5: v2 introduces focused Spearman and Pearson correlation tests with p-values in Section 5.2; v1 reports no corresponding significance analyses. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, or uncertainty intervals for benchmark performance.
descriptions.E6: v1's BLAIR results and pretraining-ablation entries are replaced by extensive encoder benchmark results, including new collaborative-filtering and Reddit-Movies outcomes. Retained scores also change: SimCSE-large's ESCI NDCG@100 is 0.0869 after rescaling v1's display, versus 0.1063 in v2. Changed metadata prevents interpreting this as a same-setting gain.
descriptions.T1: The explicit BLAIR embedding and joint-loss definitions in v1's Equations 1–3 are removed. v2 supplies formal definitions for projected representations and sequential/collaborative prediction in Section 4.1. These change the limited mathematical specification; neither version contains theorems or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The central contribution changes from specialized pretrained models with superior retrieval/recommendation performance to a benchmark of existing semantic encoders. v2 adds headline claims about disagreement with MTEB, task-dependent scaling, and Amazon-C4's usefulness as a proxy for real complex queries.
descriptions.C2: v1's explanations of BLAIR training benefits and curriculum-related overfitting are replaced by interpretations involving encoder discriminability, downstream complexity, metadata noise, and complex intent. v2 also introduces substantive limitations concerning English-only coverage, restricted model/category coverage, and incomplete review collection, plus failure analysis.
descriptions.D1: v1's checkpoint, GPU, batch-size, training-time, and pretraining-hyperparameter documentation is removed with its model study. v2 adds dataset-collection details, exact temporal cutoffs, generation and retrieval prompts, dataset-specific processing, a learning-rate search grid, and documented access to the BLaIR-Bench toolkit in Appendices A–C.
descriptions.R1: v2 repositions the work around benchmarking semantic encoders, including a first-benchmark claim. Related work expands to BEIR, MTEB/MMTEB, BRIGHT, shopping-agent benchmarks, and recent recommendation encoders, replacing much of v1's foundation-model retrieval and recommendation positioning.
descriptions.P1: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves forward, dataset and benchmark sections replace the original model-centered organization, and v2 adds limitations, ethics, and six appendices.
descriptions.P2: Figure 1 is redrawn around the benchmark, and v2 adds correlation and metadata plots. Tables are reorganized into consolidated dataset statistics, aggregate rankings, and appendix results grouped by encoder class. The original query example is retained as renumbered Table 4, rather than newly added.

P-A097A46D9E.title: Distilling Balanced Knowledge from a Biased Teacher

descriptions.M1: The two-component LTKD objective and uniform within-group weighting remain. V2 corrects the specified rebalancing step by explicitly normalizing the scaled group-probability vector in Equation 11, replacing v1's flawed class-level normalization expression. This changes the written procedure; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate long-tailed image classification on CIFAR-100-LT, TinyImageNet-LT, and ImageNet-LT, and retain the balanced-versus-long-tailed CIFAR-100 diagnostic. New group-count experiments and broader application citations do not introduce a new dataset, task, or domain actually evaluated.
descriptions.E2: Comparator membership changes across matched benchmark comparisons. V2 Table 1 replaces CIFAR-100-LT's KD and FitNet rows with DIST and CAT-KD; Table 2 replaces TinyImageNet-LT's FitNet with DIST while retaining KD. ImageNet-LT Table 3 adds DIST and CAT-KD. DKD and ReviewKD remain throughout.
descriptions.E3: V2 introduces a controlled group-count sweep over 3, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50, and 100 groups for four architecture pairs on CIFAR-100-LT at imbalance factor 100. Existing imbalance factors, balanced testing, accuracy metrics, and the alpha/beta sweep remain. Main tables show fewer architecture configurations, but the unavailable additional results prevent establishing that the full experimental suite contracted.
descriptions.E4: V2 adds per-group convergence comparisons between KD, DKD, and LTKD in Figure 4 and sensitivity to group granularity in Table 6. Existing component ablations and hyperparameter sensitivity are retained. V1's t-SNE analysis is absent from the supplied v2; whether it appears in the unavailable supplement cannot be checked.
descriptions.E5: V1 Section IV-B and v2 Section 4.2 both report three repetitions and average performance. Neither supplied PDF reports standard deviations, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a changed uncertainty-estimation practice.
descriptions.E6: V2 adds baseline scores, group-count results, and convergence findings while displaying fewer architecture-result blocks. Most matched scores remain identical, but CIFAR-100-LT ResNet50–MobileNetV2 overall accuracy at imbalance factor 10 changes from 57.46% to 57.79% (Table II to Table 1). V2 also corrects component-ablation tail gains from 7.36/9.19 to 3.70/5.53 percentage points, matching the unchanged underlying table values.
descriptions.T1: V2 Equation 11 repairs the normalization mathematics: its denominator sums scaled probabilities over groups. V1 Section III-B incorrectly repeats the numerator's scaling factor inside the class summation, causing that factor to cancel. The central KL decomposition and final loss derivation otherwise remain substantively unchanged.
descriptions.C1: The core contributions of decomposing KD, correcting teacher bias, and improving long-tailed accuracy remain. V2 strengthens teacher-surpassing language to 'nearly all cases' in the introduction and explicitly claims to be the first compression-oriented treatment of long-tailed KD in Section 2.2; v1 states the compression focus without that explicit priority claim.
descriptions.C2: V2 adds interpretations linking teacher bias to suboptimal convergence and group granularity to finer bias correction. It characterizes 100 singleton groups as continuous reweighting and credits discrete grouping with enabling beneficial within-group supervision. The original bias explanation and the head-class suppression tradeoff remain.
descriptions.D1: V2 newly specifies head, medium, and tail groups as the top 33%, next 34%, and bottom 33% of classes by training frequency. V1's SGD, momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0005, and dataset-size/resolution details are not repeated in the supplied v2. Its references to supplementary pseudocode and settings cannot establish their contents or an actual optimizer change.
descriptions.R1: The introduction shifts from general vision architectures and compression techniques toward KD applications across vision, NLP, and language models. Related work adds DIST and several long-tailed distillation references, expands discussion of CAT-KD, and strengthens the compression-oriented novelty claim. Literature coverage and positioning are revised.
descriptions.P1: The title changes from 'Biased Teacher, Balanced Student' to 'Distilling Balanced Knowledge from a Biased Teacher.' The introduction, related work, method exposition, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten and condensed. Inter-/intra-group terminology becomes cross-/within-group, and the contribution narrative is reorganized.
descriptions.P2: V2 redraws the overview diagrams, restructures and combines benchmark tables, and changes the document formatting. The retained hyperparameter plots move from vertically stacked Figure 4 to side-by-side Figure 5. A convergence figure and group-count table are added, while the t-SNE display is absent from the supplied v2.

P-CE95ABFF40.title: PPLLaVA: Varied Video Sequence Understanding With Prompt Guidance

descriptions.M1: The three core modules and Equations 1–4 remain unchanged. V3 adds an InternVL3-specific contrastive realignment stage using CLIP-L14-text with frozen InternViT-300M, and no longer includes v1's optional DPO stage in the reported training pipeline. These are limited initialization and auxiliary-training changes to the retained pooling method.
descriptions.E1: V3 removes MSVD-QA and MSRVTT-QA evaluation, adds EgoSchema and LongVideoBench, and evaluates NExT-QA, which already appeared as training data in v1. This broadens egocentric and long-video reasoning evaluation while reducing open-ended QA coverage. V3 also introduces LAION and Wukong image–text data for encoder alignment. The image benchmark suite is retained.
descriptions.E2: V3 Table 2 adds comparators such as LLaVA-OneVision, LLaVA-Video, InternVL3, and VideoLLaMA2/3 on retained video benchmarks. Earlier ActivityNet/VCG comparisons against BT-Adapter, Vista-LLaMA, and VLM-RLAIF are removed. V3 Table 5 also adds a ToME-like token-merging comparator to the retained pooling comparison.
descriptions.E3: V3 adds backbone configurations spanning 7B/8B models, a comparison at matched visual-token budgets, and a 10M-pair alignment-training stage. The reported instruction-data total changes from 1.36M to 1.16M, and v1's stated 760k comparison exception disappears. These are reported setting changes; the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun. V3's main VideoMME table also leaves subtitle conditions unspecified.
descriptions.E4: V3 adds the token-budget comparison in Figure 1(b), a token-merging alternative in Table 5, and generic-prompt attention analysis in Figure 6 and Appendix A. It removes v1's dedicated frame-count/kernel experiment and modality-interleaving/DPO ablation in Tables 8–9. The component ablation and spatial/temporal pooling sensitivity curves are retained.
descriptions.E5: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or statistical error bars. The quantitative tables and performance curves continue to present point estimates.
descriptions.E6: V3 adds extensive results for new configurations and benchmarks: Table 2 reports VideoMME overall scores of 64.5 and 67.1 for the LLaVA-Video and InternVL3 variants, and Table 5 adds token merging at 51.9 with 2048 tokens. These are newly reported settings, not demonstrated same-setting gains over v1. MSVD/MSRVTT results, DPO results, and MVBench task-level breakdowns disappear. The reported PLLaVA VCG score also changes from 2.99 to 3.12.
descriptions.T1: The certificate construction and mathematical definitions of alignment weights, pooling dimensions, weighted aggregation, and positional interpolation are retained. Equations 1–4 change only in presentation. Appendix B's new Q-Former analogy supplies conceptual motivation, without adding formal assumptions, propositions, or proofs.
descriptions.C1: V1 frames the central problem as achieving unified short- and long-video understanding through image-model transfer. V3 instead emphasizes reducing the computational cost of already capable long-context MLLMs and explicitly claims generalization across image, video, and general-purpose backbones with different encoders. The abstract and introduction drop the highlighted DPO/codebase contribution and introduce matched-token efficiency claims.
descriptions.C2: V3 introduces a learned-feature explanation for performance with uninformative prompts and adds substantive prompt-dependence and context-length limitations in Appendix B. It removes v1's discussion of the multi-image/dialogue tradeoff and DPO's hallucination benefits. Section 4.2 also newly attributes advantages to motion priors, although the described method does not identify a corresponding component.
descriptions.D1: V3 adds encoder-specific alignment and initialization details and newly specifies video-only training for ablations. Reported full-training time changes from 24 to 36 hours. It removes v1's repository link and the statement that both questions and answers enter CLIP during training. These are documentation changes; the omissions do not establish that the repository became unavailable or that training inputs changed.
descriptions.R1: V3 expands positioning around modern unified MLLMs, long-context compression, and key-content extraction, citing works such as Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, LongVA, Video-XL, LongVU, VideoAgent, and VideoTree. A new Key Content Extraction discussion distinguishes PPLLaVA from iterative frame-search methods. V1's DPO/RLHF positioning and associated references are removed.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, related work, main-results narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around efficiency and backbone generalization. Separate benchmark discussions are consolidated, and qualitative results and limitations move into appendices. Author information and publication headers also change. This is narrative restructuring beyond the addition of experiments.
descriptions.P2: Figure 1(b)'s radar chart is replaced by a token-count/performance plot. V1's detailed video benchmark tables are reorganized into v3's consolidated Table 2, and the frame-count and training-ablation tables disappear. V3 adds the generic-prompt attention montage and relocates retained qualitative figures into Appendix A; v1 Figure 6 becomes v3 Figure 8. Figure 2 also gains explanatory arrow labels.

P-B3004D0CCA.title: Efficient Weighted Sampling via Score-based Generative Models

descriptions.M1: The finite-difference guidance approximation is retained, but v2 adds time-dependent guidance scaling through the LAGS scheduler in Section 3.3 and a hard-gating alternative in Appendix B.2. Appendix C.2.2 also implements an optional projection of guidance perpendicular to the DDIM drift. These additions change the sampling procedure beyond the ISSGM-to-LAGS renaming.
descriptions.E1: V2 replaces the Circles, Spiral, Pinwheel and 8-Gaussians benchmarks with a 25-Gaussian base distribution and shaped target distributions, and removes the CSI compression task. It adds SD/SDXL human-preference alignment and MNIST class suppression/balancing. CelebA and StableCascade frequency control remain, with additional RGB-bias and low-frequency-control scenarios.
descriptions.E2: V1 evaluates MADE-MAA, NIS, NSF, CSF and TNA in Table 1; these comparisons disappear. V2 evaluates DPS, FreeDoM and DAS in the synthetic comparisons, and additionally DAS-1p in image alignment. DPS was previously cited but not evaluated as a baseline.
descriptions.E3: V1's synthetic evaluation uses Jensen–Shannon divergence and DDPM-based SDE sampling. V2 introduces DDIM evaluation using Wasserstein distance and runtime for 10,000 generated samples. The new image-alignment protocol specifies 100 diffusion steps, shared 8×PickScore weighting, and multiple alignment, perceptual-quality and diversity metrics. These are new evaluation designs, not evidence of same-setting reruns.
descriptions.E4: V2 adds scheduler-coefficient sensitivity studies, projected versus standard guidance comparisons, reward–diversity analysis and qualitative investigations of alignment versus realism in Appendix C.2. These extend the analysis beyond v1's demonstrations. Conversely, v1's CSI high-distortion failure analysis is removed.
descriptions.E5: V1 reports unexplained ± quantities in its synthetic-results table. V2 explicitly identifies mean ± standard deviation in Tables 1 and 4 and newly documents matched seeds or noise for paired visual comparisons. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or significance testing; the additional reporting does not establish that more runs were performed.
descriptions.E6: V1's synthetic divergence results and Spiral/CSI/StableCascade mean-weight entries disappear. V2 adds WD/runtime, preference, quality, diversity and MNIST results: Figure 1 reports LAGS WD 0.33, and Table 1 reports 85 seconds per SDXL image versus 4.722 times that runtime for DAS. These are new-setting results. CelebA's 35.1% to 51.2% result and the original StableCascade frequency examples are retained.
descriptions.T1: V1 states Theorem 1 without a proof and assumes an approximate second-order expansion. V2 revises the assumptions, including bounded support and a bounded Hessian of the weight itself, changes the error bound and supplies a proof in Appendix B.1. It adds Proposition 1 under an error-orthogonality assumption, plus a hard-gating derivation without that assumption.
descriptions.C1: V1 claims the first training-free score-based importance-sampling framework and emphasizes industrial and natural-image applications. V2 drops that priority claim and centers its contributions on lightweight guidance plus uncertainty-adaptive scheduling. Its abstract and introduction now claim matching or superior task performance with approximately 1.2–4.7× speedups over competing guidance methods.
descriptions.C2: V2 extends the approximation-error discussion into an explanation of early-step instability and guidance scheduling. Appendix C.2 introduces substantive interpretations of reward–diversity and reward–realism tradeoffs, metric disagreement and projection effects. Comparisons are explicitly restricted to training-free guidance, while v1's CSI failure-mechanism interpretation is removed.
descriptions.D1: Appendices B.3 and C add discrete sampling updates, noise schedules, architecture specifications, optimizer settings, training budgets, weight formulas and baseline configurations. Retained CelebA and StableCascade experiments receive checkpoint, classifier-training and Fourier-mask details absent from v1. The listed source-code repository address also changes; its availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.
descriptions.R1: V1 stresses separation from conditional sampling and says no prior baselines exist for its setup. V2 instead explains connections and adaptations to posterior guidance, positioning the contribution around inference efficiency. Appendix A expands related work, including FreeDoM, DAS, particle sampling and fairness; Appendix C also introduces Adaptive Projected Guidance.
descriptions.P1: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion around guidance efficiency, reorganizes the method and experimental narrative, and changes terminology from importance sampling/ISSGM to weighted sampling/LAGS. Retained applications move into structured appendices, accompanied by expanded explanations and a contents page.
descriptions.P2: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with new density/runtime panels, alignment plots, sensitivity curves, quality/diversity tables and image grids. V1 Figures 4 and 5 reappear as v2 Figures 13 and 21 with presentation changes. The conceptual, Spiral and CSI figures and original table structures are removed.

P-697F34B057.title: OmniBrainBench: A Comprehensive Multimodal Benchmark for Brain Imaging Analysis Across Multi-stage Clinical Tasks

descriptions.M1: The rule/GPT question augmentation, non-brain filtering, Sentence Transformers/DINOv2 deduplication, and clinical task taxonomy remain. The added open-ended evaluation and fuller construction documentation do not establish a changed model architecture, training objective, or inference algorithm.
descriptions.E1: v2 adds reported evaluation on 2,704 open-ended questions requiring free-form clinical descriptions and reasoning, whereas v1 reports multiple-choice evaluation. These questions draw on existing NEJMIC, Radiopaedia, and StrokQD sources. The 15 modalities and previously claimed 218 diagnosis labels are retained; the expanded disease appendix does not establish new disease coverage.
descriptions.E2: The corresponding Table 2 retains all 24 models and the physician reference. The new open-ended Table 3 evaluates 23 existing models, excluding InternVL3-38B, but introduces no new comparator and removes none from the retained comparison.
descriptions.E3: The new open-ended evaluation uses ROUGE1, ROUGEL, BLEU, and BERTScore, extending the evaluation protocol beyond answer accuracy. v2 also adds modality and image-count stratifications. Its explicit 6,823 closed-ended/2,704 open-ended partition clarifies benchmark composition; unchanged Table 2 scores do not establish that the earlier closed-ended experiment was rerun.
descriptions.E4: Sections 4.4–4.5 add performance analyses across 15 modalities and image-count groups from one to at least seven images. Appendix E and Figures 7–18 add success/error case studies for six models across both answer formats. These extend v1's taskwise comparisons, although the image-count analysis is not documented as a controlled image-removal ablation.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars. v2's discussion of performance variance across models does not introduce statistical uncertainty estimation.
descriptions.E6: All 400 numerical entries in Table 2 are unchanged. New Table 3 reports free-form results: Lingshu-32B leads ROUGE1 at 26.45 and BLEU at 1.90, Qwen3-VL-30B leads ROUGEL at 16.13, and GPT-5-mini leads BERTScore at 9.13. Figures 4–5 and the appendix add subgroup results and qualitative outcomes. Table 1 and Section 3.2 change OmniBrainVQA's image total from 597,853 to 600,050, although Figure 2 retains 597,853.
descriptions.T1: Neither version develops formal theoretical results, proofs, or derivations. v2 introduces standard evaluation metrics without adding new mathematical definitions or formal properties.
descriptions.C1: The central contribution remains a comprehensive brain-imaging benchmark spanning 15 modalities and 15 clinical tasks, with substantial model–clinician gaps. v2 extends the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to explicitly claim both closed- and open-ended evaluation and performance heterogeneity across both formats.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds interpretations concerning training efficiency versus model size, modality specialization, and information integration or overload as image counts vary. Appendix E introduces perception, understanding, and reasoning failure categories. These expand the interpretation, although some leadership and scaling statements conflict with Table 3 or Figure 5. The existing warning that the benchmark cannot replace clinical validation remains.
descriptions.D1: v2 specifies four NVIDIA A6000 GPUs, adds fuller question-generation templates, documents the answer-format partition and open-ended sources, changes the release-link destination, and states a CC BY-SA 4.0 license. Appendix A describes entirely public data, replacing v1's private-hospital-data disclosure. These are bounded documentation and access changes rather than evidence of altered training or inference settings.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds references for ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore, Qwen3-VL, and the original BraTS benchmark. Table 1 additionally positions benchmarks by closed/open-ended support. The broader positioning around comprehensive neuroimaging coverage remains substantially unchanged.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, related work, task descriptions, and results narrative undergo extensive editing and condensation. Experiments are reorganized into dedicated metrics, results, modality, and multi-image sections. Disease coverage and construction explanations are expanded into structured appendices, and the author/affiliation block changes.
descriptions.P2: Figure 1 gains open-ended examples, Table 1 gains answer-format columns, and the construction diagram is resized and relocated. v2 adds an open-ended results table, modality and image-count plots, glossary/disease tables, and twelve case-study figures. v1's category-tagging prompt is retained within the expanded supplementary Figure 6, rather than removed.

P-6F8912A859.title: Discovering Interpretable Algorithms by Decompiling Transformers to RASP

descriptions.M1: The reparameterization, layer-normalization linearization, multistage pruning, MLP splitting and primitive replacement procedures remain unchanged. Expanded explanations and corrected projection notation do not introduce a different algorithm.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate the same 11 algorithmic tasks and 17 formal languages. The added analyses reuse existing coverage. Appendix J.8 corrects the sorting description to agree with the existing task definition and examples; it does not establish a changed dataset.
descriptions.E2: No evaluated comparison method is added or removed. The original-model comparisons and primitive-versus-regularization comparison remain; the new experiments examine seeds and stages of the existing pipeline.
descriptions.E3: New analyses introduce fixed-configuration comparisons, graph/program diversity measures, Pearson correlations conditional on matching computation graphs, and a greater-than-90% match-accuracy filter for pruning stability. Existing experiments retain their training budgets, length ranges and primary task/match-accuracy protocols.
descriptions.E4: Appendix E expands supplementary analysis with training-seed sensitivity across eight tasks, pruning stability across 21 models, stagewise faithfulness, and primitive-use/MLP-splitting statistics. The earlier architecture, checkpoint, layer-normalization and training-length analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: v2 newly reports ten separately trained models with different seeds for each of eight fixed task/configuration combinations, including success counts across seeds. v1 lacks this controlled repeated-training analysis. No confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.
descriptions.E6: Original Tables 1–2 and program-specific scores remain unchanged. New Table 3 reports seven decompilations versus ten length-generalizing models for Unique Bigram Copy, and two versus zero for Binary Majority Interleave. Appendix E additionally reports pruning consistency for 17/21 models and stagewise match accuracies of 93%, 93%, 95% and 95%, extending the findings.
descriptions.T1: v1 states exact Transformer/program equivalence under LLNA, although LLNA permits negligible behavioral change. v2 explicitly requires exact equality in Equation 5 for Theorem 3.2 and strengthens the appendix restatement accordingly. The constructions and proofs otherwise remain.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contribution: extracting interpretable D-RASP programs from trained Transformers and providing evidence that length-generalizing small models often implement simple programs. The new analyses do not redefine that contribution.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds arguments interpreting some decompilation failures as evidence about learned mechanisms, while acknowledging possible failures despite an underlying short program. It also explains why different pruned graphs can yield the same program. Much of the expanded LLM-applicability discussion already appeared in v1's FAQ.
descriptions.D1: Table 3 documents the configurations used for the new seed study and the correlation-aggregation exclusions. Appendix J.8 corrects the misleading consecutive-integer condition in the sorting description. Existing implementation settings and repository access information are retained.
descriptions.R1: The bibliography and substantive positioning against logic translations, Tracr, Transformer Programs and circuit discovery remain unchanged. The separate Related Work section reorganizes existing discussion; additional main-text citations already appeared elsewhere in v1.
descriptions.P1: v2 adds an introductory roadmap, separates Related Work from Discussion, expands the FAQ, and makes targeted methodological clarifications and wording corrections. Most prose and the overall organization remain recognizable.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds the seed-summary Table 3, renumbers the existing primitive table, and corrects Figure 1's projection label from q==k to inp==out. Existing plots and appendix visualizations are retained, with relocation and page reflow.

P-33B8322038.title: League of LLMs: A Benchmark-Free Paradigm for Mutual Evaluation of Large Language Models

descriptions.M1: The four-phase pipeline, rotating questioner, independent answering, reference-based mutual evaluation, self-evaluation exclusion and score aggregation remain unchanged. v3 explicitly names Borda scoring and supplies fuller prompts, but these disclosures do not establish a changed algorithm.
descriptions.E1: The task experiments retain dynamically generated mathematics and ACM-style programming questions, the same eight model versions and unrestricted programming-language choice. v3 compares external benchmark rankings but does not report evaluating additional task instances from those benchmarks.
descriptions.E2: v3 Section 6 and Figure 5 introduce explicit ranking comparisons with MATH500, AIME2024, LiveCodeBench, HumanEval and mathematics/coding Chatbot Arena leaderboards. v1 only asserts agreement with unspecified mainstream benchmarks and Chatbot Arena, without corresponding comparator-specific results. The eight mutually evaluated LLMs remain unchanged.
descriptions.E3: v3 adds secondary-analysis protocols using leaderboard snapshots for Spearman correlations and pooled in-family versus out-of-family scores. Appendix D describes Top-k overlap across independent runs, whereas v1 discusses agreement among evaluators, limiting direct comparability of that statistic. The primary question-generation and evaluation design is retained.
descriptions.E4: v3 adds developer-family scoring-bias analysis and quantitative external-ranking validation, and extends consistency analysis across k = 1–7. Appendix F expands the existing Dirichlet-series case with reference and erroneous answers. Conversely, v1's programming illustrations involving quantum path counting and the Cube Garden solution are removed.
descriptions.E5: The reported independent runs increase from three to five. v3 newly supplies score and Top-k confidence intervals, across-run standard deviations, ANOVA and Tukey comparisons, Welch tests for family-score differences, and significance reporting for ranking correlations; v1 lacks these formal statistical reports.
descriptions.E6: Results and rankings change substantially: programming o3-mini moves from 53.8 and last place in v1 Figure 6 to 79.5 and second in v3 Figure 4. These are different three-run and five-run summaries, not demonstrated same-setting gains. Reported memorization cases change from 10/168 to 22/280, and Top-k consistency from 74.85% to 70.7%. v3 also adds concrete benchmark correlations and family-score differences.
descriptions.T1: v3 Appendix F, Figure 9 adds an abridged mathematical derivation for the retained Dirichlet-series example, covering convergence, a functional identity and an expression for F(0). v1 presents the question without this worked reference solution. Neither version develops formal guarantees for the evaluation framework.
descriptions.C1: v3 elevates OpenAI-family homophily to a headline empirical contribution, replacing the abstract's emphasis on Gemini's superior question generation. It also narrows broad claims about overcoming existing evaluation limitations and generalizability, positioning LOL as a complement and specifying internal ranking stability.
descriptions.C2: The programming interpretation reverses from consistency between solving and question-setting abilities to their decoupling. v3 proposes shared architecture, training data or styles as possible explanations for homophily. Its new limitations address correlated evaluator errors, open-ended tasks, restricted task/model coverage, human validation, API cost and scaling overhead.
descriptions.D1: Appendix G provides answering and evaluation prompts absent from v1 and expands the question-generation templates, including JSON formats and the mathematics answer-length constraint. v3 also specifies temperature 1, default remaining parameters, the Borda point mapping and independent validation by at least three annotators. These are additional disclosures, not established changes to existing settings.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds a dedicated comparison with LLM-as-a-Judge, citing Zheng et al. and Pan et al., and connects its design to evaluator-bias research such as Liu et al. and Ye et al. This sharpens positioning against the closest research. The earlier broad survey is condensed, including removal of benchmark-saturation discussion and associated citations.
descriptions.P1: v3 extensively rewrites and condenses retained introductory, motivational, methodological and experimental prose. It renames the framework, introduces numbered sections, separates Related Work, Discussion and Limitations, and organizes supporting material into Appendices A–G.
descriptions.P2: The conceptual and pipeline figures are largely retained, while performance plots are reordered and recaptioned. The two original prompt figures become expanded appendix displays. v3 adds six tables, benchmark-correlation and evaluator–responder heatmaps, and case-study panels, alongside changes to typesetting and figure placement.

P-571617FCF9.title: Learning a distance measure from the information-estimation geometry of data

descriptions.M1: The IEM definitions, denoiser architectures, and learned weighting function remain unchanged. Appendix D.3 adds an optimization adaptation: progressively optimizing the IEM integrand from low to high SNR using one noise sample per step and projecting distortions onto a fixed-PSNR constraint.
descriptions.E1: V2 adds DIV2K and a distinct evaluation scenario: actively minimizing or maximizing perceptual metrics while constraining distortion magnitude. This extends evaluation beyond scoring existing image pairs to testing behavior under metric-driven image optimization; previous coverage is retained.
descriptions.E2: Comparator membership in the retained benchmark and clustering experiments is unchanged. The new optimization study reuses existing comparators: DISTS, LPIPS, VIF, SSIM, TOPIQ, PieAPP, NLPD, and GMSD. It introduces no new baseline algorithm.
descriptions.E3: The new study introduces projected optimization with 1,000 Adam steps at five PSNR constraints from 30 to 10 dB, plus aggregation over 30 images. Separately, Appendix E.4 changes the reported Laplace scales from (4, 2) to (0.3, 0.1) and widens its integration ranges. Existing MOS and BAPPS protocols are retained.
descriptions.E4: Section 3.3 and Appendix D.3 add substantial optimization stress tests examining structural preservation and artifacts under metric minimization and maximization. Figures 9–12 show outcomes across distortion levels, while Figure 13 checks whether each objective was effectively optimized. These supplement the retained disagreement examples and synthetic analyses.
descriptions.E5: Figure 13 newly reports means and standard-deviation error bars for initial, minimized, and maximized metric values across 30 randomly selected DIV2K images. This measures variation across images; it does not establish additional training seeds or repeated-run significance testing.
descriptions.E6: V2 adds qualitative optimization outcomes and quantitative initial/best/worst metric results. It also revises PieAPP scores throughout Figure 4 and the corresponding BAPPS, KRCC, and PLCC plots; for example, PieAPP moves above IEM on TID2013 SRCC. Existing IEM benchmark scores are unchanged. Figure 2's numerical geometry illustrations are also revised.
descriptions.T1: Equation (4) corrects the noise terms inside the squared norms from minus to plus. Theorem 2 now specifies expansion of the squared IEM, and the pointwise I-MMSE statement replaces 'any' realization with 'almost every' signal and Wiener trajectory. The principal theorems and proof framework remain intact.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and introduction retain the same central metric, geometric, and perceptual-prediction claims. Section 3.3 adds the more specific claim that IEM may serve as a robust standalone optimization objective, extending v1's general discussion of optimization as a potential future application.
descriptions.C2: V2 interprets the new optimization results as supporting structural preservation and sensitivity to perturbations outside the data support. Appendix D.3 explains low-SNR gradient scale and variance as optimization difficulties, and Figure 13 qualifies that global optima are not guaranteed. Existing computational-cost and hyperparameter-selection limitations remain.
descriptions.D1: Appendix D.3 supplies optimization hyperparameters, SNR endpoints, projection instructions, DIV2K preprocessing, and the IQA-PyTorch implementation source. Appendix E.4 revises illustrative computation parameters. The existing architecture/training tables and code-access information are retained.
descriptions.R1: V2 replaces the Ma et al. (2018) group-maximum-differentiation citation with Wang and Simoncelli (2008), and adds references for DIV2K and IQA-PyTorch. The broader positioning against metric learning, information geometry, and score-derived Riemannian metrics remains unchanged.
descriptions.P1: Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are preserved. V2 adds dedicated maximum-differentiation subsections, makes localized wording and proof-explanation edits, updates cross-references, and adds the conference-publication header.
descriptions.P2: V2 adds the explanatory Figure 5, four optimization image grids in Figures 9–12, and the multi-panel error-bar Figure 13. Figure 2 is redrawn and several benchmark axes are rescaled. Earlier appendix figures and both tables are retained with renumbering or relocation.

P-FACAE3392B.title: BrepLLM: Enabling Large Language Models to Understand Boundary Representations

descriptions.M1: V2 removes the residual Mixture-of-Query Experts component and its third fine-tuning stage, replacing v1's three-stage adaptation with two-stage MLP/LoRA alignment. The backbone changes from Phi-2 to Qwen3-8B. Adaptive sampling, the hierarchical BrepEncoder, and CLIP-style pretraining remain.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use Text2CAD-derived Brep2Text with abstract/beginner questions for CAD captioning and generative classification. V2 expands examples within these existing tasks, including dialogue already illustrated in v1; it adds no distinct benchmark or documented controlled test scenario.
descriptions.E2: V2 Tables 1–2 add LLaVA-13B and Qwen3-VL-8B alongside the retained PointLLM, ShapeLLM, and MiniGPT-3D baselines, broadening comparison to image-based models. Appendix Table 12 also expands the qualitative comparator set beyond v1's MiniGPT-3D-only comparison.
descriptions.E3: Reported settings change substantially: BrepLLM grows from 2.9B to 8.4B parameters, face/edge sampling bounds change from [16,32] to [32,64], and the main-text judge changes from Qwen-Max to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. Image-baseline evaluation is added. Appendix A.2 still names Qwen-Max in places, leaving the evaluator documentation inconsistent.
descriptions.E4: V1's three-stage ablations and MQE timing study become two-stage studies in v2, including a Stage-II-only control and removal of the MQE analysis. Appendix A adds question/answer-length and vocabulary analyses, expanded qualitative comparisons, and additional dialogue cases.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for performance. V2's new dataset histograms describe corpus composition rather than experimental uncertainty.
descriptions.E6: Tables 1–2 replace headline results: classification average changes from 57.05% to 60.0%, captioning judge score from 58.89 under Qwen-Max to 61.36 under Qwen3-30B, and human precision from 81.85 to 83.62. Ablation values, several baseline values, and qualitative outputs also change. These are results under revised model/evaluator settings, not controlled same-setting gains.
descriptions.T1: Removing MQE also removes v1 Section 3.3's mathematical definition of residual composition, Qfinal = Qbase + Qresidual. The sampling, feature-concatenation, and contrastive-learning definitions in Equations 1–7 remain mathematically unchanged; no theorems or proofs are added.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and contribution list withdraw the residual-MQE/three-stage alignment contribution and redefine adaptation around two-stage transfer of 2D priors with LoRA. The central claims of native B-rep understanding, the Brep2Text benchmark, and leading captioning/classification performance remain.
descriptions.C2: V2 removes the explanation of late-stage MQE specialization and early-routing noise. Its sampling discussion emphasizes continued importance after full training, whereas v1 stresses diminishing dependence. Appendix A.4 newly interprets dialogue examples as evidence of occlusion robustness and hidden-geometry understanding, without a controlled robustness study.
descriptions.D1: V2 supplies dataset-generation and evaluator prompts, detailed fine-tuning learning-rate/warmup schedules and iteration counts, and TinyGPT-V initialization information absent from supplied v1. Reported hardware changes from one to four 80GB A800 GPUs, and a project-page link is added. Conflicting evaluator names limit reproducibility clarity.
descriptions.R1: Related work is reframed around procedural CAD, direct B-rep learning, and 3D language models. V2 adds discussion of SolidGen, BrepGen, NeuroNURBS, DTGBrepGen, HoLa, AutoBrep, and BrepARG, among others. It also explicitly attributes 2D-prior transfer and MQE to MiniGPT-3D and emphasizes construction-history data constraints.
descriptions.P1: V2 extensively rewrites related work and portions of the introduction, experimental narrative, and conclusion. It reverses the order of qualitative results and ablations, adds a structured appendix, and revises the title, author list, and B-rep terminology. These changes exceed simple renumbering or added results.
descriptions.P2: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, replaces the introductory dialogue illustration, revises the architecture diagram, and restructures comparison and ablation tables. New appendix displays include dataset histograms, word clouds, prompt tables, an expanded qualitative table, and dialogue panels; the encoder diagram is substantially retained.

P-FAA0875754.title: ISAC: Training-Free Instance-to-Semantic Attention Control for Multi-Instance Generation

descriptions.M1: v1 combines instance separation with a class-overlap penalty. v2 Section 3.3 extends this to explicit token-pair repulsion and attribute binding, introducing a binding loss absent from v1. Appendix C.1 also adds an alternative inference procedure that selects candidates using accumulated ISAC losses without backpropagation. The underlying clustering, MPO and attention-propagation components remain.
descriptions.E1: v2 adds HRS-Bench evaluations, color/texture/complex-composition tasks from T2I-CompBench, and layout-conditioned generation with overlapping boxes. These extend v1's counting-focused coverage substantially. IntraCompBench retains the earlier COCO-derived benchmark's classes and prompt construction; its new name does not establish new coverage. T2I-CompBench Numeracy also already appeared in v1 as T2I-CompBench++ Numeracy.
descriptions.E2: v2 adds Self-Cross to SD1.5 and SD3.5-M comparisons and evaluates A&E, SynGen, InitNO and TEBOpt against ISAC on SD3.5-M, where v1 lacked those comparisons. CountGen is newly evaluated on SDXL, while GLIGEN and CAR&SAR support the new layout comparison. Bounded Attention receives qualitative comparisons. Counting Guidance and the TokenCompose/IterComp comparisons are retained.
descriptions.E3: New protocols include reuse of released HRS-Bench box layouts, best-of-10 selection on Flux.1-dev and Qwen-Image, and FID/CMMD measurements against native SDXL outputs. Original COCO sampling and detector-ensemble procedures remain. However, v2 Section 4.1 describes exact-count/all-class success while Appendix A.2 retains fractional detection accuracy, leaving any actual change to that scoring procedure unresolved.
descriptions.E4: v2 adds a semantic-overlap heatmap, CountGen-combination analysis, distributional image-quality evaluation, attention-layer ablation and a transparent-object failure case (Figure 2, Tables 10/13/14 and Figure 15). Earlier schedule, MPO and clustering ablations remain. Conversely, v1's separate propagation/normalization diagnostics and SDXL-Turbo dynamics analysis are removed, rather than merely relocated.
descriptions.E5: V1 reports multiple images and qualitative seed examples but provides no uncertainty estimates for its Numeracy table. V2 Appendix C.4 and Table 16 newly report 30 seeds and means with standard deviations for SD1.5/SDXL Numeracy results. This reporting change is confined to that evaluation; v1's unspecified Numeracy run count prevents inferring an explicit increase in runs.
descriptions.E6: Many original COCO scores and ablation values persist, but v2 adds compositional, layout, comparator and latent-selection results. For example, its new layout experiment reports GLIGEN counting F1 of 66.58 without ISAC and 71.28 with ISAC. Numeracy values change from 54.3% to 55.0% for SD1.5+ISAC, 50.7% to 51.1% for SDXL, and 63.4% to 64.0% for SDXL+ISAC, now with 30-seed reporting; these are not established same-setting gains. Changed SD1.5 efficiency values in v2 Table 2 remain unreconciled with the older values retained in Table 15.
descriptions.T1: v2 formally defines repulsion/binding token-pair sets and the binding objective based on 1 minus MPO in Section 3.3, extending v1's class-only objective. The central MPO, foreground-mask, clustering and attention-propagation definitions remain mathematically equivalent. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The instance-first thesis remains, but v2 broadens the central contribution to attribute binding and both text-to-image and layout-to-image control. Its abstract, introduction and conclusion foreground three-benchmark validation, superiority over count-supervised approaches and IntraCompBench as a named contribution. v1 principally emphasized improved class/instance generation and the reported 52%/83% accuracies.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds substantive interpretations of CountGen's mask proposals, failures of exclusive box masking, image-quality tradeoffs and seed stability. It also identifies ambiguous parsed counts and missing 3D understanding as applicability limits. The runtime limitation remains, while v1's argument that normalization prevents transferring several baselines and its proposed SDXL-Turbo extension are removed.
descriptions.D1: v2 documents GPT-OSS-20B prompt parsing through instructions, examples and approximate cost, specifies normalized coordinates and bilinear attention upsampling, and identifies the reused layout annotations. This expands implementation information beyond v1's assumed class/count inputs. However, v1's blanket single-A100-80GB experimental hardware statement is no longer provided. Both versions still promise code upon publication.
descriptions.R1: Related work is reframed around training-free guidance, count supervision, layout control and benchmark limitations. New discussions include Self-Cross, GLIGEN, Attention Refocusing, HRS-Bench, OverLayBench and TIFA. CountGen, already cited in v1 as Make It Count, receives substantive comparative and complementarity analysis. The earlier MCR/TweedieMix discussion and several segmentation/distillation references disappear.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, related work and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Separate preliminaries are condensed into method background, the method is organized into named phases and a scheduling subsection, and experiments and appendices are reorganized. Terminology changes from class disambiguation to semantic separation accompany this broader narrative revision.
descriptions.P2: v2 replaces the opening comparison, redraws the method overview, restructures the main results table and adds heatmaps, parser examples, layout comparisons, failure illustrations and analysis tables. Several earlier standalone figures disappear. Retained displays are distinguishable from additions: for example, v1 Figure 2 becomes v2 Figure 3, and v1 Figure 15 becomes v2 Figure 22.

P-5EA5A87C72.title: Filterless Snapshot Hyperspectral Imaging using Guided Patch Diffusion

descriptions.M1: The core diffusion, patch rescaling, and guidance algorithm remains. However, v3 adds a physical-system adaptation using calibrated measured PSFs, spatial-offset augmentation, and rank-8 LoRA finetuning. Supplement Section 4.6 also introduces desheared-cube conditioning and CASSI-specific guidance; Section 4.3 adds an optional scheduled-guidance procedure.
descriptions.E1: Beyond the retained ARAD1K, ICVL, Harvard, and CAVE coverage, v3 adds real tabletop measurements from a fabricated metalens, CASSI reconstruction on KAIST at benchmark and higher resolutions, and synthetic checkerboards with controlled spatial homogeneity. These introduce new physical and input-condition coverage.
descriptions.E2: The original eight ARAD1K comparison methods remain. v3 adds UNet-Regress, a full-image MSE regression control using its backbone, and introduces MST-S/MST-L comparators in the new CASSI comparison. The CASSI baseline values are explicitly imported from cited work rather than reported as rerun experiments.
descriptions.E3: New protocols include six-scene finetuning/eight-scene prototype testing, 640×960×26 reconstruction with 10 guidance iterations, and CASSI evaluation with 28-channel outputs and uncertainty-based pixel exclusion. For retained training, reported EMA decay changes from 0.9999 to 0.99; the written PSNR formula also changes. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: v3 adds experimental PSF shift-invariance checks, a LoRA ablation, controlled checkerboard failure analysis, backbone-regression comparisons, denoising trajectories, and per-wavelength uncertainty analysis. CASSI pixel-rejection results additionally test whether uncertainty identifies reconstruction errors. Existing patch, lens, and noise analyses are largely retained.
descriptions.E5: v3 supplementary Figure 7 introduces 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for per-wavelength uncertainty–error correlations. Conversely, v2 explicitly specifies 10 reconstructions with different noise seeds, whereas v3 describes repeated sampling using an unspecified N. An increase in sampling runs is not established.
descriptions.E6: Most original ARAD1K scores remain unchanged apart from rounding. New results include UNet-Regress at 29.12 dB, prototype averages of 31.20 dB/0.894 SSIM/0.157 SAM, and CASSI averages of 35.46 dB/0.95 SSIM under their respective settings. ICVL mean SSIM changes from 0.95 to 0.94, and v2's five-scene CAVE average is omitted.
descriptions.T1: The optical and guidance derivations are substantially retained. Limited mathematical revisions include changing the stated DDIM noise distribution from N(0, sigma_t) to N(0, sigma_t^2 I), and replacing the max(x, xhat) factor in v2's PSNR definition with a unit-peak formulation in v3 supplementary Equation 10.
descriptions.C1: The central contribution remains reconstruction through local patch diffusion and global optical guidance. v3 explicitly includes experimental validation, narrows the priority claim from the first demonstration to one of the first, and reframes prospective camera benefits as a tradeoff between optical and computational complexity.
descriptions.C2: v3 adds substantive limits concerning homogeneous regions, restricted propagation of global context, and suitability for fast capture rather than fast reconstruction. It also explains misregistration tolerance and simulation-to-hardware discrepancies, interprets LoRA's effects, and expands discussion of what chromatic aberration contributes relative to RGB filtering.
descriptions.D1: v3 supplies fabrication procedures, laser-based PSF characterization, geometric and spectral calibration, and detailed LoRA settings absent from v2. It also discloses gradient checkpointing and high-resolution reconstruction times. Some information is lost: v2's explicit lens-design repository availability statement and several configuration-table details are not retained.
descriptions.R1: v3 acknowledges concurrent filterless imaging by Liu et al. and diffusion-based uncertainty work by Romero et al., while adding references supporting metamerism, LoRA, and computational techniques. Some earlier citations, including PatchScaler, disappear. The broad research positioning remains, but exclusive priority is qualified.
descriptions.P1: The paper is extensively rewritten and reorganized: diffusion background and patch training are merged, cross-dataset evaluation moves earlier, optical comparison and interpretability are combined, and the supplement gains a hierarchical structure and contents list. The title and author list also change.
descriptions.P2: The layout changes from two columns to one, with extensive figure merging and table restructuring. v2's combined reconstruction table is split between main-text filterless results and supplementary RGB results. Numerous new prototype, calibration, uncertainty, LoRA, CASSI, and failure-analysis displays expand the visual evidence.

P-4586F3B46E.title: RMNP: Row-Momentum Normalized Preconditioning for Scalable Matrix-Based Optimization

descriptions.M1: The proposed optimizer still updates momentum and applies row-wise L2 normalization. The revised Gram-matrix expressions reconcile the equations with the row normalization already specified in v1's Equation 4 and Appendix A. The expanded experiments and revised training prescriptions do not introduce a new core optimization mechanism.
descriptions.E1: v1 evaluates language-model pretraining on OpenWebText, FineWeb-Edu-100B and C4. v3 retains these tasks and adds CIFAR-10 image classification in Appendix E.6, extending coverage to a different modality and task. Larger language models and Mamba change model configurations within language modeling.
descriptions.E2: v3 adds evaluated Shampoo and SOAP learning-rate sweeps to the LLaMA-60M and LLaMA-130M comparisons in Tables 11–12. The corresponding v1 Tables 12–13 contain only Muon and RMNP. Shampoo and SOAP were cited in v1, but these direct experimental comparisons are new.
descriptions.E3: v3 adds GPT-2 1.5B and LLaMA-1B pretraining, Mamba and ResNet configurations, doubled training budgets, parameter-group ablations and clipping diagnostics. Appendix D also reports shared AdamW/matrix learning rates for LLaMA RMNP, replacing v1's independently fixed AdamW-rate prescription, and reverses the stated shape multiplier from max(1,sqrt(n/m)) to max(1,sqrt(m/n)). These reported setting revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: Beyond v1's learning-rate sweeps and Transformer diagonal-dominance analyses, v3 tests whether advantages persist with twice the training budget and whether assigning embeddings and the LM head to the matrix optimizer matters (Appendices D.3–D.4). It also adds larger-model, Mamba and ResNet dominance diagnostics and gradient-clipping analyses (Appendices B and E).
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed-based variability, confidence intervals or significance tests for the experimental comparisons. Raw and smoothed diagnostic trajectories and averages across parameters are not newly introduced uncertainty estimates.
descriptions.E6: Retained perplexity and timing tables preserve their values, while v3 adds results. Examples include RMNP/Muon perplexities of 12.58/12.97 for GPT-2 1.5B and 13.75/14.13 for LLaMA-1B (Tables 18–19). New sweeps report best Mamba perplexities of 32.32/32.95 and CIFAR-10 accuracies of 94.33%/94.65% (Tables 20–21). Additional baseline and ablation results expand the evidence under new settings.
descriptions.T1: v3 corrects the order of diagonal extraction and matrix powers in Algorithm 2 and Equations 3–4, making the preconditioner expression agree with row normalization. It also marks finite Newton–Schulz orthogonalization as approximate and clarifies the matrix-dimension/transposition convention. The convergence theorems and Appendix A proofs remain unchanged.
descriptions.C1: The abstract newly claims empirical asymptotic equivalence between orthogonalization and row-wise normalization for Transformers. This strengthens v1's claims of comparable optimization performance and observed diagonal dominance. The principal computational-complexity and convergence claims remain, while the conclusion extends the empirical claims to larger models.
descriptions.C2: v3 adds interpretations concerning generalization beyond Transformers, persistence under longer training, negligible embedding/head effects and reduced gradient-norm volatility. It also acknowledges that LLaMA-1B lacks a full learning-rate sweep. Some interpretations exceed the displayed evidence: Appendix D.4's claim that differences stay within 0.13 PPL conflicts with Tables 11 and 15, where best Muon-60M perplexity changes from 29.58 to 29.38.
descriptions.D1: Appendices D–E expand the documented training recipes with explicit embedding/head assignments, LLaMA learning-rate conventions, larger-model configurations, LLaMA-1B hardware and fixed hyperparameters, and Mamba/ResNet learning-rate grids. The embedded code pointer also changes from an anonymous 4open repository to a named GitHub repository; external availability is not established by the PDFs.
