descriptions.R1: Section 2 adds substantive discussion of Adam-mini, SRON, SCALE, SWAN, MNGD, Mano and MOGA. It acknowledges earlier row-normalization approaches and expands the distinction between curvature-based explanations and worst-case steepest-descent analyses. Pethick et al. was already discussed in v1; its relocation accompanies a broader revision of research positioning.
descriptions.P1: Most existing prose, the six-section main structure and the proof appendix remain intact. v3 expands Section 2, replaces the former discussion at the end of Section 3.2, adds an appendix contents list and organizes new material into Appendices D.3–D.4 and E. These are localized editorial and organizational changes rather than a wholesale rewrite.
descriptions.P2: v3 adds a conceptual Figure 3, revises Figure 2's formulas, combines global dominance plots using relative training progress, and merges and expands the main performance charts. Numerous training, ablation and clipping displays are added, alongside expanded comparison tables. Several earlier plots and scores are relocated or redisplayed rather than newly generated evidence.

P-BAA453C4AC.title: On the Shelf Life of Fine-Tuned LLM-Judges: Future-Proofing, Backward-Compatibility, and Question Generalization

descriptions.M1: The pairwise judging procedure, GPT-4o supervision, SFT/DPO/SFT+DPO objectives, backbones, and continual-training procedure are retained. Added prompt and split descriptions document the setup without establishing changes to the existing method.
descriptions.E1: v1 evaluates mathematics through DeepScaleR. v2 adds training and evaluation on MMLU-Pro, extending coverage to knowledge-intensive multiple-choice questions across 14 domains, including humanities, social sciences, and law. Continual-training experiments remain confined to DeepScaleR.
descriptions.E2: The zero-shot, SFT, DPO, SFT+DPO, and existing continual-training comparisons are retained. MMLU-Pro extends the existing comparator set to another dataset; no comparator is added or removed from a corresponding DeepScaleR experiment.
descriptions.E3: The added MMLU-Pro experiments use 10K training samples and 10 epochs/1,500 steps, while DeepScaleR retains 70K samples and 3 epochs/2,800 steps. Both use the existing split design, consistent accuracy, and 2.5K evaluation pairs before order reversal. The newly stated matching of questions across weak/strong splits is a disclosure, not an established alteration of the earlier protocol.
descriptions.E4: v2 Appendix C adds a focused selection-bias diagnostic: Table 3 and Figure 9 measure question retention by generator and relate it to generator strength. This examines the consequences of requiring both correct and incorrect sampled responses. Existing continual-training and preference-strength comparisons are retained.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The 20 generator responses per question were already specified in v1; v2 supplies sampling details without establishing additional repetitions.
descriptions.E6: v2 adds MMLU-Pro generator strengths and judge results, plus retention percentages for both datasets. For example, Table 4 reports MMLU-Pro strong/unseen accuracy of 52.92% versus 57.31% for weak- versus strong-trained Mistral-24B with SFT+DPO. These are newly reported comparisons; all DeepScaleR accuracy entries from v1 Table 3 are preserved in v2 Table 4.
descriptions.T1: The dual-distribution formulation, judge mapping, generalization metrics, and consistent-accuracy definition in Equations (1)–(10) are unchanged. No theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and introduction broaden the stated empirical scope from mathematics to two datasets covering multiple domains. The principal claims about future-proofing, backward compatibility, continual learning, and question generalization remain substantively unchanged.
descriptions.C2: v2 newly interprets smaller MMLU-Pro degradations as evidence of domain dependence, explains why the generator grouping is insensitive to thresholds within the observed gaps, and acknowledges a medium-difficulty selection bias from response filtering. These qualify the interpretation without replacing the central conclusions.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds code/data and project-page links, dataset identifiers, explicit question matching across weak/strong splits, and Appendix G with six prompt templates, temperature/sample allocations, top-p, prompt randomization, and greedy judge decoding. These expand reproducibility information; the linked resources' availability is not verified by the supplied PDFs.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds the MMLU-Pro reference, Wang et al. (2024c), to support the new dataset. The existing related-work discussion and positioning relative to judge training and distribution-shift research remain substantively unchanged.
descriptions.P1: v2 standardizes terminology and hyphenation, updates author notes and the publication header, expands setup explanations, and adds appendix contents and Sections F–G. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact, rather than undergoing extensive rewriting.
descriptions.P2: v2 moves the existing DeepScaleR generator-strength plot into the main text, adds Figures 8–12 and a retention table, and redesigns the accuracy table into side-by-side dataset blocks. It also adds six boxed prompts. Captions for Figures 7 and 12 incorrectly describe weak/strong bar patterns as seen/unseen questions.

P-F56361C028.title: From Inpainting to Editing: Unlocking Robust Mask-Free Visual Dubbing via Generative Bootstrapping

descriptions.M1: The two-stage DiT framework and multi-phase objectives remain. However, v2 changes the generator from single-reference conditioning to multiple references, selecting four by default, and replaces the full-face 3DMM mask with its lower-half portion (Section 3.1; Appendices A.3 and B.2). These are limited procedural changes.
descriptions.E1: Training data, HDTF, and the 440-pair benchmark retain their coverage; ContextDubBench is renamed X-DubBench. Section 4.2 newly reports identity and color stability on videos longer than one minute, a limited extension of documented evaluation scenarios, although no separate sample counts or quantitative results accompany it.
descriptions.E2: Tables 1–3 retain Wav2Lip, VideoReTalking, TalkLip, IP-LAP, Diff2Lip, MuseTalk, LatentSync, and the renamed generator baseline. The timing comparison also retains its comparator set, including MultiTalk. The new reference-count experiment is an internal ablation.
descriptions.E3: Appendix B.2 adds an HDTF experiment varying reference counts across 1, 2, 4, and 6 with 25-frame segments. Appendix E revises accelerated inference from removing approximately 10 early steps to using 25 total steps by pruning early and late stages. The standard 50-step timing comparison remains unchanged.
descriptions.E4: New Appendix B.2 and Table 6 test reference-count sensitivity and justify selecting four references. Existing conditioning, training-phase, segment-length, and timestep ablations remain. The 20-pair bootstrapping analysis moves from Section 4.1/Table 4 to Appendix F.2/Table 11; it is not newly added.
descriptions.E5: Table 3 retains identical MOS values and 95% confidence intervals. Neither version reports model-run variability, seeds, or significance tests. New success-rate voting details document annotation procedures without adding uncertainty or inter-rater reliability estimates.
descriptions.E6: New Table 6 reports reference-count results: one versus four references gives FID 8.01 versus 7.72, LPIPS 0.025 versus 0.020, and CSIM 0.892 versus 0.904. Section 4.2 adds the longer-than-one-minute stability finding. All ten original tables retain their numerical results after matching renumbering and relocation; no headline performance gain between versions is established.
descriptions.T1: The flow-matching equations, conditioning mathematics, and single-step denoising derivation remain substantively unchanged. Introducing tau as min(t, t_thres) restates the existing clipping formula. The added attention-cost explanation does not introduce a substantive formal result or proof.
descriptions.C1: Both versions claim the same central contributions: constructing synthetic-real pairs with a mask-based generator, training a mask-free editor, using timestep-adaptive multi-phase learning, and introducing a challenging benchmark with strong empirical performance. The shift from context-rich self-bootstrapping terminology to generative bootstrapping largely reframes these retained claims.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds explanations linking short-segment processing to reduced attention cost and interprets reference-count gains as saturating beyond four, motivating a quality–cost tradeoff. Appendix A.3 also adds a rationale for retaining background context through lower-half masks. Existing interpretations of bootstrapping and phase specialization largely remain.
descriptions.D1: v2 identifies A100 hardware and documents success-rate scoring by 10 evaluators, with at least five judgments per video and majority voting. It replaces the project-page link with explicit code/demo repository information, whose availability is not independently verified. Conversely, v1's specification of 50% motion-conditioning dropout is omitted.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds KeySync, RASA, and HuMo references and removes AlignHuman and the AV-HuBERT reference. The introduction additionally contrasts generated pseudo-pairs with scalability and domain-gap limitations of 3D-rendered alternatives. The broader positioning against mask-based dubbing remains.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around an explicit two-stage narrative. Generator/editor terminology becomes G_mask/G_free, the title and benchmark name change, method subsections are reorganized, and bootstrapping validation moves into an expanded experimental appendix.
descriptions.P2: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figures 1 and 2 are redesigned, Figures 4 and 5 are regrouped, and Figure 10's study interface is replaced. Tables are relocated and renumbered, a reference-count table is added, and several retained appendix illustrations are enlarged or separated.

P-0C2D8993F1.title: SONIC: Spectral Optimization of Noise for Inpainting with Consistency

descriptions.M1: The image-inpainting objective, linearization, spectral Adam optimization, gradient masking and nearest-neighbor filling remain unchanged. Appendix D adds a limited video adaptation: temporal latent masks use the first frame's mask followed by max-pooling over groups of four mask frames.
descriptions.E1: FFHQ, DIV2K and BrushBench coverage and their mask scenarios are retained. v3 adds full-image inversion of synthetic SD3.5 outputs for convergence testing and describes preliminary Wan video inpainting. The video outputs themselves are only linked externally, limiting assessment of that extension.
descriptions.E2: The original benchmark comparator sets remain. Appendix H/Table 7 adds InitNo, GoldenNoise and FreeInpaint, including FreeInpaint with BrushNet and BLD-SD3.5; Appendix I/Table 8 adds SD3 ControlNet inpainting. These expand comparisons with relevant noise-optimization and trained methods. FlowOpt and DiNG are discussed but not evaluated.
descriptions.E3: v3 introduces a randomized, single-blind 2AFC study with 37 raters and 45 scenes, controlled synthetic-image inversion using shared initializations and RMSE, SD1.5/SDXL backbone evaluations, and 10/20/30-iteration budgets. These expand evaluation design; the original main benchmark splits and inpainting settings are retained.
descriptions.E4: The original component ablations remain, but the single-example convergence analysis becomes a systematic Adam/SGD and learning-rate comparison. Appendices B/C add velocity-linearity diagnostics and latent/noise convergence analyses; Appendix J adds iteration sensitivity. New CLIP-scored qualitative cases examine disagreement between metric scores and visual consistency.
descriptions.E5: v1 contains no formal uncertainty analysis. v3 Appendix A/Table 5 introduces aggregate and per-baseline 95% confidence intervals for human preference and claims statistically significant advantages. The interval construction and significance test are unspecified, and uncertainty across repeated benchmark runs remains unreported.
descriptions.E6: v3 adds preference results of 90.0% (1,498/1,665), runtime/memory measurements, baseline scores and analysis results. Tables 1, 2 and 4 also revise existing IR, HPS, CLIP and some AS values: FFHQ SONIC IR changes from 0.114 to 0.280 and CLIP from 20.773 to 24.042, while PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FID remain fixed. The revisions are unexplained, and Table 9 retains older FFHQ values. Revised DIV2K HPS favors BLD, 0.255 versus SONIC's 0.253.
descriptions.T1: v1 provides objective and linearization equations without a theoretical treatment of the spectral advantage. v3 Appendix F adds Fourier-domain gradient derivations, SGD-equivalence and Adam-non-equivalence arguments, and short-horizon complexity assertions. These are mathematical additions; the explicit spectral objective in Equation 4 mainly restates the existing method.
descriptions.C1: The central claims of training-free initial-noise optimization and superior image-inpainting performance remain. v3 qualifies the novelty framing by explicitly acknowledging earlier noise optimization and identifying its gradient approximation with the straight-through estimator. It sharpens the contribution around Adam-based spectral preconditioning and reduced need for learning-rate tuning.
descriptions.C2: v3 expands the mechanism explanation through Adam's per-frequency normalization and globally coupled updates. It discusses learning-rate, blur and divergence tradeoffs, qualifies trajectory linearity near the final denoising steps, and explains applicability to non-flow backbones. These go beyond v1's empirical rationale and broad future-work discussion.
descriptions.D1: v3 newly specifies the spatial-ablation learning rate of 0.05, identifies Claude Sonnet 4.5, and adds implementation settings and exact runtime/memory information. The original implementation recipe and prompt templates largely persist. The explicit code-release promise disappears, but the PDFs do not establish a change in actual code availability.
descriptions.R1: The introduction and related work broaden positioning around earlier GAN inversion, diffusion/flow noise optimization and back-propagation workarounds. Added discussion includes straight-through estimation, D-Flow, DiNG, InitNo and GoldenNoise. The relationship to concurrent FlowOpt is refined from a similar update equation to explicit straight-through equivalence and differentiation through spectral preconditioning.
descriptions.P1: v3 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work and methodological explanations, replaces contribution bullets with themed paragraphs, and standardizes terminology around initial noise samples, spectral preconditioning and spatial constraints. The supplement is reorganized into Sections A–L, with existing prompts and qualitative grids moved to K/L.
descriptions.P2: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation, relocating and resizing figures and tables. Figure 5 is rebuilt as a multi-configuration convergence plot, and new study/analysis figures and Tables 5–9 are added. The original three supplementary qualitative grids are retained as Figures 16–18, rather than new results.

descriptions.M1: The BMM retriever, SSTA mechanism, 2D RVQ-VAE, masked/residual transformers, and RAG-CFG are unchanged. Algorithm 1 and the training and inference descriptions match.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use HumanML3D and KIT-ML for the same generation and retrieval tasks. The supplementary user study and qualitative motion scenarios retain their coverage.
descriptions.E2: Comparator membership is unchanged in Tables 1–3. Figure 6 still compares ReMoMask with MoGenTS, TMR, and ReMoDiffuse; the user study still compares against MoMask, ReMoDiffuse, and ground truth.
descriptions.E3: The reported splits, preprocessing, metrics, model configurations, and training settings match. Both user-study descriptions specify 20 prompts, over 50 participants, anonymized models, and randomized presentation. Figure 6's revised examples do not establish a changed experimental procedure.
descriptions.E4: The existing qualitative comparison in Figure 6 uses revised baseline examples, changing the visual evidence for motion realism and text alignment. The component and momentum-queue ablations in Tables 4–5 remain unchanged.
descriptions.E5: Both versions retain point estimates and user-preference percentages without adding repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.
descriptions.E6: Tables 1–5 and the user-study percentages in Figures 3–4 are unchanged. Figure 6 replaces some qualitative outputs, including MoGenTS's walking/rest example and ReMoDiffuse's balancing example, and exchanges TMR's examples between the clumsy- and slow-walking prompt columns. These revisions do not establish a performance gain.
descriptions.T1: Equations 1–18 retain the same mathematical definitions, objectives, and operations. No assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or revised.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and state-of-the-art performance claims. Revised illustrations do not alter their stated scope.
descriptions.C2: Result interpretations and limitations are unchanged, including retrieval weaknesses, deployment cost, limited long-motion validation, abstract-text difficulties, and missing physical verification. No explanation accompanies the substituted Figure 6 examples.
descriptions.D1: Architecture specifications, hyperparameters, hardware, training duration, and code/project URLs remain identical. The revision supplies no additional implementation or reproducibility information.
descriptions.R1: The related-work discussion, cited works, bibliography, and positioning relative to prior motion-generation and retrieval methods are unchanged.
descriptions.P1: Figure labels receive small wording and punctuation edits, including changing three Figure 6 prompts from 'a person' to 'a man.' The main prose, supplementary narratives, and section organization remain unchanged.
descriptions.P2: Figures 5–6 are enlarged and rebuilt with sharper individual motion panels and typeset labels; Figure 6 also gains row separators. Existing citation and project links become clickable. Tables and the remaining figures retain their presentation apart from small typographic differences.

P-76D01654DB.title: ID-Crafter: VLM-Grounded Online RL for Compositional Multi-Subject Video Generation

descriptions.M1: The reported attention procedure changes substantively. v1 Section 3.2.1 uses concatenated inter-subject self-attention followed by self-attention over subjects, text and video. v4 Appendix A.1 specifies gated inter-subject cross-attention and residual cross-modal attention, with these blocks inserted in the first 20 DiT layers. This goes beyond renaming or disclosing reward settings.
descriptions.E1: The same training sources, subject categories, 180 subject-text evaluation pairs and video-editing task are retained. v4 Table S.8 tabulates dataset quantities already reported in v1 Appendix C. New ablations and human judgments do not establish additional data domains or task coverage.
descriptions.E2: v4 Table 3 newly evaluates offline DPO against online GRPO and the existing SFT/base model. The generator comparators in Table 1 and Figure 4 remain unchanged. The new human study uses existing comparators: VACE-14B, Vidu, Phantom and Kling.
descriptions.E3: v4 replaces Table 2's Text-Video Alignment metric with Q-Align and changes the reported GmeScore encoder from Qwen2-VL to Qwen2.5-VL. It introduces a five-model, four-criterion human evaluation using 200 questionnaires from 30 participants. The architecture table also revises DiT depth from 60 to 30/40 layers. These are reported setting changes; they do not establish that all retained experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: v1 provides whole-component ablations and qualitative RL examples. v4 adds quantitative online-versus-offline optimization and reward-component ablations in Table 3, individual attention-stage ablations in Table S.5, mean-versus-minimum identity-reward sensitivity in Table S.7, and training dynamics in Figure S.7.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. v4's moving-average training curves and human preference percentages add results without introducing uncertainty estimates.
descriptions.E6: v4 newly reports online-RL results of 55.16% Total Score and 66.10% FaceSim, extensive ablation results, and human preference rates of 54%, 60%, 43% and 65% across four criteria. Existing values also change: VACE-14B GmeScore changes from 67.27% to 73.27%, and Ours-14B FaceSim from 60.50% to 60.71%. Revised metrics and configurations prevent treating every difference as a same-setting performance gain.
descriptions.T1: v4 adds explicit mathematical definitions for mean/minimum facial fidelity, holistic fidelity, aesthetic/naturalness rewards and gated attention. v1 specifies only a generic quality-plus-identity reward. The underlying rectified-flow and GRPO formulations remain, and neither version presents theoretical guarantees or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The central claims about multi-subject generation, hierarchical attention, VLM guidance and superior generation quality remain. v4 additionally claims to pioneer online RL for multi-subject video generation and frames its contribution explicitly around balancing identity preservation and motion quality.
descriptions.C2: v4 adds substantive explanations involving credit assignment, online exploration, reward hacking, worst-subject identity collapse and mitigation of copy-paste artifacts. It also changes the computational-cost framing: v1 identifies high cost as a limitation, whereas v4 Appendix E argues that attention overhead is marginal and RL adds a one-time cost. Misuse and dataset-curation safeguards are newly discussed.
descriptions.D1: v1's reward-calculation appendix is empty. v4 supplies reward weights, noise and normalization settings, and an RL hyperparameter table including learning rate, AdamW settings, batch size and gradient clipping. It revises architectural specifications, states that evaluation data are disjoint from training, reports approximately one-minute inference, and adds a project address. The PDFs still describe model/data release prospectively.
descriptions.R1: v4 adds targeted references including Identity-GRPO, RAFT, CustomVideo, Vimi, Seedance, Waver and DPO, while removing the earlier VGGT/PartCrafter inspiration citations. It adds a specific novelty claim about integrating VLM reasoning into open-source Wan. The broad related-work organization and principal competing approaches remain.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction and method motivations are extensively rewritten around VLM-grounded online RL. The model and title are renamed, author information changes, editing is folded into the analysis section, and the supplement is reorganized with an overview and additional subsections. The earlier LLM-writing declaration is removed.
descriptions.P2: The document changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. The teaser and several pipeline, dataset and prompt illustrations are redesigned; existing qualitative figures are resized or relocated. New displays include RL and sensitivity tables, training curves and preference charts. v1 Figures 7–10 survive as v4 Figures S.9–S.12 rather than constituting new analyses.

P-6854D605DC.title: From Local to Global: Revisiting Structured Pruning Paradigms for Large Language Models

descriptions.M1: GISP retains first-order importance, normalized structural aggregation, global ranking, iterative rescoring, and perplexity or margin objectives. Algorithm 1 and Appendix A.2 provide fuller specifications without establishing a changed pruning procedure. The new LoRA experiment evaluates subsequent adaptation.
descriptions.E1: V2 adds MedQA medical multiple-choice evaluation and calibration in Appendix A.5. Existing language-modeling, commonsense and mathematical-reasoning coverage remains. The Qwen3 extension uses the existing GSM8K task.
descriptions.E2: Appendix A.4 and Table 12 add a structured adaptation of SparseLLM using Wanda-sp as its local solver. Existing baseline comparisons remain. Newly discussed GBLM, Wanda++ and Pruner-Zero are not reported as evaluated comparators.
descriptions.E3: V2 introduces Qwen3 evaluation, post-pruning LoRA adaptation on an additional 2M CMQA samples, calibration-budget sweeps, finer sparsity evaluations, and a 60% pruning experiment. New inference profiling uses an A6000 with batch size 1 and latency, throughput and memory metrics. These extend the evaluation design while retaining the original principal experiments.
descriptions.E4: V2 adds calibration-budget and sampling robustness studies, post-pruning adaptation, efficiency analysis, higher-sparsity testing and Qwen3 structural profiles. Figure 3(b) also extends the once-for-all analysis with individual-pruning results at 25%, 35% and 45% sparsity. Earlier iteration and objective ablations remain.
descriptions.E5: V1 specifies seed 0 but reports no comparable uncertainty analysis. V2 adds a separate calibration-resampling study using seeds 0–2 with mean and standard deviation, plus standard deviations across calibration budgets and a shaded trajectory plot. These new reporting practices concern calibration robustness, not all benchmark comparisons.
descriptions.E6: Original Tables 1–6, the DeepSeek portion of Table 7, and matched appendix result tables retain their numerical entries. V2 adds results for Qwen3, MedQA, SparseLLM, robustness, adaptation and efficiency. For example, new MedQA results at 20% pruning are 31.26% for GISP and 21.92% for Wanda-sp.
descriptions.T1: Appendix A.2 adds exact mathematical specifications for the linear schedule and parameter-count normalization, particularly Equations 7 and 9, where v1 provided procedural descriptions. The existing Taylor expansion and objective equations remain, with no new theorem or proof.
descriptions.C1: Both versions retain the central claims of stable iterative global pruning, nested subnetworks enabling once-for-all deployment, and task-aligned importance improving downstream performance. The expanded model evidence in the abstract supports these retained contributions without redefining them.
descriptions.C2: V2 adds interpretations of calibration robustness and subsequent adaptation, conjectures explaining SparseLLM's limited gains under structured pruning, and architecture-specific explanations contrasting Llama2 and Qwen3 sparsity patterns. The original limitations concerning computational cost and untested MoE architectures remain.
descriptions.D1: V2 adds Algorithm 1, explicit scheduling and normalization details, an official implementation link, GSM8K-specific sampling counts, inference hardware settings and quantified mask-storage requirements. It also clarifies that CMQA calibration produces one shared multitask subnetwork; this clarification does not establish a changed experiment.
descriptions.R1: V2 adds discussion and citations for GBLM, Wanda++, Pruner-Zero and SparseLLM, distinguishing their gradient or reconstruction approaches from GISP. MedQA and Qwen3 references are also added. The existing related-work discussion is retained after relocation.
descriptions.P1: V2 revises the abstract and selected method and calibration explanations, presents the one-shot procedure as numbered steps, and moves Related Works from Section 5 to Appendix A.1. New sections are integrated while much of the existing narrative remains unchanged.
descriptions.P2: V2 adds an algorithm block, robustness and Qwen3 figures, and tables for the new comparisons and analyses. Table 7 expands to include Qwen3; Figure 3(b) gains intermediate markers and axis ticks. Existing tables are rearranged, and the original sparsity-profile Figure 4 becomes Figure 5.

P-B8A03620E1.title: SAEmnesia: Erasing Concepts in Diffusion Models with Supervised Sparse Autoencoders

descriptions.M1: The supervised concept-latent assignment, TopK SAE, reconstruction/assignment/decorrelation/sparsity losses and latent-steering procedure remain unchanged. The two-latent nudity variant already appears in v2. v3 describes applying existing score-based selection to unseen concepts without introducing a distinct algorithmic component.
descriptions.E1: v3 adds style erasure and sequential style erasure to the existing object-erasure and nudity tasks (Appendix A.15). Styles were already training labels in v2, but were not evaluated as erasure targets. Ring-A-Bell additionally introduces a black-box adversarial prompt scenario beyond the retained white-box evaluation.
descriptions.E2: SalUn is added to the main object comparison in Table 1, although it already appeared in v2's adversarial figure. Conversely, v2 Figure 9's nine non-SAE adversarial comparators disappear from the corresponding v3 comparison, which retains SAeUron. New Table 12 compares against an untouched model and Surkov et al.'s unsupervised SAE on SDXL-Turbo.
descriptions.E3: Section 4.1 replaces the stated training templates with one-sentence anchor prompts and identifies templates as test prompts. The reported two-latent nudity multiplier changes from -60 to -600 (v2 Table 9; v3 Table 13); neither revision establishes a rerun. New protocols include training on half the styles and testing the remainder, six-style sequential erasure, Ring-A-Bell using seven prompt pairs per object, SDXL-Turbo evaluation without CRA, and timing ten images.
descriptions.E4: v3 adds tests of generalization beyond supervised concepts, black-box attack robustness, sequential style-erasure scalability and a training/inference cost breakdown. These address substantive questions absent from v2. Existing loss variants, Cats-Dogs overlap counts, class-interference heatmaps, k-NN validation and multiplier analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.
descriptions.E5: The four-seed accuracy mean-and-standard-deviation analysis is unchanged (v2 Table 2; v3 Table 5). Additional timing tables extend the use of ± summaries to new results without specifying a new uncertainty estimator or significance procedure. The ten-image timing sample does not establish an increase in accuracy-evaluation runs.
descriptions.E6: White-box before/after UA changes from 73.30/28.30 to 97.60/57.50 for SAEmnesia and from 26.19/2.22 to 83.70/34.20 for SAeUron (v2 Figure 9 and text; v3 Table 2). These are unexplained replacements, not established same-setting gains. v3 adds style, sequential-style, held-out, black-box, SDXL-Turbo and timing results; examples include style averages of 98.19 versus 98.10 and held-out averages of 73.75 versus 72.32. Existing main object scores and nudity detection counts remain unchanged.
descriptions.T1: Equations (1)–(11), including the concept score, centralization condition, supervised losses, intervention rule and alternative cross-entropy loss, retain their mathematical substance. Parameter-symbol changes are not new definitions or derivations. Neither version adds formal theorems or proofs.
descriptions.C1: v3 materially recalibrates the headline performance claim: the 9.22-point object advantage is explicitly over the SAE baseline, while SalUn has the higher object-only average, 94.28 versus 91.51. It adds a claim of best combined object/style performance at 94.85. The centralization contribution, search reduction and nine-object sequential advantage remain.
descriptions.C2: New Section 5 discusses transformer adaptation, unseen concepts, within-group interference and vocabulary-capacity limits. Appendix A.13 qualifies SDXL-Turbo findings through classifier domain mismatch, and the adversarial mechanism explanation becomes an explicit hypothesis. New style interpretations sometimes overstate the evidence: A.15 claims matching or improving every metric despite slightly lower IRA and CRA in Table 14.
descriptions.D1: v3 newly specifies TopK k=32, expansion factor 16, Adam, learning rate 5×10^-6, batch size 128, A100 hardware, and a 27-configuration loss-weight search using validation loss over five epochs. It adds timing/resource information and a source-code location. These expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to previously undisclosed settings. The earlier disclosure of corrected SAeUron metric computation is removed.
descriptions.R1: Section 2 replaces the historical and concept-resurgence overview with expanded positioning against methods including RECE, SLUG, ConceptPrune and ScaPre. New experiments introduce Ring-A-Bell and Surkov et al.'s SAE work. Several earlier citations, including Cao and Yang and the resurgence studies, disappear. The changes exceed bibliographic updates and accompany narrower claims relative to SAE-based competitors.
descriptions.P1: v3 rewrites selected abstract, related-work, setup and results passages, updates author information and terminology, introduces dedicated Limitations and Impact Statement sections, and moves hyperparameter discussion earlier in the appendix. Most method exposition and existing analysis prose and ordering remain recognizable; the added scientific material does not constitute wholesale rewriting.
descriptions.P2: v3 adopts a conference layout with running headers and a single-column appendix, redraws Figure 2, reformats the main comparison table, and replaces the adversarial bar chart with Table 2. It combines v2 Figures 10–12 into Figure 9's panels, adds a style-erasure image grid and several tables, and relocates/resizes existing grids, heatmaps and multiplier plots.

P-8537D2BC9B.title: River-LLM: Large Language Model Seamless Exit Based on KV Share

descriptions.M1: The KV-shared Exit River, quantized exit layers, cosine-similarity exit decision, prefill/generation procedures, and backbone offloading remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate BoolQ, HellaSwag, ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, and HumanEval. The long-context memory scenarios are also retained.
descriptions.E2: Comparator membership is unchanged: backbone/full quantization in Table 3, the four alternative KV strategies in Figures 3 and 8, HQQ/AWQ configurations in Table 4, and Balcony/EE-LLM in the memory comparisons.
descriptions.E3: The same four model configurations, NVIDIA A40 hardware, shot settings, exit thresholds, batch-size-one generation tests, metrics, and 4K–64K memory evaluation settings are reported.
descriptions.E4: The KV-similarity analysis, exit-depth fidelity analysis, accuracy-throughput trade-offs, quantization-backend comparison, and memory-scaling analysis are retained without substantive revision.
descriptions.E5: Both versions report averages over 10 tests in Section 5.3 and the same correlation/significance reporting in Figure 6. No repeated-run, seed, or uncertainty-reporting practice changes.
descriptions.E6: Tables and plotted results remain unchanged, but two reported findings are corrected. The headline speedup minimum becomes 1.53×, already present for Phi4-mini on MATH in Table 3. Section 5.2 replaces HumanEval outperformance with an accuracy match, consistent with Table 2's 57.3 for both the Llama3.1 8B backbone and River-LLM at threshold 0.7.
descriptions.T1: The seamless-exit conditions, cosine-similarity decision rule in Equation 1, and O(d) decision-cost argument are unchanged. No mathematical assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and introduction revise the claimed practical speedup range from 1.71–2.16× to 1.53–2.16×. The core training-free, KV-sharing contributions are unchanged; the conclusion still states the earlier range.
descriptions.C2: Despite correcting the HumanEval performance observation, v3 retains the same noise/overthinking explanation and broader interpretations of KV integrity and memory savings. The limitations concerning larger models and prefill-dominant workloads are unchanged.
descriptions.D1: Implementation and reproducibility descriptions remain unchanged, including W4A16 exit weights, FP16 KV caches, HQQ, compilation optimization, hardware, and offloading. No new River-LLM code or data availability is reported.
descriptions.R1: The same cited works and research positioning are retained, including the mixed-precision discussion in Appendix A.4. Expanded author lists and revised dates, venues, links, and MiniCache metadata are bibliographic updates.
descriptions.P1: There are targeted wording and terminology edits, standardized references, and expanded bibliographic entries. The main narrative, section ordering, and Appendix A.1–A.4 organization remain intact.
descriptions.P2: All nine figures and six tables are retained. Table 1 and Figure 6 receive caption edits; footer page numbers disappear, and bibliography/appendix reflow moves Table 6 from the left to the right column and extends Appendix A.4 onto another page.

P-43603E709C.title: Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models

descriptions.M1: V3 Section 3.2 adds entropy-based transition monitoring, replaces v1's arithmetic-mean answer confidence with a geometric mean, and introduces DEER-PRo, which combines multiple prompted answers using mean confidence minus a mean-absolute-deviation penalty. These change the inference procedure. Branch-parallel decoding itself was already proposed in v1.
descriptions.E1: V3 retains the six original benchmarks and adds GSM8K, AIME 2025, OlympiadBench, and LiveCodeBench, with results in Tables 1, 3, 8, and 13. This extends elementary mathematics, advanced competition mathematics, and competitive programming coverage. Discussion of non-English applicability does not establish an added language evaluation.
descriptions.E2: V1 primarily compares DEER with Vanilla CoT and its own transition-marker variants. V3 Table 1 adds evaluated comparisons against TCC, CoD, NoThinking, Dynasor-CoT, and SEAL. SEAL results are limited to GSM8K and MATH-500 on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B; its participation should not be generalized to the other comparisons.
descriptions.E3: V3 changes the documented length measure from words to tokens and adds compression-rate reporting. It adds Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-671B, and Nemotron model configurations, token-budget sweeps, and a separate 32,768-token sampling evaluation with top-p 0.95 and temperature 0.6 (Table 8). These extend v1's documented 16,384-token greedy evaluation.
descriptions.E4: V3 extends the threshold and trigger studies with token-budget and decoding sensitivity, entropy-trigger and arithmetic/geometric-mean comparisons, early-exit rate/accuracy diagnostics, hidden-state analysis, confidence-distribution analysis, and additional case comparisons. Conversely, v1 Figure 2's AIME pilot panels and Table 2's non-MATH Alternatively comparisons are absent from v3.
descriptions.E5: V1 documents single-sample greedy evaluation without confidence intervals. V3 reports four sampling rounds for small contest datasets and a separate uncertainty experiment using four independent runs on GSM8K, MATH, and GPQA and eight on AMC23 and AIME24, with 95% confidence intervals in Table 9. Seeds and interval-construction details are unspecified, and the relationship to retained single-sample greedy descriptions is unclear.
descriptions.E6: Many results are replaced or added. For example, v1 Table 1's R1-Distill-Qwen-7B MATH-500 accuracies of 86.0% for Vanilla and 87.4% for DEER are replaced by 87.4% and 89.8% in v3 Table 1 under revised method and evaluation conditions, not a demonstrated same-setting gain. V3 also adds comparator, DEER-PRo, additional-benchmark, and branch-parallel latency results.
descriptions.T1: V1 contains method equations but no comparable theoretical treatment. V3 Appendix B introduces an independent Gaussian prompt-noise model, false-positive probability derivations, a claimed exponential improvement theorem, and a MAD derivation. Appendix H adds attention-cost and KV-cache memory analyses under explicit assumptions about cached decoding and answer-induction overhead.
descriptions.C1: The training-free early-exit thesis remains, but v3 adds DEER-PRo's prompt-robust calibration as a core contribution and broadens its explicit effectiveness claim across model families and ten benchmarks. The abstract revises headline shortening and accuracy-gain ranges from 31-43% and 1.7-5.7 points to 19.1-80.1% and 0.3-5.0 points across the expanded evaluations.
descriptions.C2: V3 adds substantive explanations linking linguistic markers to high entropy and hidden-state discontinuities, and threshold robustness to polarized confidence scores. It interprets the different compression and accuracy benefits across task difficulties and identifies low intermediate-answer confidence as a limitation on Nemotron's efficiency gains. V1's performance-ceiling extrapolation is removed; its QwQ delimiter limitation is retained.
descriptions.D1: V3 adds a code-repository link, exact answer-inducing prompts, shared and variant-specific thresholds, DEER-PRo parameters, and an eight-H100 hardware specification. It documents the vLLM implementation, quantized DeepSeek-R1 evaluation through KTransformers, and confidence estimation from the first 50 code-answer tokens. These are reproducibility disclosures; relocated pseudocode and the existing branch-parallel diagram are not new details.
descriptions.R1: V3 retains the original efficient-reasoning taxonomy but expands the cited research and comparative positioning. Section 5 and Appendix M add Dynasor-CoT and SEAL and incorporate newer reinforcement-learning, confidence-guided compression, reasoning-path compression, distilled pruning, and manifold-steering work. This extends the discussion beyond v1's narrower concurrent-work comparisons.
descriptions.P1: V3 reorganizes and rewrites the narrative: generation-pattern preliminaries move into Method, pilot setup and much experimental detail move to dedicated appendices, ablations receive a separate section, and related work is split between a concise main section and Appendix M. It also adds ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements and revises terminology from LRLM to LRM.
descriptions.P2: V3 redesigns Table 1 as a highlighted multi-baseline matrix with token and compression columns, adds numerous analysis tables and plots, and introduces a rotated comprehensive results table. Figure 2 is rearranged and loses its AIME panels; the branch-parallel diagram and pseudocode move to the appendix. The original three appendix case figures remain, renumbered and supplemented with additional comparisons.

P-E08E289DF2.title: When Personalization Legitimizes Risks: Uncovering Safety Vulnerabilities in Personalized Dialogue Agents

descriptions.M1: The benchmark construction procedures, detection heuristics, reflective-reminder generation, and personalized inference procedure remain unchanged. Corrections from 'legitimization' to 'legitimation' do not change the method.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same LoCoMo-derived personas, 750 base queries, 1,986 persona-grounded queries, thematic augmentations, privacy probes, and representation-analysis datasets. The deployment scenarios added in Appendix F are discussed, not newly evaluated.
descriptions.E2: The evaluated comparator sets remain unchanged: LDAgent, A-mem, Mem0, MemOS, MemU, and stateless baselines, with the same subsets participating in the hard-query and intervention comparisons. Newly cited methods are not added as experimental baselines.
descriptions.E3: Section 3.4 corrects the reported backbone for Figure 4 from GPT-4o-mini to Qwen3-235B-A22B, matching the caption and Table 6 already present in v1. This is a limited configuration-reporting correction, not evidence of rerunning experiments; other evaluation settings remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: The thematic-memory, representation, privacy, memory-volume, explicit-persona, and intervention analyses are retained. Both case studies move from Appendix F to G without substantive changes. The new discussion supplies no additional experimental analysis.
descriptions.E5: Both versions retain the 160-response human evaluation, two independent annotators, adjudication, and the same agreement-reporting procedure. No repeated-run, uncertainty, or significance-testing practice changes; the revised agreement percentage is a result change under E6.
descriptions.E6: Human–automatic evaluator agreement changes from 96.4% to 96.3% in Appendix B.2. The stateless Base Setting entries change from 19.00 to 23.13 in Table 5 and from 11.29 to 11.75 in Table 6, aligning them with Table 1. Other table results and plotted findings are unchanged.
descriptions.T1: The ASR definition and PCA-based reasoning remain unchanged, with no added or revised formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs. The new feedback-loop discussion is qualitative.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: intent legitimation, PS-Bench, mechanistic evidence, and detection–reflection mitigation. The headline 15.8%–243.7% relative ASR increase is unchanged.
descriptions.C2: New Appendix F expands interpretation through a proposed persistent feedback loop and downstream risks in personal assistants, companion agents, and enterprise deployments. The limitations also explicitly exclude tool-augmented agents. These extend the applicability and risk discussion without new empirical validation.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds a code-repository location in the abstract; v1 only states a future commitment to release data and evaluation protocols. Hardware, deployment arrangements, implementation descriptions, and substantive prompt contents remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds references concerning over-personalization, safety alignment, representations, and role-play safety, and elaborates comparison with role-playing jailbreaks in Appendix F.1. The original positioning around benign personalization rather than adversarial memory manipulation remains intact.
descriptions.P1: v2 removes repetition in Section 3.4, corrects terminology and cross-references, adds acknowledgments and a corresponding-author designation, and inserts a discussion appendix before the retained case studies. The main narrative and section organization remain largely unchanged.
descriptions.P2: All 17 figures and 11 tables are retained. Appendix heatmaps and tables are repositioned, Table 8 persona labels lose the '_R3' suffix, and Figure 10's incorrect topic-relevance caption is replaced with an intent-legitimation description. The plotted graphics are unchanged.

P-40F84DF27F.title: DriverGaze360: OmniDirectional Driver Attention with Object-Level Guidance

descriptions.M1: The Video Swin backbone, shared decoder, attention and attended-object heads, training losses, and extraction/calibration algorithms are unchanged. The new panoramic comparison does not modify the proposed method.
descriptions.E1: Training and evaluation retain DriverGaze360 and DADA-2000, with the same driving scenarios and participant coverage. The added panoramic baselines use the existing task rather than introducing another dataset or test scenario.
descriptions.E2: Section 11 and Table 7 add evaluated PanoConv and PAVER baselines adapted to rectilinear inputs. The five original comparison methods in Tables 4 and 5 remain unchanged.
descriptions.E3: The documented splits, 16-frame inputs, resolutions, metrics, optimizer and training budget are unchanged. The added comparison uses the existing rectilinear inputs; no separate evaluation protocol revision is reported.
descriptions.E4: The attention-only, object-segmentation and attended-object ablation in Table 6 and the qualitative examples are retained unchanged. Table 7 adds ordinary baseline comparisons, not a new robustness test or ablation.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for model performance. The new table continues the existing point-estimate reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: Table 7 adds PanoConv scores of 1.450/0.599/0.425/5.540 and PAVER scores of 3.375/0.089/0.070/0.236 in KLD/CC/SIM/NSS order. The proposed method's scores are repeated from Table 4; Tables 4–6 and existing qualitative findings are unchanged.
descriptions.T1: The metric definitions, loss equations and supplementary fixation-map formulation are mathematically unchanged. No new formal assumptions, theoretical results or proofs are introduced.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same dataset, joint-prediction and attended-object extraction contributions, along with the same performance and generalization claims.
descriptions.C2: New Section 12 explicitly identifies simulation-induced differences in behavior and gaze, advises caution about real-world generalization, and proposes domain adaptation. Section 11 also qualifies the panoramic comparison by distinguishing rectilinear inputs from equirectangular imagery.
descriptions.D1: The stated project address changes from av.dfki.de to dfki-av.github.io. v2 clarifies rectilinear camera geometry and credits CVC-provided navigation-route code. Existing training and hardware details remain unchanged; baseline adaptation details are not supplied.
descriptions.R1: Section 2.2 adds discussion and citations for SAGE and ASIAFNet. Supplementary Section 11 adds PanoConv and PAVER and explains their input-representation distinction, broadening positioning against related approaches.
descriptions.P1: v2 adds acknowledgments and supplementary Sections 11–12 and expands the related-work paragraph. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain unchanged, without extensive rewriting.
descriptions.P2: Table 7 is added, Algorithm 1 moves from page 6 to page 5, and Table 1's caption moves above the table. Paragraph spacing and placement shift, while the existing figures and result-table designs are retained.

P-631E79EEB3.title: Analyzing the Training Dynamics of Image Restoration Transformers: A Revisit to Layer Normalization

descriptions.M1: v2 Equations 3–5 and v3 Equations 2–3 specify the same method: joint spatial-channel normalization followed by rescaling attention/FFN outputs using the preceding normalization's standard deviation. The new theory, backbone experiments, and ablation variants do not revise the proposed i-LN procedure.
descriptions.E1: The original training corpora, benchmark datasets, and four restoration tasks are retained. Appendix E.2 adds a complex synthetic degradation scenario for ×4 super-resolution, applying the Real-ESRGAN pipeline to DF2K training images and the same five SR test sets. This is a bounded extension of input conditions within the existing SR task.
descriptions.E2: Table 1 retains the original normalization comparator set. v3 adds LN with gradient clipping and LN with KL-divergence regularization as evaluated alternatives in Table 8, and compares SRFormer with LN versus i-LN in Table 7. These extend the comparisons without replacing the original comparison framework.
descriptions.E3: v3 introduces full-sized HAT experiments using 500K iterations for ×2 SR followed by 250K iterations of warm-start ×4 fine-tuning, an SRFormer configuration, and batch-size 2/4/8 tests. These expand the evaluation design. The old HAT† results are retained under HAT2; newly disclosed settings for those existing experiments do not establish reruns.
descriptions.E4: v3 completes the component ablation by adding LN plus rescaling without spatial holisticness (Table 3). It extends RPE analysis across ablation variants, shallow/deep layers, and training stages (Figure 12), and adds gradient-clipping/KLD analyses, seed-stability tests, batch-size sensitivity, and additional qualitative cases. These address questions beyond the retained v2 analyses.
descriptions.E5: v2 does not document a repeated-seed evaluation protocol. v3 introduces multi-seed training trajectories in Figure 11 and five individual seed results with averages in Table 9. This expands repeatability and variability reporting, although formal confidence intervals and significance tests are not supplied.
descriptions.E6: Table 2 and the previously reported ablation and low-precision scores are retained. v3 adds rescaling-only, full-sized HAT, SRFormer, regularization, and complex-degradation results; Table 9 reports average Urban100 PSNR of 21.95 for LN versus 22.14 for i-LN under the new degradation protocol. Some normalization-specific Set5 results disappear from Table 1. Table 6 prints Set14 ×2 SSIM as 0.8276 for i-LN versus 0.9274 for LN while bolding i-LN.
descriptions.T1: v2 provides normalization equations and intuitive motivation without formal propositions or proofs. v3 adds definitions of inter-pixel structure and structure preservation, propositions concerning LN and holistic LN*, and derivations in Appendix G. The new analysis explicitly concerns normalization before the learned affine transformation.
descriptions.C1: The central diagnosis, two-component i-LN contribution, and claims about restoration quality, feature stability, and low-precision robustness remain. v3 explicitly extends the introduction's applicability claims to real-world IR and presents theoretical insights as an additional contribution in the abstract.
descriptions.C2: v3 expands the mechanism discussion: it explains cumulative outlier growth through residual paths, connects normalization bypassing to equal-statistics degeneracy, interprets SRFormer's permutation as partially holistic normalization, and discusses why gradient clipping fails while KLD sacrifices reconstruction fidelity. These extend the original bypassing and bias-alignment interpretations.
descriptions.D1: Beyond v2's brief settings paragraphs, v3 supplies a model-variant inventory, detailed architecture and optimization tables, degradation implementations, channel-entropy pseudocode, computational costs, and a code-repository link. Some inconsistencies remain: Table 5 describes HAT2 training as 300K iterations, whereas Table 14 specifies 500K.
descriptions.R1: The original IR-transformer and abnormal-feature positioning largely remains. v3 adds references to Real-ESRGAN, SRFormer, BasicSR, and rate-distortion/VAE research supporting its new experiments and regularization discussion. It also adds a specific interpretation of SRFormer's normalization behavior, without broadly redefining the paper's research position.
descriptions.P1: The abstract and introduction are condensed and rewritten. Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, observations become a standalone section, and experiments are reorganized into ablation and LN/i-LN property sections. Terminology changes from spatial consistency to spatial holisticness, and indexed backbone names clarify model variants.
descriptions.P2: The original Table 3 is split into separate ablation and quantization tables, Table 1 loses its Set5 columns, and existing plots and panels are rearranged or reformatted. v3 adds numerous experimental and configuration tables, entropy pseudocode, multi-run plots, expanded RPE displays, and qualitative comparison panels. These are display changes beyond renumbering or page-count growth.

P-FD52D8B586.title: Flash-VAED: Plug-and-Play VAE Decoders for Efficient Video Generation

descriptions.M1: Independence-aware pruning, stage-specific operator replacement, shortcut injection and three-phase distillation remain unchanged, including the losses and backbone-specific pruning configurations. Appendix B applies existing optimizations to additional backbones and discusses potential extensions without introducing a changed method.
descriptions.E1: Appendix B.1 adds reconstruction evaluation on the DAVIS 2019 Challenge test set at 720p, extending coverage to complex motion, occlusions and fine details. Training data, UCF-101 and VBench coverage are retained. Higher-resolution latency testing already existed in v1.
descriptions.E2: Section 4.3 and Figure 11 add L1-norm channel pruning alongside the existing random-pruning comparator. New Table 7 also compares channel-pruning-only and operator-optimization-only variants. The principal LightVAE and Turbo-VAED comparator sets remain unchanged.
descriptions.E3: v2 adds RAFT-based warping error, parameter-count and peak-VRAM measurements, and protocols for DAVIS evaluation and Causal Forcing deployment with seven selected VBench dimensions. Additional backbone diagnostics are also reported. The existing training settings and original benchmark protocols remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: The revision expands diagnostic evidence: stronger pruning comparisons, component-specific resource ablations, DAVIS robustness testing, transfer to Causal Forcing, and SVD/operator-optimization analyses on HunyuanVideo and CogVideoX. The original resolution/frame-count study and training ablations are retained.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates for the experiments. The added SVD explained-variance results concern feature redundancy, not statistical uncertainty.
descriptions.E6: Original table values are retained, while new results appear. Table 2 reports Wan warping errors of 0.018662 for Flash-VAED and 0.026640 for LightVAE. DAVIS Table 6 reports corresponding PSNR values of 32.03 and 27.92. Table 7 adds memory and parameter results; Table 8 adds Causal Forcing scores, including multi-view consistency of 0.318 versus the original decoder's 0.424. New pruning curves, qualitative examples and additional-backbone findings further expand the evidence.
descriptions.T1: The method equations and Appendix A.1 computational-cost derivation are unchanged apart from numbering and formatting. New Equations 7–8 explain the adopted optical-flow warping metric; they do not introduce new theoretical reasoning, assumptions or proofs.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same method, latent-alignment and efficiency claims, including approximately 6× decoding speedup, up to 96.9% reconstruction-performance retention and up to 36% pipeline acceleration. Added experiments support these existing claims.
descriptions.C2: New appendix discussions explain spatial generalization through convolutional structure, interpret component-specific resource savings, and discuss applicability to additional convolutional and transformer architectures. Appendix B.9 newly identifies failures involving tiny moving objects and dense faces, linking blur, flicker and detail loss to limited decoder capacity.
descriptions.D1: v2 documents implementation choices for added evaluations, including pretrained RAFT flow estimation from ground-truth frames and L1-based channel scoring from weights. Existing hardware, optimizer settings, loss coefficients, gradient masking, full prompts and code-access information are retained.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds references supporting DAVIS, temporal consistency, Causal Forcing and architectural/future-work discussion, while removing the Jetson technical brief and stereo-compression reference. The main related-work positioning remains stable. Publication updates and the retitled VLMQ reference concern retained works.
descriptions.P1: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. Changes include local wording and typo corrections, affiliation and acknowledgment updates, and expanded appendix organization. The original Appendix B.1–B.3 material is retained as B.6–B.8.
descriptions.P2: The document switches from a lab-branded format to an ICML layout, redesigning the opening page and rearranging or resizing existing displays. v2 adds four tables and two qualitative comparison figures, and redraws Figure 11 with an additional curve and revised axis ticks.

P-286337222C.title: LitVISTA: A Benchmark for Narrative Orchestration in Literary Text

descriptions.M1: The three-role VISTA framework, single-pass graph reconstruction task, and both evaluation prompts remain unchanged. New serialization explanations address intermediate heads already present in v1's examples; they do not establish a changed prediction procedure.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same LitBank-based English literary coverage and oracle and raw-text reconstruction tasks. Shortening the displayed Alice example does not establish reduced training or evaluation coverage.
descriptions.E2: Table 2 retains the same 27 models, and Appendix E.1 retains the same six end-to-end comparators. All four models illustrated in Appendix E.2 remain represented despite shorter output excerpts.
descriptions.E3: The 8:1:1 split, oracle versus raw-text conditions, one-shot prompts, and temperature settings remain unchanged. Expanded descriptions of annotation filtering and evaluation clarify existing procedures without establishing revised experimental settings.
descriptions.E4: The long-range dependency, lexical-role, and end-to-end error analyses remain. Supporting case evidence is reduced: Appendix C shortens the Alice annotation, and Appendix E.2 omits portions of three representative model outputs.
descriptions.E5: Both report annotation consistency of 0.49 and 0.76 without changing statistical estimation or uncertainty reporting. V2 explains why adjudication has no independent agreement score. Neither reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
descriptions.E6: Tables 1–2, plotted results, and the uniformly zero end-to-end finding are unchanged. Appendix E.2 removes 27 displayed prediction rows: IDs 8–16 from GPT-5-Thinking, DeepSeek-v3.2, and Gemini-3-Pro-Preview-Thinking. Retained entries are unchanged.
descriptions.T1: Appendix B.2 revises Axiom 5.1 to specify ultimate backbone dependence and adds Axioms 5.1.1–5.1.2 distinguishing ultimate dependence from operational serialization. These qualify the formal treatment of intermediate references; the main equations and remaining axioms are retained.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion explicitly position narrative reconstruction as a diagnostic proxy for generation, with the conclusion excluding direct generation evaluation. They also foreground the existing end-to-end extraction failures. The framework, benchmark, and principal oracle findings remain the core contributions.
descriptions.C2: V2 adds the limitation that participants and character interactions are not explicitly modeled. It also qualifies graph scores as incomplete measures of literary understanding and explains how upstream extraction affects pipeline scores. Existing oracle, domain, scalability, and subjectivity limitations remain.
descriptions.D1: Section 3.2 adds the protocol designer's role, annotator pair composition, limited trigger filtering, and dependency-handling details. V1's 1.5-month annotation duration is omitted. The evaluation prompts, temperature information, and dataset access link remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: V2 removes citations to Bruner (1990), Grimshaw (1990), Ricoeur (1979), Stewart (1986), Tenny (1995), and Graciotti et al. (2025). This prunes supporting literature while retaining the broad research positioning. Bibliographic updates to retained works do not constitute new cited research.
descriptions.P1: The revision edits the abstract, introductory framing, annotation account, evaluation setup, and conclusion. Section 3.2 is reorganized into background, details, and summary subsections; acknowledgements are added, and appendix explanations and examples are streamlined. This is a broad editorial revision despite stable experiments.
descriptions.P2: All six numbered figures retain identical image content, and both main tables retain their structure. Figures move with the revised text, Figure 3's caption specifies independent annotation, Appendix A and E prose adopts two columns, and several example displays are shortened.

P-4CC0786920.title: Regret-Based Federated Causal Discovery with Unknown Interventions

descriptions.M1: The two-phase minimax-regret framework remains, but Equation (4) changes from intersecting the server graph with the client skeleton to undirected-consensus masking. Under the new rule, a server-directed edge becomes undirected in the mask when the client edge is undirected. This changes orientation-stage scoring beyond merely renaming the operator.
descriptions.E1: V1 evaluates linear Gaussian structural models only. V2 retains this coverage and adds nonlinear causal-discovery scenarios using randomly selected tanh, sine, and quadratic mechanisms in Appendix B, extending the tested functional regimes.
descriptions.E2: V1's empirical comparison is between I-PERI's own CPDAG and Φ-CPDAG outputs. V2 adds evaluated comparisons against PERI, NOTEARS-ADMM, FedDAG, and FedCDH in Table 1 and the linear-data figures. These methods were not evaluated as baselines in v1.
descriptions.E3: The reported experimental grids change: Figure 6's client counts move from 3, 5, 10, 20 to 2, 4, 8, 10, and heterogeneous sample sizes change from 1000/2000/5000 to 500/1000/2000. Variable-count experiments extend to 20 variables. New nonlinear experiments introduce five-bin discretization and PC with a chi-squared independence test; SHD and F1 remain the evaluation metrics.
descriptions.E4: The comparison between initial CPDAG recovery and orientation refinement is retained. V2 adds a targeted sensitivity analysis of the client discovery algorithm: Figure 8b directly compares PC and GES, alongside GES-based baseline experiments in Figure 8a.
descriptions.E5: V1 shows shaded bands without specifying their meaning or the run count. V2 reports averages over 10 seeds, means with standard deviations in Tables 1–2, and confidence intervals in figure captions. It also discloses selecting seeds to obtain client CPDAG F1 above 0.85. This expands statistical reporting, although interval construction remains unspecified and an increase in runs cannot be inferred.
descriptions.E6: V2 replaces and expands the original phase-comparison curves with baseline, runtime, PC/GES, and nonlinear results. For example, linear Table 1 reports SHD 4.44 for I-PERI versus 8.40 for PERI at eight variables, whereas nonlinear Table 2 reports 9.33 versus 9.10. These are newly reported results under revised or added conditions, rather than established performance gains between versions.
descriptions.T1: The Φ-CPDAG definition expands from orienting intervened-graph v-structures to incorporating every oriented edge in client CPDAGs. Appendix A revises the convergence arguments and replaces v1's citation-only sensitivity proof with an explicit derivation presented as correcting prior work. The displayed sensitivity bound itself is unchanged between versions.
descriptions.C1: The central contributions—unknown-intervention discovery, Φ-MEC identification, convergence, and privacy guarantees—remain. V2's introduction additionally calls Φ-MEC the best recoverable class under private, regret-only information exchange, strengthening v1's claim that it is a tighter equivalence class.
descriptions.C2: V2 adds an explicit limitation that inaccurate client CPDAGs, especially erroneous orientations, propagate into the server's Φ-CPDAG. It also explains that nonlinear applicability depends on the client discovery method. The existing causal-assumption limitations and interpretation of parametric interventions remain.
descriptions.D1: V2 newly documents PC and BIC use in the main experiments, the client intervention arrangement, nonlinear generation and preprocessing, and the chi-squared test. It also supplies a reproducibility-code link. These extend v1's implementation information; the PDFs do not establish that newly disclosed choices were absent from the earlier implementation.
descriptions.R1: V2 expands its treatment of federated causal discovery into constraint-based, score-based, and optimization-based approaches, with numerous additional citations. It explicitly distinguishes its setting from Abyaneh et al.'s known-intervention federated work. The existing comparison with centralized unknown-intervention research is largely retained and moved into the introduction.
descriptions.P1: Existing introductory, methodological, and privacy passages are extensively rewritten. Related-work discussion moves from the discussion section to the introduction, masking and inclusion definitions move into Section 3, and the appendices receive explicit Proofs and Experimental Results sections. Terminology and explanations are revised throughout.
descriptions.P2: Figures 2–3 are redrawn with separate client-graph and masking panels, and Figure 4 is rearranged. V1's Figure 5 and illustrative regret table are replaced by a different equivalence-class comparison and empirical tables. The experimental displays are redesigned and expanded with runtime and appendix plots.

P-5938814B39.title: LinVideo: A Post-Training Framework towards O(n) Attention in Efficient Video Generation

descriptions.M1: The Hedgehog kernel, learnable layer-selection scores, constraint and regularization losses, ADM objective, score estimator, and optional subsequent DMD2 distillation remain unchanged. Applying the framework to Wan14B and documenting the existing two-stage procedure do not introduce a new proposed method.
descriptions.E1: Both versions study text-to-video generation using synthetic model trajectories and evaluate VBench and VBench-2.0. OpenVid is newly disclosed as the prompt source, without evidence of a dataset replacement. Model size, resolution and frame-count differences concern experimental configurations within this retained coverage.
descriptions.E2: The main comparators remain FlashAttention2, DFA, XAttention, SVG and SVG2; the Manual, Heuristic and objective controls also remain. Appendix F quantifies the direct-distillation failure already reported qualitatively in v1 Section 4.3. SLA receives an explicit exclusion explanation but is not evaluated in either version.
descriptions.E3: Section 5.1 adds a configuration: Wan14B at 720p, replacing 22/40 attention layers and training on 32 H100 GPUs, alongside the retained Wan1.3B configuration. Appendix C specifies annealed and fixed-alpha comparison settings. Conversely, v1 Figure 7's latency sweep over 81, 161 and 321 frames is removed. Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments changed or were rerun.
descriptions.E4: The appendix supplies alpha-schedule sensitivity results, visual evidence of temporal jitter under the naive objective, and a quantitative comparison of direct versus sequential distillation and linearization. Several questions were mentioned in v1, but their supporting appendix evidence was absent. V2 also removes the frame-length scaling analysis from v1 Figure 7.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. Appendix A's videos-per-prompt counts disclose evaluation sample sizes rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: The Wan1.3B quality scores in Tables 1–4 are retained. V2 adds Wan14B results, including 1127-second inference at 1.71× speedup and 92.56-second distilled inference at 20.9×, plus VBench-2.0 totals of 59.62 and 58.22 respectively. Appendix Tables I–II add alpha-ablation and direct-distillation scores, while the longer-frame latency results disappear. These are additional or removed results, not same-setting improvements over v1.
descriptions.T1: Appendix D adds the previously unavailable derivation of Equation (13), starting from the general score–velocity relationship, substituting the rectified-flow schedules and subtracting the two scores. The main equations and formal assumptions remain unchanged.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and contribution summary replace the 1.25–2.00× acceleration claim with 1.43–1.71× and expand the distilled-model claim from 15.92× to 15.9–20.9×. These ranges reflect different reported configuration coverage. The central data-free post-training, selective-transfer and ADM contributions remain the same.
descriptions.C2: Appendices B–C explain how alpha changes the regularizer's gradient landscape and interpret the new ablation as supporting schedule robustness. Appendix F makes the training-stability rationale for sequential linearization and distillation explicit. These extend the interpretation without changing the main mechanism claims or introducing a substantially different applicability boundary.
descriptions.D1: Appendices A and G disclose the OpenVid prompt source, 81-frame inputs with 21 latent frames, FSDP, 10% warm-up, batch sizes 48/64, initial learning rate 0.0001, alpha decay from 20 to 2, and the 128-prompt heuristic-selection procedure. Evaluation counts of five videos per VBench prompt and three or twenty per VBench-2.0 prompt are also supplied.
descriptions.R1: V2 shortens the early-video survey and removes citations including Stable Video Diffusion, Tune-A-Video and Make-A-Video, while adding OpenVid and FSDP. It corrects the implementation paragraph's DMD2 citation and explains SLA's exclusion through its stated GPU-kernel restriction. The central positioning against sparse attention and intra-layer mixed attention is retained.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction and method prose receive localized rewriting, and related work is shortened. The separate Efficiency Discussion is absorbed into Main Results, the ablation subsection is renumbered, and supplementary material is organized into Appendix A–H. The main narrative and method exposition remain largely intact.
descriptions.P2: Figure 4 changes from a radar chart to labeled bar panels for both model sizes. Table 1 gains latency columns and model groups, while Table 2 incorporates latency information previously plotted separately. The frame-scaling plot is removed, and the appendix adds Figures I–IV and Tables I–II. V1 Figure 8 is retained as v2 Figure 6, rather than constituting a new analysis.

P-E46DBC7960.title: Freqformer: Image-Demoiréing Transformer via Effective Frequency Decomposition

descriptions.M1: The decomposition kernel, dual branches, SA-CA, hierarchical fusion, learnable FCT and two-stage losses remain unchanged. The explicit description of resized low-frequency inference resolves an inconsistent overview in v1; v1 Section 3.2 already specified small inputs during both training and inference.
descriptions.E1: TIP2018 and LCDMoire move from related-work discussion to actual training and evaluation, alongside retained FHDMi and UHDM experiments. This broadens coverage beyond high-resolution benchmarks to 256×256 natural-scene images and a synthetic, text-focused dataset. Adding adapted RAW/video comparator architectures does not establish evaluation on RAW or video datasets.
descriptions.E2: Table 2 adds RRID and DTNet on FHDMi/UHDM and STD-Net on FHDMi. The ablations additionally introduce Block DCT and DAT comparisons. Conversely, v1 Table 5's dedicated comparison against ESDNet on separate frequency branches disappears, although ESDNet remains in other experiments.
descriptions.E3: Existing FHDMi/UHDM splits, metrics, crop/resize sizes and 150-epoch training stages are retained. Added experiments specify TIP2018's 135,000/15,000 training/test split and 256/256 crop/resize sizes, LCDMoire's 10,000/100 training/validation split and 512/512 sizes, and an 8×8 Block-DCT control. These extend the protocol without documenting a redesign of the original benchmark evaluations.
descriptions.E4: The transform analysis expands from one Haar experiment to quantitative Haar/DCT comparisons and qualitative artifact examples in Table 3 and Figure 7. Table 6 adds full-convolution SCP and DAT architecture controls. The separate branchwise ESDNet analysis is removed, while the resizing and learnable-FCT studies survive as renumbered Tables 4–5.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The expanded results retain the same single-score reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: New benchmark results include TIP2018/LCDMoire PSNRs of 30.63/45.62, plus added comparator and ablation entries. Freqformer's UHDM PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS change from 22.22/0.8018/0.2434 to 22.24/0.8021/0.2424; FHDMi scores remain unchanged. Haar PSNR changes from 13.32 to 23.01, and Table 6 scores and timings are replaced without establishing identical conditions. Section 3.2's high-frequency resizing PSNR changes from approximately 30 to 25 dB. Section 4.1 adds 0.58 versus 0.25 s/image for Freqformer versus ESDNet-L and revises Freqformer's computation from 2.49 to 2.46 TFLOPs.
descriptions.T1: The mathematical method and losses are retained. The added equality expressing the high-frequency residual as the original image minus its low-frequency component restates the existing recurrence. No substantive new formal assumptions, theorems or proofs appear.
descriptions.C1: The central contributions and compact, state-of-the-art restoration claim remain. The abstract strengthens the comparative premise by attributing spatial discontinuity, channel redundancy and reconstruction errors to discrete Haar/block-DCT representations, extending v1's narrower discussion of underexploited wavelet approaches.
descriptions.C2: Section 3.1 adds explanations involving shift variance, secondary aliasing, block-DCT stationarity and channel redundancy. Section 4.1 newly qualifies the efficiency discussion: Freqformer has fewer FLOPs but slower inference than ESDNet-L, tentatively attributed to less optimized attention operations. The central texture/color interpretation remains unchanged.
descriptions.D1: v2 adds implementation information for new experiments, including the Haar variant's band-specific modules and 10.921M parameters, and clarifies inference. However, it omits v1's explicit initial learning rate of 0.0002. The abstract changes the code-availability statement from publicly available to a future release; the PDFs do not establish the repository's actual availability.
descriptions.R1: Section 2.2 broadens from wavelet-based to frequency-based methods, adding DCT positioning against MBCNN and FHDe2Net and revising the critique of FHDe2Net. STD-Net and generative-restoration references are added. The existing research lineage and principal novelty positioning remain.
descriptions.P1: The section sequence and much of the method exposition remain, with localized rewrites, clearer inference wording and reordered ablation discussion. The title changes 'Efficient' to 'Effective,' asymmetric training terminology becomes more prominent, author/affiliation information changes, and acknowledgements are added.
descriptions.P2: The document adopts a different template with narrower text, running headers and reorganized displays. New Figures 3 and 7 illustrate transform differences and ablation outputs.
