Tables 1, 2 and 6 expand; the old branch-comparison table disappears. Ablation tables move from text-wrapped placements to full-width blocks, and qualitative comparisons replace a UHDM example and introduce RRID panels.

P-52314E9C29.title: CardioComposer: Leveraging Differentiable Geometry for Compositional Control of Anatomical Diffusion Models

descriptions.M1: The VAE–diffusion architecture, geometric moment losses, gradient guidance and appendix alternative losses are retained. Section 4.2 corrects the softmax description from near-binary outputs to values between 0 and 1, without changing the procedure.
descriptions.E1: Both versions use the same cardiac, aortic, spinal and knee datasets, synthetic ellipsoid task, and compositional and editing scenarios. Section 5.8 is shortened, but the corresponding anatomical coverage remains documented in the appendix.
descriptions.E2: Both retain explicit concatenation with adaptive null guidance, implicit concatenation with classifier-free guidance, and cross-attention with classifier-free guidance. The compositional comparison retains the same implicit-conditioning dropout baseline.
descriptions.E3: Data splits, sample counts, model configurations, guidance sweeps and denoising budgets are unchanged. Section 5.3 newly specifies averaging fidelity errors across substructures; this documents aggregation without establishing a changed evaluation procedure.
descriptions.E4: The disentanglement, compositionality, dataset-scaling, synthetic-ellipsoid, reconstruction/topology, editing-scale and alternative-moment analyses are retained. Appendix Sections 8.8–8.13 become 9.8–9.13 without substantive analysis changes.
descriptions.E5: Run/seed disclosures and uncertainty-reporting practices are unchanged. Neither version reports repeated-run confidence intervals or significance tests; the retained references to seed label maps concern input anatomies.
descriptions.E6: Table 1, appendix Tables 8, 9 and 11, and all result figures retain the same results. For example, zero-constraint FD in Table 1 remains 1622 for Implicit and 34.6 for Ours in both versions.
descriptions.T1: Equations (1)–(8), including moment definitions, covariance normalization and the extent/stretch/orientation decomposition, are unchanged. No mathematical derivation, formal assumption, theorem or proof is added or removed.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same claims of inference-time geometric control, disentangled attributes and compositional generation across anatomical systems. The new code-release sentence supplies access information rather than a new scientific contribution.
descriptions.C2: Section 6 removes the proposed remedy of developing localized substructure-selection methods for cross-sectional control. The limitations concerning weight tuning, class-based substructures and topological failures, and the interpretations of experimental results, otherwise remain.
descriptions.D1: v3 adds a code-release URL in the abstract and explicitly documents substructure averaging in Section 5.3. Figure 12's caption drops the statement that a separate diffusion model is trained for each anatomical dataset. Detailed appendix implementation settings remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: Section 2 replaces Madani et al. (2019) with Dong et al. (2023) for the coronary-cylinder modeling example. Other reference changes update publication metadata or consolidate duplicate Kong citations; the substantive research positioning remains unchanged.
descriptions.P1: v3 corrects grammar, citation formatting and explanatory wording, removes repetition, and shortens Section 5.8 and the limitations discussion. It adds acknowledgments and renumbers the appendix while retaining the overall narrative structure.
descriptions.P2: All 16 figures and 11 tables are retained. v3 changes conference headers and affiliation placement, resizes Table 1, shifts figure/text placement through reflow, and shortens Figure 12's caption. The underlying figure graphics are unchanged.

P-655C9D9CD7.title: Nesterov Finds GRAAL: Optimal and Adaptive Gradient Method for Convex Optimization

descriptions.M1: Algorithm 1 retains its update equations, but its required parameter condition changes: Eq. (19) doubles the gamma*theta^2/(1+theta)^2 term, tightening the admissible constants. No algorithm component is added.
descriptions.E1: Neither version uses datasets or empirical evaluation tasks. The extension to (L0, L1)-smooth functions concerns theoretical applicability, not evaluated task coverage.
descriptions.E2: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. The added AdaNAG discussion and Table 1 compare theoretical guarantees, without adding evaluated baselines.
descriptions.E3: Neither version reports experimental protocols, data splits, evaluation metrics, training budgets, or testing procedures. Revised mathematical parameter conditions do not establish an experimental setting change.
descriptions.E4: Neither version contains ablations, empirical sensitivity analyses, robustness tests, or case studies. The additional appendix develops convergence proofs.
descriptions.E5: Repeated runs, seeds, uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, and significance tests are absent from both versions.
descriptions.E6: Neither version reports measured performance values or empirical findings. The new iteration bounds and theoretical comparison entries are changes to theory and research positioning.
descriptions.T1: Section 4 and Appendix C add generalized smoothness assumptions, Lemmas 5–8, Theorem 3, and Corollary 3, establishing near-optimal complexity under (L0, L1)-smoothness with initialization-dependent additive terms. Theorem 1 gains explicit descent terms under tighter parameter conditions. Appendix A also expands the positivity proof and corrects the Corollary 1 derivation to retain its distance term.
descriptions.C1: v1 centers its contribution on accelerated convergence for Lipschitz-smooth objectives. v2 adds near-optimal guarantees for (L0, L1)-smooth objectives and claims the first adaptive algorithm achieving them. The abstract and contribution list explicitly qualify optimality by additive terms.
descriptions.C2: v2 explains why geometric stepsize growth matters when curvature varies exponentially, discusses generalized-smooth initialization requirements and additive-complexity tradeoffs, and conjectures that AC-FGM and AdaNAG cannot achieve comparable near-optimal guarantees. v1 primarily discusses AC-FGM's difficulty recovering from small initial stepsizes.
descriptions.D1: Parameter guidance expands beyond v1's eta0 <= 1/L condition: v2 states eta0 L0 exp(L1||x0-x*||) <= 1 and gives the specific initialization used for Table 1's theoretical comparison. These are analytical prescriptions, not reported implementation settings; no code, hardware, or runtime information is added.
descriptions.R1: v2 expands positioning through AdaNAG and generalized-smooth optimization literature, including Li et al., Gorbunov et al., Vankov et al., and Tyurin. Sections 1.4, 3.2, and 4.2 discuss their guarantees, adaptation restrictions, and novelty relationships. Li and Lan's 2023-to-2025 citation change is a publication update to the same work.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, contribution list, and comparison discussion are revised; convergence-rate language is recast as iteration complexity, and B_f notation becomes D_f. The existing narrative and section sequence largely remain, while Section 4 and Appendix C principally introduce new scientific content.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds Table 1 with theoretical complexity, optimality, and adaptivity columns, colored checkmarks, and a highlighted proposed-result row. Algorithm 1 moves from page 4 to page 5 without display changes; the overall single-column layout remains.

P-ACF5E37789.title: REGLUE Your Latents with Global and Local Semantics for Entangled Diffusion

descriptions.M1: The proposed compressor, global/local/VAE fusion, velocity and alignment objectives, and sampling procedure remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendix B. Newly evaluated fusion, compression, and regularization variants are diagnostic ablations; they do not replace the proposed architecture or training objective.
descriptions.E1: v2 adds focused food-image generation on Food-101 and higher-resolution ImageNet generation at 512×512 (Appendix A.7, Table 14). v1's generation experiments cover ImageNet at 256×256. Existing Cityscapes probing and reduced-data ImageNet experiments are retained.
descriptions.E2: Table 4 adds RAE and REPA-E to the retained comparison methods, flagging their different latent spaces and the class-balanced evaluation of the 800-epoch REPA-E result. Table 1 also adds PCA-based combinations with global tokens, alignment, and multi-layer features as explicit comparison controls.
descriptions.E3: The stated default CFG scale changes from 2.8 to 2.3, retaining the guidance interval and sampling steps. v2 expands evaluation through CMMD, DINOv2-based FD/FD-infinity, inference throughput, total training compute, and additional compression/fusion/resampling controls. Existing main training budgets and the 50,000-sample evaluation remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: v2 adds matched PCA combination controls, a frequency-profile diagnostic, alternative-metric checks, compute-efficiency analysis, and fusion/resampling ablations (Table 1, Figure 3, Tables 11 and 13–16). The KL study expands to multiple weights and probing accuracy, while the GAN-loss experiment is removed. The CFG sweep expands; earlier channel, layer, VFM, and limited-data analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: Both versions report point results without repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional metrics in v2 are presented as point estimates, without a newly described uncertainty-estimation procedure.
descriptions.E6: Additional new results include Food-101 FID 4.6 versus REG's 7.6 and ImageNet-512 FID 14.4 versus 18.1, plus new metric, compute, and ablation entries. Table 4's 80/160-epoch REGLUE FIDs change from 1.61/1.53 to 1.59/1.46 alongside the changed CFG setting, so these are not identical-setting gains. At the retained CFG scale 2.7, FID changes from 1.53 to 1.52. Main unguided benchmark FIDs remain unchanged.
descriptions.T1: Equations 1–11, interpolation assumptions, token definitions, and training objectives retain the same mathematical content. The new frequency analysis is empirical; no theorem, proof, or formal derivation is added.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, four introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about global–local entanglement, nonlinear semantic compression, complementary alignment, and faster convergence. New experiments provide additional support without redefining these core contributions.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds a substantive mechanism explanation linking high-frequency suppression to diffusability and interprets stronger KL regularization as damaging semantic content. It also discusses metric dependence, compute efficiency, and fusion tradeoffs. Appendix C narrows the outstanding high-resolution limitation to larger models and adds mixed preliminary results from jointly decoding semantic and VAE latents.
descriptions.D1: v2 specifies throughput measurement on one A100 with batch size 64 and clarifies inclusion of DINOv2 and the compressor in compute accounting. Compressor-size reporting is explicitly reframed around encoder counts in Table 6. Most architecture, optimization, hardware/training-time disclosures, and the code-access statement remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds references concerning Food-101, alternative evaluation metrics, diffusability, encoder/tokenizer alignment, and representation autoencoders, while removing the EQ-VAE citation. The related-work narrative and central positioning relative to REPA, ReDi, and REG remain largely unchanged.
descriptions.P1: Most abstract, introduction, method, and conclusion wording and section order are retained. Changes concentrate on local experimental explanations, revised captions and cross-references, renamed or added appendix subsections, and a supplementary title page and contents list.
descriptions.P2: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, extensively resizing and repositioning displays. The overview moves later, and the compressor diagram and convergence samples move into the supplement. v2 adds the frequency plot and several tables and expands existing table columns and rows. The final sample grids retain the same images.

P-8C205582FE.title: PM-KVQ: Progressive Mixed-precision KV Cache Quantization for Long-CoT LLMs

descriptions.M1: v2 adds an evaluated PM-KVQ plus QuestAttention combination, extending inference to sparse attention (Appendix C.6, Table 10). The core progressive quantization schedule, Equivalent Right Shift, sensitivity-based allocation, positional-interpolation calibration and Section 3 pipeline remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: v2 adds IFEval instruction following with short outputs, extending coverage beyond competition mathematics and code generation (Appendix C.2, Table 6). Existing evaluation and calibration datasets are retained. Changing CMIMC-2025 to CMIMC-2024 in the setup prose aligns it with the existing Table 2 label rather than establishing a dataset replacement.
descriptions.E2: The original Table 2 comparators are retained. v2 additionally evaluates KVTuner for mixed-precision reasoning accuracy (Table 8), QuestAttention as the control for combined sparse attention and quantization (Table 10), and QServe for calibration time (Table 11). This broadens the evaluated comparison methods and controls.
descriptions.E3: New protocols include A100-80G throughput measurements at 16K/24K/32K output lengths with different feasible batch sizes, memory-triggered truncation of higher-bit KIVI, and additional memory/bit-width configurations. IFEval introduces strict/loose prompt and instruction metrics with one response per prompt. MiKV's preserved cache is described as BF16 instead of FP16, a reported setting revision that does not establish rerunning the retained results.
descriptions.E4: v2 adds analyses of throughput versus output length, higher-bit KIVI under memory limits, hardware-memory sensitivity, sparse-attention compatibility, preparation overhead, and response-length distributions (Section 4.3; Appendices C.3 and C.5–C.8). The original shrinking and interpolation ablations and block-sensitivity analyses are retained; moving Figure 3 into the main text is not a new analysis.
descriptions.E5: Table 2 retains its existing plus/minus reporting unchanged. Neither version supplies explicit seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or additional experiment-level repetition information. The new tables use point estimates, a practice already present in v1's ablations.
descriptions.E6: Table 2 and the original ablation tables retain identical numerical results. Additional new results include throughput of 2.73–5.18 times the original 16-bit models, IFEval scores, and KVTuner comparisons: AIME-2024 pass@1 is 40.21 for PM-KVQ versus 34.17 for KVTuner. Tables 7 and 9–12 add memory-constrained accuracy, sparse-attention results, calibration timing and response-length counts.
descriptions.T1: Appendix D introduces Theorem D.1 and a detailed quotient-and-remainder proof of Equivalent Right Shift, whereas v1 states the equivalence without proof. This adds substantive formal reasoning for the existing formula. However, the new proof contains an incorrect inequality in Equation (25).
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion add a principal claim of 2.73–5.18 times higher throughput than the original 16-bit models. This expands the claimed contribution from accuracy under memory constraints to measured inference acceleration. The original methodological contributions and up-to-8% accuracy claim are retained.
descriptions.C2: v2 adds substantive interpretations of the accuracy–throughput tradeoff, memory-constrained comparisons, short-output applicability and sparse-attention compatibility. Appendix C.8 explains different benefits for short responses and long responses whose early tokens use higher precision. Section 4.4.3 explicitly qualifies aggressive interpolation scaling. The original limitations remain essentially unchanged in Appendix E.
descriptions.D1: V2 documents using KIVI's inference engine and 2/4-bit CUDA kernels, alongside newly implemented 8/16-bit and shrinking kernels. It also discloses BF16 model weights, OpenCompass scoring, KVTuner quantization settings, throughput configurations and preparation times. Both versions advertise the same code repository.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds references to KVTuner, Quest, IFEval and OpenCompass and connects them to the additional evaluations. The original related-work coverage and central positioning remain largely intact. The switch from numbered to author–year citations does not itself change research positioning.
descriptions.P1: The main narrative remains recognizable, with localized shortening, wording corrections and expanded explanations. Small-model sensitivity discussion moves into the main ablations; Broader Impacts becomes an Ethics Statement, and reproducibility and LLM-use statements are added. The conference header and author-role note also change.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds a throughput table and seven appendix tables, expanding the visual presentation of evidence. Existing ablation tables are renumbered, Figure 3 moves into the main text, and Figure 2 is relocated. The original figures retain their graphical content, while conference typography, headings and page layout replace the preprint styling.

P-234A0EE02C.title: Apertus: Democratizing Open and Compliant LLMs for Global Language Environments

descriptions.M1: Table 1 revises the reported Apertus-70B hidden dimension from 4096 to 8192. This is a localized architecture-specification correction; the PDFs do not establish retraining or a new model procedure. The architecture components and training algorithms otherwise remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: Training corpora, evaluation tasks, languages, and domains remain unchanged. The additional checkpoint and RULER scores concern existing benchmark coverage; 32k and 64k contexts were already represented in v1.
descriptions.E2: Comparator membership remains unchanged. SmolLM3-3B already has a plotted endpoint in v1 Figure 7; v2 adds its intermediate checkpoints. Table 23 retains the same model rows.
descriptions.E3: Table 12 corrects the reported Swiss Charter Q&A training-example count from 943,427 to 226, making it consistent with the unchanged regional subtotal of 943,427. This revises a stated sample count without establishing that training data or experiments actually changed.
descriptions.E4: Figure 7 extends the analysis of performance over pretraining by adding SmolLM3-3B intermediate-checkpoint trajectories for global, English, EU, and Swiss evaluations, where v1 showed endpoints only. The architecture, filtering, and Goldfish ablations and memorization robustness analyses otherwise remain unchanged.
descriptions.E5: Repeated-run and seed information, uncertainty reporting, and statistical procedures are unchanged. The additional checkpoint and RULER results do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.
descriptions.E6: Figure 7 adds SmolLM3-3B checkpoint results. Table 23 fills seven missing RULER cells, including 64k scores of 56.9 for Apertus-70B and 67.3 for Apertus-70B-Instruct, and changes SmolLM3-3B's 64k score from 66.0 to 65.9. These are added or corrected results, rather than demonstrated improvements to the Apertus models.
descriptions.T1: Section 2.3 changes the displayed Goldfish-loss factor from G_i x_i to G_i(x_i), a localized correction to the formal loss expression. The accompanying masking procedure, Appendix F algorithm, QRPO derivation, and other mathematical definitions remain unchanged.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, principal contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about scale, openness, data compliance, multilingual capability, and memorization mitigation.
descriptions.C2: Interpretations and limitations concerning compliance tradeoffs, memorization, multilingual performance, safety, and deployment remain unchanged. The additional results receive no new substantive interpretation.
descriptions.D1: Table C.4 newly specifies an initialization standard deviation of 0.008944. V2 also adds a posttraining-data repository entry and an explicit access link for the SFT mixture in Section 4.1.3. These disclosures do not establish changed initialization or training procedures.
descriptions.R1: v2 adds Foroutan et al. (2025c), Revisiting Multilingual Data Mixtures in Language Model Pretraining, to the related-publications list and bibliography. The broader research positioning remains unchanged.
descriptions.P1: Editing is limited: v2 removes a duplicated sentence from Table 6's caption, adjusts punctuation, and updates front matter and cross-references. The narrative and section organization remain substantially unchanged.
descriptions.P2: Figure 7 adds checkpoint curves within its existing panels. Table 23 moves the context-length unit into individual column labels, Table C.4 gains a row, and Table 13 moves from page 35 to page 36. Other differences mainly involve local reflow.

P-2DC6EB9D01.title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

descriptions.M1: The ridge objective, fixed-feature linear model, GD updates and existing ReLU training procedures are unchanged. The Fourier-feature experiment instantiates the already general fixed-feature framework.
descriptions.E1: Appendix B adds synthetic regression with Gaussian-corrupted labels and learning a single Fourier-feature teacher. The existing realizable linear, non-realizable ReLU-feature and zero-teacher neural-network tasks remain.
descriptions.E2: Neither version evaluates competing baseline algorithms against a proposed method. Comparisons remain between training and test behavior, theoretical bounds and empirical observations, or hyperparameter choices.
descriptions.E3: Existing Section 5 settings remain unchanged. Appendix B introduces threshold accuracy using squared error at most 0.01, noise controls with standard deviations 0.01, 0.05 and 0.1, and configurations for the added experiments.
descriptions.E4: Figure 5 adds a paired comparison of squared loss and threshold accuracy from the same simulation. Figure 6 adds label-noise robustness and sensitivity analysis. The original hyperparameter sweeps are retained.
descriptions.E5: The new Figure 5 explicitly discloses that its two plots come from one simulation. Figure 1's reporting of 50 independent runs is unchanged; no increase in existing run counts or new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is reported.
descriptions.E6: Figures 1–4 retain identical results. New Figures 5–7 report an accuracy plateau, grokking under Gaussian label noise with little timing variation across the tested noise levels, and delayed generalization with Fourier features. These are additional findings under supplementary conditions.
descriptions.T1: The main theorem statements and Appendix A proofs are unchanged apart from a cross-reference. V3 removes v1's Lemma B.7 on Gaussian sample-covariance eigenvalue deviations and adds the threshold-accuracy definition. Lemmas B.1–B.6 are retained as C.1–C.6.
descriptions.C1: The abstract and contribution list retain the three-stage grokking guarantee, quantitative hyperparameter dependence, nonlinear-network empirical extension and first-end-to-end-result novelty claim. Added emphasis on linearity restates the existing contribution's scope.
descriptions.C2: V3 adds interpretations involving changes in implicit priors and metric-dependent accuracy plateaus. It also suggests applicability to decaying step sizes and gradient flow, explicitly discusses noisy-label theory as open, and notes careful tuning for Fourier features. Existing core mechanism explanations and proof limitations remain.
descriptions.D1: Appendix B supplies hyperparameters for the new experiments, Gaussian label-noise generation details, and the Fourier-feature construction with Gaussian frequencies and uniform phases. Existing implementation descriptions remain; no new code or data access information is provided.
descriptions.R1: V3 adds Gunasekar et al. (2018), Vardi and Shamir (2021), and Lauditi et al. (2025) for the implicit-bias discussion, and removes Wainwright (2019) with Lemma B.7. Section 1.1 also adds context about grokking without explicit regularization; core novelty positioning remains.
descriptions.P1: Localized prose edits and expanded discussion accompany new acknowledgements and an experiments appendix, with former Appendix B becoming C. Affiliations and the publication footer are updated. Main section order and most exposition remain intact.
descriptions.P2: V3 adds three appendix figures showing paired accuracy/loss curves, noise comparisons and Fourier-feature training. Original Figures 1–4 retain their graphics and captions. Text reflows, but the overall layout and existing displays are preserved.

P-AD753045F3.title: InvAD: Inversion-based Reconstruction-Free Anomaly Detection with Diffusion Models

descriptions.M1: The feature-space diffusion model, DDIM inversion, and scoring procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 removes the redundant absolute value around max(A)-min(A), which is already nonnegative. Specifying bilinear interpolation adds implementation detail without establishing a changed procedure.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate MVTecAD, VisA, MPDD, and the same BMAD medical datasets. The new ablations vary model settings and stratify existing MVTecAD cases by anomaly size; they introduce no additional dataset, domain, or task.
descriptions.E2: Comparator membership in the benchmark and generalizability experiments remains unchanged. The added attribution for the existing no-inversion ablation does not introduce a new comparison row; the new schedule and resolution variants are ablation settings.
descriptions.E3: New protocols compare four inversion schedules at S=3, 10, and 100, and feature resolutions of 8x8, 16x16, and 24x24 using anomaly-size-stratified mAD. Existing benchmark settings remain unchanged; warmup and cosine decay are still documented in Table 11 despite shortening the main-text description.
descriptions.E4: Supplementary Section 9 adds targeted sensitivity analyses of inversion scheduling and feature resolution, including small-anomaly performance. These extend the existing step-count, component, backbone, scoring, and qualitative analyses, which are retained.
descriptions.E5: Both versions retain the same statement about fixing library seeds and disabling nondeterministic GPU operations where possible. Neither supplies repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the new tables add no uncertainty estimates.
descriptions.E6: Existing benchmark and ablation scores are retained. Tables 13-14 add results: uniform scheduling at S=3 yields 83.35 mAD versus 81.48-82.37 for alternatives, while overall mAD for 8x8, 16x16, and 24x24 features is 82.05, 83.70, and 81.44. These are additional ablation findings, not improved main benchmark scores.
descriptions.T1: The diffusion equations and DDIM-inversion derivation are retained, including supplementary Equations 9-21. The scoring simplification is mathematically equivalent, and the added scheduling formulas specify experimental controls rather than new theoretical reasoning.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the reconstruction-free inversion contribution, strong detection-performance claims, approximately twofold inference speedup, and applicability to existing diffusion models. The additional experiments support retained claims without redefining their scope.
descriptions.C2: v4 adds discussion of feature compression potentially obscuring small anomalies and interprets the resolution ablation as showing that higher resolution is not monotonically beneficial. It also explains the uniform-schedule choice and expands the fairness rationale for EfficientNet. Existing reverse-scoring explanations and limitations remain.
descriptions.D1: Section 3.3 specifies bilinear anomaly-map interpolation, and Section 4.7 clarifies the existing no-inversion ablation's skipped algorithm steps and scoring attribution. v4 adds a project-page link while retaining the original code link in the supplement. Hardware, hyperparameters, and training-time disclosures remain unchanged.
descriptions.R1: v4 adds Li et al.'s prototype-oriented diffusion work and Rippel et al.'s pretrained-feature anomaly-detection work, supporting limited positioning and attribution additions. Most other reference changes concern formatting or bibliographic metadata rather than different cited research.
descriptions.P1: v4 makes local wording and spelling corrections, renames Abs to Diff, updates author/contact notes, and standardizes references. Funding acknowledgment becomes a separate section, and the supplement gains an ablation section; the main narrative structure remains substantially intact.
descriptions.P2: v4 adds Tables 13-14 and reflows the supplement, relocating the unchanged Figure 4 plots. It also corrects the RESC detection-column heading in Table 3 and updates scoring labels in Table 9 and Figure 4. Existing visual designs are largely retained.

P-ADD1870CD9.title: Towards Foundation Models for Zero-Shot Time Series Anomaly Detection: Leveraging Synthetic Data and Relative Context Discrepancy

descriptions.M1: TimeRCD retains the same tokenization, Transformer backbone, anomaly/reconstruction heads, training objectives, inference procedure, and synthetic-data generation method.
descriptions.E1: Appendix D.1 replaces WADI with SMAP, correcting its dataset list: v1 already includes SMAP in Table 8 and the corresponding result tables. The same 14 benchmark datasets, synthetic test scenarios, and pre-training data coverage are retained.
descriptions.E2: The zero-shot and full-shot comparator sets in Table 1 are identical. Comparator membership also remains unchanged in the contextual experiments and data/head ablations in Appendix E.
descriptions.E3: The evaluation protocol, four metrics, baseline window sizes, training settings, dataset-specific context selections, and ablation/scaling budgets match throughout Section 3 and Appendices D–E.
descriptions.E4: The contextual-versus-point-anomaly tests, window-size sensitivity analysis, pre-training data comparisons, scaling studies, and anomaly/reconstruction-head ablations are unchanged, including their appendix evidence.
descriptions.E5: Seed information and uncertainty displays are unchanged, including Table 3’s optional generator-seed control. No repeated-run counts, uncertainty-estimation procedures, or significance tests are added or revised.
descriptions.E6: All matched numerical scores, rankings, plotted trends, and qualitative examples are unchanged. This includes the main results in Tables 1–2 and the extended experimental results in Tables 9–13 and Appendix E’s figures.
descriptions.T1: The task definition, model equations, ODE-to-ARX construction, and Appendix C’s formal definitions of trends, seasonality, and anomaly types are unchanged.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction’s three contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about RCD, fully synthetic pre-training, and zero-shot anomaly-detection performance.
descriptions.C2: Interpretations of context length, injection trade-offs, data scaling, and reconstruction-head necessity are unchanged. The conclusion retains the same limitation and future direction concerning the standard Transformer backbone.
descriptions.D1: v3 adds a first-page code-availability footnote identifying the Time-RCD GitHub repository. This provides new access information; existing implementation and training details remain unchanged. The PDFs alone do not establish repository accessibility or completeness.
descriptions.R1: The references and Appendix B are unchanged, as is the positioning relative to reconstruction-based TSAD, contrastive methods, and synthetic-data pre-training.
descriptions.P1: v3 removes affiliation lines, corrects an author email, adds the code footnote, and corrects WADI to SMAP in Appendix D.1. The substantive prose and section organization remain unchanged.
descriptions.P2: The shortened author block and added footnote produce limited reflow on pages 1–4, including slight repositioning of Figures 2–3. No figures or tables are added, removed, or redesigned.

P-7A7741A751.title: UniRec-0.1B: Unified Text and Formula Recognition with 0.1B Parameters

descriptions.M1: Section 4 retains the FocalNet encoder, six-layer decoder, hierarchical supervision, semantic-decoupled tokenizer, cross-entropy objective and inference processing. The redrawn architecture diagram and scaling discussion do not establish a change to the proposed method.
descriptions.E1: Documented training and evaluation coverage remains UniRec40M, UniRec-Bench and OmniDocBench with the same languages, levels and domains. v2's new dataset-comparison table describes prior datasets without establishing their experimental use. Table recognition was already evaluated within the full-page parsing comparisons.
descriptions.E2: Corresponding recognition, document-parsing and timing tables retain identical comparator membership. Newly cited works such as Dolphin-v2 and DocHumming are not added to these evaluations. Figure 1(b) identifies parameter scales without specifying additional comparator methods.
descriptions.E3: Figure 1(b) adds a reported model-size sweep measuring recognition performance and latency. Existing training settings, benchmark partitions, metrics and timing procedures remain unchanged. Architectures and experimental controls for the new sweep are unspecified.
descriptions.E4: Figure 1(b) introduces a distinct cross-task capacity analysis investigating recognition saturation and the accuracy–latency tradeoff, extending the analysis beyond component ablations and recognition examples. The HST/SDT ablations and all appendix case studies remain unchanged.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or error bars for its results. The new scaling curves do not introduce uncertainty reporting.
descriptions.E6: v2 adds scaling curves reporting text/formula saturation near 0.1B parameters, continuing table-performance gains and increasing latency, plus finer timing labels in Figure 1(d). Existing benchmark, ablation and timing values match exactly between v1 Tables 2–5 and v2 Tables 3–6; appendix results also remain unchanged.
descriptions.T1: The model equations, token definitions and loss formulation are unchanged. The added 'scaling law analysis' is an empirical plot and interpretation, without a new mathematical law, derivation, assumption or proof.
descriptions.C1: The introduction adds the claim that text/formula recognition saturates around 0.1B parameters while tables benefit from larger models, strengthening the rationale for task specialization. It also explicitly asserts that named competing systems lack HST/SDT designs. The principal dataset, method and speedup contributions remain unchanged.
descriptions.C2: v2 attributes continued table-recognition gains to greater task complexity and interprets differing scaling behavior as support for dividing recognition tasks between models. Existing explanations of component benefits and appendix limitations, including superscript/subscript failures in Figure 9, are retained.
descriptions.D1: Section 3.1 removes explicit arXiv, Wikipedia and PyMuPDF documentation links provided in v1. The OpenOCR code/dataset link, implementation settings, hardware and training-time disclosures remain unchanged. No reproducible setup is supplied for the new scaling analysis.
descriptions.R1: Section 2 adds dedicated training-data positioning, supported by a systematic comparison of dataset tasks, annotation levels, languages and sizes in new Table 1. This expands the justification for UniRec40M's contribution. Additional literature includes Union14M-L, BCTR, Infinity-Doc, DocHumming and Dolphin-v2.
descriptions.P1: The introduction is locally rewritten around scaling and task specialization, related-work subsection headings become paragraph headings, and a training-data discussion and acknowledgements are added. Other sections receive limited wording corrections; the overall organization remains stable.
descriptions.P2: Figure 1 becomes a full-width four-panel display, adding scaling curves and replacing timing pie charts with stacked bars. Figure 3 is substantially rearranged into a horizontal diagram. v2 also adds the dataset-comparison table and reformats existing table headers and placement; appendix displays are unchanged.

P-B07B1F717B.title: Robust Fine-Tuning from Non-Robust Pretrained Models: Mitigating Suboptimal Transfer With Epsilon-Scheduling

descriptions.M1: Section 6.3 adds an automatic scheduling variant: validation-accuracy convergence selects T1, followed by a linear perturbation increase through the remaining training. The original two-hinge scheduler, adversarial objective, and model architectures remain unchanged.
descriptions.E1: Appendix E and Table 12 add ImageNette classification evaluations with SWIN and CNX at 4/255 and 8/255. The five original downstream datasets and their tasks are retained.
descriptions.E2: New Table 4 adds auto as an evaluated scheduling comparator alongside fix and sched on Aircraft, Caltech, and Cars. Existing comparisons remain. Expanded discussion of TWINS, AutoLoRA, and RoLi does not introduce evaluations of those methods.
descriptions.E3: The added automatic-scheduler experiment introduces validation-dependent timing, using five-epoch patience and 2% tolerance, with the ramp continuing to training completion. Existing experiments retain their splits, preprocessing, 50-epoch budget, APGD training/evaluation steps, and accuracy metrics.
descriptions.E4: Section 6.3 and Table 4 add a targeted test of whether validation-based timing can replace manually selected schedule boundaries. The original T1/T2 sensitivity sweeps, uniform-sampling comparison, robust-backbone analysis, and AutoAttack checks are retained.
descriptions.E5: v1 provides no significance tests. New Appendix D and Table 9 introduce paired t-tests covering all three principal metrics at both perturbation budgets, with 30 paired model–dataset configurations per test. This adds formal statistical assessment across the central comparison; it does not establish additional training runs or report seed-level uncertainty.
descriptions.E6: The original numerical result tables are unchanged. Table 4 adds auto results, with expected robustness below sched in all 12 configurations. Table 12 adds ImageNette results; for example, SWIN at 8/255 has expected robustness 86.93 for scheduler versus 82.43 for fix. Tables 9–11 add statistical outcomes and numerical averages. Table 10 contains a small inconsistency: ViT-fix clean accuracy at 8/255 averages to 15.52 from Table 2, versus the reported 15.59.
descriptions.T1: The adversarial-risk, scheduling, expected-robustness, and numerical-integration equations are retained. The added Dirac-distribution endpoint example explains the existing metric; the new theoretical open questions supply no theorem, proof, or substantive derivation.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, contribution summary, and conclusion retain the same central claims about suboptimal transfer, delayed adaptation, Epsilon-Scheduling, and expected robustness. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining their scientific scope.
descriptions.C2: The expanded limitations explicitly question whether delayed adaptation is the sole cause of suboptimal transfer and identify unresolved mechanisms and relevant pretraining properties. Section 6.3 also interprets automatic scheduling as effective despite lower expected robustness than the manually specified scheduler.
descriptions.D1: v1 mentions a code repository without giving the study's repository address. v2 adds an explicit link and a reproducibility statement describing implementation, HPO results, figure/table data, reproduction scripts, and setup instructions. It also specifies the automatic scheduler's patience and tolerance. Existing Appendix A implementation and compute details remain.
descriptions.R1: Section 2 expands the discussion of TWINS, AutoLoRA, and RoLi to explain their reported reliance on robust pretraining. Section 6.3 changes the linear-warmup attribution from Cao et al. to Debenedetti et al. The bibliography and principal novelty positioning otherwise remain unchanged.
descriptions.P1: The title replaces Adversarial Scheduling with Epsilon-Scheduling, and v2 makes local wording and affiliation edits. It adds short discussions, a reproducibility statement, and Appendices D–E while retaining most prose and the original section sequence.
descriptions.P2: v2 adopts the ICLR presentation with redesigned front matter and running headers, relocates figures and tables throughout the document, and adds five tables: automatic scheduling, significance tests, two aggregate summaries, and ImageNette results. All twelve original figures remain; original appendix tables are renumbered rather than removed.

P-164B7569EE.title: CraftMesh: High-Fidelity Generative Mesh Manipulation via Poisson Seamless Fusion

descriptions.M1: The image-editing, mesh-generation, Boolean/SDF fusion pipeline and its geometry and texture losses remain unchanged. Added alignment and texture-conditioning descriptions clarify implementation without establishing a changed procedure; the fusion block is also renamed.
descriptions.E1: Section 4.1 broadens the evaluation collection beyond v2's six illustrated sculpture/fantasy objects to assets selected from Objaverse-XL, Google Scanned Objects, and internet sources, including scanned household objects. The underlying mesh-editing tasks and drag-based demonstrations remain.
descriptions.E2: VoxHammer joins FocalDreamer, MagicClay, and Instant3dit in Table 1 and Figure 4. Trellis and Hunyuan3D 2.5 are alternative CraftMesh generation backends, rather than additional competing editing methods.
descriptions.E3: The stated evaluation expands from six objects to 100 models with three editing prompts per model. Section 4.5 also introduces alternative-generator configurations. The four evaluation metrics and reported GPU, iteration budgets, and optimization times remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: Section 4.5 adds a backend sensitivity analysis comparing MeshyAI, Trellis, and Hunyuan3D 2.5. Existing geometry/texture component ablations and qualitative distribution-, gradient-, and boundary-loss removal tests remain.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates for the experimental results.
descriptions.E6: Both tables replace the retained methods' numerical scores and add results. CraftMesh's Table 1 scores change from 22.768/13.594/3.203/5.071 to 20.801/18.479/4.710/5.928 for CLIPsim/CLIPdir/NIQE/NIMA. These concern different evaluation collections, not same-setting performance changes. CraftMesh still leads the main comparison on all four metrics; VoxHammer and alternative-backend results are newly reported.
descriptions.T1: v3 adds an asymptotic complexity comparison asserting O(kn^2) for image-space Poisson processing versus O(n^3) for volumetric processing in Sections 1 and 3.2.1, without a derivation or proof. The existing mathematical definitions and equations remain, with texture-loss equations reordered.
descriptions.C1: The first contribution changes from introducing the 'first framework' to introducing 'a framework,' narrowing the novelty claim. v3 emphasizes SDF-domain Poisson fusion while retaining the central claims of high-fidelity editing, structural consistency, and versatility.
descriptions.C2: v3 newly explains that repetitive textures disrupt gradient-domain color propagation, motivating distribution alignment. It also interprets backend comparisons as attributing gains to fusion rather than a particular generator. The stated limitations concerning generative-model dependence and complex/open/noisy meshes remain unchanged.
descriptions.D1: v3 adds a project-page address, an alignment-method citation, and explicit edited-image conditioning for texture generation. It removes the post-acceptance implementation-release promise and the explicit description of supervision viewpoints as random. The PDFs do not establish actual code availability.
descriptions.R1: v3 adds references to Google Scanned Objects, VoxHammer, and Imaginarium, and removes Deep Image Analogy. It refines positioning against classical Poisson mesh editing through connectivity and gradient-incompatibility arguments; most related-work coverage remains.
descriptions.P1: The abstract and selected introduction, related-work, and method paragraphs are rewritten. The fusion terminology changes, texture-loss explanations are reordered, and affiliations, contact information, and acknowledgments are revised. The overall section organization remains intact.
descriptions.P2: Figure 2 adds explicit texture-generation conditioning inputs, Figure 4 gains a VoxHammer column, and Tables 1–2 gain comparison rows. Front matter and surrounding text are reflowed, while the six-figure, two-table organization and retained demonstrations remain recognizable.

P-8FA7B3E0EF.title: Excited Pfaffians: Generalized Neural Wave Functions Across Structure and State

descriptions.M1: The architecture, sample-pooling strategy and spin snapping remain. However, the written computational specification changes: Eq. 7 uses squared overlap, the normalizer and bridge-system expressions are revised, and the pretraining Procrustes rotations are corrected. These are limited formula-level corrections; the PDFs do not establish an implementation change or rerun.
descriptions.E1: Both versions cover the same Li–Ne atoms, 12 molecules, 33-state beryllium calculation, carbon-dimer dissociation and crossing geometries, and ethylene torsion and pyramidalization. The added analyses reuse this coverage; their different model configurations and compute budgets do not introduce new tasks or populations.
descriptions.E2: Appendix I newly evaluates the naive architecture with separate orbitals per state against Excited Pfaffians; v1 only discussed its memory requirements. Appendix N also includes Szabo et al. (2024) in the expanded runtime comparisons, whereas v1 Appendix L's compute estimates focused on NES. Existing accuracy comparators remain.
descriptions.E3: Appendix N replaces assumption-based compute estimates with A100 timing protocols: Adam/KFAC measurements at 1,000 walkers are scaled to 4,000, while SPRING is measured at 4,000. It adds a 12-state NES comparison with approximately 4,500 steps per geometry under the proposed method's compute budget. Appendix I introduces a single-determinant architecture control. The reported VMC learning-rate schedule also changes from 0.02/(1+1/10000) to 0.02/(1+t/10000), without establishing that existing experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: New Appendix E tests whether MSIS sample pooling remains effective across systems and electron/atom counts. Appendix I tests the efficiency and convergence consequences of sharing orbitals, and Appendix N.1 examines NES accuracy under a matched compute budget. These extend the retained MSIS-removal ablation and state-crossing analyses.
descriptions.E5: New Figure 11 reports effective-sample-size averages over states with standard-deviation error bars. These describe variation across states, not repeated training runs. Existing parenthesized energy uncertainties remain unchanged, and neither version documents an increased seed or repeated-run count.
descriptions.E6: The original energy values in v1 Tables 4–8 are retained in v2 Tables 9–13. Additional new results include normalized effective sample sizes, architecture convergence and optimizer-dependent timings: Table 5 reports cumulative C2 speedups of 208 times with Adam and 46 times with KFAC versus SPRING. New Table 6 reports a first excitation of 1.3817 eV for budget-limited NES versus 0.4294 eV for the proposed method. These are added comparisons, not improvements to the retained energy results.
descriptions.T1: Appendix D corrects the joint-variance expression in Eq. 43 by removing extraneous state-count factors and revising the intermediate equality. It also removes v1's assertion that estimating normalization ratios changes the bound only by O(1/Nb). Equation 9 now explicitly concerns overlap magnitude. These repair or narrow the existing mathematical treatment without introducing a new theoretical framework.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction and discussion retain the same central contributions: MSIS variance reduction, efficient shared-orbital Excited Pfaffians, generalization across structures and compounds, and many-state calculations. The principal novelty and headline carbon-dimer and beryllium claims remain; new experiments mainly provide additional support.
descriptions.C2: The ethylene state-swap explanation changes from self-reinforcing overlap-penalty ordering in v1 Appendix J to a Rydberg–valence crossing and a parameter-similarity hypothesis in v2 Appendix L. v2 also interprets the C2 swap as an avoided crossing, explicitly excludes transfer to unseen structures, and adds qualifications concerning conical intersections and residual spin-state mixtures.
descriptions.D1: New Appendix O.2 states that the implementation is publicly available and supplies a code link. The added comparisons disclose hardware, determinant constraints and NES pretraining requirements. Table 12 also corrects the ethylene caption from separate to joint training, consistent with v1's main text and Figure 12; this does not establish a newly joint experiment. Most existing implementation documentation is retained.
descriptions.R1: v2 explicitly relates MSIS to the balance heuristic through Veach and Guibas (1995) and Owen and Zhou (2000). Additional citations support effective sample size, transfer limitations and state-crossing interpretations, while the Folx reference is removed. These refine selected connections to prior work without substantially changing the overall research positioning.
descriptions.P1: The six-section main narrative and most prose remain. Changes include localized background and limitations edits, rewritten compute-time and ethylene explanations, inserted appendix sections, and corrected terminology, affiliation/contact text and conference footer. The additional scientific content does not entail wholesale narrative restructuring.
descriptions.P2: v2 adds quantitative displays: Figures 11, 12 and 17 show effective sample size, architecture convergence and runtime scaling, while Tables 2–6 present sample counts, timings and budget-limited excitation energies. Original figures are retained and relocated or renumbered; Figure 2's caption is shortened and several table captions are corrected.

P-F67745A7E6.title: SpeeDe3DGS: Speedy Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting with Temporal Pruning and Motion Grouping

descriptions.M1: The TSP, TSS, and GroupFlow procedures, objectives, grouping rules, and inference transformations remain unchanged. The annealing period of 20,000 iterations added beside Equation 7 was already specified in v2 Section 5. Adaptive grouping appears only as future work.
descriptions.E1: Both versions evaluate the same D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, NeRF-DS, Nerfies, and iPhone coverage, including the 50-scene MonoDyGauBench evaluation and standalone experiments. The new TSS ablation reuses NeRF-DS without introducing another task or scenario.
descriptions.E2: Tables 2–7 retain EffGS, STG-decoder, STG, RTGS, 4DGS, and DeformableGS with the same proposed variants. The newly cited motion-modeling methods are not added as evaluated baselines.
descriptions.E3: Table 11 introduces controlled TSS sweeps over beta values 0.05, 0.1, and 0.2 and annealing periods 15K, 20K, and 25K. Appendix A.6 also replaces v2's conflicting RTX A4000 statement with RTX 3090 rendering and RTX A5000/A6000 training settings matching existing captions. This documents a correction, without establishing reruns.
descriptions.E4: New Appendix A.4 and Table 11 test sensitivity to TSS perturbation magnitude and annealing duration, including a TSP-only control. Existing component, group-count, and pruning-percentage ablations and qualitative analyses are retained.
descriptions.E5: Both versions report three-run averages. The new TSS table follows this existing practice; it introduces no additional seed information, uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
descriptions.E6: Table 11 adds results for four nondefault TSS configurations, with PSNR ranging from 23.80 to 23.82 and SSIM from 0.8510 to 0.8517. Its TSP-only and default-TSS values reproduce v2 Table 1. Existing benchmark scores, per-scene values, and figure results remain unchanged.
descriptions.T1: Equations 1–12 retain the same mathematical content, including the sensitivity approximation and grouped SE(3) transformations. Explaining the existing mat and quat notation and discussing the J=N limiting case add exposition, without a new formal result, assumption, or proof.
descriptions.C1: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same three contributions and scientific scope. The headline 6.78× pruning speedup, 13.71× combined rendering speedup, and 2.53× shorter training claims are unchanged.
descriptions.C2: v2 already discusses fidelity loss under aggressive pruning and limited motion groups. New Appendix A.8 expands this with inherited baseline limitations, locally rigid motion after densification, the J=N limit, and adaptive grouping as future work. Appendix A.4 also attributes weak TSS parameter sensitivity to small interframe changes.
descriptions.D1: The rewritten per-scene appendix removes the unexplained ASP statement and reconciles GPU documentation with the retained timing-table captions. It clarifies the standalone codebase and metric-to-dataset mapping. v4 also attributes the existing TSS defaults to DeformableGS; those values were already disclosed in v2.
descriptions.R1: Section 2.2 adds MoSca, Gaussian-Flow, and Shape of Motion and removes RigGS. It refines the comparison by distinguishing neural inference, complex deformation computation, and reliance on 2D priors, replacing the earlier blanket characterization of costly neural inference.
descriptions.P1: v4 makes localized wording and grammar corrections, explains quaternion-conversion notation, and rewrites portions of related work, limitations, and per-scene documentation. It inserts two appendix subsections and updates cross-references while retaining the overall narrative and section organization.
descriptions.P2: v4 adds Table 11 and adjusts spacing around Tables 8–10 to accommodate it. Appendix text and Figure 5 placement reflow, and the per-scene tables are renumbered. All six figures retain their imagery, and existing table structures remain substantially unchanged.

P-14684BA9D2.title: ZARA: Training-Free Motion Time-Series Reasoning via Evidence-Grounded LLM Agents

descriptions.M1: Both versions use pairwise feature-importance knowledge, frozen placement-specific embeddings, class-wise retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion, and three agent roles executed in four stages. The appendix prompts remain substantively unchanged. Expanded explanations and additional backbone evaluations do not establish a changed algorithm.
descriptions.E1: The eight original datasets remain. V2 adds eight directed transfer scenarios among UCI-HAR, USC-HAD, PAMAP2, WISDM, and MHealth, using shared activities and aligned sensor placements. These extend evaluation from held-out subjects to knowledge transfer across heterogeneous datasets.
descriptions.E2: The ten baselines in Table 1 and the supervised Moment-S, Moment-L, and Mantis comparators in Table 2 are retained. Added Qwen/GPT rows are ZARA configurations; the transfer experiments extend comparisons using its existing full-knowledge and no-knowledge conditions.
descriptions.E3: Section 4.3 and Appendix A.3.2 introduce transfer protocols with shared labels, placement mappings, resampling, and pair-specific evaluation samples while retaining target-domain retrieval. V2 also evaluates Qwen-30B, Qwen-80B, and GPT-4.1-mini backbones. Existing subject splits largely remain; PAMAP2's reported test total changes from 210 to 240, without establishing that experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: V2 adds analyses of whether knowledge transfers across datasets, comparing absent, target-domain, and source-domain knowledge with retrieval held fixed. It also examines additional LLM backbones and token consumption by agent stage. The original component ablations, retrieval-backbone comparisons, and per-class analyses remain.
descriptions.E5: Both versions specify temperature zero and report point estimates without repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Feature means and standard deviations supplied to agents, and cross-validation used for knowledge construction, are retained rather than newly introduced uncertainty reporting.
descriptions.E6: V2 adds Qwen-30B, Qwen-80B, and GPT results with average macro F1 of 70.2, 73.0, and 77.2, plus transfer results and token measurements. Original Gemini results and matched ablations remain unchanged. Table 1 exchanges Gemini Plot's UCI-HAR accuracy/F1 from 31.7/20.6 to 20.6/31.7 while retaining the old averages, introducing an inconsistency.
descriptions.T1: V2 removes v1's explicit O(|F|) update-cost assertion for adding an activity. The pairwise knowledge representation and cosine-similarity/RRF mathematics remain equivalent; neither version presents formal theorems or proofs.
descriptions.C1: V2 replaces the unqualified zero-shot and unseen-activity framing with parameter-frozen, training-free inference using labeled references, emphasizing evidence-grounded reasoning. Its contributions also explicitly claim transferable motion priors, and the conclusion extends the state-of-the-art claim to cross-dataset settings.
descriptions.C2: New Section 7 acknowledges labeled retrieval requirements, limited architectural comparisons, and computational overhead. Section 4.3 explains why retrieval remains target-domain and attributes transfer asymmetries to source-user diversity and data density, including cases where transferred knowledge hurts. These expand applicability boundaries and interpretation.
descriptions.D1: V2 adds Qwen checkpoint identifiers, detailed transfer preprocessing and mappings, token-cost information, and clearer UniMTS checkpoint-use documentation. It corrects Opportunity's appendix class count from 12 to 4. Conversely, v1's default retrieval k=100 is omitted. The code URL, feature catalog, prompts, and most implementation details remain.
descriptions.R1: V2 adds targeted references on retrieval, agent memory, TableTime, Qwen, LLaSA, and RelCon, while removing the conventional-HAR paragraph and several associated citations. Positioning emphasizes statistical grounding and explains excluded recent comparators, but retains the principal HAR and foundation-model comparison landscape.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodological motivation, result discussions, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around training-free, evidence-grounded reasoning. V2 introduces numbered sections, separates cross-subject and cross-dataset evaluation, organizes the appendix into subsections, and adds limitations and acknowledgements.
descriptions.P2: Tables 1 and 2 are restructured into paired accuracy/F1 columns, and Figure 1 is rearranged. V2 adds the transfer figure and token table, consolidates dataset statistics into another table, and extensively reflows appendix displays and prompt panels. Retained ablation and per-class plots are matched across renumbering.

P-B9005B47F1.title: Target-aware Image Editing via Cycle-consistent Constraints

descriptions.M1: The two learnable noises, source-to-target-to-source cycle, alignment and reconstruction losses, Euler denoising, and inference procedure remain unchanged in Section 3. SD-1.5 compatibility was already demonstrated in v1 Appendix A.5; its greater prominence in v2 does not introduce a new adaptation.
descriptions.E1: V2 adds evaluation on a DIV2K subset containing approximately 70 images and 280 editing pairs at 1024×1024 resolution. This extends the retained 512×512 PIE-Bench coverage to higher-resolution images and longer prompts that can require multiple edits, with quantitative and qualitative results.
descriptions.E2: The quantitative PIE-Bench comparator sets are retained in v2 Table A2; P2P and P2P-Zero correspond to v1's DDIM-based entries. However, v2 Figure 4 omits ODE-Inversion from five reused PIE-Bench qualitative cases previously compared against it in v1 Figure 10. ODE-Inversion remains in other comparisons.
descriptions.E3: V2 introduces a paired user-study protocol using 30 randomly sampled PIE-Bench images, more than 20 participants, and four preference criteria. It also adds a four-condition transfer evaluation on 50 manually crafted examples and expands the lambda and guidance-scale sweeps. The stated default FlowCycle settings for the retained SD-3 and SD-1.5 experiments remain unchanged.
descriptions.E4: V2 adds the previously missing lambda=0 alignment-loss ablation and broader sensitivity tests in Figures A8–A9. It extends qualitative transfer evidence with a target-specific optimized reference, a quantitative 50-example comparison in Figure A11, and an editing-deviation case study in Figure 7. The original transfer examples and optimization-step curve remain, relocated to the appendix.
descriptions.E5: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. V2's new user-study win rates and transfer results do not introduce uncertainty estimation; describing results as significant does not establish a statistical test.
descriptions.E6: V2 adds DIV2K results, transfer measurements, expanded ablation results, and user preferences. Table A3 reports overall win rates of 82.9%, 76.5%, 70.6%, and 64.7% against ODE-Inversion, SDEdit, iRFDS, and FlowEdit, respectively. The retained PIE-Bench comparison scores and runtime measurements are unchanged, while v1 Tables 2–3, reporting 18 metrics across 11 groups, are removed.
descriptions.T1: The flow-matching formulation and FlowCycle equations (1)–(14) are unchanged. The FlowEdit injection-drift derivation moves from v1 Appendix A.6 to v2 Appendix A.1 with equivalent mathematics. New mechanism discussion and empirical ablations do not add formal assumptions, proofs, or theoretical results.
descriptions.C1: Both versions retain the central claims that target-agnostic corruption limits editing and that FlowCycle's target-aware corruption, learned through dual cycle constraints, improves consistency and editing quality. The revised contribution list foregrounds broader benchmark and backbone validation of these claims; the abstract's substantive claims and novelty claim remain unchanged.
descriptions.C2: V2 interprets the expanded ablations as showing that alignment is necessary but performance is relatively insensitive to positive lambda values, whereas v1 emphasized the consistency–alignment tradeoff. It also qualifies transfer as inferior to target-specific optimization, proposes reuse as an efficiency mitigation, and discusses adaptation to larger editing deviations. These refine the existing interpretation rather than replace it.
descriptions.D1: V2 documents DIV2K preparation using LLaVA-1.5 captions, manual caption refinement, handcrafted target prompts, and a dataset access link. Conversely, the SD-1.5-specific SDEdit settings and DDIM result provenance stated in v1 Appendix A.5 are no longer explicitly documented. FlowCycle's own hyperparameters and code link are retained.
descriptions.R1: V2 adds references for DIV2K, CLIPScore, LLaVA-1.5, SelfTok, and Qwen-Image, and removes the separate score-based SDE reference associated with v1's DDPM applicability discussion. The corruption/restoration taxonomy and positioning relative to prior cycle-consistency methods remain substantially unchanged.
descriptions.P1: V2 changes the title, reorganizes the experimental narrative to integrate datasets and backbones, and removes the separate comparison/ablation subsection hierarchy. The appendix is extensively reordered and consolidated, separating benchmark details, computational cost, transfer analysis, and quantitative results. Much of the introduction and method wording is retained.
descriptions.P2: The paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout with figure and table restructuring. V1's benchmark tables are merged into v2 Table A2, main quantitative comparisons become scatterplots, and the hyperparameter table is replaced by plots. Qualitative panels are redistributed, new study and transfer displays are added, and the image gallery is expanded.

P-28069F45F6.title: ReasoningGuard: Safeguarding Large Reasoning Models with Inference-time Safety Aha Moments

descriptions.M1: The core attention-sink identification, safety phrase, IAS ranking, and adaptive sampling procedure remain unchanged. v2 additionally evaluates ReasoningGuard combined with Llama Guard 3 or GuardReasoner, adding optional post-generation filtering to the inference pipeline (Appendix D.5.2, Table 15).
descriptions.E1: AdvBench, SorryBench, MMLU, GPQA Diamond, MATH500, and XSTest are retained. Attack-input scenarios change: automated AutoRAN replaces manually constructed H-CoT attacks, and cipher-based Mousetrap attacks are added. This extends adversarial conditions within the existing tasks.
descriptions.E2: v2 adds evaluated RealSafe-R1, SafeKey, SAFEPATH-FT, and SAFEPATH-ZS comparisons, plus Llama Guard 3 and GuardReasoner filtering baselines. Gradient Cuff disappears. PPL remains in a narrower appendix comparison, while SafeDecoding is restricted to the 7B/8B models. These change comparator membership.
descriptions.E3: v2 replaces the AdvBench Llama Guard classification metric with the proportion receiving GPT-4o harmfulness score 5, retaining mean GPT scores. It adds Phi-4 and Qwen3 model configurations, controlled IAS sampling and NF4-versus-unquantized experiments, and reasoning-length metrics. Its reported decoding policy also extends nucleus decoding beyond utility evaluations; these statements do not establish which experiments were rerun.
descriptions.E4: New analyses examine IAS–harmfulness associations, varied instructive/misleading/irrelevant safety phrases, quantization sensitivity, reasoning-length preservation, and combinations with guard filters. A mathematical utility case is added and the failure example is replaced. Existing window, sampling, scaling-factor, decoding, and phrase-component ablations are retained or relocated.
descriptions.E5: v2 introduces Spearman rank-correlation estimation for reasoning lengths and IAS boxplots reporting distributional spread, means, and medians. These extend descriptive statistical reporting. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
descriptions.E6: v2 adds extensive results for new comparators, attacks, and analyses, while removing detailed QwQ utility, jailbreak, and XSTest results. Retained entries also change: ReasoningGuard's R1-Llama-8B no-attack GPT harmfulness scores change from 1.02/1.00 in v1 Table 10 to 1.40/1.00 in v2 Table 17. Changed metrics and incompletely specified subsets prevent interpreting the overall revisions as matched performance gains.
descriptions.T1: The attention, sink-selection, IAS, and token-complexity mathematics are substantively retained. Last-layer notation clarifies implementation, and the added Spearman formulas explain a standard evaluation statistic. The new IAS-sufficiency discussion supplies an empirical interpretation, not a formal theorem or proof.
descriptions.C1: The central contribution remains a lightweight, training-free safeguard using attention-guided safety reflection and sampling. The abstract broadens its explicit effectiveness claim from three attacks and seven safeguards to four attacks and nine safeguards; the introduction also extends the claimed model-family coverage.
descriptions.C2: v2 interprets high IAS as sufficient but unnecessary for safety, connects utility preservation with reasoning-length consistency, and explains complementary roles and streaming limitations of post-hoc filters. It also qualifies comparison coverage because of unavailable training data and computational limits. These extend the scientific interpretation; the IAS sufficiency wording exceeds what the conditional observational analysis establishes.
descriptions.D1: v2 specifies last-layer attention, identifies 14B/32B models as quantized, documents IAS-analysis sampling and filtering, and supplies implementation/checkpoint references for added attacks and defenses. GPU hardware and task-time estimates are retained. Exact evaluation subset sizes and random seeds remain unspecified.
descriptions.R1: Section 2.3 shifts from a general jailbreak-defense taxonomy to LRM-specific training-based and training-free alignment, positioning ReasoningGuard against closely related SAFEPATH and SafeKey approaches. AutoRAN, GuardReasoner, and additional model references are introduced, while several general defense references are removed.
descriptions.P1: The abstract, introduction, related work, and experimental narrative receive broad paragraph-level revisions. v2 reorganizes the appendices around a dedicated IAS analysis, restructures utility and ablation subsections, adds a model-transferability section, and separates limitations and ethical considerations from their earlier locations.
descriptions.P2: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figures 1–2 are reorganized, the radar chart and ablation panels are revised, and tables are restructured with comparator groups and average columns. New IAS boxplots, phrase-example tables, and analysis tables expand the visual presentation.
